docs.title: The Bearded Tech Guy AIR-1 review
Simon Says Home Assistant AIR-1 review
AIR-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What sensors are included in the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 uses a SEN55 which includes sensors for PM1, PM2.5, PM4, PM10 (particulate matter), VOC Index (volatile organic compounds), NOx Index (nitrogen oxides), temperature, and humidity. Addon sensors include the SCD40 CO2 and the MiCS gas sensor.

2. What does the AIR-1 measure?

  • The AIR-1 measures a variety of air quality metrics, including particulate matter (dust, pollen, etc.), VOCs, NOx, temperature, and humidity. The optional CO2 sensor can track carbon dioxide levels.

3. How do I connect the AIR-1 to Homey?

  • The AIR-1 joins your Wi-Fi, and the Apollo Automation app for Homey talks to it directly over your local network through the ESPHome native API, with no cloud account. Once you add it, its readings show up on the device in Homey, ready for flows and Insights. The app runs on Homey Pro; Homey Cloud isn't supported.

Next step: add your AIR-1 to Homey

Connect the sensor to your Wi-Fi through its hotspot, then add it with the Apollo Automation app. The getting started guide walks you through both.

Get started with Homey

4. Does the AIR-1 require cloud connectivity or a subscription?

  • No, the AIR-1 is fully local and does not require any cloud services or subscriptions. It talks to Homey directly over your local network, so your data stays in your home and under your control.

5. What are common use cases for the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 is ideal for monitoring indoor air quality, such as tracking dust levels in woodworking shops, ensuring optimal air quality during sleep, or automating air purifiers when certain thresholds are met. The CO2 sensor is particularly useful for identifying high CO2 levels, which can affect sleep and concentration.

6. How do I set up flows with the AIR-1?

  • Any AIR-1 reading can start a flow in Homey. For example, run an HVAC fan when CO2 levels are high, or send a notification when particulate matter reaches unhealthy levels. The high CO2 notification example walks you through one.

7. How does the optional CO2 sensor work?

  • The optional SCD40 CO2 sensor measures carbon dioxide levels and helps you understand when CO2 concentrations in a room become too high, which can cause fatigue, drowsiness, and worse for humans and pets alike. It’s particularly useful in offices, bedrooms, and other enclosed spaces.

8. What is particulate matter (PM) and why is it important?

  • Particulate matter (PM) refers to tiny particles in the air that can be harmful when inhaled. The AIR-1 measures various sizes of particulate matter (PM1, PM2.5, PM4, PM10), helping you track dust, pollen, and other particles that affect air quality. It’s especially useful for people with allergies or respiratory conditions.

9. What is VOC and why should I monitor it?

  • VOCs (volatile organic compounds) are chemicals that can be emitted from everyday items like cleaning products, paints, and furniture. Prolonged exposure to high levels of VOCs can affect indoor air quality and health. The AIR-1’s VOC sensor helps you monitor these levels and take action when necessary, such as increasing ventilation.

10. What is the NOx Index and why is it measured?

  • NOx (nitrogen oxides) are harmful gases that contribute to air pollution and can affect respiratory health. The AIR-1 gives an NOx index number, allowing you to keep track of indoor air quality and make adjustments if necessary. "The NO x Index describes the current NO x condition in a room relative to the sensor’s recent history. In this way, the NO x Index behaves like a human nose. "

11. How accurate are the air quality readings from the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 uses a high-quality SEN55 sensor with a 10-year lifespan, designed for continuous use. Its readings are highly accurate for particulate matter, VOC Index, and NOx Index. However, keep in mind that the ESP32-C3 generates some heat, which may require you to apply a temperature and humidity offset. Set it with SEN55 temperature offset and SEN55 humidity offset under Calibration offsets in the device's Settings in the Homey app.

12. My AIR-1 never shows a DPS310 pressure reading in Homey. Is something wrong?

  • No, your device is fine. A small subset of units shipped without the DPS310 sensor because the part was discontinued by the manufacturer. If your AIR-1 never reports a pressure value, your unit is one of these. Every other sensor on the device works normally.

13. How can I use the RGB LED for notifications?

  • The RGB LED is the AIR-1's light in Homey. Turn it on or off, dim it, or change its color from the device or in a flow: for example, turn it red when air quality is poor, green on trash night, or blue when CO2 levels are safe.
  • On current firmware, the LED can also follow air quality by itself. Choose NowCast AQI, CO2, or VOC Index under Air Quality LED Source on the sensor's own web page: in a browser, open http://apollo-air-1-xxxxxx.local, where xxxxxx is the last 6 characters of the device's name in Homey. This setting isn't in Homey.

14. How do I update the firmware on the AIR-1?

  • Homey doesn't install firmware updates: the Apollo Automation app has no update action. On current firmware, the AIR-1's own web page has a Firmware Update button that downloads and installs the latest release over Wi-Fi. Open http://apollo-air-1-xxxxxx.local in a browser, where xxxxxx is the last 6 characters of the device's name in Homey, and press it. The sensor needs internet access to download the update.
  • You can also flash the latest firmware over USB with the Apollo installer, as described in Factory re-flash AIR-1.

15. How do I calibrate the CO2 sensor?

  • You usually don't need to. The latest AIR-1 firmware enables automatic self-calibration, which keeps the SCD40 accurate as long as the sensor sees fresh air (about 420 ppm) at least once a week.
  • If your AIR-1 sits in a space that rarely gets fresh air (a sealed office, a basement, a grow room), turn automatic self-calibration off and calibrate by hand every 1 to 2 years instead. The CO2 Auto Calibration switch isn't in Homey: turn it off on the sensor's own web page (see question 13 for the address). Then follow the manual calibration guide, which uses the Calibrate SCD40 to 420 ppm maintenance action in the device's Settings in Homey.

16. Does the AIR-1 work outdoors?

  • The AIR-1 is primarily designed for indoor use. It could be used outdoors in a sheltered environment, but it is not weatherproof. If you need outdoor air quality monitoring, ensure the device is protected from the elements.

17. What is the power source for the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 is powered via a USB-C connection. It can be plugged into any standard wall outlet using a 5V adapter.

18. My AIR-1 CO2 sensors are having a sawtooth pattern, is there any explanation?

  • Some users have noticed the AIR-1 with the "Apollo" side facing up will produce strange behavior with the CO2 sensor readings fluctuating way more than they should. Turning the AIR-1 to the other side makes this problem go away!

19. Can I integrate multiple AIR-1 sensors in my smart home?

  • Yes. Add each AIR-1 with the Apollo Automation app. Each one shows up as its own device in Homey with its own readings, so you can monitor air quality across different rooms or spaces at the same time.

20. How customizable is the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 is fully customizable via ESPHome. You can adjust sensor settings, create automations, modify reporting intervals, and even customize the RGB LEDs. Additionally, we provide open-source CAD drawings and code for further customization.

21. How frequently does the AIR-1 report data?

  • By default, the SEN55 readings (particulate matter, VOC Index, NOx Index, temperature, and humidity) update every 10 seconds, pressure every 30 seconds, and CO2 and the MiCS gas readings every 60 seconds. These intervals are set in the AIR-1 firmware, and Homey has no setting for them, so changing an interval means editing the firmware with ESPHome.

22. Does the AIR-1 require specific software?

  • With Homey, you need the Apollo Automation app, which adds the AIR-1 and its readings to Homey. Monitoring and flows all happen in Homey from there.

23. Is the AIR-1 compatible with other smart home platforms?

  • Yes. Besides Homey (through the Apollo Automation app), the AIR-1 works with Home Assistant and with other platforms that support the ESPHome API. See Supported platforms.

24. What's the difference between the AIR-1 and other air quality sensors?

  • The AIR-1 is unique because it offers local control with no cloud or subscription required. It also provides a wide range of sensor data (PM, VOC, NOx, CO2, temperature, humidity) in a compact, affordable package. The addition of the RGB LEDs and open-source nature makes it highly customizable.

25. What are the optional addons for the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 offers two optional addons: an SCD40 CO2 sensor and the MiCS gas sensor. These can be added to enhance air quality monitoring with very accurate CO2 measurements and the ability to detect multiple gases with the MiCS gas sensor.

26. What's in the box?

  • The AIR-1 comes with the fully assembled board and case, a USB-C power cable, and access to all our documentation, open-source code, and CAD models. You'll also receive a sticker of Apollo, our mascot.

27. How do I install the AIR-1?

  • Plug the AIR-1 into a wall outlet using the USB-C cable, connect it to your Wi-Fi through its hotspot, and add it in Homey with the Apollo Automation app. The getting started guide walks you through each step.

28. What is the warranty on the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 comes with a one-year warranty. If you encounter any issues, we provide support via email, Discord, and our community channels to ensure you're satisfied with the product.

29. Can the AIR-1 be used to monitor 3D printer fumes?

  • Yes, the AIR-1 can monitor air quality around 3D printers, especially particulate matter (PM) and VOCs emitted during the printing process. It can trigger alerts or flows when levels become unhealthy.

30. How long does it take to set up the AIR-1?

  • Setup typically takes around 5 to 10 minutes: once the AIR-1 is powered and connected to Wi-Fi, you add it in Homey with the Apollo Automation app.

31. How secure is the AIR-1?

  • The AIR-1 operates entirely on your local network and does not send data to the cloud. All information is processed and stored locally, ensuring the security and privacy of your home automation setup.

32. Can I use the AIR-1 for safety monitoring (e.g., CO2 or gas leaks)?

  • The AIR-1's CO2 and gas sensors are intended for air quality monitoring but DO NOT MEET the safety standards for CO2 or gas leak detection as defined by the NBIC, NFPA, or IFC. For safety purposes, dedicated gas or CO2 monitors should be used.

33. My NOx Index never shows a value and the logs mention an SEN54. How do I fix it?

  • A small number of AIR-1 units report their sensor as an SEN54, which has no NOx element, on the model register, even though the NOx-capable SEN55 is actually fitted and working. That left the NOx Index without a value. The 26.7.23.1 firmware forces the correct SEN55 model, so updating to the latest firmware (see question 14) brings NOx back. Once it updates, give the reading a little time to appear: like the VOC Index, the NOx Index needs a short conditioning period after boot before it reports a value.

34. Is the connection between the AIR-1 and Homey encrypted?

  • When the AIR-1 has an API encryption key, yes. Homey asks for the key when you add the device and only connects with it. If the key changes later, open the device's Settings in Homey, choose Repair, and enter the new key. A device without a key connects without encryption, on your local network only.

35. I build the AIR-1 YAML myself and validation fails on a version error. What do I need?

  • Firmware 26.7.23.1 needs ESPHome 2026.7.2 or newer, and firmware 26.10.8.1 and later need ESPHome 2026.8.0 or newer. Update ESPHome Device Builder and validate again. Firmware installed with the Firmware Update button or the Apollo installer isn't affected, since those builds are compiled for you.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Apollo AIR-1 is a compact, feature-rich air quality sensor designed for Home Assistant users. It operates locally over Wi-Fi using ESPHome, without the need for a cloud or subscription. Powered by USB-C, the AIR-1 offers open-source software and CAD drawings for customization.

Key features include monitoring PM levels (dust, pollen), VOCs, CO2 (optional), temperature, humidity, and even gas levels with an optional sensor. The device also integrates RGB LEDs for notifications and Bluetooth tracking for added automation.

Perfect for monitoring air quality in your home, office, or workshop, the AIR-1 is highly customizable and comes with full community support through Discord and access to open-source tools on GitHub.

docs.title: Add the SCD40 CO₂ sensor to your AIR-1
Adding CO<sub>2</sub> to AIR-1
docs.text:
Tip

If you have the Original Design of the AIR-1 please click here

You'll open the case, attach the SCD40 sensor to the mezzanine connector on the back of the board, and close the case again.

1. Unplug your AIR-1 from power and lift the top of the case or "lid".

2. Remove the lid completely by grabbing the lid from the other side and gently lifting upwards.

3. Hold the PCB and orient it correctly where Apollo (the dog) is facing you in.

4. Gently slide the pcb out by sliding it to the left as shown in the images below.

5. Flip the PCB over and identify the bottom right corner where the small black mezzanine connector lives. You will see an "X" indicating which corner needs to be lined up with the SCD40 CO2 sensor. There is an X on the SCD40 sensor's PCB as well, you can see it in the image below but it is slightly cut off on the PCB itself. There is also a "gold dot" in the top left of the SCD40 when oriented properly.

6. Gently push the SCD40 CO2 module onto the black mezzanine connector.

7. Gently slide the PCB back into the 3d printed case as shown below.

8. Gently push the case back together as shown below.

9. Please refer to our CO2 calibration guide to calibrate the CO2 module after installation. This is required for all CO2 addons purchased from us separately from a product (such as buying it to addon to an existing Apollo device).

docs.title: Adding GPIO header to AIR-1
docs.text:
You'll open the case, attach the GPIO Header to the mezzanine connector on the board, and close it up in the new lid that came with the addon.

1. Unplug your AIR-1 from power and lift the top of the case or "lid".

2. Remove the lid completely by grabbing the lid from the other side and gently lifting upwards.

3. Hold the PCB and orient it correctly where Apollo (the dog) is facing you in.

4. Gently slide the pcb out by sliding it to the left as shown in the images below.

5. Flip the PCB over and identify the Top Right corner where the small black mezzanine connector lives. You will see an "X" indicating which corner needs to be lined up with the PCB of the GPIO Header. There is an X on the GPIO Header's PCB as well, you can see it in the images below.

6. Match up the X on the PCB of the GPIO Header and the X on the AIR-1 PCB and then gently push the GPIO Header onto the black mezzanine connector.

7. Flip the AIR-1 PCB over and gently slide it back into the new AIR-1 Lid which came with your GPIO Header addon! Please do not use much force, the PCB should slide in relatively smoothly, with a tiny bit of force needed. There are three channels in the plastic where the PCB slides into!

8. Gently push the case back together as shown below.

9. You are now done and your AIR-1 is now able to be used with the GPIO Header addon! Here is the pinout image below and here's a great wiki article showing you how to add a small led strip!

Warning

If you plan to use a lot of leds or your gpio project requires a lot of power then you need to use a dedicated power supply and not try to use too much power (under 350mA) from the GPIO of the device! You can power the AIR-1 via the vcc (5v) and GND pins but please do not power it via the pins AND the USB-C port, it should be one or the other.

docs.title: Air quality notification
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

This flow watches the CO2 reading on your Apollo AIR-1 and tells you when the air in your home is less than ideal. When CO2 rises above 999 ppm, the AIR-1's light turns red and everyone who's home gets a push notification with the current reading. When CO2 drops below 900 ppm, the light turns green, and 5 minutes later the flow turns it off.

Before you start

This guide uses the Homey web app in a web browser, because the flow is built with Homey's Advanced Flow editor.

docs.title: Add the CO2 triggers
docs.text:
Start with two trigger cards: one for when CO2 gets too high, and one for when it comes back down.

1. Open a web browser, such as Firefox, and go to the Homey webapp. Click the Flow tab on the left side.

2. Click New Flow, then Advanced Flow.

3. Click Add and select When.

4. In the search bar at the top, type co2 becomes and select the card for the sensor you want to track. This guide uses CO2 becomes greater than for the Apollo AIR-1 device.

5. Left-click on your flow area to place the card. Your flow canvas now shows this card:

6. Select ppm and type in your value. This guide uses 999.

7. Repeat steps 4 and 5, but this time select CO2 becomes less than and place it on your flow canvas. Fill in your less-than ppm value, such as 900.

Use 900, even though the screenshots show 1000

From step 7 on, the screenshots show 1000 ppm on the less-than card; use 900. The gap between 900 and 999 keeps the light from flickering between red and green when CO2 hovers around 1000 ppm.

Both triggers are now on your canvas.

docs.title: Set the light color
docs.text:
Next, link each trigger to a color on the AIR-1's light: red for high CO2, green once it drops.

8. Click Add, select Then, search for set a color, and choose the AIR-1 device option.

9. Draw a line from CO2 becomes greater than 999 ppm to the Set a color card. Click the 3 dots and select a color. This guide uses red to indicate a problem.

10. Repeat steps 8 and 9 for the other trigger: add another Set a color card, connect it to CO2 becomes less than 900 ppm, and select green.

The light now turns red when CO2 is high and green when it drops.

docs.title: Send a push notification
docs.text:
Now add a message that tells everyone at home what the CO2 level is and what to do about it.

11. Click Add, select Then, search for push, and choose Send message to user.

12. Draw a line from the red Set a color card to the push notification card. Then write the message:

  • Type The CO2 level in the bedroom is currently CO2 ppm. Open the Window, turn on HVAC, etc to lower this value!
  • Delete the second CO2 (the one right before ppm) and leave your cursor in its place.
  • Click the small tag icon, type CO2, and select the blue CO2 option under Apollo AIR-1. The tag puts the live CO2 reading into the message.

13. Click User and choose Everyone who's home or your preferred option.

High CO2 now sends the alert along with the red light.

docs.title: Turn the light off after 5 minutes
docs.text:
Finally, switch the light off 5 minutes after it turns green, so it doesn't stay on once the air is clear.

14. Click Add, select Delay, and place it on your flow canvas. Change it to minutes and enter 5 for a 5 minute delay. Then drag a line from the green Set a color card to the delay.

15. Click Add, select Then, search for turn off, and choose the AIR-1 device option.

16. Drag a line from the delay you added in step 14 to the Turn off card. Click Save at the top and give your flow a name. Your finished flow looks like this:

17. Optional: add a note that reminds you what this flow does. Click Add, then Note, and type CO2 level alert with RGB LEDs on the note. Your flow now looks like this:

You're done! Your flow is saved, and the next time CO2 rises above 999 ppm, your AIR-1 turns red and everyone who's home gets the alert.

Run into issues? Join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: AIR-1 general tips
docs.text: The AIR-1 has multiple different types of sensors and this guide will help you understand which ones you should be concerned with and expected safe or not safe thresholds to alert or automate on.

docs.title: SEN55 environmental sensor
docs.text: The SEN55 is the powerhouse of the AIR-1 with multiple sensors such as particulate matter, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), oxidizing gases, such as nitrogen oxides (NOx), as well as humidity & temperature.

docs.title: Particulate matter
docs.text:
Per the EPA: particulate matter (also called particle pollution): the term for a mixture of solid particles and liquid droplets found in the air. Some particles, such as dust, dirt, soot, or smoke, are large or dark enough to be seen with the naked eye. Others are so small they can only be detected using an electron microscope. Sources of pm particles here.

PM10 : inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 10 micrometers and smaller; and

PM2.5 : fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller.

  • How small is 2.5 micrometers? Think about a single hair from your head. The average human hair is about 70 micrometers in diameter, making it 30 times larger than the largest fine particle.

We suggest triggering alert automations, hvac or a fan turning on, etc when PM particles are rising

This article goes over lots of ways to reduce pm particles in your home!

docs.title: Safe PM levels
docs.text: Particulate Matter (PM) refers to a mixture of solid particles and liquid droplets found in the air. These are often classified by size, as smaller particles pose greater risks to health due to their ability to penetrate deeper into the lungs.

docs.title: What do PM1, PM2.5, PM4, and PM10 mean?
docs.text:
PM Type

Size (µm)

Description

PM1

≤ 1.0

Ultrafine particles that can reach deep into the lungs and bloodstream.

PM2.5

≤ 2.5

Fine particles; linked to respiratory and cardiovascular issues.

PM4

≤ 4.0

Less commonly regulated; typically used in industrial settings.

PM10

≤ 10

Inhalable particles; may irritate eyes, nose, and throat.

PM2.5 and PM10 are the most widely monitored and regulated for public health purposes.

The PM 1, PM2.5, PM4, and PM10 are all four useful even if PM 2.5 and PM 10 are the most common!

docs.title: Recommended safe exposure limits
docs.text:

docs.title: U.S. EPA Air Quality Index (AQI) – PM2.5
docs.text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) defines safety thresholds for PM2.5 based on a 24-hour average:

PM2.5 (µg/m³)

AQI Category

Health Implications

0.0 – 12.0

Good

Air quality is satisfactory.

12.1 – 35.4

Moderate

Acceptable; some risk for sensitive individuals.

35.5 – 55.4

Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups

Increased risk for those with heart/lung issues, children, and older adults.

55.5 – 150.4

Unhealthy

Everyone may begin to experience health effects.

150.5 – 250.4

Very Unhealthy

Health alert: serious effects possible.

>250.5

Hazardous

Emergency conditions for all populations.

docs.title: NowCast AQI
docs.text:
NowCast AQI takes your PM2.5 and PM10 readings and converts them into a single 0–500 number using the EPA's formula. That number maps directly to the AQI categories in the table above: bigger = worse.

The AIR-1 calculates this automatically, and the Apollo Automation Homey app shows it as NowCast AQI on your AIR-1 device in Homey.

NowCast AQI is easier to automate and understand than raw PM

Instead of comparing µg/m³ values across PM1, PM2.5, PM4, and PM10, you get one number. Set an automation to trigger at 100 (Moderate) or 150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups) and anyone in your household can understand why it fired.

docs.title: Indoor air quality notes
docs.text:
• PM1 and PM2.5 are especially important for indoor air monitoring since these smaller particles are more likely to come from cooking, candles, smoking, or inadequate ventilation.
  • Use an air purifier with a HEPA filter to reduce PM1–PM2.5 concentrations indoors.
  • Keep PM2.5 below 12 µg/m³ indoors for general safety; below 5 µg/m³ for ideal long-term health protection.

PM Size

Safe Range

Health Concern

No official limit. Keep as low as possible

Ultrafine particles (most dangerous)

≤ 12 µg/m³ (EPA), ≤ 5 µg/m³ (WHO annual)

Penetrates lungs and bloodstream

Industrial contexts only (no public health limits)

Less regulated
