docs.title: VOC Index
docs.text:
Per Sensirion,

The VOC Index

describes the current VOC status in a room relative to the sensor’s

recent history. In this way, the VOC Index behaves like a human nose

We suggest triggering alert automations, hvac or a fan turning on, etc when the VOC Index rises above 100

Per Sensirion:

a VOC Index above 100 means that there are more

VOCs compared to the average (e.g., induced by a VOC event from

cooking, cleaning, breathing, etc.) while a VOC Index below 100 means

that there are fewer VOCs compared to the average

docs.title: VOC quality
docs.text:
This uses the VOC index and a scale to output an easier to use variable.

0-79: Improved -> 80-149: Normal -> 150-249: Abnormal -> 250-399: Very abnormal -> 400+: Extremely abnormal

We suggest triggering alert automations, hvac or a fan turning on, etc when the VOC Quality changes to Abnormal or Very Abnormal or Extremely Abnormal.

This lets you automate based on the air quality changing over the past 24 hours, but you will still want to automate on particulate matter as well!

docs.title: NO<sub>X</sub> Index
docs.text:
Per Sensirion,

The NO x Index describes the current NO x condition in a

room relative to the sensor’s recent history. In this way, the NO x Index

behaves like a human nose.

We suggest triggering alert automations, hvac or a fan turning on, etc when NOx rises above 1

Per Sensirion:

On the NO x Index scale, this offset is always mapped to

the value of 1, making the readout as easy as possible: an NO x Index

above 1 means that there are more NO x compounds compared to the

average (e.g., induced by cooking on a gas stove), while an NO x Index

close to 1 means that there are (nearly) no NO x gases present, which is

the case most of the time (or induced by fresh air from an open window,

using an air purifier, etc.).

docs.title: SCD40 CO<sub>2</sub> sensor
docs.text:
The optional CO2 sensor addon is a great way to add the ability to track CO2. CO2 levels in a closed, poorly ventilated bedroom can quickly rise to concentrations that may impair focus or even pose health risks. Notice the CO2 levels dropping in the image below when the HVAC was turned on overnight!

The latest AIR-1 firmware keeps the SCD40 calibrated automatically. The sensor assumes it sees fresh air (about 420 ppm) at least once a week and corrects its baseline to match, so you no longer need to re-calibrate it manually every 1 to 2 years.

Auto calibration needs regular fresh air

If your AIR-1 sits in a space that rarely gets fresh air (a sealed office, a basement, a grow room), automatic self-calibration will slowly drag the CO2 readings down. Turn off the CO2 Auto Calibration switch in your device's settings and follow the manual calibration guide every 1 to 2 years instead.

Wisconsin Department of Health CO2 Level Chart

We suggest triggering alert automations, hvac or a fan turning on, etc when CO2 is over 1000

Opening a window, turning on a fan, the HVAC in the house, etc are all great ways to get CO2 to go down!

docs.title: MiCS-4514 gas sensor
docs.text: The MiCS-4514 is a very unique sensor able to distinguish between multiple gases such as Carbon Monoxide, Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2), Ethanol, Hydrogen, Ammonia, and Methane.

docs.title: Prevent Sleep
docs.text:
Put your sensors to sleep!

All of our battery powered devices are able to go to sleep to save battery life. Our non-battery sensor devices like the AIR-1 and PLT-1 can also sleep to get better temperature and humidity measurements.

The temperature offsets needed will be much lower for your sensors as the microcontroller will not put off as much heat when it is sleeping and then waking for short periods to report the sensor values.

You'll set how long your sensor sleeps, then turn off Prevent Sleep so it can start sleeping.

1. Head to the ESPHome Integrations page and click on the name of your Apollo device.

2. Scroll down until you see Prevent Sleep and Sleep Duration.

3. Type in how long you want your sensor to sleep in the Sleep Duration box. Check the unit next to the box: it is minutes on the AIR-1 (default 5), PLT-1 (default 5), and TEMP-1 (default 8), and hours on the BTN-1 (default 24), PLT-1B (default 12), and TEMP-1B (default 12). We recommend leaving the default values.

Read this before turning off Prevent Sleep!

When "Prevent Sleep" is toggled off, your sensor will immediately begin sleeping. Please make sure you are ready to make this sensor sleep before toggling off prevent sleep.

4. When you are ready, toggle off Prevent Sleep and your sensor will go to sleep. It will wake up on the Sleep Duration interval from step 3. If you need to keep your sensor awake, head to our OTA Awake helper tutorial!

5. You can wake your sensor by following this guide or you can power cycle your device. If there is a battery in it, the battery will need to be removed or the reset button pressed.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The AIR-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your AIR-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your AIR-1. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The Default Update column is how often each sensor refreshes while the AIR-1 is awake. By default Prevent Sleep is on, so the device stays awake and reports continuously at these intervals. Turn Prevent Sleep off to let the AIR-1 deep-sleep between readings for more accurate onboard SEN55 temperature and humidity (the ESP chip's heat skews them while it is awake); it then wakes for about 2 minutes, reports, and sleeps for the Sleep Duration.

To update firmware on a sleeping device, click Update on the Firmware Update entity and it installs the next time the device wakes (the firmware keeps itself awake until the update finishes, so you don't need to do anything else). The optional OTA helper is a separate toggle that overrides Prevent Sleep to keep a device awake on demand.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light Three RGB Neopixel LEDs. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn them on or off. Calibrate SCD40 To 420ppm Forces a fresh-air calibration of the SCD40 CO₂ sensor to the outdoor baseline (about 420 ppm). Run it outdoors or next to an open window. Only needed when CO2 Auto Calibration is off. Clean SEN55 Runs the SEN55 fan auto-clean cycle to clear the particulate sensor and refresh its readings. Sensor Default Update Details Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) 60s True NDIR reading from the SCD40. Shows Unknown if you do not have the CO₂ module. You can re-calibrate it to the outdoor baseline. SEN55 Temperature 10s Ambient air temperature. Adjusted by the SEN55 Temperature Offset. SEN55 Humidity 10s Relative humidity in the air. Adjusted by the SEN55 Humidity Offset. SEN55 VOC Index 10s Volatile organic compounds from paints, cleaning products, and solvents. How the VOC Index works. SEN55 NOX Index 10s Nitrogen oxides produced by burning fossil fuels and other combustion. VOC Quality follows SEN55 VOC A plain-language scale built on the VOC Index (details): 0-79 Improved, 80-149 Normal, 150-249 Abnormal, 250-399 Very abnormal, 400+ Extremely abnormal. DPS310 Pressure 30s Barometric air pressure. A small subset of devices do not include a DPS310 sensor. If this reads Unknown, your device may be one of these units. PM <1µm Weight Concentration 10s Ultra-fine particles smaller than 1 micrometer, often present in smoke or exhaust. PM <2.5µm Weight Concentration 10s PM2.5, generated by combustion and industrial activity. PM <4µm Weight Concentration 10s Particulate matter smaller than 4 micrometers. PM <10µm Weight Concentration 10s PM10, which includes dust, pollen, and mold. NowCast AQI follows PM2.5 / PM10 US EPA NowCast Air Quality Index, calculated from the PM2.5 and PM10 readings. PM 0.3 To 1 µm 10s Particles between 0.3 and 1 micrometer. Disabled by default. PM 1 To 2.5 µm 10s Particles between 1 and 2.5 micrometers. Disabled by default. PM 2.5 To 4 µm 10s Particles between 2.5 and 4 micrometers. Disabled by default. PM 4 To 10 µm 10s Particles between 4 and 10 micrometers. Disabled by default. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. SEN55 Temperature Offset 6.0 °C Calibrates the SEN55 temperature reading to a known value. See the temperature & humidity calibration guide. SEN55 Humidity Offset 0 % Calibrates the SEN55 humidity reading to a known value. See the temperature & humidity calibration guide. DPS310 Pressure Offset 0.0 hPa Applies a calibration offset to the DPS310 pressure reading. Range is -100 to +100 hPa in 0.1 hPa steps. Disabled by default. A small subset of devices do not include a DPS310 sensor; if this option reads Unknown, your device may be one of these units. CO2 Auto Calibration On Keeps the SCD40 CO₂ sensor calibrated automatically. The sensor assumes it sees fresh air (about 420 ppm) at least once a week and corrects its baseline to match. Turn it off if the device sits in a space that rarely gets fresh air, then calibrate manually with Calibrate SCD40 To 420ppm every 1 to 2 years. Sleep Duration 5 min How long the AIR-1 stays in deep sleep between wake cycles (only used when Prevent Sleep is off). Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it reports continuously. Turn it off to let the AIR-1 deep-sleep between readings for more accurate onboard SEN55 temperature and humidity. Air Quality LED Source Off Colors the three onboard RGB LEDs by air quality. Choose NowCast AQI, CO2, or VOC Index and the LEDs shift from green to red as that reading climbs. Leave it on Off to keep the LEDs free for your own automations. See the LED Indicator guide. Air Quality LED Brightness 100 % Dims the air-quality LEDs, from 5% to 100%. Applies the moment you change it. Only has an effect while Air Quality LED Source is set to something other than Off. Bluetooth Proxy Off Turns the AIR-1 into a Bluetooth proxy so nearby Bluetooth devices reach Home Assistant through it. Toggles on without reflashing. Firmware Channel Stable Sets which firmware the Firmware Update entity pulls. Stable is the tested release; Beta gets new features earlier. Switch back to Stable any time to return to the stable build. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. Separate from the Apollo Firmware Version and ESPHome Version sensors above. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: MICS Gas Sensor (optional)
docs.text:
Read this before relying on the gas readings

The MICS gas sensor is an optional add-on, so many AIR-1 units do not include it. It's a DFRobot SEN0377 (MICS-4514) module, and it's best treated as a "does it detect this gas or not" indicator rather than a precise measurement. It does not meet safety standards for gas monitoring, so do not rely on it as a CO or gas-leak alarm. It also has a known quirk where methane can spike when other gases are present.

Gas Default Update Details Carbon Monoxide (CO) 60s Dangerous, odorless gas produced by combustion. Baseline is 4.16 ppm, not 0 ppm. Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) 60s Harmful gas from vehicle emissions and industrial processes. Baseline is 0.16 ppm, not 0 ppm. Ammonia (NH₃) 60s Comes from agricultural emissions, cleaning products, or industrial processes. Baseline is 0 ppm. Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) 60s Vapors from cleaning agents, sanitizers, or alcohol-based products. Baseline is 0 ppm. Hydrogen (H₂) 60s Can indicate leaks or industrial processes. Baseline is 0 ppm. Methane (CH₄) 60s Can indicate natural-gas leaks or agricultural emissions. Detects concentrations above 1000 ppm. Baseline is 0 ppm.

docs.title: AIR-1 boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the AIR-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You'll hold the boot button while you plug in the USB-C cable, so the device starts in boot mode.

1. Position the AIR-1 so that the USB-C port is facing you. On the left side of the USB-C port, locate a small opening to press the boot button (the right button).

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your AIR-1 then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You'll plug the device into your computer, then hold the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and locate the boot and reset buttons as shown in the image below.

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your AIR-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button, next to the USB-C port). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the AIR-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash AIR-1
docs.text:
If your Apollo AIR-1 becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods, you can re-flash the factory firmware. This guide walks you through it in your browser, step by step.

Before you start

  • Use Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium-based browser. The factory re-flash needs one.
  • If your AIR-1 has already been added to Homey, remove it from Homey before you continue.

1. Put your AIR-1 in boot mode: hold down the boot button, then plug in the USB cable.

2. Go to the Apollo AIR-1 installer page.

3. Click Connect & Install.

4. Select the open COM port, then click Connect.

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.AIR-1.

6. Click INSTALL.

7. When you see Installation complete!, the install is finished. Click Next, then close the browser window.

Your AIR-1 is back on its factory firmware.

Power cycle your AIR-1 before you do anything else

Your AIR-1 is still in boot mode. Remove its power, then power it back on so it boots in normal mode.

Next step: set up your AIR-1 as a new device

With the factory firmware on and the AIR-1 power cycled, follow the getting started guide to connect it to Wi-Fi and add it to Homey as a new device.

Proceed to the getting started guide

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials
docs.text:
You'll clear the saved Wi-Fi details so the device broadcasts its hotspot again and you can connect it to your new Wi-Fi.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Press and hold the Boot button for 10 seconds.

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo AIR-1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: BTN-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. My BTN-1 is registering single clicks but not multiple, what is wrong?

  • The BTN-1 is likely sleeping and when being woken up it only can register a single button press. We are looking into ways to avoid this but it might be an ESPHome limitation.

2. How long will the BTN-1 last on battery if it's not sleeping?

  • It's expected to last 18 hours on a single charge if you need to take it on the go, great for all ESP-NOW projects!

3. Why won't my BTN-1 multi presses work? Single press works fine!

  • The device is most likely sleeping. When sleeping, no multi clicks are supported. Only a physical button single press because that wakes the device up.

4. How do I connect the BTN-1 to Homey?

  • The BTN-1 joins your Wi-Fi, and the Apollo Automation app for Homey talks to it directly over your local network through the ESPHome native API, with no cloud account. Add it the same way as any Apollo device. The app runs on Homey Pro; Homey Cloud isn't supported.

Next step: add your BTN-1 to Homey

Connect the BTN-1 to your Wi-Fi through its hotspot, then add it with the Apollo Automation app.

Get started with Homey

5. Does the BTN-1 support Zigbee firmware?

  • The BTN-1 uses an 8MB C6 mini MCU so it technically does support zigbee. We might have official firmware for this in the future!

6. What kind of things can I do with the BTN-1?

  • Each button can start any flow in Homey. The Button pressed card fires for Button 1 to Button 4 with a press type of Click, Double click, Triple click, or Hold, so one BTN-1 gives you 16 different triggers.
  • Flows can also color the key lights with Set button light color, and switch them off with Turn off button light.

7. What kind of power supply is required for the BTN-1?

  • The BTN-1 is powered via USB-C and can be plugged into a standard wall outlet using a 5V 1A or bigger power supply.

8. What addons are available for the BTN-1?

  • The BTN-1 will have an upcoming OLED screen and NFC connector addon!

9. Is the BTN-1 secure?

  • The BTN-1 communicates with Homey over your local network through the ESPHome API. This provides a local connection without the need for cloud services. No data is sent to external servers, ensuring privacy.

10. What is the warranty for the BTN-1?

  • The BTN-1 comes with a standard one-year warranty. If you experience any issues, our support team is available through Discord, email, or the website to assist with troubleshooting or replacement.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Customizable Buttons: 4 Cherry MX-compatible hot-swappable mechanical switches. RGB indicator LEDs below the switches give feedback; the keys themselves are not backlit. No soldering required for switch changes.

Modular Design: Supports large top attachments like e-ink displays for status updates and NFC readers/emitters for contactless interactions. Side attachments include additional buttons, rotary dials, OLED screens, LED matrices, and sensor mezzanines.

Power & Connectivity: USB-C or battery powered with Wi-Fi connectivity for wireless control and smart home integration.

Versatile Applications: Perfect for streamers, content creators, smart home enthusiasts, and IoT projects. Compatible with macro software and home automation platforms.

Compact & Durable: Small desktop footprint with sturdy enclosure designed for both desktop and mounted use in various environments.

docs.title: Prevent sleep
docs.text:
Your Apollo BTN-1 can sleep between presses to make its battery last. While it sleeps, Homey can't reach it. Press Button 1, 2, 3, or 4 and the BTN-1 wakes up, reconnects, reports that press to Homey, and goes back to sleep.

The BTN-1 ships with Prevent sleep turned on, so it stays connected and Homey receives every press type right away. That's what most flows need, but it drains the battery far faster. Turn Prevent sleep off when your flows only use clicks and a few seconds' delay is fine.

Before you start

  • Add your BTN-1 to Homey with the Apollo Automation app. See Getting started.
  • Homey can only change these settings while the BTN-1 is awake and connected. If it's asleep, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. In that case, wake it first.

docs.title: The sleep settings in Homey
docs.text:
Both settings sit in your BTN-1's Settings in the Homey app, under Battery settings (if battery is present). They're device settings only, so there's no flow card that turns sleep on or off.

Setting What it does on the BTN-1 Prevent sleep Checked, the BTN-1 stays awake and reports every press right away. Unchecked, it sleeps between presses. A new BTN-1 has it checked. Sleep duration How many hours the BTN-1 sleeps before it wakes on its own and checks in with Homey, from 0 to 800. The default is 24. A button press wakes it sooner.

Prevent sleep also decides which presses reach Homey:

Prevent sleep checked Prevent sleep unchecked Press types Homey receives Click, Double click, Triple click, and Hold Only the press that wakes the BTN-1, always as a Click When a press arrives Up to half a second after you let go At least 5 seconds after the press, once the BTN-1 has reconnected In the Homey app Connected Device disconnected between presses

docs.title: Wake your BTN-1 first
docs.text:
A sleeping BTN-1 can't receive a change from Homey, so wake it before you open its settings. Press and release the reset button on the back of the BTN-1, on the left in the photo below. Button 1, 2, 3, or 4 wakes it too, but Homey receives that press as a Click of that button and runs any flow you've tied to a click of it. The boot button can't wake a sleeping BTN-1.

Homey reconnects to the BTN-1 on its own, and the Homey app no longer shows it as Device disconnected. Unless Prevent sleep is on, the BTN-1 goes back to sleep about 10 seconds after Homey connects, or after about 90 seconds if Homey doesn't connect at all, so have the Homey app open and ready. How to wake up your sensor has more on waking it.

docs.title: Let your BTN-1 sleep
docs.text:
Set how long the BTN-1 sleeps first, then let it go to sleep. Make the two changes one at a time: the BTN-1 falls asleep the moment Prevent sleep turns off, so a change sent along with it may never arrive.

Read this before you uncheck Prevent sleep

The BTN-1 goes to sleep as soon as Prevent sleep is off. From then on, Homey receives only clicks, a few seconds late, and can't change any setting until you wake the BTN-1 again. Finish any other settings first.

  1. In the Homey app, open your BTN-1's Settings.
  2. Under Battery settings (if battery is present), set Sleep duration to the hours you want between check-ins, and save the change. Leave it at 24 unless you want the BTN-1 to check in with Homey more often; every check-in uses some battery.
  3. Uncheck Prevent sleep and save.

Your BTN-1 is now asleep. Press any of its four buttons and it wakes, sends that press to Homey as a Click, and goes back to sleep about 10 seconds after Homey connects. It also wakes on its own after each Sleep duration.

Device disconnected is normal between presses

While the BTN-1 sleeps, Homey shows it as Device disconnected. That's expected: Homey reconnects on its own each time the BTN-1 wakes up.

docs.title: Keep your BTN-1 awake
docs.text:
To get every press type back, change a setting, update the firmware, or troubleshoot, turn Prevent sleep back on. The boot button on the back of the BTN-1 is the most reliable way, because it works even when Homey can't reach the BTN-1. What the BTN-1 does depends on how long you hold it:

How long you hold the boot button What the BTN-1 does Under 1 second Lights up its buttons for a quick status check. Prevent sleep doesn't change. 1 to 3 seconds Nothing. 3 to 10 seconds Turns Prevent sleep on once you let go. Aim for 4 to 5 seconds. 10 seconds or more Resets the BTN-1 to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets your BTN-1 to factory settings, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again.

Press the reset and boot buttons one after the other, never together: holding the boot button while you press reset puts the BTN-1 in boot mode for flashing firmware instead.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the BTN-1.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

Your BTN-1 turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked once the BTN-1 is connected, and every press type reaches Homey again. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the BTN-1 was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

Rather use the Homey app? Wake the BTN-1, then right away check Prevent sleep in its Settings, under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save. You only have about 10 seconds after Homey connects, which is why the boot button is more reliable. How to wake up your sensor walks you through it.

Next step: put your buttons to work

With Prevent sleep on, each press type on your BTN-1 can start its own flow in Homey. Build your first one: a light that turns on with a click and off with a hold.

Turn a light on and off with your BTN-1

docs.title: Attaching switches and keycaps to your BTN-1
docs.text:
Your Apollo BTN-1 uses mechanical keyboard switches with keycaps on top. The step-by-step instructions for installing both live in the Physical setup section of the BTN-1 getting started guide.

Install switches and keycaps

Use your own Cherry MX switches

We sell Cherry MX Brown switches because they're mostly silent, but some people prefer a very "clicky" switch. You can buy off-the-shelf mechanical keyboard switches (Cherry MX Red, Brown, Blue, and others) and place them on your BTN-1.

docs.title: How to wake up your sensor
How to wake up your sensor
docs.text:
Once Prevent sleep is off, your Apollo TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 sleeps between reports to make its battery last, and Homey can't reach it while it sleeps. In the Homey app, a sleeping sensor shows as Device disconnected, and if you try to change a setting, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. The sensor wakes on its own after each Sleep duration and reconnects to Homey. Wake it yourself when you want fresh readings right away, or need it awake to change a setting, update the firmware, or troubleshoot.

Using a USB-powered TEMP-1?

Your TEMP-1 normally stays awake in Homey, so there's nothing to wake. If it keeps losing its connection to Homey, it may have been set to sleep earlier, for example in Home Assistant. Turn Prevent sleep back on with its boot button.

docs.title: Wake your sensor
docs.text:
Pressing the reset button restarts your sensor, so it wakes up right away, connects to your Wi-Fi, and reports to Homey. On a BTN-1, any of its four buttons wakes it too. The boot button can't wake a sleeping sensor. Once the sensor is awake, the boot button is what keeps it awake. Select your device below to find both buttons.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1

The buttons are on the board inside the case. To reach the reset button, gently pry the lid off at the small slit near the top of the case. You can press the boot button with the lid off too, or with a paperclip through the small opening on the right side of the case when the USB-C port faces you. Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode has more photos.

To wake the TEMP-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

This is the boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake.

You can press both buttons with a pin through small openings in the case. Putting the PLT-1B in boot mode shows where the openings are.

To wake the PLT-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

The boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake, sits next to the USB-C port.

To wake the BTN-1, press and release the reset button, on the left in the photo below. The boot button, which you'll use to keep the BTN-1 awake, is on the right.

Pressing Button 1, 2, 3, or 4 also wakes the BTN-1. Homey receives that press as a Click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any flow you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

Your sensor is now awake. Homey reconnects to it on its own, and the Homey app no longer shows it as Device disconnected. It doesn't stay awake for long, though. Unless Prevent sleep is on, it sends fresh readings and goes back to sleep about 20 seconds after Homey connects (about 10 seconds for the BTN-1), or after about 90 seconds if Homey doesn't connect at all. Not sure your TEMP-1B or PLT-1B woke up? The sensor connection check tells you in a few seconds.

docs.title: Keep your sensor awake
docs.text: A wake-up doesn't last long enough to change settings or troubleshoot comfortably. Turn on Prevent sleep and your sensor stays awake until you turn it off again. You can turn it on from the sensor itself or from the Homey app, where it sits in your sensor's Settings under Battery settings (if battery is present).

docs.title: With the buttons on the sensor
docs.text:
The buttons work even when Homey can't reach the sensor, which makes this the most reliable way. It's also the better choice for the BTN-1, which stays awake for only about 10 seconds after Homey connects. Press the two buttons one after the other, never together: holding the boot button while you press reset puts the sensor in boot mode for flashing firmware instead.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets your sensor to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the sensor.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

Your sensor turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked once the sensor is connected. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the sensor was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

docs.title: From the Homey app
docs.text:
The sensor stays awake for only about 20 seconds after Homey connects, or about 10 seconds for the BTN-1, so have the Homey app open and ready before you start.

  1. Wake the sensor with the reset button.
  2. In the Homey app, open your sensor and wait until it no longer shows Device disconnected.
  3. Right away, open its Settings, check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save.
  4. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, press the reset button once more.

Your sensor now stays awake until you uncheck Prevent sleep again. If the sensor was already on its way back to sleep at step 3, it still keeps the change and starts up with Prevent sleep on after the reset in step 4. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. instead, the change didn't reach the sensor: start again from step 1, or use the buttons.

The Prevent sleep guide for the TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 covers both settings in detail, including Sleep duration. On a BTN-1, Prevent sleep also decides which presses reach Homey.

Next step: let your sensor sleep again

Staying awake drains the battery far faster. Once you're done, turn Prevent sleep off and choose how long the sensor sleeps between reports.

TEMP-1B: Prevent sleep PLT-1B: Prevent sleep BTN-1: Prevent sleep

docs.title: Use all four buttons and press types
Use all four buttons and press types
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 2

🌱 New here? Try these first:

Turn a light on and off with your BTN-1 Difficulty: Level 1

Your Apollo BTN-1 has four buttons, and each one reports four press types: Click, Double click, Triple click, and Hold. That is up to 16 actions from one device.

In Home Assistant, a single BTN-1 blueprint covers every press. Homey has no blueprints, and the BTN-1 doesn't need one there: every press starts its own flow with the Button pressed card. This guide shows you how to plan your presses, build the flows, and light up the buttons so you can see what each press did.

Before you start

  • Add your BTN-1 to Homey with the Apollo Automation app. See Getting started.
  • Build your first BTN-1 flow with the step-by-step guide. This page builds on it.
  • Keep Prevent sleep on. See Keep the BTN-1 awake.

docs.title: The Button pressed card
docs.text:
Every flow on this page starts with the same trigger card, Button pressed. On it, you pick two things:

  • Button: Button 1, Button 2, Button 3, or Button 4.
  • Press type: one of the four below.
Press type How to press the button Click Press and release quickly, in under 0.3 seconds. Double click Two quick clicks, less than half a second apart. Triple click Three quick clicks, less than half a second apart. Hold Press and hold for 1 to 5 seconds, then let go.

Each card only runs for the button and press type you picked, so a flow for Button 2 never fires when you press Button 3.

Not sure which button is which? Open your BTN-1 in Homey and press a button. The matching reading, Button 1 to Button 4, shows the press type Homey received. Use a different press type each time, so you can see which reading updates.

docs.title: Plan your presses
docs.text:
Sixteen presses are a lot to keep in your head, so sketch a plan before you build anything. Here is an example:

Button Click Double click Triple click Hold Button 1 Desk lamp on Monitor light on Desk lamp and monitor light off Button 2 Ceiling light on Ceiling light off Button 3 Fan on Fan off Button 4 Hallway light on Every light in the plan off

A few rules of thumb:

  • Put the actions you use most on Click. It is the quickest press, and the only one a sleeping BTN-1 reports.
  • Pair opposites on one button, such as Click for on and Hold for off.
  • Leave a cell empty if you don't need it. A press with no flow does nothing.

docs.title: Build one flow per press
docs.text:
Each filled cell in your plan becomes one flow. Build them one at a time, starting with the presses you will use most.

  1. In the Homey mobile app, tap Flow in the bottom bar, then tap + at the top right.
  2. Under When..., tap Add Card. Open Apollo Automation under Apps, choose your BTN-1, and choose Button pressed.
  3. Tap Button and pick the button from your plan. Tap Press type and pick the press type, then tap the check mark at the top right.
  4. Under Then..., tap Add Card and add the action from your plan, for example Turn on or Turn off for a light under Zones & Devices. Add more Then... cards if the press should do several things.
  5. Tap Next. Name the flow after the button and press, for example BTN-1 Button 2 Click, and tap Save Flow.

Repeat these steps for every press in your plan. Each flow shows in My Flows, and each press on the BTN-1 runs the flow you built for it.

docs.title: Light up the buttons
docs.text:
Each button on the BTN-1 has its own color LED, and the Apollo Automation app gives you two action cards to drive them. Add them under Then... from your BTN-1, the same way you add Button pressed under When....

Card Asks for What it does Set button light color Button light (Button 1 to Button 4) and Color Turns that button's LED on in the color you pick, at full brightness. Turn off button light Button light Turns that button's LED off.

Three ways to use them:

  • Show what's on: in each Click flow, add Set button light color for the same button. In the matching Hold flow, add Turn off button light. Each LED now shows which devices you last turned on from the BTN-1.
  • Confirm the press type: give each press type its own color, for example green for Click and blue for Double click, so you can see which press the BTN-1 registered.
  • A status light for the house: the cards work in any flow, not only flows that start with a button press. Light Button 4 red when a door opens, and turn it off when the door closes.

Each LED also has its own on/off switch on the BTN-1 in Homey, labeled LED 1 to LED 4.

docs.title: Put every press on one canvas
docs.text: Separate flows are quick to build in the mobile app. If you'd rather see your whole BTN-1 in one place, build an Advanced Flow in the Homey web app instead. An Advanced Flow can hold several When cards: add one Button pressed card for each press in your plan, and draw a line from each one to its own Then cards. The High CO2 notification example walks you through the Advanced Flow editor.

docs.title: Keep the BTN-1 awake
docs.text:
Double clicks, triple clicks, and holds only reach Homey while the BTN-1 is awake and connected.

A sleeping BTN-1 only reports clicks

The BTN-1 ships with Prevent sleep on, so it stays connected and reports every press. If you turn it off to save battery, the BTN-1 sleeps between presses. Homey receives the press that wakes it as a Click of that button, whatever press type you used, and only after the BTN-1 has reconnected, at least 5 seconds later. It then goes back to sleep.

To use every press type, open the device in Homey, go to its Settings, and check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present). Homey can only change this setting while the BTN-1 is awake, so wake it first with its reset button. How to wake up your sensor shows where the reset button is and how to keep the BTN-1 awake, and Prevent sleep explains what each sleep setting does on the BTN-1.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Most problems come down to press timing, a sleeping BTN-1, or a card pointing at the wrong device.

Symptom What to check A flow never runs Check that it is switched on in My Flows and that every Apollo card in it points at your BTN-1. The app offers the BTN-1 cards on every Apollo device, but only a BTN-1 has the buttons and LEDs. The wrong flow runs, or none Press the button and watch its Button 1 to Button 4 reading on the BTN-1 in Homey. It shows the last press type Homey received. A double click runs your Click flow twice Click faster. The two clicks must be less than half a second apart. A triple click also runs your Double click flow Click faster. The BTN-1 reports a double click once the button has been released for 0.2 seconds, so the third click has to come sooner than that. A hold does nothing Hold for 1 to 5 seconds. A press longer than a click but shorter than 1 second isn't reported, and neither is a press longer than 5 seconds. Only clicks work, and they arrive several seconds late The BTN-1 is sleeping. Turn on Prevent sleep, as described in Keep the BTN-1 awake.

docs.title: Turn a light on and off with your BTN-1
Turn a light on and off with your BTN-1
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

Every button on your Apollo BTN-1 tells Homey how you pressed it, and each press type can start its own flow. In this guide you build two flows in the Homey mobile app. The first turns a light on when you click Button 1 and lights that button's LED; the second turns both off again when you hold Button 1.

Before you start

  • Add your BTN-1 to Homey with the Apollo Automation app. See Getting started.
  • Add the light you want to control to Homey.
  • Keep Prevent sleep on. It is on out of the box; Keep your BTN-1 awake explains why it matters.

docs.title: How button presses reach Homey
docs.text:
All four buttons on your BTN-1 share one trigger card: Button pressed. When you add it to a flow, you pick a Button, from Button 1 to Button 4, and a Press type:

Press type How to press the button Click Press and release quickly, in under 0.3 seconds. Double click Two quick clicks, less than half a second apart. Triple click Three quick clicks, less than half a second apart. Hold Press and hold for 1 to 5 seconds, then let go.

The card runs your flow every time the BTN-1 reports that button and press type. A Click flow ignores a double click, and two clicks with a pause between them run it twice.

The BTN-1 reports a press up to half a second after you let go, once it knows no further click is coming. Hold fires when you release the button, not while you are still holding it.

docs.title: Flow 1: Turn the light on with a click
docs.text:
This flow has one trigger and two actions: it turns your light on and sets Button 1's LED to a color, so the button itself shows that the light is on.

  1. In the Homey mobile app, tap Flow in the bottom bar, then tap + at the top right (or Create a Flow if you have none yet).
  2. Under When..., tap Add Card. Open Apollo Automation under Apps, and choose your BTN-1.
  3. Choose the card Button pressed.
  4. Tap Button and pick Button 1. Tap Press type and pick Click, then tap the check mark at the top right.
  5. Under Then..., tap Add Card. Find your light under Zones & Devices, choose Turn on, and tap the check mark.
  6. Under Then..., tap Add Card again. Open Apollo Automation under Apps, choose your BTN-1, and choose Set button light color.
  7. Tap Button light and pick Button 1. Tap Color, pick a color, and tap the check mark.
  8. Tap Next. Name the flow, for example BTN-1 light on, and tap Save Flow.

The flow now shows in My Flows. Click Button 1 and your light turns on, with the button lit in the color you picked.

Pick your BTN-1, not another Apollo device

The Apollo Automation app offers Button pressed, Set button light color, and Turn off button light on every Apollo device you have added, but only a BTN-1 has the buttons and LEDs they work with. If a flow never runs, check that each of its Apollo cards points at your BTN-1.

docs.title: Flow 2: Turn the light off with a hold
docs.text:
The second flow mirrors the first. Build it the same way, with these changes:

  1. Under When..., choose Button pressed, then pick Button 1 and Hold.
  2. Under Then..., choose Turn off for the same light.
  3. For the second Then... card, choose Turn off button light from your BTN-1 and pick Button 1 under Button light.
  4. Name the flow BTN-1 light off and tap Save Flow.

Now Button 1 runs your light: a click turns it on, a hold turns it off, and the LED follows along.

docs.title: Keep your BTN-1 awake
docs.text:
Your BTN-1 can only report a double click, triple click, or hold while it is awake and connected to Homey.

A sleeping BTN-1 only reports clicks

The BTN-1 ships with Prevent sleep on, so it stays connected and reports every press. If you turn it off to save battery, the BTN-1 sleeps between presses. Homey receives the press that wakes it as a Click of that button, whatever press type you used, and only after the BTN-1 has reconnected, at least 5 seconds later. It then goes back to sleep.

To use every press type, open the device in Homey, go to its Settings, and check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present). Homey can only change this setting while the BTN-1 is awake, so wake it first with its reset button. How to wake up your sensor shows where the reset button is and how to keep the BTN-1 awake, and Prevent sleep explains what each sleep setting does on the BTN-1.

docs.title: Test your flows
docs.text:
Run the flows end to end by clicking and holding Button 1 while you watch the light. To check a single flow without pressing the button, tap the play button next to it in My Flows; it runs its Then cards once, and a green check mark confirms it ran.

Your BTN-1 also shows you what Homey received. Open it in Homey and look at the Button 1 reading: it shows the last press type, such as Click or Hold.

If a flow doesn't run:

  • Watch the Button 1 reading as you press. If it doesn't show the press type you used, check your timing: release within 0.3 seconds for a click, or hold for 1 to 5 seconds.
  • Check that both flows are switched on in My Flows.
  • Check that the BTN-1 is awake, and that every Apollo card in the flow points at your BTN-1.

docs.title: Take it further
docs.text:
• More presses on the same button: build flows for Double click and Triple click on Button 1, for example to turn on a second light.
  • A status light for the house: Set button light color works in any flow, not only flows that start with a button press. For example, light Button 4 red when a door opens, and turn it off with Turn off button light when the door closes.

Next step: put all four buttons to work

Button 1 is set up. The next guide shows you how to plan and build flows for all four buttons and all four press types, up to 16 actions from one BTN-1.

Use all four buttons and press types

docs.title: Sticky pads
docs.text: Your BTN-1 comes with two sets of 4 sticky pads or feet to stick on the bottom of the BTN-1 itself or on the optional BTN-1 Mount addon. These are great for setting the device on your desk!

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text: The BTN-1 with the stand addon allows you to mount the device using M3 screws to attach using one of three mounting scenarios as shown below. It also allows for magnetic mounting from one orientation!

docs.title: Desk mount
docs.text: I used a block of wood instead of mounting it directly to my desk in this example.

docs.title: BTN-1 getting started
docs.text: This will guide you through adding on switches and keycaps to your BTN-1 then adding it to your Wi-Fi and Home Assistant!

docs.title: Installing brown switches
docs.text: Line up the two gold pins with the holes on your BTN-1, then press down gently. Be careful, as the pins can bend or get damaged if too much force is used.

docs.title: Installing keycaps
docs.text: Line up the + on the keycap with the + on the top of the switch you installed. It may require a little pressure, but it should press on smoothly. Once placed, lightly tap to ensure the keycap is fully seated.

docs.title: Flip power switch
docs.text: Only the battery version has a power switch. If yours has one, ensure it's turned on. With the device on its side, flipping the switch away from you turns it on, and flipping it toward you turns it off.

docs.title: Connecting through hotspot
docs.text:
To connect through the sensor's onboard hotspot follow the below:

1. Plug the BTN-1 in via USB-C. A 5v 1amp power supply will work fine

If your sensor is restarting or not broadcasting Wi-Fi try another USB-C cable and power supply!

The BTN-1 is sensitive to power fluctuations and needs constant 5v power. It draws 1amp or less so most used phone chargers will work. Make sure it's a quality one!

Still no hotspot? Follow the Reset Wi-Fi Credentials guide to make it broadcast again.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to "Apollo BTN1 Hotspot".

3. Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your sensor. If this does not automatically open the dashboard, please open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

4. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your sensor to connect to or scroll to the bottom and type in your Wi-Fi network then click "Save".

Tip for Mesh Wi-Fi systems or multiple Access Points

If you have multiple access points or a mesh system please manually type in your Wi-Fi network so it will join with the strongest signal!

5. Once connected, the sensor's dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your sensor to your Wi-Fi.

Click here for next steps!

docs.title: Connecting with Improv via BLE
docs.text:
With Improv via BLE, you add your device to your Wi-Fi and to the ESPHome integration right from Home Assistant.

Pre-requirement: Bluetooth proxy or Bluetooth Home Assistant hardware required

Bluetooth built in such as a raspberry pi or at least one ESP32 BLE Proxy is required to use this to set up your Apollo device. If you have already followed the "Connecting through Hotspot" please skip this section.

1. Navigate to settings -> integrations then click the "ADD" button below your new Apollo device then click Submit.

2. Once prompted, type in your Wi-Fi name and password in the two fields then click Submit. Click on Close once it finishes.

3. Click on Add then click on Submit. Choose an area and then click Finish.

4. Your device is now added to your Wi-Fi and added to the ESPHome Integration in Home Assistant. You should now be ready to set up a blueprint and start using your BTN-1!

docs.title: Connecting to ESPHome Device Builder
docs.text:
Skip the ESPHome Device Builder unless...

Feel free to skip to the next section by clicking here unless you need to rename your sensor or do manual edits to the yaml

You can add the ESPHome Device Builder app in Home Assistant to update your device or edit the yaml. If you don't have the ESPHome Device Builder app installed you can search ESPHome Device Builder in the app store and install it.

Make sure to fill out your Wi-Fi details in the secrets section by clicking on the secrets button.

# Your Wi-Fi SSID and password - keep the quotes and just replace the name and password between the quotes!
wifi_ssid: "your-wifi-ssid-here"
wifi_password: "your-wifi-pass-here"

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder dashboard.

2. Click Show in the top right to show your discovered devices then click on Take Control then click Install. This can take multiple minutes or longer on low-end hardware.

3. Once you see "INFO OTA successful" you are done. Click "STOP" to exit.

4. Your new device is now adopted into the ESPHome Device Builder and you can move on to Integrating with Home Assistant via the ESPHome Integration below!

docs.title: Connecting to Home Assistant via ESPHome integration:
docs.text:
1. Head to the ESPHome Integration then click on Add then click Submit. When prompted click Finish then give it a location and click Finish or click Skip and Finish.

2. Your device is now added to Home Assistant via the ESPHome integration, and you can navigate to it by going to settings -> ESPHome integration -> click on the name of your new device!

Click here to set up a blueprint and automate using your BTN-1!

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your BTN-1. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The BTN-1 is a battery-powered device that can deep-sleep to save battery. Prevent Sleep is on out of the box, so it stays awake and reports continuously (required for OTA updates). The Default Update column is how often each entity refreshes while the BTN-1 is awake. Turn Prevent Sleep off and the BTN-1 wakes for about 90 seconds (on a button press or after the Sleep Duration), reports its values, then deep-sleeps again. While asleep it does not respond to Home Assistant.

ControlsSensorsEventsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does BTN 1 Light RGB light behind the first button. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color, or use the toggle to turn it on or off. Defaults to off. BTN 2 Light RGB light behind the second button. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color, or use the toggle to turn it on or off. Defaults to off. BTN 3 Light RGB light behind the third button. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color, or use the toggle to turn it on or off. Defaults to off. BTN 4 Light RGB light behind the fourth button. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color, or use the toggle to turn it on or off. Defaults to off. Sensor Default Update Details Battery level per wake cycle Remaining battery charge as a percentage, from 0 to 100%. Read from the MAX17048 fuel gauge. Battery voltage per wake cycle Current battery voltage, for real-time monitoring of the cell. Wake-up Button Pressed per wake cycle Which button woke the device from deep sleep (1 to 4). Resets to 0 after the press is handled. Event What it reports Button 1 Fires a click, double_click, triple_click, or hold event for the first button. Great for automating. Button 2 Fires a click, double_click, triple_click, or hold event for the second button. Great for automating. Button 3 Fires a click, double_click, triple_click, or hold event for the third button. Great for automating. Button 4 Fires a click, double_click, triple_click, or hold event for the fourth button. Great for automating. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Sleep Duration 24 h How many hours the BTN-1 stays in deep sleep between wake cycles (only used when Prevent Sleep is off). Range is 0 to 800 hours. Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it responds to Home Assistant continuously. Required for OTA updates; turn it off to save battery. While the device is asleep it does not respond to Home Assistant until it wakes again. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Disabled by default. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the BTN-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the BTN-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
This method puts your device into boot mode using only the boot button.

If you have the battery model skip to Method 2!

If your BTN-1 has a battery in it, it will not properly enter boot mode while the battery is connected and has a charge. Please move to Method 2 of the guide.

1. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer.

2. Disconnect power from your BTN-1, then hold the right (boot) button while plugging in a USB-C data cable to the BTN-1. Once connected, release the button.

3. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
This method uses the boot and reset buttons, and it's the one to use if your device has a battery.

1. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer and connect the other end to your BTN-1.

2. With the device facing you, locate the reset (left) and boot (right) buttons.

3. Put your BTN-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the BTN-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Reflashing the BTN-1
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the steps below.

This factory re-flash needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

1. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer and connect the other end to your BTN-1.

2. With the device facing you, locate the reset (left) and boot (right) buttons.

3. Put your BTN-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the BTN-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Open the Apollo BTN-1 installer in a Chromium-based browser such as Chrome or Edge and click Connect & Install. Select the open com port and click Connect.

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.BTN-1, then click Install again.

6. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

Head to the Getting Started article to set up your BTN-1 as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your BTN-1
docs.text:
Resetting the Wi-Fi credentials makes your device broadcast its hotspot again so you can enter new Wi-Fi details.

1. Plug the BTN-1 into power.

2. Long press the Boot button (the button on the right) for 10 seconds.

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo BTN1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: Disassembly
docs.text:
You'll remove the lid, lift out the green PCB, and disconnect the battery.

If you have a BTN-1 with a battery you should flip the power switch to off

The BTN-1 ships with a lithium ion battery, however, this means it needs a master shutoff switch, which is on the left side of your BTN-1

1. Flip the battery switch towards you to the off position. Users with no battery skip to step 2.

2. With the BTN-1 USB-C port facing upwards, unplug the USB-C cable and remove the lid.

3. Gently lift the BTN-1 green PCB out of the device at an angle so the buttons clear the case easier.

4. Remove the 2-pin JST connector and remove the battery.

docs.title: Reassembly
docs.text:
To put everything back together, you'll reconnect the battery, seat the PCB, and snap the lid back on.

1. Re-attach the 2-pin JST connector and place the battery writing side down with the wires on the left side of the case.

2. Gently place the BTN-1 green PCB back in the case at an angle so the buttons will slide into cutout in the case.

3. Line up the lid of the case with the holes for the rgb leds then gently press down to snap it into place.

4. Flip the power switch back on.

docs.title: Choosing an mmWave sensor
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave sensors detect the moving and still energy of people and animals, which makes them excellent for presence detection in a room. They are not meant to detect vehicles, so for a car an ultrasonic sensor is a better fit. This guide compares our three current mmWave sensors so you can pick the right one for your space.

  • MSR-2

    Best still detection, for one person.

    MSR-2 overview

  • MTR-1

    Tracks multiple people across zones.

    MTR-1 overview

  • R PRO-1

    Best of both worlds, plus PoE.

    R PRO-1 overview

docs.title: Compare
docs.text: MSR-2 MTR-1 R PRO-1 Targets tracked 1 Up to 3 Up to 3 Multi-zone tracking  3 zones  3 zones Still detection  Excellent  Limited  With LD2412 add-on PoE / Ethernet Horizontal FoV 120° 120° 120°150° with LD2412 Vertical FoV 70° 70° 70° Power USB-C USB-C PoE (802.3af) or USB-C mmWave module LD2410B LD2450 LD2450, optional LD2412

docs.title: Field of view
docs.text:
Each sensor watches a cone that fans out in front of it, like the beam of a flashlight. The cone is wider side to side than it is top to bottom.

120° sensor Horizontal FoV: 120° side to side (up to 150° on the R PRO-1 with the LD2412) 70° sensor Vertical FoV: 70° top to bottom

docs.title: Zone tracking (MTR-1 and R PRO-1)
docs.text:
The LD2450 module tracks up to three moving targets and reports each one's X and Y position. You draw rectangular zones in those coordinates to decide where presence counts.

Setting LD2450 zone coordinates

  • X1 must always be less than X2, and Y1 must always be less than Y2.
  • The X axis is where you can get tripped up, especially when both values are negative: -3456 is less than -2345.
  • The Y axis is easier since it is never negative.
  • The Plotly chart still draws the rectangles even if the X1/X2 or Y1/Y2 values are reversed, so double-check the order.
  • Zones cannot overlap.

To set up zones, follow the guide for your device: MTR-1 zones or R PRO-1 (LD2450) zones.

docs.title: Still detection (MSR-2 and R PRO-1 with the LD2412)
docs.text: The MSR-2, and the R PRO-1 once you add the optional LD2412, detect a single target using gates: fixed distance bands rather than X and Y coordinates. This is what makes them so good at catching someone who is barely moving, like sleeping or sitting still. To add the second module to an R PRO-1, follow Add the LD2412 to your R PRO-1.

docs.title: Reducing false triggers
docs.text:
mmWave detects motion, so things that move or reflect the radar signal can trigger a sensor even when no one is there. Common culprits include:

  • Mirrors and other reflective surfaces
  • Fans and spinning blades
  • Moving air from HVAC vents and registers
  • Curtains, blinds, or plants swaying in a draft

The MSR-2 (LD2410) and the R PRO-1 with the LD2412 let you tune the sensitivity of each gate, so you can dial down the distance bands where a fan or vent sits and tune these false positives out. With the LD2450 (MTR-1 and R PRO-1) you can instead draw your zones to exclude the problem area.

See the Radar Tuning guide to adjust sensitivity.

docs.title: 1. How much power do your sensors use?
docs.text: • All Apollo sensors use 1amp or less, some of them 350-500mA.

docs.title: 2. What all can the MSR-2 LD2410B mmWave sensor go through?
docs.text: • It can reliably go through drywall and some other materials such as thin wood and some couches.

docs.title: 3. My MSR-2 is triggering and no one is there.
docs.text: • We have seen this happen before. First, restart the radar with Restart radar under Maintenance in the device's Settings in the Homey app. If that doesn't help, factory reset the radar with Factory Reset Radar on the sensor's own web page: in a browser, open http://apollo-msr-2-xxxxxx.local, where xxxxxx is the last 6 characters of the device's name in Homey. If it still triggers, try a factory re-flash. We also see success with users re-seating their LD2410B mmWave sensor.

docs.title: 4. How do I reset my Wi-Fi?
docs.text: • Plug in your device then hold down the boot button for 10 seconds. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

docs.title: 5. My lux sensor doesn't seem to be working, how do I fix it?
docs.text:
• The light reading updates every 60 seconds by default, which isn't great for flows that react to lux values. On the MSR-2, MTR-1, and PLT-1, shorten it to a more responsive 3 to 5 seconds with LTR390 Update Interval on the sensor's own web page. In a browser, open the sensor's address, such as http://apollo-mtr-1-xxxxxx.local for an MTR-1, where xxxxxx is the last 6 characters of the device's name in Homey. On the MSR-2, the page hides this setting at first, so click Show All to list it. Homey has no setting for it.
  • On other sensors, the interval is fixed in the firmware, and changing it means editing the firmware with ESPHome. If you also run Home Assistant, this short guide shows how.

docs.title: 6. Do I need to press Clean SEN55 for my AIR-1 or set up a flow for it?
docs.text: • No, your AIR-1 will self-clean once a week per this recommended documentation from the manufacturer.

docs.title: 7. Can your sensors be used with OpenHAB?
docs.text: • Yes, please install this binding and then restart OpenHAB and our devices will show up to configure!

docs.title: 8. My Apollo device doesn't show up when I add it in Homey.
docs.text:
• Make sure the device is powered on and connected to the same network as your Homey. If it still isn't listed, choose Enter an address instead on the first page of the pairing wizard and enter the device's IP address or hostname, plus its encryption key if it has one.
  • Homey finds devices with mDNS, which doesn't cross every VLAN, so a device on a separate network may only show up by address. To make discovery work across networks, see Connection issues and the mDNS guides for UniFi and OPNsense.

docs.title: 9. My CO2 values are way off from my other Apollo devices.
docs.text: • If your sensor is exposed to high levels of vibrations or too much airflow, the SCD40 CO2 sensor will have issues working properly.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Apollo Automation is a small startup based in Lexington, Kentucky, dedicated to creating innovative, high-quality, and affordable smart home automation hardware. Founded in 2023 by a group of friends, the company was born out of frustration with existing solutions that lacked transparency and customization options. Named after Trevor’s dog, Apollo, the team set out to build products that offer complete local control without reliance on cloud services or subscriptions!

Apollo Automation focuses on designing and manufacturing open-source hardware and software that puts control in the hands of its users. The company engages closely with the Homey community, providing fully customizable devices that integrate with the platform. Their mission is to empower customers to build and control their own smart homes with ease, reliability, and privacy. Through monthly livestreams and an active Discord community, Apollo Automation remains accessible, transparent, and driven by user feedback, ensuring that their products meet the evolving needs of their customers.
