docs.title: Temp and humidity calibration and offset examples
Simple and advanced temperature and humidity offsets
docs.text: Your Apollo device's temperature and humidity readings can differ from the true value. This page explains why, then shows how to correct them: simple offsets you set from the device page, or advanced template sensors that estimate the true values from all of your readings.

docs.title: Why readings can be off
docs.text:
The BME280 and SCD40 sensors are known for measuring temperature and humidity precisely. Like any sensor, though, they can sometimes give inaccurate readings. One significant cause is heat from the ESP chip, which warms the air inside the enclosure and skews the readings.

Temperature and humidity are also linked. When the air temperature rises, the air can hold more moisture, which can lower the relative humidity. When the temperature falls, the air can hold less moisture, so the humidity rises. This relationship plays a big part in how the sensors detect and interpret readings, which makes accurate readings even more important.

docs.title: Add simple offsets
docs.text:
Add two offset boxes to your device so you can correct its SCD40 temperature and humidity readings from Home Assistant.

1. In ESPHome Device Builder, open your device's YAML and paste the following at the bottom:

sensor:
  - id: !extend scd40
    humidity:
      name: "Humidity"
      id: "humidity"
      filters:
        - lambda: return x - id(scd40_humidity_offset).state;
    temperature:
      name: "Temperature"
      id: "temperature"
      filters:
        - lambda: return x - id(scd40_temperature_offset).state;
number:
  - platform: template
    name: SCD40 Humidity Offset
    id: scd40_humidity_offset
    restore_value: true
    initial_value: -18.86
    min_value: -70.0
    max_value: 70.0
    entity_category: "CONFIG"
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    optimistic: true
    update_interval: never
    step: 0.1
    mode: box
  - platform: template
    name: SCD40 Temperature Offset
    id: scd40_temperature_offset
    restore_value: true
    initial_value: 14.54
    min_value: -70.0
    max_value: 70.0
    entity_category: "CONFIG"
    unit_of_measurement: "°C"
    optimistic: true
    update_interval: never
    step: 0.1
    mode: box

2. Click Save, then Install.

3. In Home Assistant, open your device's page in the ESPHome integration. Fill in your offsets in the two new boxes, SCD40 Humidity Offset and SCD40 Temperature Offset.

Give the new offsets up to 1 minute to take effect. The next section explains how to choose the right values.

docs.title: How the offsets work
docs.text:
You can adjust the BME280 and SCD40 Temperature Offset entities by hand to match the conditions in your home. The firmware subtracts each offset from the raw temperature or humidity reading, and the result is what the sensor's entity shows in Home Assistant. For example, the scd40_temperature entity equals the raw SCD40 temperature reading minus scd40_offset.

The default offsets come from our NIST-certified thermometer and are calibrated for our environment, so they might not be accurate in your home. To fine-tune them, compare your sensor with a reference thermometer and adjust the offsets by the difference between the two readings.

You may also notice the bme280_humidity_calibrated, scd40_humidity_calibrated, bme280_temperature_calibrated, and scd40_temperature_calibrated entities. These use the linear filter in the ESPHome firmware to adjust the readings based on data we collected. Because every home is different, they might not always be precise either.

docs.title: Advanced: model the relationship between sensors
docs.text:
Another way to get accurate readings is to model how the ESP chip temperature and the other sensors relate to a reference temperature. A template sensor in Home Assistant does this for you: it combines your sensor's live readings into an estimated true temperature and humidity, using either a decision tree or our regression coefficients (the multipliers in the example below).

Add the example below to your Home Assistant configuration YAML. Its entity IDs belong to one Apollo MSR-1 (apollo_msr_1_a79e24), so replace them with your own device's entity IDs.

sensor:
  - platform: template
    sensors:
      estimated_reference_temperature:
        friendly_name: "Estimated Temperature"
        unit_of_measurement: '°C'
        value_template: >
          {{
            0.3228 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_esp_temperature') | float +
            0.8702 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature') | float +
            -0.1285 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature') | float +
            -0.0491 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity') | float +
            0.0851 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity') | float +
            -17.4840
          }}


      estimated_reference_humidity:
        friendly_name: "Estimated Humidity"
        unit_of_measurement: '%'
        value_template: >
          {{
            -1.2468 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_esp_temperature') | float +
            -2.1959 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature') | float +
            2.9604 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature') | float +
            0.2380 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity') | float +
            1.8283 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity') | float +
            40.1686
          }}

docs.title: Collect your own data
docs.text:
To gather your own data with a reference sensor and an MSR-1 in your home, we recommend logging the readings to a CSV file. The YAML below logs once a minute to match the reference sensor. As its comments show, the notify entry goes in configuration.yaml and the automation goes in automations.yaml.

#Configuration.yaml
notify:
  - platform: file
    name: sensor_csv_log
    filename: /config/sensor_log.csv
    timestamp: False

#Automations.yaml
  - id: log_sensor_data_to_csv
    alias: "Log Sensor Data to CSV"
    trigger:
      platform: time_pattern
      minutes: "/1"  # Log data every minute to match reference sensor
    action:
      - service: notify.sensor_csv_log
        data_template:
          message: >
            {{ now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_esp_temperature') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_uptime') | default('NA') }}

docs.title: Advanced accuracy with GPIO
docs.text: For the highest accuracy, connect a temperature and humidity sensor to the exposed mezzanine connector on the back of your Apollo board. This modification can dramatically improve both temperature and humidity readings, giving you data that's as accurate as possible.

docs.title: Apollo battery devices - sensor connection check
Sensor connection check
docs.text:
Not sure whether your battery device is online? Run this quick check. You restart the device and press its boot button, and the RGB light flashes a color that shows whether it's connected to Wi-Fi, to Homey, or to nothing. Select your device below. Each button name links to a page that shows where that button is.

TEMP-1BPLT-1B

1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the device.

2. Then press the boot button and let go.

1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the device.

2. Then press the boot button and let go.

The RGB light on your device then flashes a color that shows its connection status:

  • Blue: connected to Wi-Fi and Homey
  • Green: connected to Wi-Fi only, not to Homey
  • Yellow: no Wi-Fi connection

Read the first flash, not the second

A few seconds later the light flashes a second time, green or red. That second flash is the device's built-in sensor self-test, not its connection status, so read the connection status from the first color.

Keep your sensor awake with Prevent Sleep

To keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time, open the device in Homey, go to its settings, and turn on Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present). Homey can only change this setting while the sensor is awake, so press the reset button first. To learn more, see the Prevent Sleep guide for the TEMP-1, TEMP-1B, or PLT-1B.

docs.title: How to wake up your sensor
How to wake up your sensor
docs.text:
Once Prevent sleep is off, your Apollo TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 sleeps between reports to make its battery last, and Homey can't reach it while it sleeps. In the Homey app, a sleeping sensor shows as Device disconnected, and if you try to change a setting, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. The sensor wakes on its own after each Sleep duration and reconnects to Homey. Wake it yourself when you want fresh readings right away, or need it awake to change a setting, update the firmware, or troubleshoot.

Using a USB-powered TEMP-1?

Your TEMP-1 normally stays awake in Homey, so there's nothing to wake. If it keeps losing its connection to Homey, it may have been set to sleep earlier, for example in Home Assistant. Turn Prevent sleep back on with its boot button.

docs.title: Wake your sensor
docs.text:
Pressing the reset button restarts your sensor, so it wakes up right away, connects to your Wi-Fi, and reports to Homey. On a BTN-1, any of its four buttons wakes it too. The boot button can't wake a sleeping sensor. Once the sensor is awake, the boot button is what keeps it awake. Select your device below to find both buttons.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1

The buttons are on the board inside the case. To reach the reset button, gently pry the lid off at the small slit near the top of the case. You can press the boot button with the lid off too, or with a paperclip through the small opening on the right side of the case when the USB-C port faces you. Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode has more photos.

To wake the TEMP-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

This is the boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake.

You can press both buttons with a pin through small openings in the case. Putting the PLT-1B in boot mode shows where the openings are.

To wake the PLT-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

The boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake, sits next to the USB-C port.

To wake the BTN-1, press and release the reset button, on the left in the photo below. The boot button, which you'll use to keep the BTN-1 awake, is on the right.

Pressing Button 1, 2, 3, or 4 also wakes the BTN-1. Homey receives that press as a Click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any flow you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

Your sensor is now awake. Homey reconnects to it on its own, and the Homey app no longer shows it as Device disconnected. It doesn't stay awake for long, though. Unless Prevent sleep is on, it sends fresh readings and goes back to sleep about 20 seconds after Homey connects (about 10 seconds for the BTN-1), or after about 90 seconds if Homey doesn't connect at all. Not sure your TEMP-1B or PLT-1B woke up? The sensor connection check tells you in a few seconds.

docs.title: Keep your sensor awake
docs.text: A wake-up doesn't last long enough to change settings or troubleshoot comfortably. Turn on Prevent sleep and your sensor stays awake until you turn it off again. You can turn it on from the sensor itself or from the Homey app, where it sits in your sensor's Settings under Battery settings (if battery is present).

docs.title: With the buttons on the sensor
docs.text:
The buttons work even when Homey can't reach the sensor, which makes this the most reliable way. It's also the better choice for the BTN-1, which stays awake for only about 10 seconds after Homey connects. Press the two buttons one after the other, never together: holding the boot button while you press reset puts the sensor in boot mode for flashing firmware instead.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets your sensor to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the sensor.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

Your sensor turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked once the sensor is connected. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the sensor was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

docs.title: From the Homey app
docs.text:
The sensor stays awake for only about 20 seconds after Homey connects, or about 10 seconds for the BTN-1, so have the Homey app open and ready before you start.

  1. Wake the sensor with the reset button.
  2. In the Homey app, open your sensor and wait until it no longer shows Device disconnected.
  3. Right away, open its Settings, check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save.
  4. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, press the reset button once more.

Your sensor now stays awake until you uncheck Prevent sleep again. If the sensor was already on its way back to sleep at step 3, it still keeps the change and starts up with Prevent sleep on after the reset in step 4. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. instead, the change didn't reach the sensor: start again from step 1, or use the buttons.

The Prevent sleep guide for the TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 covers both settings in detail, including Sleep duration. On a BTN-1, Prevent sleep also decides which presses reach Homey.

Next step: let your sensor sleep again

Staying awake drains the battery far faster. Once you're done, turn Prevent sleep off and choose how long the sensor sleeps between reports.

TEMP-1B: Prevent sleep PLT-1B: Prevent sleep BTN-1: Prevent sleep

docs.title: CO<sub>2</sub> calibration
docs.text:
Your sensor calibrates itself

The latest Apollo firmware enables the SCD40's automatic self-calibration by default on every device with the CO2 sensor (AIR-1, R PRO-1, MSR-2, and MTR-1). As long as the sensor sees fresh air (about 420 ppm) at least once a week, it corrects its own baseline and you never need to calibrate manually. Airing out the room once a week is enough.

If your device sits in a space that rarely gets fresh air (a sealed office, a basement, a grow room), automatic self-calibration will slowly drag the readings down. Turn off the CO2 Auto Calibration switch in your device's settings and calibrate manually with the steps below instead.

Calibrate manually every 1 to 2 years when auto calibration is off

The SCD40 CO2 sensor has a long lifetime (over 10 years), but with automatic self-calibration turned off it needs re-calibration back to the 420 ppm baseline every 1 to 2 years.

You'll take your sensor outside into fresh air and calibrate it from its settings in Homey.

1. Bring your sensor outside and plug it in. You might need a USB battery bank if you live in an apartment or otherwise cannot get power outside of your building.

2. Open your Homey app or desktop browser and navigate to the Homey Dashboard.

3. Navigate to your device, such as via the "Favorite Devices" section and right click (or on mobile short hold) then click on Settings.

4. Scroll down until you see "Maintenance" and select it on mobile, then click on "Calibrate SCD40 to 420ppm" and you should see the CO2 readings at 420 ppm or near it.

It might take several attempts clicking the "Press" button for it to equalize correctly. If you don't see the SCD40 reporting 400-500 ppm then click the button again.

5. Now your CO2 sensor should be calibrated! Be sure to set up some nice flows and check out the insights so you can monitor the CO2 levels.

Dangerous CO2 level considerations

CO2 levels in a closed, unventilated bedroom can quickly rise to concentrations that may impair focus or even pose health risks.

Note the steep decline in CO2 ppm detected due to the door and window being opened and fan turned on.

Wisconsin Department of Health CO2 Level Chart

docs.title: mmWave tuning videos
docs.text:
Radar Engineering Mode (REM)

If your Apollo MSR-2 reports presence in an empty room, turn on Radar Engineering Mode (REM) to watch the energy in each radar gate, then raise the threshold of any gate that triggers on its own. You do this on the MSR-2's built-in web page, because the Apollo Automation app for Homey doesn't show these controls.

Both videos are from Apollo and use the MSR-1, which has the same LD2410B radar as your MSR-2. If a video tunes the radar in Home Assistant, follow along on your MSR-2's web page instead, using the quick summary below.

docs.title: Radar gates and zones
docs.text: A quick introduction to the gates and zones of the LD2410B radar.

docs.title: Tuning with Radar Engineering Mode
docs.text: How to tune the radar with Radar Engineering Mode.

docs.title: Quick summary
docs.text:
Here's the whole process in five steps, all on your MSR-2's web page. You need a phone or computer on the same network as the sensor.

  1. Open the web page. Take the last 6 characters of your MSR-2's name in Homey, such as c64a28 in Apollo MSR-2 c64a28, and go to http://apollo-msr-2-c64a28.local/ with your own characters. If that doesn't load, go to http://<device IP> instead.
  2. In the Configuration section, turn on Radar Engineering Mode.

  3. In the Diagnostic section, watch the gate energy readings, g0 move energy and g0 still energy through g8 move energy and g8 still energy. Each gate covers 0.75 m, counted out from the sensor.

  4. Move a gate's threshold slider, such as g6 move threshold or g6 still threshold, to the right to make that gate less sensitive, or to the left to make it more sensitive.

  5. Turn Radar Engineering Mode back off when you're done.

Your MSR-2 now detects people where you want it to. To confirm it in Homey, open your MSR-2 and watch Has Target as you walk around the room.

Quote from popular YouTuber Make It Work Tech

I ended up maxing out the sliders on all gates and then bringing them down just enough to pick up human presence. Definitely easier than using the LD2410B app. - MakeItWorkTech

Open-plan kitchen and living room: light the kitchen only

You'll tune the gates so only movement in the kitchen turns on the kitchen lights.

  1. Stand in the spots where you want the MSR-2 to trigger, and in the spots where it shouldn't.
  2. Watch which gates rise in each spot.
  3. Move the sliders for the living room gates to the right, so walking past no longer turns on the kitchen lights. Move the still threshold sliders for the kitchen gates to the left, so the lights stay on while you read a recipe or do the dishes.

Next step: tune gate by gate

The full guide walks you through finding your MSR-2's address, reading the gate energy against each threshold, and the radar settings you can change in Homey itself.

Tune the MSR-2 radar from its web page

docs.title: How to tune the MTR-1 using Home Assistant
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to set up your MTR-1's three zones by entering the X and Y coordinates for each one. First you add a card to your dashboard that shows the radar's live targets, then you use it to work out the coordinates for each zone, in millimeters. You can enter the values in Home Assistant, as shown below, or directly on the device's web page by visiting its IP address or hostname.local.

Tuning with the HLK Radartool app is much easier, and it's the method we suggest for setting up your MTR-1.

docs.title: Add the target card to your dashboard
docs.text:
Start by adding a Plotly card that draws the radar's coverage area, your three zones, and the targets the radar sees.

1. Install HACS.

2. Download Plotly inside HACS.

3. In the tool below, enter your device's full name and, if you like, rename the three zones. Then click Generate YAML and Copy YAML.

Not sure of your device name? Go to the ESPHome Integrations page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome), select your device, and look for the full name. Unless you've renamed it, it looks something like apollo_mtr_1_c64a28, ending in six random characters.

4. Open a dashboard and click the pencil icon to edit it. Click one of the large + signs, type "manual", and select the Manual card.

Shown with an R PRO-1 card; the MTR-1 steps are the same.

5. Delete any text in the card, paste the YAML you copied in step 3, and click Save.

Your dashboard now has a card like the one above, showing the radar's coverage area and your three zones.

docs.title: Open your MTR-1's device page
docs.text:
The target sensors and zone settings are on your MTR-1's page in the ESPHome integration.

1. Head to the ESPHome Integrations page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome).

2. Click your device, as shown in the image below.

docs.title: Switch the target sensors to millimeters (imperial units only)
docs.text:
Metric users can skip this section

If your Home Assistant uses the metric system, go straight to Enter your zones.

If you use the imperial system, your Target 1-3 X and Y sensors report in inches (in). For the targets to show up correctly on the card, change all three X and all three Y target sensors to millimeters (mm).

1. In the Sensors section, find the Target 1-3 X and Y sensors and select one of them.

2. Select the Settings cog in the top right.

3. Change the unit of measurement to mm and select Update.

4. Repeat steps 1 to 3 for each of the other target sensors, so all three X and all three Y sensors are updated. Your X and Y targets now look like this.

5. Check your Plotly card. Your targets now appear on it.

Your card now shows live targets, so you're ready to draw zones around them.

docs.title: Enter your zones
docs.text:
Now use the live targets on the card to find the coordinates for each zone, and enter them on your MTR-1's device page.

1. Scroll down to the Configuration section, where you see the empty boxes for the X and Y coordinates of zones 1-3.

Suggested settings

  • Turn on Multi Target Tracking to help the MTR-1 detect up to three targets better.
  • Zone Type lets you select Disabled, Detection, or Filter:
    • Disabled: disables zone area detection.
    • Detection: only detects targets in the specified zone. With no zones set, it detects nobody.
    • Filter: excludes the zone from detection.

2. Walk, sit, or stand in the area where you want a detection or non-detection zone, and watch where your target appears on the card. Then enter the Zone 1-3 X and Y values to draw zones around the targets you want to detect or filter out. X values go from -4860 mm to 4860 mm, and Y values go from 0 mm to 7560 mm.

Helpful hints for understanding zones

  • X1 must always be less than X2, and Y1 must always be less than Y2.
  • The Y axis is simpler, since it's never negative.
  • The X axis is where you can get tripped up, especially when both values are negative: -3456 is less than -2345.
  • The Plotly chart still draws the rectangles even if the X1/X2 and Y1/Y2 values are reversed, so check the order yourself.
  • Zones can't overlap.

Your zones now show on the card, and your MTR-1 uses them to detect or filter out targets.

Zones reset after a restart?

If your zone configurations aren't saved when you restart the device, try turning on LD2450 Bluetooth for a few seconds and then turning it off again. You can also try turning on Multi Target Tracking. This should wake up the mmWave module and retrieve your saved zones.

docs.title: HLK Radar Tool app
docs.text:
Finding your MTR-1's web server address

Some steps below require opening your device's web server in a browser. To find your address:

  1. In Homey, open your MTR-1 device and note the last 6 characters of its name. For example, Apollo MTR-1 c64a28 gives you c64a28.
  2. Build your URL: http://apollo-mtr-1-c64a28.local/

If the .local address doesn't load, use your router to find the device's IP address and use that instead.

docs.title: Configure zones
docs.text:
Ensure that the LD2450 firmware version is V2.02.23090617 or later for proper integration functionality.

The newer version of the firmware includes an "auto calibrate" function so you might want to test it out!

The HLK-LD2450 mmWave sensor is used in the MTR-1. Click Here for the datasheet.

iPhoneAndroid

Click here to download

Click here to download

With the app installed, you'll turn on the radar's Bluetooth, connect to it from the HLKRadarTool app, and set up your zones.

1. Open your MTR-1's web server (see address tip above), scroll down until you see LD2450 Bluetooth, and toggle it on.

2. Open the HLKRadarTool App and select your device.

You need to be close to your device!

The LD2450 mmWave sensor is a very tiny sensor with no external antenna, which means it cannot connect to Bluetooth devices unless they are very close. Sometimes this means you need to be within a few feet of the sensor to connect directly to it!

3. Select Set in the top right.

4. Select Area Detection, then toggle Area 1, 2, or 3 and you will see a box with the corresponding number pop up. Then you can press and hold the box to move it and resize it. When your zones are set then select Submit and you should see Setup successfully.

There are three ways to use your MTR-1!

You can use any of these three choices to control your MTR-1 differently. The most common option is Area Detection, which lets you set up three areas and track three targets within them.Close detection (Disabled on the web server): zone detection is offArea Detection (Detection): only detects targets inside your zonesArea Filtering (Filter): ignores targets inside your zones

Close detection lets you use the sensor as a basic presence sensor, and Area Filtering lets you filter out an area and detect everything else, which is useful to avoid a fan!

5. If set up correctly the zones should be saved as different colors. You should be all set!

Helpful Hints to understand zones better!

  • X1 must always be less than X2, and Y1 must always be less than Y2.

  • The Y axis is easier since it's never negative.

  • The X axis is where you can get tripped up, especially when both values are negative: -3456 is less than -2345.
  • The zones cannot overlap.

docs.title: Adding Apollo devices to hidden networks
Adding Apollo devices to hidden networks
docs.text:
A Wi-Fi network with a hidden SSID needs the ESPHome fast_connect option, which connects your Apollo device to the network directly instead of scanning for it first. In this guide you add that option to your device's YAML in ESPHome Device Builder and install the update over Wi-Fi.

Before you start

You need ESPHome Device Builder. If you do not have it installed, install the standalone ESPHome Device Builder first. It runs on a computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux), so you don't need Home Assistant.

1. Open ESPHome Device Builder.

2. Click Edit on your Apollo device, as shown below. If your Apollo device only appears under Discovered, click Take control on it first.

Keep Homey connected

If ESPHome Device Builder adds an API encryption key to your device, Homey can't connect to the device after the install. Device Builder adds a key when you take control of a device with Enable encryption turned on, and that option is on by default in the Take control dialog. To reconnect, copy the key with Show encryption key in the device's menu in ESPHome Device Builder. Then open the device's settings in Homey, choose Repair, and enter the key.

3. Copy the code inside the code block below.

  fast_connect: True

4. Paste it on a new line inside the wifi: section of your device's YAML, as shown in the screenshot below. Make sure the spaces at the start of the line match the lines around it, and that there are no red lines under any of the code.

5. Click Save, then Install in the top right.

6. Click Wirelessly and let it finish compiling, then installing.

7. When you see OTA Successful, the install has finished. Click Close in the bottom right.

You're finished! Your Apollo device can now connect to your Wi-Fi with a hidden SSID.

Understand the downside of fast_connect

fast_connect (optional, true or false): when enabled, your device connects directly to your Wi-Fi network without doing a full scan first. This is required for hidden networks and can significantly improve connection times. It defaults to off. The downside is that your device connects to the first network it sees, even if that network is very far away and better ones are available. Read more about the downsides in the ESPHome Wi-Fi documentation.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This will walk you through the process of connecting your new Apollo Automation sensor to Homey. If at any point you get stuck, join our Discord for some help.

docs.title: Connecting through hotspot:
docs.text:
To get your new Apollo sensor connected to your Wi-Fi, follow the steps below!

1. Plug the sensor into a quality power brick. They require 5v and under an amp so most phone chargers will be fine. ESP devices are sensitive to power fluctuations and users have had some issues with really cheap power bricks. If your device is restarting or unavailable please try a different power brick.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to "Apollo MSR2 Hotspot", it might take a minute for the Wi-Fi network to show up.

3. Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your sensor.

If this does not automatically open the dashboard, please open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

4. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your sensor to connect to or scroll to the bottom and type in your Wi-Fi network then click "Save".

Tip for Mesh Wi-Fi systems or multiple Access Points

If you have multiple access points or a mesh system please manually type in your Wi-Fi network so it will join with the strongest signal!

5. Once connected, the sensor's dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your sensor to your Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Adding Apollo Automation app in Homey:
docs.text:
You'll install the Apollo Automation app on your Homey from a desktop PC or a browser.

1. Navigate to this website and click "Install App". For now this needs to be done from a desktop PC or a browser.

2. Select the Homey device you want to install it on and then click "Install App" again!

3. Your device will install the Apollo Automation Homey App then move to the next section.

docs.title: Connecting to Homey:
docs.text:
Next, you'll add your Apollo sensor to Homey from the Homey app on your phone.

1. Open the Homey App on your phone and navigate to the Devices tab at the bottom then select the (+) icon in the top right and choose "New Device". Choose "Allow" if it pops up asking to find Bluetooth devices, or you can change this later in settings.

2. Select Apollo Automation under Brands in the bottom left then choose "Every Apollo Sensor". When prompted, click "Connect".

3. Your Apollo devices will automatically show up and if not, please first connect it to your Wi-Fi following the steps outlined here.

4. Select the device you want to add, in this case an Apollo MTR-1 and click Continue at the bottom.

5. Click Continue Setup and choose a Zone to place your device in. If you are new to Homey you can choose Home and move it to another Zone later after you create more zones!

6. Change any other default settings like the Name, icon, etc or click Finish in the bottom right.

7. You are done! Your sensor is now ready to create flows and add as a favorite to your dashboard!

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.text: This will walk you through the process of connecting your new Apollo Automation sensor to Homey. If at any point you get stuck, join our Discord for some help.

docs.title: Connecting through hotspot:
docs.text:
To get your new Apollo sensor connected to your Wi-Fi, follow the steps below!

1. Plug the sensor into a quality power brick. They require 5v and under an amp so most phone chargers will be fine. ESP devices are sensitive to power fluctuations and users have had some issues with really cheap power bricks. If your device is restarting or unavailable please try a different power brick.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to "Apollo MSR2 Hotspot", it might take a minute for the Wi-Fi network to show up.

3. Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your sensor.

If this does not automatically open the dashboard, please open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

4. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your sensor to connect to or scroll to the bottom and type in your Wi-Fi network then click "Save".

Tip for Mesh Wi-Fi systems or multiple Access Points

If you have multiple access points or a mesh system please manually type in your Wi-Fi network so it will join with the strongest signal!

5. Once connected, the sensor's dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your sensor to your Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Adding Apollo Automation app in Homey:
docs.text:
You'll install the Apollo Automation app on your Homey from a desktop PC or a browser.

1. Navigate to this website and click "Install App". For now this needs to be done from a desktop PC or a browser.

2. Select the Homey device you want to install it on and then click "Install App" again!

3. Your device will install the Apollo Automation Homey App then move to the next section.

docs.title: Connecting to Homey:
docs.text:
Next, you'll add your Apollo sensor to Homey from the Homey app on your phone.

1. Open the Homey App on your phone and navigate to the Devices tab at the bottom then select the (+) icon in the top right and choose "New Device". Choose "Allow" if it pops up asking to find Bluetooth devices, or you can change this later in settings.

2. Select Apollo Automation under Brands in the bottom left then choose "Every Apollo Sensor". When prompted, click "Connect".

3. Your Apollo devices will automatically show up and if not, please first connect it to your Wi-Fi following the steps outlined here.

4. Select the device you want to add, in this case an Apollo MTR-1 and click Continue at the bottom.

5. Click Continue Setup and choose a Zone to place your device in. If you are new to Homey you can choose Home and move it to another Zone later after you create more zones!

6. Change any other default settings like the Name, icon, etc or click Finish in the bottom right.

7. You are done! Your sensor is now ready to create flows and add as a favorite to your dashboard!

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: Renaming Apollo devices
docs.text:
1. Open the Homey App or dashboard in a browser and right click a device or short hold and then select "Rename".

2. Type in the new name and then hit enter. That's it, you're done!

docs.title: Common connection issues
docs.text:
Work through these checks if your Apollo device won't stay connected or Homey can't find it.

1. Try a couple of different power cord and power brick combinations. This matters a lot more than you'd think!

2. Check your Wi-Fi list for the device's hotspot. If the hotspot is showing up, the device is not connected to a network. Connect to the hotspot and add your Wi-Fi network, as shown in Connecting through hotspot.

3. Check your router's list of connected devices. Your device shows up with the Apollo name followed by a 6-digit hex value, which is the end of its hardware (MAC) address.

Look at the mDNS wiki articles as well

Auto discovery depends on mDNS, which is used to tell which devices are on your network. If a firewall blocks mDNS, or your network doesn't forward mDNS traffic, auto discovery can run into issues. If you use UniFi or OPNsense, see the UniFi mDNS guide or the OPNsense mDNS guide.

docs.title: OPNsense Auto Discover Device mDNS Issue
OPNsense mDNS auto discover issue
docs.text:
If mDNS is unchecked then Home Assistant and ESPHome will not auto discover new devices

If you have different networks that Home Assistant and ESPHome devices are on, then you will need mDNS working across both networks and firewall rules allowing access between them. Below is a guide for installing the mDNS Repeater plugin on OPNsense to fix this issue.

Install the mDNS Repeater

1. Click System -> Click Firmware -> Click Plugins -> Search for "mdns" -> Click the “+” symbol to install os-mdns-repeater.

2. Confirm that the installation was successful.

3. Refresh the page and then go to Services -> mDNS Repeater (if it isn't there after refreshing your screen, verify the plugin install was successful.)-> Check off "enable" -> select your networks containing Home Assistant / ESPHome IoT devices -> click save.

Now the Home Assistant/ESPHome auto-discover issue should be fixed!

docs.title: Removing devices from Homey
docs.text:
1. Open your Homey app or desktop browser and navigate to the Homey Dashboard.

2. Navigate to your device, such as via the "Favorite Devices" section and right click (or on mobile short hold) then click "Delete".

docs.title: UniFi Auto Discover Device mDNS Issue
Ubiquiti UniFi mDNS auto discover issue
docs.text:
If mDNS is unchecked then Home Assistant and ESPHome will not auto discover new devices

If your Home Assistant (or Homey) hub and your ESPHome devices are on different networks, you need mDNS working across both networks and firewall rules that allow traffic between them. Below are guides for fixing this from your PC or the UniFi mobile app.

docs.title: Method 1: Browser
docs.text:
You can turn on Multicast DNS for your Default Network from a browser on your PC.

1. Log into your UniFi network through your default IP address which is usually http://192.168.1.1

2. Select Network.

3. Select Settings.

4. Select Networks.

5. Select the Default Network

6. Check Multicast DNS

7. Now the Home Assistant/ESPHome auto-discover issue should be fixed!

docs.title: Method 2: UniFi mobile app
docs.text:
You can also turn on Multicast DNS for your Default Network from the UniFi mobile app.

1. Open the UniFi app.

2. Tap Settings/Gear Icon

3. Tap Networks

4. Tap Default Network

5. Tap the Multicast DNS slider

6. Now the Home Assistant/ESPHome auto-discover issue should be fixed!

docs.title: High CO<sub>2</sub> notification
docs.text:
This guide will show you how to create a flow that sends a notification to everyone who's home when the CO2 is over a set threshold, 1000 ppm in this example.

This guide is made using the web browser due to using Advanced Flows version of Homey!

1. First we need to open a web browser such as Firefox and head to the Homey webapp and click on the Flow tab on the left side.

2. Click "New Flow" then "Advanced Flow".

3. Click "Add" and select "When".

4. In the search bar at the top, type in "co2 becomes" and select the card for the sensor you want to track. We are choosing "CO2 becomes greater than" for the Apollo AIR-1 device.

5. Place your card on your flow area with a left click. You should have this node on your flow canvas.

6. Select "ppm" and type in your value, we will use 999.

7. Duplicate steps 4 and 5 above but this time select "CO2 becomes less than" and place it on your flow canvas. Make sure to fill in your less than ppm value such as 900 (the screenshot shows 1000; use 900). The gap between 900 and 999 keeps the light from flickering between red and green when CO2 hovers around 1000 ppm.

8. Click "Add" and select "Then" and search for "set a color" and choose the AIR-1 device option.

9. Draw a line to connect "CO2 becomes greater than 999 ppm". Click the 3 dots and select a color. We have chosen red to indicate a problem.

10. Duplicate steps 8 and 9 but this time select green for the color when "CO2 becomes less than 900 ppm" (the screenshot shows 1000; use 900).

11. Click "Add" and select "Then" and search "push" and choose "Send message to user".

12. Draw a line to connect set a color to the push notification. Write in "The CO2 level in the bedroom is currently CO2 ppm. Open the Window, turn on HVAC, etc to lower this value!" Then replace the second "CO2" and click the little tag icon and type in CO2 then select the blue CO2 option under Apollo AIR-1.

13. Click "User" and choose "Everyone who's home" or your preferred option.

14. Click "Add" and select "Delay" and then place it on your flow canvas. Change to minutes and input 5 for adding a 5 minute delay then drag a line from "set a color" to the delay (the screenshot shows 1000; use 900).

15. Click "Add" and select "Then" and search for "turn off" and choose the AIR-1 device option.

16. Drag a line from the Delay in step 14 to the Turn off card and that's it! Click save at the top and give your flow a name. Your finished flow should look like this (the screenshot shows 1000; use 900).

17. As a bonus, you can add a note reminding you what this automation does. Click "Add" then click "Note" and type in "CO2 level alert with RGB LEDs" on the note. Your flow should now look like this (the screenshot shows 1000; use 900).

18. You are done! Your sensor is now ready to create flows and add as a favorite to your dashboard!

Run into issues? Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: Turn on a light when someone enters a region
Turn on a light when someone enters a region
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

Regions turn one radar into several spots you can automate on their own: the desk, the sofa, the workbench. In this guide you build two flows in the Homey mobile app. The first turns a light on the moment someone steps into a region; the second turns it off once the region has been empty for a while. The example uses a region called Server on an Apollo R PRO-1, and works the same way on an MTR-1 with any region you have drawn.

Before you start

  • Draw at least one region with the Zone Mapper tool, set to Detect people here. See the guide for your R PRO-1 or MTR-1.
  • Add the light you want to control to Homey.

docs.title: Why use the region trigger
docs.text:
Every detect region gives your sensor three flow cards: A region became occupied, A region became empty, and A region is occupied. Start your flow with A region became occupied and pick your region. It fires every time someone walks into that spot, even when someone else is already elsewhere in the room.

The sensor's whole-room card, The occupancy alarm turned on, only fires when the room goes from empty to occupied. Pairing it with a Server is occupied condition misses the moment someone who is already in the room walks over to the server, so the light stays off.

docs.title: Flow 1: Turn the light on
docs.text:
This flow has one trigger and one action, so it needs no And card.

  1. In the Homey mobile app, tap Flow in the bottom bar, then tap + at the top right (or Create a Flow if you have none yet).
  2. Under When..., tap Add Card. Open Apollo Automation under Apps, and choose your sensor.
  3. Choose the card A region became occupied.
  4. Tap Region and pick Server, then tap the check mark at the top right.
  5. Under Then..., tap Add Card. Find your light under Zones & Devices, choose Turn on, and tap the check mark.
  6. Tap Next. Name the flow, for example Server area light on, and tap Save Flow.

The flow now shows in My Flows. Walk into the region and the light turns on.

Only detect regions are listed

The region picker lists your Detect people here regions. Areas set to Ignore this area never report occupied, so they don't appear.

docs.title: Flow 2: Turn the light off
docs.text:
The second flow mirrors the first. Build it the same way, with two changes:

  1. Under When..., choose A region became empty and pick Server.
  2. Under Then..., choose Turn off for the same light.
  3. Name it Server area light off and tap Save Flow.

Now the light follows the region: on when someone arrives, off when they leave.

docs.title: Set the hold time
docs.text:
A region stays occupied for its Hold time after the last person leaves, 5 seconds by default. That is what stops the light from flickering off when someone leans back or steps away for a moment.

For a desk or a workbench, raise it. Open the dashboard with your Radar regions widget, tap the region with Select active, and set Hold time under More to 60 seconds or longer. Press Save. Flow 2 now waits that long before it turns the light off.

docs.title: Test your flows
docs.text:
Run the flows end to end by walking in and out of the region while you watch the light. To check a single flow without moving, tap the play button next to it in My Flows; it runs its Then cards once, and a green check mark confirms it ran.

If a flow doesn't fire:

  • Open the Radar regions widget and watch the dots. If your dot doesn't land inside the region, make the region larger with Bigger or the arrows.
  • Check that the region is set to Detect people here and is Enabled.
  • Check that both flows are switched on in My Flows.

docs.title: Take it further
docs.text:
• One flow for many regions: pick Any region in the trigger instead of a single region. The Region name token tells the flow which one fired, for example in a notification.
  • Count people: A region became occupied also passes a Target count token, the number of people in the region.
  • Keep other automations in check: add A region is occupied as an And condition. For example, add Sofa is not occupied (with Invert on) to the flow that turns your living room lights off.

See Use regions in flows for the full list of region cards.

docs.title: LED-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What is the maximum power output of the LED-1?

  • The LED-1 is able to safely offer 10 amps of power using either 5 V, 12 V, or a 24 V when using an external power supply.
  • The device can also be powered via USB-C-PD (Power Delivery) with 5 V or 12 V at 3 amps.
  • The device can also be powered by USB-C with 5 V at 3 Amps.
  • The device has a built-in replaceable fuse that will trip if 10 Amps is exceeded. The output voltage is the same as the input voltage, so please make sure you buy the same 5 V, or 12 V, or 24 V power supply and LED strips.

2. How long of an LED strip can I use with the LED-1?

  • The length of LED strips depends more on other factors like voltage drop. Ultimately, we suggest going 3 meters with 5 V for each output, so 3 meters + 3 meters connected to separate outputs. You can go up to 5 meters at 24 V without seeing much voltage drop though!

3. Can I use a remote with the LED-1?

  • Although the device does not come with IR, it does support the WizMote over "ESP-NOW" and this works great inside of WLED!

4. How does the microphone work?

  • Audio-reactive WLED is built into the WLED firmware we ship with the LED-1. Make sure to enable it from the "info" pane and then try using an effect with the little Musical Note Image next to them!

5. My LEDs are the wrong color how do I fix it?

  • You might have SK6812 or some other leds other than the default WS2812B and WLED needs to be configured to know that you are using a different type of LEDs. Head to the LED Outputs section of wled docs to learn more.

6. Can I use the LED-1 without Home Assistant or even Wi-Fi? Even on my boat/RV?

  • Yes! You can directly connect to the access point of your WLED device without a network using a phone or laptop. Look for "WLED-AP" in your Wi-Fi client list and enter in the password "wled1234", head to http://4.3.2.1 or http://wled.me then control your device!

7. My LEDs are very dim how do I fix it?

  • Head to the settings of WLED and make sure the brightness limiter is off. You also might have a very long LED strip and you might need power injection to make it work properly.

8. How much power does it use?

  • The LED-1 uses under 1 Amp of power for itself but will use up to 10amps at 5-24 Volts based on the power supply used.

9. Can I reflash this with stock WLED firmware?

  • Yes! The LED-1 runs regular WLED. Flash it with the LED-1 reflash guide, then set the pins in WLED from the LED-1 pinout guide.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Apollo LED-1 is a compact, versatile LED Controller for Home Assistant. Fully open-source and expandable, the LED-1 integrates with Home Assistant using the WLED Integration, making it ideal for automating lighting. Access to support and customization resources is available via our Discord and GitHub.

Key Features:

  • Powered via either USB-C (5 V only), USB-C PD (5 V or 12 V) or external power supply (5 V, 12 V, or 24 V).
  • Two fused outputs able to handle 10 Amps total, either from one output or both but max of 10 Amps.
  • Built in MEMS digital microphone for WLED Audio Reactive functionality.
  • Built in relay to kill power to LEDs for less power usage (great for battery projects).

docs.title: Controlling Govee lights with the LED-1
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to use the Apollo LED-1 to control your Govee permanent outdoor lights fully locally, without a cloud-based app. So far, the steps cover preparing a project box, wiring power into the LED-1, and preparing the LED cable.

This guide is still being written

The steps below get the LED-1 connected. More steps are coming.

1. Gather the parts and tools for this project.

Parts

  • Apollo LED-1
  • Govee permanent lights
  • Project box
  • Barrel plug connector
  • White 3-wire LED connecting wire
  • Waterproof sealant

Tools

  • Screwdriver
  • Wire strippers
  • Hobby knife
  • Tweezers

2. Unscrew the 4 screws and remove the project box lid.

3. Remove two of the rubber grommets. Use the hobby knife to cut a small slit in each one for the power and data connections. For an outdoor setup, the two bottom grommets might be best, to help keep water from getting in.

4. Connect the barrel plug to the WAGO connector, the large white component at the bottom left of the board, below the USB-C port. Connect the RED (+) wire to the top terminal and the BLACK (-) wire to the bottom terminal. To insert each wire, use the tweezers to press down the top of the WAGO connector, insert the wire, and then release to lock it in place.

5. Use the hobby knife to remove the cable sheathing from the 3-pin LED connector. Cut carefully, because the cable can roll.

You've finished the steps written so far: the grommets are cut, the barrel plug is wired to the LED-1, and the 3-pin LED connector is stripped and ready.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Congrats on your new Apollo LED-1! This guide walks you through powering it, wiring up your LEDs, and connecting it to Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Choose how to power it
docs.text:
You can power the LED-1 in three ways:

  • USB Power: 5V, up to 3 amps
  • USB Power Delivery: 5V or 12V, up to 3 amps
  • External Power Supply: a dedicated power supply using either 5V, 12V, or 24V

Pick the tab that matches your setup.

USB PowerUSB Power DeliveryExternal Power Supply

1. Connect a USB-C cable to a 5V 3A or larger power supply, and plug the other end into your LED-1.

Use a cable rated for 3 amps

We suggest a quality USB-C cable that can handle 3 amps or more. If you're not sure whether yours supports 3 amps, buy a new cable from our store or a reputable seller such as Amazon or Monoprice.

1. Decide whether you're using 5V or 12V with USB-C PD. If you're using 12V, first flip the switch on the LED-1 board (the board render on the LED-1 introduction page shows where it is). If you're using 5V, skip to the next step.

2. Connect your USB-C PD wall charger to the USB-C cable, then plug the other end into the USB-C port of the LED-1.

Your LED-1 now outputs either 5V or 12V to the + and - terminals of Output 1 and Output 2.

An external power supply is the best way to get the longest distance and the most power out of your device. You can get up to 10 amps of power at 5V, 12V, or 24V.

1. Connect your power supply's output wires to the input terminals of your LED-1. Be very careful to connect the positive red wire to the + sign and the negative black wire to the - sign.

If you still need a power supply, check out our power supply suggestions.

Cut off the barrel connector

Most power supplies have a barrel connector that's only rated for 3 amps. We suggest cutting the barrel connector off and splitting out the red and black wires to put directly into the LED-1.

Unplug the power!

Before you move on to wiring up your LEDs, make sure to unplug your LED-1.

docs.title: Wire up LEDs
docs.text:
Use LEDs that match your power supply's voltage

The LED-1 outputs the same voltage that is input to the device. It protects itself, but not the LED strips connected to it. Connect 5V LED strips if you're using a 5V power supply, and do the same with 12V and 24V.

Next, connect your LED strip to the first output of the LED-1.

1. Grab a male JST-SM 3-pin connector, such as the extra one included with your LED strips. Carefully note which wire is which: red is positive, green is data, and white is ground.

2. Find the two WAGO connectors on the LED-1 labeled "Output 1" and "Output 2". Insert the wires into Output 1:

  • Red power wire: far left terminal of Output 1
  • Green data wire: middle terminal of Output 1
  • White ground wire: third terminal of Output 1

3. If you have a second LED strip, repeat step 2 for it using Output 2.

Your LEDs are wired up and ready for power.

docs.title: Connect to Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Your device is now ready to connect to your Wi-Fi. Once it's connected, you can control it from Home Assistant, the WLED app for iPhone and Android, or a web browser.

1. Plug in your power supply or USB-C power. The LED-1 boots within a couple of seconds.

2. On your phone, open the list of available Wi-Fi networks and select WLED-AP.

3. Wait for the "Welcome to WLED!" page to pop up. If it doesn't, open a web browser and go to http://4.3.2.1/. You should see the same page shown below.

When the "Welcome to WLED!" page opens, you're connected to your LED-1.

docs.title: Add the LED-1 to Home Assistant
docs.text: Home Assistant should discover your LED-1 automatically using the WLED integration.

docs.title: Power supplies
docs.text:
Meanwell power supplies are best but most power supplies off Amazon will be sufficient. As a rule of thumb, over 80% usage on a power supply is bad. So if you want to run with 3amps, buy a 4 or 5amp power supply so that the power supply is not running at its maximum potential amperage.

Most power supplies will have a barrel connector only rated for 3 amps on it, so we suggest that you cut the barrel connector off and split out the red and black wires to put directly into the LED-1.

The LED-1 will output the same voltage that is input and that could damage LEDs!

The LED-1 will protect itself, but not the led strips connected to it. So if you connect a 24 volt power supply to the device, it will send 24v out to the LED strips. Make sure to pair your LEDs and Power supplies with the same voltage!

docs.title: LED strips
docs.text:
• WS2812B which are 5V RGB LED strips.
  • SK6812 which are 5V RGBW LED strips.
  • WS2814 which are 24V RGBW-CCT FCOB LED strips.

Not all LEDs are the same!

We suggest buying only BTF Lighting off of amazon or directly from us (we source only BTF Lighting). They also have an Aliexpress store!

docs.title: LED connectors
docs.text:
JST-SM 3 pin connectors are helpful to connect multiple led strips or to solder them onto led strips to create multiple smaller sections. These have a maximum rating of 3 amps.

10mm Width Transparent Connector Kit You might want to use these 24v FCOB connectors for the WS2814 LEDs suggested above. Make sure to choose the same width of led strip + connector (10mm, 12mm, etc).

docs.title: Additional tools
docs.text:
Wago Connectors are a great option for connecting wires together without soldering.

Wire Strippers are very helpful especially if you need to cut the end off a barrel connector to expose the red and black wires for powering your device. Make sure they are able to strip 18/20/22 gauge wires.

Soldering Iron such as a TS80P. Here's a tutorial on how to use it.

docs.title: How to replace the LED-1 10 A fuse
How to replace the 10 A fuse
docs.text:
Follow these steps to open the case, swap in a new fuse, and close the case again.

1. Gently pry open the lid. This can be a tight fit so you will want to use a small tool not your fingernail. Remove the lid and set aside.

2. Gently lift the LED-1 PCB out of the case. Be careful not to use a lot of force this could break components

3. Flip the LED-1 PCB over and locate the replaceable fuse.

4. Gently remove the fuse using tweezers.

5. Orient the new fuse with the writing facing up then place it inside the fuse bay.

6. Gently push down on the fuse to make sure it is fully seated.

7. Flip PCB over and angle it the same way you disassembled and rest the side of the pcb on the "shelf" as shown in the image below.

8. Align the holes on the case so they line up with the Wago connectors.

9. Press down on the case lid to secure it to the bottom of the case.

10. You're all done. Enjoy your LED-1!

Click here to head to our general tips wiki for best practices!

docs.title: Putting the LED-1 in boot mode
Putting the LED-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the LED-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

1. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer.

2. Push and hold the boot button (the right button). While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your LED-1 then let go of the button.

3. Proceed to the flashing guide!

docs.title: How to find the IP address and hostname of your LED-1
How to find IP address and hostname of your LED-1 device.
docs.text:
You can find your device's IP address and hostname with the WLED Native app on your phone.

1. Download the WLED Native app for iOS and Android.

iOSAndroid

Click here to download

Click here to download

2. Make sure you have already connected it to the same Wi-Fi network that your pc and phone are on as shown here.

3. Your LED-1 should be detected automatically. Select it, then click the Config tab in the top right corner.

WARNING ~ DO NOT UPDATE IT ~ WARNING

There will be a red badge or circle in the top right showing you an update is available. DO NOT DO THIS, IT WILL BREAK YOUR CONFIG.

4. Select WiFi Setup and at the bottom you will see a box with .local at the end. The letters inside of the box are your hostname and the IP is directly below it. You can change the hostname to whatever you like (using letters, numbers, and dashes only). Click Save and Connect when done.

5. You can now access your device from a browser at http://the-ip-address-here or http://the-hostname-you-entered.local

6. Edit the User Interface settings section under the Server description with a friendly name that is shown for your device!

docs.title: Factory re-flash LED-1
docs.text:
Follow these steps to flash your Apollo LED-1 with regular WLED from the official WLED web installer. Use Chrome or Edge, since the installer needs a browser that can talk to the USB serial port.

1. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer.

2. Push and hold the boot button (the right button). While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your LED-1 then let go of the button.

3. Open the WLED web installer. Leave Mode on Basic, keep the newest version selected in the version dropdown, and keep Plain selected. Basic installs a 4MB build, which works on the LED-1.

4. Click Install, pick your LED-1's serial port, and follow the prompts. When the installer shows that installation is complete, close it.

5. The device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled. To reboot it, either unplug the power cable or press the reset button labeled RST (the left button; the boot button BT is on the right).

6. Set the LED-1's pins in WLED. Regular WLED doesn't know how the LED-1 is wired, so it needs the GPIO numbers from the LED-1 pinout guide. Open your LED-1 in WLED (the Connect to Wi-Fi steps show how), click Config, and set the pins in this order:

  • Under Usermods, in the AudioReactive section, set the microphone pins: SD to GPIO 12, WS to GPIO 27, and SCK to GPIO 14. Check Reboot after save? and click Save. Do this first, because WLED's default microphone settings use GPIO 15, which Output 2 needs.
  • After the LED-1 restarts, open Config → LED & Hardware. Set the LED outputs to GPIO 13 (Output 1) and GPIO 15 (Output 2), clicking + to add the second output. Set the relay to GPIO 22 and the button to GPIO 0, then click Save. If your LEDs stay dark while WLED shows them on, check Invert under Relay and save again.

Head to the Getting Started article to set up your LED-1 as a new device!

docs.title: Choose your M-1 firmware
docs.text: Most M-1 pages on this wiki have a WLED and a WLED-MM tab. Pick your firmware once and the rest of the wiki follows it, so this page is only here to help you work out which one you have.

docs.title: Which one do I have?
docs.text:
Open your M-1 in a browser and tap Info. The version is at the top.

Version shown Your firmware 16.0.1 or newer WLED 14.5.1 WLED-MM

docs.title: WLED
docs.text:
The stock, upstream WLED release, and what new M-1 units ship with. HUB75 matrix support is now built into WLED itself, so the M-1 no longer needs a fork to drive the panel.

It brings Pixel Forge, an image and scrolling-text tool that runs on the device, and it can arrange panels in a 2x2 grid instead of only a single row.

WLED requires a Rev6 M-1 controller. The revision is printed on the back of the board.

docs.title: WLED-MM
docs.text:
WLED MoonModules, the fork that added HUB75 support before upstream WLED had it. Units shipped before the switch came with this, and every guide on this wiki still covers it under the WLED-MM tab.

On a Rev6 controller you can move to stock WLED over the air and keep your settings. See Upgrade to WLED.

docs.title: ESPHome
docs.text:
hub75-studio replaces WLED entirely with an ESPHome firmware built for the M-1. You get native Home Assistant entities and YAML you control, at the cost of the WLED effect library and app. Pick this one deliberately.

Set Up ESPHome

docs.title: Game Day Scoreboard
docs.text:
Game Day Scoreboard turns the M-1 into a live sports scoreboard for your team: the next game, the live score and clock, and a splash in your team's color when they score (in basketball, when they win), across the NFL, college football, MLB, the NBA, the WNBA, men's college basketball, the NHL, MLS, and the Premier League. It reads the scores from ESPN by itself, serves its own settings page, and shows up in Home Assistant as an ESPHome device. It needs a Rev6 controller.

Set Up Game Day Scoreboard

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
1. Why am I seeing half a screen worth of color? Is my new M-1 Broken?

  • It is not broken, the matrix settings need to be set. Units on WLED arrive already configured, so this usually means the device was reflashed or its settings were wiped. Run through Matrix Settings and pick your firmware tab.

2. Why am I seeing vertical sideways lines? Is my new M-1 Broken?

  • Re-seat the M-1 controller on the back of your M-1 matrix and it should now be working reliably!

3. What is the maximum power output of the M-1?

  • The M-1 is able to safely offer 3 Amps of power using 5 Volts when using the USB-C cable and stock power supply. That covers one 64x64 panel, so every extra panel needs its own power module.

4. Scrolling Text does not show as an effect, what am I doing wrong?

  • The 2D setup has not been configured, so WLED does not know it is driving a matrix. Check Config then 2D Configuration is set to a 64 x 64 panel. Full steps for both firmwares are on Matrix Settings.

5. Can I use a remote with the M-1?

  • Although the device does not come with IR, it does support the WizMote over "ESP-NOW" and this works great inside of WLED! On WLED this works with the firmware your M-1 already ships with. On the older WLED-MM 14.5.1 it needed a specially compiled build, so if you want a remote and you are still on 14.5.1, migrate to WLED first. See Add a WizMote Remote for the pairing steps.

6. How does the microphone work?

  • Audio-reactive WLED is built into the firmware we ship with the M-1, and on WLED it is on from the factory with the pins already set. Plug in the add-on and pick an effect with the little Musical Note Image next to it. The microphone is an optional add-on and needs a Rev6 or newer controller. See Add Microphone.

7. Can I use the M-1 without Home Assistant or even Wi-Fi? Even on my boat/RV?

  • Yes! The M-1 broadcasts its own open Wi-Fi network named Apollo M-1, with no password. Join it from a phone or laptop, head to http://4.3.2.1, and control the device from there. Builds older than 16.0.1 add a serial number to the end of the network name.

8. How much power does it use?

  • The M-1 uses under 1 Amp of power for itself but will use up to 3amps at 5v for one panel.

9. Can I reflash this with stock WLED firmware?

  • Yes, as of WLED 16.0.1. HUB75 matrix support is now part of upstream WLED, so the M-1 no longer needs the MoonModules fork. Flash it from the Apollo installer, which offers WLED 16.0.1 alongside the older WLED-MM builds. WLED 16.0.1 requires a Rev6 controller.

10. I am on WLED-MM 14.5.1. Should I update?

  • If you have a Rev6 controller, yes. You get Pixel Forge, panel-grid layouts like 2x2, and everything upstream WLED ships from here on. The update is over the air and keeps your settings. See Upgrade to WLED.

11. How do I factory reset the M-1?

  • On WLED, hold the button for ten seconds. That restores every factory setting including the display size, and you reconnect it to Wi-Fi afterward. On WLED-MM a reset does not restore the display settings, so use the reflash guide instead.

12. Why can't I upload a GIF from the WLED phone app?

  • The app's file picker grays out image files, which is a bug in the app rather than anything on the M-1. Open the device in any browser instead and use Pixel Forge.

13. Part of my panel is dark or the colors look wrong.

  • Work through the panel troubleshooting table, which matches what you are seeing to the likely cause.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Apollo Automation M-1 LED Matrix is a vibrant, high-performance display featuring 4096 pixels in a HUB75 format. Powered entirely by our new 5V 3Amp controller, it requires no additional power sources, keeping your setup clean and simple. The compact controller hides discreetly behind the matrix for a sleek installation.

Pre-flashed with WLED firmware, the M-1 offers a fun user experience right out of the box. Customize your display with animations, effects, and colors, or use Pixel Forge, built into WLED, to turn your own images and scrolling text into displays without leaving the device. You can also connect up to four panels, either in a row or as a 2x2 square, though extra power injection will be needed for the full effect.

New units ship with WLED 16.0.1. Older units shipped WLED-MM 14.5.1, and the M-1 can also run ESPHome, including the Game Day Scoreboard, which turns it into a live scoreboard for your team. See Choose Your Firmware to find the right setup guide.

Use Cases:

  • Dynamic indoor or outdoor digital signage for advertising or information displays.
  • Interactive art installations and digital murals.
  • Real-time data visualization like weather, stock prices, or social media feeds.
  • Custom notifications and alerts in smart homes or workplaces.
  • Scoreboards and event displays at sports venues or conferences.
  • Ambient lighting with customizable patterns and colors for mood setting.
  • DIY projects for gaming or retro pixel art displays.
