(Better) HLK Radar Tool app
docs.text:
Finding your MTR-1's web server address

Some steps below require opening your device's web server in a browser. To find your address:

  1. In Homey, open your MTR-1 device and note the last 6 characters of its name. For example, Apollo MTR-1 c64a28 gives you c64a28.
  2. Build your URL: http://apollo-mtr-1-c64a28.local/

If the .local address doesn't load, use your router to find the device's IP address and use that instead.

docs.title: Configure zones
docs.text:
Ensure that the LD2450 firmware version is V2.02.23090617 or later for proper integration functionality.

The newer version of the firmware includes an "auto calibrate" function so you might want to test it out!

The HLK-LD2450 mmWave sensor is used in the MTR-1. Click Here for the datasheet.

iPhoneAndroid

Click here to download

Click here to download

With the app installed, you'll turn on the radar's Bluetooth, connect to it from the HLKRadarTool app, and set up your zones.

1. Open your MTR-1's web server (see address tip above), scroll down until you see LD2450 Bluetooth, and toggle it on.

2. Open the HLKRadarTool App and select your device.

You need to be close to your device!

The LD2450 mmWave sensor is a very tiny sensor with no external antenna, which means it cannot connect to Bluetooth devices unless they are very close. Sometimes this means you need to be within a few feet of the sensor to connect directly to it!

3. Select Set in the top right.

4. Select Area Detection, then toggle Area 1, 2, or 3 and you will see a box with the corresponding number pop up. Then you can press and hold the box to move it and resize it. When your zones are set then select Submit and you should see Setup successfully.

There are three ways to use your MTR-1!

You can use any of these three choices to control your MTR-1 differently. The most common option is Area Detection, which lets you set up three areas and track three targets within them.Close detection (Disabled on the web server): zone detection is offArea Detection (Detection): only detects targets inside your zonesArea Filtering (Filter): ignores targets inside your zones

Close detection lets you use the sensor as a basic presence sensor, and Area Filtering lets you filter out an area and detect everything else, which is useful to avoid a fan!

5. If set up correctly the zones should be saved as different colors. You should be all set!

Helpful Hints to understand zones better!

  • X1 must always be less than X2, and Y1 must always be less than Y2.

  • The Y axis is easier since it's never negative.

  • The X axis is where you can get tripped up, especially when both values are negative: -3456 is less than -2345.
  • The zones cannot overlap.

docs.title: Putting the MTR-1 in boot mode
Putting the MTR-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the MTR-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You'll hold the boot button while you plug in the USB-C cable.

1. Position the MTR-1 as shown in the image below and locate the small opening to press the boot button (the right button).

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your MTR-1 then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You'll plug the device into your computer, then hold the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and locate the boot button (the right opening, shown in the image above) and the reset button (the left opening, shown in the image below).

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your MTR-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the MTR-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash MTR-1
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the steps below.

This factory re-flash needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

If your device has already been added to Homey, please remove it from Homey before continuing.

1. Position the MTR-1 as shown in the image below and locate the small opening to press the boot button (the right button).

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your MTR-1 then let go of the button.

3. Open the Apollo MTR-1 installer.

4. Click Connect & Install.

5. Select the open com port then click Connect.

6. Click Install ApolloAutomation.MTR-1.

7. Click "INSTALL".

8. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

9. Please proceed to the getting started guide and set up your sensor as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials
docs.text:
You'll reset the device's Wi-Fi credentials, then connect it to your new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power

2. Long press the Boot button (the button on the right) for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo MTR-1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: Teardown and reassembly of the MTR-1
Teardown and reassembly of the MTR-1
Calibrating Soil Moisture
docs.text:
This guide will take you through calibrating your PLT-1's moisture sensor. The sensors come with a default calibration, so this method is only necessary if you want to make your own adjustments.

1. Take your PLT-1 out of the soil and clean off the probe. It's important to remove all dirt for the most accurate calibration.

2. Make sure the PLT-1 probe is sitting in the air or on a dry, non-conductive surface, and is plugged in.

3. Select Settings and then Devices & Services

4. Select the ESPHome Integration

5. Select your PLT-1 device

6. Scroll down to the diagnostics section and select entity not shown.

7. Select the entity "Soil ADC."

8. Select the gear icon

9. Select Enable

10. Give the sensor a minute for this new entity to populate.

11. Once the Soil ADC value is populated, enter it into the "Dry Voltage" entity.

12. Now, place the stake/probe portion of the PLT-1 into a cup of water. Be careful not to submerge the entire sensor. Only the exposed PCB below the "Apollo" label and the horizontal line can be exposed to water.

13. Grab the "Soil ADC" value again and enter it into the "100% Water Voltage" entity.

14. You can now return your PLT-1 to your plant. Congratulations, your sensor is calibrated!

docs.title: PLT-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What sensors are included in the PLT-1?

  • The PLT-1 comes with sensors to measure soil moisture, air temperature, humidity, LUX, and UV. There is also an optional DS18b20 waterproof soil temperature probe available for measuring soil temperature.

2. How does the capacitive soil moisture sensor work?

  • The capacitive soil moisture sensor measures the water content in the soil by detecting changes in the dielectric permittivity of the soil, which is affected by moisture. It’s more durable than resistive sensors because it doesn’t corrode and is protected with a conformal coating.

3. How is the PLT-1 powered?

  • The PLT-1 operates with USB-C power at 5 volts using 1amp or less (5W).

4. What’s the difference between the battery and non-battery versions?

  • The PLT-1B is battery-operated (18650) and slightly larger, while the non-battery (NB) version is compact and requires USB-C power at 5 volts using 1amp or less (5W). They both have all of the same components for measuring soil moisture, air temp/humidity, lux/uv, etc.

5. How does the optional soil temperature probe work?

  • The optional DS18b20 waterproof soil temperature probe is 20 cm / 7.8 inches long. It measures the temperature directly in the soil and can be used to monitor the conditions for specific plants that require precise temperature control for optimal growth.

6. Is the PLT-1 weatherproof? Can I use it outdoors?

  • The PLT-1 is primarily designed for indoor use. While some components, such as the waterproof soil temperature probe, can withstand harsher environments, the main body of the sensor is not rated for outdoor use unless adequately protected.

7. How does the PLT-1 connect to Homey?

  • The PLT-1 joins your Wi-Fi, and the Apollo Automation app for Homey talks to it directly over your local network through the ESPHome native API, with no cloud account. Once you add it, its readings show up on the device in Homey, ready for flows and Insights. The app runs on Homey Pro; Homey Cloud isn't supported.

Next step: add your PLT-1 to Homey

Connect the sensor to your Wi-Fi through its hotspot, then add it with the Apollo Automation app. The getting started guide walks you through both.

Get started with Homey

8. What kind of flows can I set up with the PLT-1?

  • Any PLT-1 reading can start a flow in Homey. For example, send a notification when soil moisture drops, turn on a grow light when the light level falls, or adjust your heating or cooling based on the air temperature and humidity around your plants.

9. How often does the PLT-1 send sensor data?

  • Most readings update every 60 seconds by default. The intervals are set in the sensor's firmware, and Homey has no setting for them. The light and UV interval is the one you can change without editing the firmware: set LTR390 Update Interval (1 to 300 seconds) on the sensor's own web page. In a browser, open http://apollo-plt-1-xxxxxx.local, where xxxxxx is the last 6 characters of the device's name in Homey. Changing the other intervals means editing the firmware with ESPHome.

10. Can I customize the PLT-1’s functionality?

  • Absolutely! With ESPHome, users can modify firmware, settings, and even print custom cases for the PLT-1. Our YAML is on GitHub and our .STEP and .STL CAD files are available for community use.

11. What are the RGB LED and piezo buzzer used for?

  • The RGB LED is the PLT-1's light in Homey. Turn it on or off, dim it, or change its color from the device or in a flow, for example to glow red when the soil gets dry.
  • The piezo buzzer is played through an ESPHome action, and the Apollo Automation app has no flow card for it, so Homey can't sound the buzzer. If you also run Home Assistant, it can: see the piezo buzzer guide.

12. What is the benefit of using a conformal coating on the soil moisture sensor?

  • The conformal coating protects the sensor from moisture-related degradation, improving its lifespan and durability.

13. What plants are compatible with the PLT-1?

  • The PLT-1 works with all kinds of indoor plants. Look up the light, humidity, and soil moisture your plant likes, then use those values as thresholds in your Homey flows, so you hear about it when a reading drifts out of range.

14. Can I monitor multiple plants with one PLT-1?

  • The PLT-1 is designed to monitor a single plant’s environment. To monitor multiple plants, additional sensors are recommended.

15. What makes the PLT-1 better than other plant sensors?

  • The PLT-1 pairs a durable capacitive soil moisture sensor with real-time reporting of several environmental factors, all in one compact device that works with Homey on your local network.

16. Is the PLT-1 compatible with other smart home platforms?

  • Yes. Besides Homey (through the Apollo Automation app), the PLT-1 works with Home Assistant, and it may work with other platforms through the ESPHome API or MQTT. See Supported platforms.

17. Do I need coding knowledge to use the PLT-1?

  • No. Adding the PLT-1 to Homey and building flows takes no code. YAML knowledge only matters if you want to customize the firmware with ESPHome.

18. Can I access data from the PLT-1 remotely?

  • Yes. The PLT-1 reports to your Homey over your local network, and the Homey app shows its readings wherever you are, as long as your Homey is reachable remotely.

19. Can I use multiple PLT-1 sensors with one Homey?

  • Yes. Add each PLT-1 with the Apollo Automation app. Each one shows up as its own device in Homey, so you can monitor several plants or spaces.

20. Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) – -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.

  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) – -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The PLT-1 is equipped with a capacitive soil moisture sensor, providing enhanced accuracy and durability over resistive alternatives. The sensor’s ground contact portion is coated with a conformal layer, ensuring long-lasting performance and resistance to environmental factors. It also features an AHT20-F air temperature and humidity sensor, which includes dust protection, an LTR390 UV sensor for Lux/UV measurements, an RGB LED, a piezo buzzer, and an optional DS18B20 waterproof soil temperature probe (20 cm / 7.8 inches).

Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The PLT-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your PLT-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: Flower Card
docs.text:
The Flower Card shows a plant's moisture, temperature, light, and humidity as bars on a Home Assistant dashboard.

Before you start

This page is for Home Assistant. The Flower Card is a Home Assistant dashboard card, and it works with the two Home Assistant integrations below: the Plant integration and the Open Plant Book integration.

docs.title: Plant integration
docs.text:
Home Assistant Plant Integration

You set up your plants in the Home Assistant UI, and manage all of their configuration there or with automations and scripts. If you're a registered OpenPlantBook user, the integration can fetch plant data from it automatically. Registration is free.

docs.title: Open Plant Book integration
docs.text:
Open Plant Book Integration

This integration fetches plant information from OpenPlantBook and uploads your plant sensors' data to it. It adds these service calls to Home Assistant for the OpenPlantbook API:

  • Search plant
  • Get plant details
  • Upload plants sensors data

Its sister integration, the Plant integration, is built on it. The Plant integration uses this API to add threshold values, such as moisture, temperature, and conductivity, based on the plant species.

docs.title: Add the Flower Card
docs.text:
Flower Card GitHub

Add the card to your dashboard with this YAML. Replace plant.my_plant and sensor.demo_battery with your own entity IDs.

type: custom:flower-card
entity: plant.my_plant
show_bars:
- illuminance
- humidity
- moisture
- temperature
battery_sensor: sensor.demo_battery

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your PLT-1. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

Automate your plant care

Want soil-moisture alerts and watering reminders? Import the PLT-1 Plant Sensor Alerts blueprint to get low-moisture notifications and automations without building them by hand.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light One RGB Neopixel LED. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Useful for visual plant-health alerts (for example, green when fine, red when soil is too dry). Sensor Default Update Details Soil Moisture 60s Water content of the soil as a percentage, calculated from the soil voltage against the 100% Water Voltage and Dry Voltage calibration values. Ideal range depends on the plant. Soil Temperature 60s Reading from the optional DS18B20 soil temperature probe. Shows Unknown if no probe is connected. Air Temperature 60s Air temperature around the plant from the AHT20 sensor. Adjusted by the Air Temperature Offset. Air Humidity 60s Relative humidity of the air around the plant from the AHT20 sensor. Adjusted by the Air Humidity Offset. LTR390 Light 60s* Ambient light level in lux. *Polls at the LTR390 Update Interval (60s by default). LTR390 UV Index 60s* UV index measured by the LTR390. *Polls at the LTR390 Update Interval. Soil ADC 5s Raw soil voltage from the ADC, used to calculate Soil Moisture. Diagnostic, disabled by default. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. 100% Water Voltage 1.55 Soil voltage that corresponds to fully saturated (wet) soil. Lowers the Soil Moisture scale. Tune this for your plant and probe. Dry Voltage 2.7 Soil voltage that corresponds to completely dry soil. Sets the point where Soil Moisture reads 0%. Air Temperature Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset applied to the Air Temperature reading. Air Humidity Offset 0 % Calibration offset applied to the Air Humidity reading. LTR390 Update Interval 60 s How often the LTR390 light and UV sensors poll (1 to 300 seconds). Sleep Duration 5 min How long the PLT-1 deep-sleeps between readings when Prevent Sleep is off. Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it reports continuously. Turn it off to let the PLT-1 deep-sleep between readings for more accurate onboard AHT20 temperature and humidity. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available. Click Update and it installs the next time the device wakes; the optional OTA helper overrides Prevent Sleep to keep the device awake on demand. Separate from the Apollo Firmware Version and ESPHome Version sensors. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Prevent sleep
docs.text: Your Apollo PLT-1 runs on USB power, but its firmware can still sleep between readings: it wakes up, reports, and goes back to sleep. Sleeping keeps the board from warming itself up, so the air temperature reads closer to the room. The PLT-1 ships with Prevent sleep on, so it stays awake and reports all the time.

docs.title: Sleep isn't available for the PLT-1 in Homey
docs.text:
In Homey, your PLT-1 stays awake. You'll see Prevent sleep and Sleep duration in your PLT-1's Settings in the Homey app, under Battery settings (if battery is present), but the Apollo Automation app only lets you change Prevent sleep on a sensor with a battery. If you uncheck it on the PLT-1, Homey refuses the change and shows Battery settings are not supported on this device.

Staying awake is how Homey expects a USB-powered sensor to work, so there's nothing you need to change here.

Leave Sleep duration as it is

Homey shows Sleep duration in hours, but the PLT-1 reads the number as minutes: the default of 5 means 5 minutes. It only applies while Prevent sleep is off, so you don't need to change it in Homey.

Using Home Assistant too?

Home Assistant can turn sleep on for the PLT-1. See the Home Assistant Prevent Sleep guide. While the PLT-1 sleeps, Homey loses its connection between reports.

docs.title: Correct the air temperature instead
docs.text:
If you wanted sleep to stop the board's own warmth from nudging the air temperature up, an offset fixes the reading without it. You need a reference thermometer you trust.

  1. Put the reference thermometer next to your PLT-1 and give both time to settle.
  2. Compare the PLT-1's air temperature reading in Homey with the reference.
  3. In your PLT-1's Settings, under Calibration offsets, set Air temperature offset to how many degrees Celsius the PLT-1 reads too high, and save. For example, if the PLT-1 shows 23.5 °C and the reference shows 22 °C, enter 1.5.

The PLT-1's air temperature in Homey now matches your reference thermometer. The offset only changes the air reading, not the soil temperature probe.

Homey set to Fahrenheit?

The offset is always in degrees Celsius. Divide the difference you see in °F by 1.8: a reading 2.7 °F too high is an offset of 1.5.

docs.title: If your PLT-1 was set to sleep before
docs.text:
If Prevent sleep was turned off earlier, for example in Home Assistant, the PLT-1 remembers it and keeps sleeping after you add it to Homey, so Homey keeps losing the connection. Homey can't change Prevent sleep on the PLT-1, so turn it back on with the boot button. Putting the PLT-1 in boot mode shows where the button is.

Don't hold the boot button while you plug in

Plugging in with the boot button held puts the PLT-1 in boot mode for flashing firmware instead. Also let go before 10 seconds: holding the boot button that long resets the PLT-1 to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi.

  1. Unplug the PLT-1 and plug it back in to wake it.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

The PLT-1 turns Prevent sleep back on and stays connected to Homey, and Prevent sleep shows as checked in its settings. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the PLT-1 was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so unplug it and plug it back in once more, and it stays awake this time.

Keep the main body dry

The main body of the PLT-1 isn't rated for outdoor use. Don't leave it outside for long periods or let it get wet. If it will sit in damp air or could see rain, put it inside another, protective case.

docs.title: Putting the PLT-1 in boot mode
Putting the PLT-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the PLT-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You can put your device into boot mode with only the boot button and a USB-C cable.

1. Position the PLT-1 as shown in the image below and locate the small opening to press the boot button.

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your PLT-1 then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You can also put your device into boot mode by holding the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and locate the boot button (on the side, shown in the image above) and the reset button (near the USB-C port, shown in the image below).

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your PLT-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (on the side, shown in the image above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (near the USB-C port, shown in the image below).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the PLT-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash PLT-1
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the below guide.

This needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

If your device has already been added to Homey, please remove it from Homey before continuing.

Follow these steps to put your device in boot mode and install the factory firmware.

1. Put your device in boot mode by holding down the boot button and then plugging in the USB cable.

2. Navigate to the Apollo PLT-1 installer and choose USB Power since you are using a PLT-1.

3. Click Connect & Install.

4. Select the open com port then click Connect.

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.PLT-1.

6. Click "INSTALL".

7. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

8. Please proceed to the getting started guide and set up your sensor as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your PLT-1
Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your PLT-1
docs.text:
You can clear the Wi-Fi details saved on your device and connect it to a new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo PLT1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: Calibrating Soil Moisture
docs.text:
This guide will take you through calibrating your PLT-1's moisture sensor. The sensors come with a default calibration, so this method is only necessary if you want to make your own adjustments.

1. Take your PLT-1 out of the soil and clean off the probe. It's important to remove all dirt for the most accurate calibration.

2. Make sure the PLT-1 probe is sitting in the air or on a dry, non-conductive surface, and is plugged in.

3. Select Settings and then Devices & Services

4. Select the ESPHome Integration

5. Select your PLT-1 device

6. Scroll down to the diagnostics section and select entity not shown.

7. Select the entity "Soil ADC."

8. Select the gear icon

9. Select Enable

10. Give the sensor a minute for this new entity to populate.

11. Once the Soil ADC value is populated, enter it into the "Dry Voltage" entity.

12. Now, place the stake/probe portion of the PLT-1 into a cup of water. Be careful not to submerge the entire sensor. Only the exposed PCB below the "Apollo" label and the horizontal line can be exposed to water.

13. Grab the "Soil ADC" value again and enter it into the "100% Water Voltage" entity.

14. You can now return your PLT-1 to your plant. Congratulations, your sensor is calibrated!

docs.title: PLT-1B FAQ
docs.text:
1. What sensors are included in the PLT-1B?

  • The PLT-1B comes with sensors to measure soil moisture, air temperature, humidity, LUX, and UV. There is also an optional DS18b20 waterproof soil temperature probe available for measuring soil temperature.

2. How does the capacitive soil moisture sensor work?

  • The capacitive soil moisture sensor measures the water content in the soil by detecting changes in the dielectric permittivity of the soil, which is affected by moisture. It’s more durable than resistive sensors because it doesn’t corrode and is protected with a conformal coating.

3. How is the PLT-1B powered?

  • The PLT-1B operates with a rechargeable 18650 Flat Top battery (not included), giving it portability for plant monitoring without being tied to an outlet. Example battery to use: https://imrbatteries.com/products/samsung-30q-18650-3000mah-15a-battery.

4. Can you charge the battery by plugging in the device?

  • No, you cannot charge the battery through the USB port. You need an external 18650 charger such as a nitecore 2 or 4 bay.

5. How long does the battery last in the PLT-1B?

  • Battery life depends on sleep/wake intervals. Waking every 8 hours provides around 6 months of battery life, and waking every 12 hours or more can extend it to about a year.

6. How does the optional soil temperature probe work?

  • The optional DS18b20 probe (20 cm / 7.8 inches) measures soil temperature directly, providing critical data for plants that need specific temperature conditions.

7. Is the PLT-1B weatherproof? Can I use it outdoors?

  • The PLT-1B is primarily designed for indoor use, but components like the waterproof soil probe are suited for harsh conditions. The main body is not rated for outdoor use without additional protection.

8. How does the PLT-1B connect to Homey?

  • The PLT-1B joins your Wi-Fi, and the Apollo Automation app for Homey talks to it directly over your local network through the ESPHome native API, with no cloud account. Once you add it, its readings show up on the device in Homey, ready for flows and Insights. The app runs on Homey Pro; Homey Cloud isn't supported.

Next step: add your PLT-1B to Homey

Connect the sensor to your Wi-Fi through its hotspot, then add it with the Apollo Automation app. The getting started guide walks you through both.

Get started with Homey

9. What kind of flows can I set up with the PLT-1B?

  • Any PLT-1B reading can start a flow in Homey. For example, send a notification when soil moisture drops, turn on a grow light when the light level falls, or adjust your heating or cooling based on the air temperature and humidity around your plants.

10. How often does the PLT-1B send sensor data?

  • A new PLT-1B ships with Prevent sleep checked, so it stays awake and reports most readings every 60 seconds. That drains the battery fast. Once you uncheck Prevent sleep, the PLT-1B wakes up, sends all its readings to Homey, and goes back to sleep to save battery. How long it sleeps is the Sleep duration setting, in hours (12 by default). Both settings are under Battery settings (if battery is present) in the device's Settings in the Homey app. A shorter sleep gives fresher readings and a shorter battery life. See Prevent sleep for the details.

Change settings while the PLT-1B is awake

Homey can only send a setting while the sensor is awake and connected. If it's asleep, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. Keep the sensor awake and try again.

11. Can I customize the PLT-1B functionality?

  • Absolutely! With ESPHome, users can modify firmware, settings, and even print custom cases for the PLT-1B. Our YAML is on GitHub and our .STEP and .STL CAD files are available for community use.

12. What are the RGB LED and piezo buzzer used for?

  • The RGB LED is the PLT-1B's light in Homey. Turn it on or off, dim it, or change its color from the device or in a flow, for example to glow red when the soil gets dry. Commands reach the sensor only while it's awake.
  • The piezo buzzer is played through an ESPHome action, and the Apollo Automation app has no flow card for it, so Homey can't sound the buzzer. If you also run Home Assistant, it can: see the piezo buzzer guide.

13. What is the benefit of using a conformal coating on the soil moisture sensor?

  • The conformal coating protects the sensor from moisture-related degradation, improving its lifespan and durability.

14. What plants are compatible with the PLT-1B?

  • The PLT-1B works with all kinds of indoor plants. Look up the light, humidity, and soil moisture your plant likes, then use those values as thresholds in your Homey flows, so you hear about it when a reading drifts out of range.

15. Can I monitor multiple plants with one PLT-1B?

  • The PLT-1B is designed to monitor a single plant’s environment. To monitor multiple plants, additional sensors are recommended.

16. What makes the PLT-1B better than other plant sensors?

  • The PLT-1B pairs a durable capacitive soil moisture sensor with real-time reporting of several environmental factors, all in one compact, battery-powered device that works with Homey on your local network.

17. Is the PLT-1B compatible with other smart home platforms?

  • Yes. Besides Homey (through the Apollo Automation app), the PLT-1B works with Home Assistant, and it may work with other platforms through the ESPHome API or MQTT. See Supported platforms.

18. Do I need coding knowledge to use the PLT-1B?

  • No. Adding the PLT-1B to Homey and building flows takes no code. YAML knowledge only matters if you want to customize the firmware with ESPHome.

19. Can I access data from the PLT-1B remotely?

  • Yes. The PLT-1B reports to your Homey over your local network, and the Homey app shows its latest readings wherever you are, as long as your Homey is reachable remotely.

20. What’s the difference between the battery and non-battery versions?

  • The PLT-1B is battery-operated (18650) and slightly larger, while the non-battery (NB) version is compact and requires USB-C power at 5 volts using 1amp or less (5W). They both have all of the same components for measuring soil moisture, air temp/humidity, lux/uv, etc.

21. Can I use multiple PLT-1B sensors with one Homey?

  • Yes. Add each PLT-1B with the Apollo Automation app. Each one shows up as its own device in Homey, so you can monitor several plants or spaces.

22. Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) – -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) – -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.

docs.title: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text: When looking at the PLT-1B in the below orientation, the reset button is on the left and the boot button is on the right by the USB-C port.

docs.title: LTR390 UV
docs.text: For the most accurate UV and LUX readings, be sure to expose the sensor circled in the image below to light.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The PLT-1B (18650 battery) is equipped with a capacitive soil moisture sensor, providing enhanced accuracy and durability over resistive alternatives. The sensor’s ground contact portion is coated with a conformal layer, ensuring long-lasting performance and resistance to environmental factors. It also features an AHT20-F air temperature and humidity sensor, which includes dust protection, an LTR390 UV sensor for Lux/UV measurements, an RGB LED, a piezo buzzer, and an optional DS18B20 waterproof soil temperature probe (20 cm / 7.8 inches).

Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The PLT-1B should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your PLT-1B if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: How to insert the battery
docs.text:
18650 battery and charger required!

The PLT-1B does NOT include a battery nor a charging circuit. You will need to supply your own flat-top, unprotected 18650 Li-ion cell, and a separate 18650 charger. Recommended cell: Samsung 30Q 18650 3000mAh.

Follow these steps to open the case, insert the battery, and close it again.

1. Gently press your thumb on the case above the stake and the lid should pop off.

2. Hold the case and push the stake down a bit, then gently lift it out of the bottom case section.

3. Flip the PLT-1B over and identify the + and - markings. The + is on the left side and the - is on the right side. Double check before going any further.

4. The top of the battery (the positive end, marked with a + and a small ring around the terminal) goes on the left side, matching the + on the PLT-1B.

5. Hold the PCB. You'll need to use a bit of force to push in the battery. Start with the right - side, then push in the left + side.

6. Flip the sensor back over and lay the PCB inside the case so it sits flat.

7. Line up the notch in the top left of the lid, then gently press down until the lid snaps into place.

You have now installed or reinstalled the battery!

docs.title: Sensor connection check
docs.text:
Not sure whether your battery device is online? Run this quick check. You restart the device and press its boot button, and the RGB light flashes a color that shows whether it's connected to Wi-Fi, to Homey, or to nothing. Select your device below. Each button name links to a page that shows where that button is.

TEMP-1BPLT-1B

1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the device.

2. Then press the boot button and let go.

1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the device.

2. Then press the boot button and let go.

The RGB light on your device then flashes a color that shows its connection status:

  • Blue: connected to Wi-Fi and Homey
  • Green: connected to Wi-Fi only, not to Homey
  • Yellow: no Wi-Fi connection

Read the first flash, not the second

A few seconds later the light flashes a second time, green or red. That second flash is the device's built-in sensor self-test, not its connection status, so read the connection status from the first color.

Keep your sensor awake with Prevent Sleep

To keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time, open the device in Homey, go to its settings, and turn on Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present). Homey can only change this setting while the sensor is awake, so press the reset button first. To learn more, see the Prevent Sleep guide for the TEMP-1, TEMP-1B, or PLT-1B.

docs.title: How To Wake Up Your Sensor
How to wake up your sensor
docs.text:
Once Prevent sleep is off, your Apollo TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 sleeps between reports to make its battery last, and Homey can't reach it while it sleeps. In the Homey app, a sleeping sensor shows as Device disconnected, and if you try to change a setting, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. The sensor wakes on its own after each Sleep duration and reconnects to Homey. Wake it yourself when you want fresh readings right away, or need it awake to change a setting, update the firmware, or troubleshoot.

Using a USB-powered TEMP-1?

Your TEMP-1 normally stays awake in Homey, so there's nothing to wake. If it keeps losing its connection to Homey, it may have been set to sleep earlier, for example in Home Assistant. Turn Prevent sleep back on with its boot button.

docs.title: Wake your sensor
docs.text:
Pressing the reset button restarts your sensor, so it wakes up right away, connects to your Wi-Fi, and reports to Homey. On a BTN-1, any of its four buttons wakes it too. The boot button can't wake a sleeping sensor. Once the sensor is awake, the boot button is what keeps it awake. Select your device below to find both buttons.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1

The buttons are on the board inside the case. To reach the reset button, gently pry the lid off at the small slit near the top of the case. You can press the boot button with the lid off too, or with a paperclip through the small opening on the right side of the case when the USB-C port faces you. Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode has more photos.

To wake the TEMP-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

This is the boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake.

You can press both buttons with a pin through small openings in the case. Putting the PLT-1B in boot mode shows where the openings are.

To wake the PLT-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

The boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake, sits next to the USB-C port.

To wake the BTN-1, press and release the reset button, on the left in the photo below. The boot button, which you'll use to keep the BTN-1 awake, is on the right.

Pressing Button 1, 2, 3, or 4 also wakes the BTN-1. Homey receives that press as a Click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any flow you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

Your sensor is now awake. Homey reconnects to it on its own, and the Homey app no longer shows it as Device disconnected. It doesn't stay awake for long, though. Unless Prevent sleep is on, it sends fresh readings and goes back to sleep about 20 seconds after Homey connects (about 10 seconds for the BTN-1), or after about 90 seconds if Homey doesn't connect at all. Not sure your TEMP-1B or PLT-1B woke up? The sensor connection check tells you in a few seconds.

docs.title: Keep your sensor awake
docs.text: A wake-up doesn't last long enough to change settings or troubleshoot comfortably. Turn on Prevent sleep and your sensor stays awake until you turn it off again. You can turn it on from the sensor itself or from the Homey app, where it sits in your sensor's Settings under Battery settings (if battery is present).

docs.title: With the buttons on the sensor
docs.text:
The buttons work even when Homey can't reach the sensor, which makes this the most reliable way. It's also the better choice for the BTN-1, which stays awake for only about 10 seconds after Homey connects. Press the two buttons one after the other, never together: holding the boot button while you press reset puts the sensor in boot mode for flashing firmware instead.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets your sensor to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the sensor.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

Your sensor turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked once the sensor is connected. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the sensor was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

docs.title: From the Homey app
docs.text:
The sensor stays awake for only about 20 seconds after Homey connects, or about 10 seconds for the BTN-1, so have the Homey app open and ready before you start.

  1. Wake the sensor with the reset button.
  2. In the Homey app, open your sensor and wait until it no longer shows Device disconnected.
  3. Right away, open its Settings, check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save.
  4. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, press the reset button once more.

Your sensor now stays awake until you uncheck Prevent sleep again. If the sensor was already on its way back to sleep at step 3, it still keeps the change and starts up with Prevent sleep on after the reset in step 4. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. instead, the change didn't reach the sensor: start again from step 1, or use the buttons.

The Prevent sleep guide for the TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 covers both settings in detail, including Sleep duration. On a BTN-1, Prevent sleep also decides which presses reach Homey.

Next step: let your sensor sleep again

Staying awake drains the battery far faster. Once you're done, turn Prevent sleep off and choose how long the sensor sleeps between reports.

TEMP-1B: Prevent sleep PLT-1B: Prevent sleep BTN-1: Prevent sleep

docs.title: Flower Card
docs.text:
The Flower Card shows a plant's moisture, temperature, light, and humidity as bars on a Home Assistant dashboard.

Before you start

This page is for Home Assistant. The Flower Card is a Home Assistant dashboard card, and it works with the two Home Assistant integrations below: the Plant integration and the Open Plant Book integration.

docs.title: Plant integration
docs.text:
Home Assistant Plant Integration

You set up your plants in the Home Assistant UI, and manage all of their configuration there or with automations and scripts. If you're a registered OpenPlantBook user, the integration can fetch plant data from it automatically. Registration is free.

docs.title: Open Plant Book integration
docs.text:
Open Plant Book Integration

This integration fetches plant information from OpenPlantBook and uploads your plant sensors' data to it. It adds these service calls to Home Assistant for the OpenPlantbook API:

  • Search plant
  • Get plant details
  • Upload plants sensors data

Its sister integration, the Plant integration, is built on it. The Plant integration uses this API to add threshold values, such as moisture, temperature, and conductivity, based on the plant species.

docs.title: Add the Flower Card
docs.text:
Flower Card GitHub

Add the card to your dashboard with this YAML. Replace plant.my_plant and sensor.demo_battery with your own entity IDs.

type: custom:flower-card
entity: plant.my_plant
show_bars:
- illuminance
- humidity
- moisture
- temperature
battery_sensor: sensor.demo_battery

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This will walk you through the process of connecting your new Apollo Automation sensor to Homey. If at any point you get stuck, join our Discord for some help.

docs.title: Connecting through hotspot:
docs.text:
To get your new Apollo sensor connected to your Wi-Fi, follow the steps below!

1. Plug the sensor into a quality power brick. They require 5v and under an amp so most phone chargers will be fine. ESP devices are sensitive to power fluctuations and users have had some issues with really cheap power bricks. If your device is restarting or unavailable please try a different power brick.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to "Apollo MSR2 Hotspot", it might take a minute for the Wi-Fi network to show up.

3. Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your sensor.

If this does not automatically open the dashboard, please open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

4. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your sensor to connect to or scroll to the bottom and type in your Wi-Fi network then click "Save".

Tip for Mesh Wi-Fi systems or multiple Access Points

If you have multiple access points or a mesh system please manually type in your Wi-Fi network so it will join with the strongest signal!

5. Once connected, the sensor's dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your sensor to your Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Adding Apollo Automation app in Homey:
docs.text:
You'll install the Apollo Automation app on your Homey from a desktop PC or a browser.

1. Navigate to this website and click "Install App". For now this needs to be done from a desktop PC or a browser.

2. Select the Homey device you want to install it on and then click "Install App" again!

3. Your device will install the Apollo Automation Homey App then move to the next section.

docs.title: Connecting to Homey:
docs.text:
Next, you'll add your Apollo sensor to Homey from the Homey app on your phone.

1. Open the Homey App on your phone and navigate to the Devices tab at the bottom then select the (+) icon in the top right and choose "New Device". Choose "Allow" if it pops up asking to find Bluetooth devices, or you can change this later in settings.

2. Select Apollo Automation under Brands in the bottom left then choose "Every Apollo Sensor". When prompted, click "Connect".

3. Your Apollo devices will automatically show up and if not, please first connect it to your Wi-Fi following the steps outlined here.

4. Select the device you want to add, in this case an Apollo MTR-1 and click Continue at the bottom.

5. Click Continue Setup and choose a Zone to place your device in. If you are new to Homey you can choose Home and move it to another Zone later after you create more zones!

6. Change any other default settings like the Name, icon, etc or click Finish in the bottom right.

7. You are done! Your sensor is now ready to create flows and add as a favorite to your dashboard!

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your PLT-1B. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How the PLT-1B sleeps

The PLT-1B runs on an 18650 battery. By default Prevent Sleep is on, so it stays awake and reports continuously at these intervals, which drains the battery. Turn Prevent Sleep off to let it deep-sleep between readings for the Sleep Duration (12h) and conserve the cell: it wakes for about 90 seconds, reports its readings, then sleeps again. The Default Update column is how often each sensor refreshes while it is awake.

To update firmware on a sleeping device, click Update on the Firmware Update entity and it installs the next time the device wakes (the firmware keeps itself awake until the update finishes, so you don't need to do anything else). The optional OTA helper is a separate toggle that overrides Prevent Sleep to keep a device awake on demand.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light One RGB Neopixel LED. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Useful for visual alerts tied to plant health, such as green when readings are fine and red when moisture is low. Accessory Power Controls power delivery to the sensors. On sends power to the whole device. Off powers only the ESP chip, and while off you cannot turn on the RGB Light. Sensor Default Update Details Air Temperature 60s Air temperature around the plant, from the AHT20. Adjusted by the Air Temperature Offset. Air Humidity 60s Relative humidity of the air around the plant, from the AHT20. Adjusted by the Air Humidity Offset. Soil Moisture 60s Water content of the soil as a percentage, calculated from the soil probe voltage using the 100% Water Voltage and Dry Voltage calibration values. Soil Temperature 60s Reading from the optional DS18B20 soil temperature probe. Shows Unknown if the probe is not connected. LTR390 Light 60s* Ambient light level in lux. *Polls at the interval set by the LTR390 Update Interval number (60s by default). LTR390 UV Index 60s* UV index measured by the LTR390. *Polls at the LTR390 Update Interval. Battery level on wake Remaining 18650 battery charge as a percentage, from the MAX17048 fuel gauge. Battery voltage on wake Current 18650 battery voltage, from the MAX17048 fuel gauge. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Air Temperature Offset 0.0 °C Calibrates the AHT20 air temperature reading to a known value. Range is -70 to 70 °C in 0.1 steps. Air Humidity Offset 0 % Calibrates the AHT20 air humidity reading to a known value. Range is -70 to 70 % in 0.1 steps. 100% Water Voltage 1.55 Soil probe voltage that corresponds to fully saturated (100% wet) soil. Tune this to calibrate the Soil Moisture reading. Range is 0 to 5 V in 0.01 steps. Dry Voltage 2.7 Soil probe voltage that corresponds to completely dry soil. Tune this to calibrate the Soil Moisture reading and to trigger low-moisture automations. Range is 0 to 5 V in 0.01 steps. LTR390 Update Interval 60 s How often the LTR390 light and UV sensors poll (1 to 300 seconds). Sleep Duration 12 h How long the PLT-1B stays in deep sleep between wake cycles (only used when Prevent Sleep is off). Range is 0 to 800 hours. Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it reports continuously. Required for OTA updates and live readings; turn it off to save battery. Accessory Power On Powers the sensors. Turn off to power only the ESP chip. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot. Soil ADC 5s Raw soil probe voltage used to calculate Soil Moisture. Disabled by default.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Prevent sleep
docs.text:
Your Apollo PLT-1B can sleep between readings: it wakes up, reports to Homey, and goes back to sleep until the next report. Sleeping is what makes the battery last. It also keeps the board from warming itself up, so the air temperature readings need less offset.

The PLT-1B ships with Prevent sleep turned on, so it stays awake and reports all the time. That's handy while you set it up, but it drains the battery far faster. Once the sensor is in its pot, turn Prevent sleep off and let it sleep.

Before you start

  • Add your PLT-1B to Homey. See Getting started.
  • Homey can only change these settings while the sensor is awake and connected. If it's asleep, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. In that case, keep it awake first.

docs.title: The sleep settings in Homey
docs.text:
Both settings sit in your PLT-1B's Settings in the Homey app, under Battery settings (if battery is present). They're device settings only, so there's no flow card that turns sleep on or off.

Setting What it does Prevent sleep Checked, the sensor stays awake. Unchecked, it sleeps between reports. A new PLT-1B has it checked. Sleep duration How many hours the sensor sleeps between reports, from 0 to 800, with up to two decimals: 0.5 is 30 minutes. The default is 12.

docs.title: Let your PLT-1B sleep
docs.text:
Set how long the sensor sleeps first, then let it go to sleep. Make the two changes one at a time: the sensor falls asleep the moment Prevent sleep turns off, so a change sent along with it may never arrive.

Read this before you uncheck Prevent sleep

The PLT-1B goes to sleep as soon as Prevent sleep is off, and Homey can't reach it again until it wakes up. Put the sensor where you want it and finish any other settings, such as soil calibration, first.

  1. In the Homey app, open your PLT-1B's Settings.
  2. Under Battery settings (if battery is present), set Sleep duration to the hours you want between reports, and save the change. Leave it at 12 unless you need fresher readings.
  3. Uncheck Prevent sleep and save.

Your PLT-1B is now asleep. It wakes up after each Sleep duration, connects to Homey, sends fresh readings, and goes back to sleep about 20 seconds after it connects.

Device disconnected is normal between reports

While the PLT-1B sleeps, Homey shows it as Device disconnected. That's expected: Homey reconnects on its own each time the sensor wakes up.

docs.title: Keep your PLT-1B awake again
docs.text: To change a setting, calibrate the soil readings, update the firmware, or troubleshoot, the sensor has to stay awake. Turn Prevent sleep back on from the sensor itself or from the Homey app.

docs.title: With the buttons on the sensor
docs.text:
The buttons work even when Homey can't reach the sensor, which makes this the most reliable way. The sensor connection check has photos of the reset and boot buttons.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets the PLT-1B to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again. A short press of under 3 seconds runs the connection check instead.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the sensor. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

The sensor turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked again once the sensor is connected. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the sensor was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

docs.title: From the Homey app
docs.text:
The sensor stays awake for only about 20 seconds after Homey connects, so have the Homey app open and ready before you start.

  1. Wake the sensor with the reset button, or take the battery out and put it back in.
  2. In the Homey app, open your PLT-1B and wait until it no longer shows Device disconnected.
  3. Right away, open its Settings, check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save.
  4. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, press the reset button once more.

Your PLT-1B now stays awake until you uncheck Prevent sleep again. If the sensor was already on its way back to sleep at step 3, it still keeps the change and starts up with Prevent sleep on after the reset in step 4. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. instead, the change didn't reach the sensor: start again from step 1, or use the buttons.

Keep the main body dry

The main body of the PLT-1B isn't rated for outdoor use. Don't leave it outside for long periods or let it get wet. If it will sit in damp air or could see rain, put it inside another, protective case.

Next step: check your sensor's connection

Not sure whether your PLT-1B woke up and reached Homey? The light on the sensor tells you in a few seconds.

Run the sensor connection check

docs.title: Putting the PLT-1B in boot mode
Putting the PLT-1B in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the PLT-1B into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You can put your device into boot mode with only the boot button and a pin.

1. Position the PLT-1B as shown in the image below and locate the small opening to press the boot button.

2. Use a pin to press and hold the boot button, while holding the boot button plug the PLT-1B back into your computer/power and then release the boot button

3. Continue with uploading the firmware

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You can also put your device into boot mode by holding the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Plug in the device

2. Put your PLT-1B in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (next to the USB-C port, shown in the images above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (labeled RST, shown in the images below).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the PLT-1B. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware

docs.title: Re-flash the PLT-1B factory firmware
docs.text:
If your PLT-1B becomes unresponsive and you've tried the other troubleshooting steps, re-flash its factory firmware. The Apollo web installer does this from your browser while the PLT-1B is plugged into your computer by USB.

Before you start

  • Use Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium-based browser.
  • If your PLT-1B has already been added to Homey, remove it from Homey before you continue.

Remove the battery

The re-flash doesn't work properly while the battery is still supplying power to the PLT-1B. If you run into issues during these steps, remove the battery.

Follow these steps to put your PLT-1B in boot mode and install the factory firmware.

1. Put your PLT-1B in boot mode: hold down the boot button, then plug in the USB cable.

2. Open the Apollo PLT-1 installer. The PLT-1B uses the same page as the PLT-1.

3. Choose Battery Power, then click Connect & Install.

4. Select the open COM port, then click Connect.

No device in the list?

If no device shows up, click Cancel and install the recommended driver from the pop-up.

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.PLT-1B.

6. Click INSTALL.

7. When you see Installation complete!, the install is finished. Click Next, then close the browser window.

Power cycle your PLT-1B before anything else

Your PLT-1B is still in boot mode. Power cycle it (remove its power, then power it again) so it starts in normal mode.

8. Follow the getting started guide to set up your PLT-1B as a new device.

Once you finish the getting started guide, your PLT-1B is running its factory firmware again and set up as a new device.

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your PLT-1B
Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your PLT-1B
docs.text:
You can clear the Wi-Fi details saved on your device and connect it to a new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo PLT1B Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
1. What type of fluid level sensor does the PUMP-1 use?

  • The fluid input and fluid output sensors are non-contact capacitive sensors. They detect water through the wall of the container rather than by touching it, so they mount flat against the outside of your bottle or reservoir. They are rated to read through up to 5mm of plastic and often manage more.

2. Can I submerge the fluid level sensors?

  • No. The sensors are not sealed against water and are meant for external placement only. Submerging one can damage both the sensor and the PUMP-1 it is plugged into. Mount the sensor on the outside of the container at the height you want to detect.

3. What is the maximum distance this pump can push water?

  • The PUMP-1 has been successfully tested with 33 feet of tubing and a vertical lift of 14 feet, while still maintaining strong head pressure. This demonstrates its capability to move water efficiently over long distances and significant elevation gains.

4. What is the pump model used for the PUMP-1?

  • The pump model is a DSB413-A.

5. What is the flow rate of the PUMP-1?

  • 900mL a minute in our testing!

6. What is the Inner Diameter (ID) and Outer Diameter (OD) of the tubing?

  • The Inner Diameter is 7mm (7/25) and the Outer Diameter is 10mm.

7. What voltage does the Apollo PUMP-1 operate on?

  • The PUMP-1 runs on 5V DC power, compatible with most standard USB power sources.

8. Is the PUMP-1 safe to use with drinking water or pet bowls?

  • Yes, the PUMP-1 is made with food-safe materials suitable for potable water. This requires you to regularly clean the device to make sure no bacteria is present.

9. Can I use the PUMP-1 to automate watering for plants?

  • Absolutely! It’s designed to work with our PLT-1 plant sensor for automated watering.

10. Can the pump detect when to stop watering automatically?

  • Yes, the PUMP-1 has two ports for non-contact fluid sensors that detect water presence to stop the pump when watering is complete or if your water source is empty.

11. What other uses does the PUMP-1 support?

  • Besides plant watering, it’s great for filling fish tanks, robot vacuum mop tanks, pet bowls, coffee pots, liquid transfer projects, and can also be used as a drain pump.

12. How large is the PUMP-1?

  • The pump measures 3.4in x 1.3in x 1.8in (86.4mm x 33mm x 45.7mm), making it compact.

13. How do I control the pump?

  • The PUMP-1 can be controlled manually using the button or integrated into smart home systems for automated operation based on sensor input or schedules.

14. Is the PUMP-1 durable?

  • Yes, it is designed for long-term use with proper maintenance and includes safety features like max run-time limits.

15. Can I extend the fluid input sensor and fluid output sensor?

  • Yes, you can use a JST PH 2.0 3 pin connector such as these off Amazon.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Apollo PUMP-1 is a versatile, compact, and food-safe fluid pump designed to integrate with our PLT-1 plant sensor to automate your watering needs. It features two ports for non-contact fluid sensors that detect water through the wall of your bottle or reservoir, allowing the pump to automatically stop when watering is complete or if your water bottle runs empty, protecting your system from damage.

Perfect for smart home gardeners, the PUMP-1 takes the hassle out of plant care by delivering precise, controlled watering automatically.

Beyond plants, the PUMP-1 is ideal for a variety of other uses such as filling fish tanks, robot vacuum mop tanks, pet bowls, coffee pots, and more. Its reliable performance, food-safe materials, and smart home integration make it a perfect addition to any home automation setup.

Experience effortless and safe fluid control with the Apollo PUMP-1. Smart, simple, and adaptable.

docs.title: Attaching the bottle to the PUMP-1
docs.text:
You'll fit the input fluid level sensor into the base, then slide the water bottle into it.

1. Begin by placing the small white connector through the hole in the base of the water bottle and gently press the input fluid level sensor into place.

Make sure to orient your fluid level sensor correctly as shown in the gif below

The fluid sensor needs to be placed with the flat side with no writing facing outwards and the side with the ears flush with the back towards the plastic enclosure.

2. (Optional) Gently press the cable into the built-in cable slots located on the underside of the 3D-printed base. This helps keep the wiring neat and secure.

3. Slide the bottle into the base until it is securely seated.

Click here to learn how to attach the inlet and outlet tubes!

docs.title: Attaching fluid level sensors to the PUMP-1
Installing fluid input sensor
docs.text:
1. Begin by placing the small white connector through the hole in the base of the water bottle and gently press the input fluid level sensor into place.

Make sure to orient your fluid level sensor correctly as shown in the gif below

The fluid sensor needs to be placed with the flat side with no writing facing outwards and the side with the ears flush with the back towards the plastic enclosure.

docs.title: Connecting fluid input sensor
docs.text: 1. Insert the small white connector into the right-side port on your PUMP-1 device. Ensure it is fully seated for proper operation. The small bump on top of the white connector must be facing upwards when inserting it. This ensures proper alignment and a secure connection.

docs.title: Connecting fluid output sensor
docs.text:
1. Insert the small white connector into the left-side port on your PUMP-1 device. Ensure it is fully seated for proper operation. The small bump on top of the white connector must be facing upwards when inserting it. This ensures proper alignment and a secure connection.

Do not submerge the fluid sensors.

They are intended for external placement only.

2. Attach the fluid output sensor to the outside of the water reservoir of your choice. Common examples include Keurig water tanks, fish tanks, or similar containers. This sensor detects whether the water level is above or below a specific threshold, providing a reliable indication of fluid presence at that height. You can secure the sensor using double-sided tape, a Command™ strip, or even a small dab of hot glue, whichever method works best for your setup. Ensure the sensor remains firmly in place and maintains good contact with the surface.

docs.title: Attaching inlet and outlet tubes to the PUMP-1
docs.text:
1. Attach the two tubes to the pump as shown below. The fluid input tube is the left tube on the same side as the USB-C port and the fluid output tube is the tube on the right on the side of the PUMP-1.

Click here to learn how to attach the Fluid Sensor addons!

docs.title: Fluid sensor
docs.text:
The fluid level sensor is a non-contact capacitive sensor. It detects water through the wall of the container, so it should be securely taped or mounted flat against the outside surface of your chosen water reservoir. The sensor is rated to read through up to 5mm of plastic and often manages more.

Do not submerge the fluid level sensor or place it inside your reservoir. It is not sealed against water, and submerging one can damage both the sensor and the PUMP-1 it is plugged into.

docs.title: Pump control
docs.text: There is a disabled entity by default called Pump Control which will turn the pump on or off and run it instead of using the Run Pump entity. The Pump Control entity will ignore the Pump Run Seconds however this entity is still affected by the Max Safe Run Time. For example, if Max Safe Run Time is set to 120 seconds, then when you turn on the Pump Control entity, it will run for 120 seconds and then turn off unless you manually turn it off sooner.

docs.title: Siphon concerns
docs.text:
If you plan to use the PUMP-1 with the output reservoir positioned lower than the input reservoir, please note that a siphon-like effect can occur. In this setup, small amounts of water may continue to drip even when the pump is turned off.

Depending on your application, this may not be a concern. If it is, there are many helpful resources online that explain ways to reduce or prevent this effect.

To clarify, this is not the pump actively siphoning from the source reservoir. It is water remaining in the outlet tubing flowing downward due to gravity when the discharge end is lower than the source.

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your PUMP-1. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The Default Update column is how often each entity refreshes. The Fluid Input and Fluid Output sensors are event-driven, so they report the moment water rises above or falls below the sensor rather than on a fixed interval.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light One RGB Neopixel LED. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Pump Run Seconds Amount of time in seconds to run the pump when you press Run Pump. Range is 1 to 120 seconds. Defaults to 10s. Run Pump Runs the PUMP-1 pump for the number of seconds set in Pump Run Seconds. Run Pump Until Output Wet Runs the pump until the Fluid Output sensor changes to Wet. Disabled by default. Sensor Default Update Details Fluid Input on change Non-contact capacitive sensor that seats into the base of the PUMP-1 water bottle and reads the fluid through the bottle wall. Reports Wet while water is present and Dry once the bottle is empty. Fluid Output on change Non-contact capacitive sensor you can mount on the exterior of any container to detect water on the other side, such as a Keurig reservoir or fish tank. Reports Wet when the water level is above the sensor and Dry when it falls below. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Max Safe Run Time 60 s Maximum time the pump will run before shutting off. Range is 5 to 600 seconds. Pump Control — Toggles the pump on and off via a switch. Still stopped by Max Safe Run Time. Disabled by default. Stop Pump When Input Dry Off Turns the pump off when the sensor in the base of the water bottle detects no water. This check is automatically skipped when Invert Water Logic is enabled. Stop Pump When Output Wet Off Turns the pump off when the Fluid Output sensor (mounted on a Keurig tank, fish tank, or similar container) detects that the water level has risen above its monitoring point. Invert Water Logic Off Flips the meaning of the Fluid Input sensor so that Dry = destination is low (start pumping) and Wet = destination is full (stop pumping). Use this when the Input sensor is placed at the low-water mark inside a destination tank (for example, a CPAP reservoir) rather than at the bottom of a supply bottle. Disabled by default. Auto Refill Off When enabled together with Invert Water Logic, the pump automatically starts a fill cycle whenever the Fluid Input sensor reads Dry. The pump stops when the Fluid Output sensor reads Wet or when Max Safe Run Time is reached, whichever comes first. Requires Invert Water Logic. Disabled by default. Pump Safety Override Off Disables the safety features. Disabled by default. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Disabled by default. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.
