docs.title: Sensor connection check
docs.text:
Not sure whether your battery device is online? Run this quick check. You restart the device and press its boot button, and the RGB light flashes a color that shows whether it's connected to Wi-Fi, to Homey, or to nothing. Select your device below. Each button name links to a page that shows where that button is.

TEMP-1BPLT-1B

1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the device.

2. Then press the boot button and let go.

1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the device.

2. Then press the boot button and let go.

The RGB light on your device then flashes a color that shows its connection status:

  • Blue: connected to Wi-Fi and Homey
  • Green: connected to Wi-Fi only, not to Homey
  • Yellow: no Wi-Fi connection

Read the first flash, not the second

A few seconds later the light flashes a second time, green or red. That second flash is the device's built-in sensor self-test, not its connection status, so read the connection status from the first color.

Keep your sensor awake with Prevent Sleep

To keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time, open the device in Homey, go to its settings, and turn on Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present). Homey can only change this setting while the sensor is awake, so press the reset button first. To learn more, see the Prevent Sleep guide for the TEMP-1, TEMP-1B, or PLT-1B.

docs.title: How To Wake Up Your Sensor
How to wake up your sensor
docs.text:
Once Prevent sleep is off, your Apollo TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 sleeps between reports to make its battery last, and Homey can't reach it while it sleeps. In the Homey app, a sleeping sensor shows as Device disconnected, and if you try to change a setting, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. The sensor wakes on its own after each Sleep duration and reconnects to Homey. Wake it yourself when you want fresh readings right away, or need it awake to change a setting, update the firmware, or troubleshoot.

Using a USB-powered TEMP-1?

Your TEMP-1 normally stays awake in Homey, so there's nothing to wake. If it keeps losing its connection to Homey, it may have been set to sleep earlier, for example in Home Assistant. Turn Prevent sleep back on with its boot button.

docs.title: Wake your sensor
docs.text:
Pressing the reset button restarts your sensor, so it wakes up right away, connects to your Wi-Fi, and reports to Homey. On a BTN-1, any of its four buttons wakes it too. The boot button can't wake a sleeping sensor. Once the sensor is awake, the boot button is what keeps it awake. Select your device below to find both buttons.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1

The buttons are on the board inside the case. To reach the reset button, gently pry the lid off at the small slit near the top of the case. You can press the boot button with the lid off too, or with a paperclip through the small opening on the right side of the case when the USB-C port faces you. Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode has more photos.

To wake the TEMP-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

This is the boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake.

You can press both buttons with a pin through small openings in the case. Putting the PLT-1B in boot mode shows where the openings are.

To wake the PLT-1B, press and release the reset button. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.

The boot button, which you'll use to keep the sensor awake, sits next to the USB-C port.

To wake the BTN-1, press and release the reset button, on the left in the photo below. The boot button, which you'll use to keep the BTN-1 awake, is on the right.

Pressing Button 1, 2, 3, or 4 also wakes the BTN-1. Homey receives that press as a Click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any flow you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

Your sensor is now awake. Homey reconnects to it on its own, and the Homey app no longer shows it as Device disconnected. It doesn't stay awake for long, though. Unless Prevent sleep is on, it sends fresh readings and goes back to sleep about 20 seconds after Homey connects (about 10 seconds for the BTN-1), or after about 90 seconds if Homey doesn't connect at all. Not sure your TEMP-1B or PLT-1B woke up? The sensor connection check tells you in a few seconds.

docs.title: Keep your sensor awake
docs.text: A wake-up doesn't last long enough to change settings or troubleshoot comfortably. Turn on Prevent sleep and your sensor stays awake until you turn it off again. You can turn it on from the sensor itself or from the Homey app, where it sits in your sensor's Settings under Battery settings (if battery is present).

docs.title: With the buttons on the sensor
docs.text:
The buttons work even when Homey can't reach the sensor, which makes this the most reliable way. It's also the better choice for the BTN-1, which stays awake for only about 10 seconds after Homey connects. Press the two buttons one after the other, never together: holding the boot button while you press reset puts the sensor in boot mode for flashing firmware instead.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets your sensor to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the sensor.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

Your sensor turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked once the sensor is connected. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the sensor was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

docs.title: From the Homey app
docs.text:
The sensor stays awake for only about 20 seconds after Homey connects, or about 10 seconds for the BTN-1, so have the Homey app open and ready before you start.

  1. Wake the sensor with the reset button.
  2. In the Homey app, open your sensor and wait until it no longer shows Device disconnected.
  3. Right away, open its Settings, check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save.
  4. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, press the reset button once more.

Your sensor now stays awake until you uncheck Prevent sleep again. If the sensor was already on its way back to sleep at step 3, it still keeps the change and starts up with Prevent sleep on after the reset in step 4. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. instead, the change didn't reach the sensor: start again from step 1, or use the buttons.

The Prevent sleep guide for the TEMP-1B, PLT-1B, or BTN-1 covers both settings in detail, including Sleep duration. On a BTN-1, Prevent sleep also decides which presses reach Homey.

Next step: let your sensor sleep again

Staying awake drains the battery far faster. Once you're done, turn Prevent sleep off and choose how long the sensor sleeps between reports.

TEMP-1B: Prevent sleep PLT-1B: Prevent sleep BTN-1: Prevent sleep

docs.title: TEMP-1B alert outside a temperature range
TEMP-1B alert outside a temperature range
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

Your Apollo TEMP-1B sends its temperature probe reading to Homey whenever it's awake, and every new reading can start a flow. In this guide you build two flows in the Homey mobile app that keep watch on a freezer: the first sends a push notification when the probe gets too warm, the second when it gets too cold.

Before you start

  • Add your TEMP-1B to Homey with the Apollo Automation app. See Getting started.
  • Plug the temperature probe into the TEMP-1B. Open your TEMP-1B's Settings and, under Probes and offsets for TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B, set Select probe to Temperature. With Food selected, the temperature probe sends no readings.
  • Install the Homey mobile app on every phone that should get the alert.
  • Decide how quickly you need to hear about a problem. A sleeping TEMP-1B only reports when it wakes; How often your TEMP-1B reports explains the trade-off with battery life.

docs.title: How often your TEMP-1B reports
docs.text:
Your flows can only react to readings the TEMP-1B sends, and it only sends them while it's awake.

  • With Prevent sleep on, the TEMP-1B stays connected and reports the probe about once a minute. This drains the battery fastest.
  • With Prevent sleep off, it sleeps between readings and reports once each time it wakes, every 12 hours unless you change Sleep duration. An alert can arrive that long after the problem started.

For a freezer, set Sleep duration (in hours) to the longest delay you're comfortable with, for example 1 for a reading every hour. Shorter sleeps use more battery. Both settings are under Battery settings (if battery is present) in your TEMP-1B's Settings, and Prevent sleep walks you through changing them.

Change settings while the TEMP-1B is awake

Homey can only change the TEMP-1B's settings while it's awake. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up., wake the sensor and try again. See How to wake up your sensor.

docs.title: Pick your range
docs.text:
Find out what your freezer normally swings between before you set any limits. That way the alert only fires when something is actually wrong.

  1. Place the probe in the freezer and run its flat cable out through the door seal. Keep the TEMP-1B itself outside the freezer, somewhere cool and dry: only the probe and its cable can handle the cold.
  2. Leave it for a few hours so the reading settles. Most freezers should sit at or below -18 °C (0 °F).
  3. In Homey Insights, look at your TEMP-1B's Temperature Probe history. Note the highest and lowest readings.
  4. Pick a maximum a little above the highest reading and a minimum a little below the lowest. This guide uses -10 °C and -30 °C; yours will likely differ.

You now have a range that covers normal use and flags a real problem.

Enter your limits in degrees Celsius

The Temperature Probe reading, and the Temperature token the flows below compare, are always in °C. If you think in Fahrenheit, convert first: -10 °C is 14 °F, and -30 °C is -22 °F.

docs.title: Flow 1: Too warm
docs.text:
This flow runs each time the probe reading changes, checks it against your maximum, and sends the alert when the freezer is too warm.

  1. In the Homey mobile app, tap Flow in the bottom bar, then tap + at the top right (or Create a Flow if you have none yet).
  2. Under When..., tap Add Card. Open Apollo Automation under Apps, and choose your TEMP-1B.
  3. Choose the card Temperature probe changed. It hands the new reading to the rest of the flow as the Temperature token.
  4. Under And..., tap Add Card and add Homey's built-in condition for comparing numbers. Set it to check that the Temperature token is greater than -10.
  5. Under Then..., tap Add Card and choose Send Message to User from Push Notifications.
  6. Type a message, for example Check the freezer! The TEMP-1B probe reads, and add the Temperature token after it.
  7. Tap User and pick who gets the alert, such as Everyone, then tap the check mark at the top right.
  8. Tap Next. Name the flow, for example Freezer too warm, and tap Save Flow.

The flow now shows in My Flows. The next probe reading above -10 °C sends the alert to your phone.

docs.title: Flow 2: Too cold
docs.text:
The second flow mirrors the first. Build it the same way, with these changes:

  1. In the And... condition, check that the Temperature token is less than -30.
  2. Change the message, for example to The freezer is colder than usual. The TEMP-1B probe reads, followed by the Temperature token.
  3. Name the flow Freezer too cold and tap Save Flow.

Both ends of your range are now covered: you hear about it whether the freezer warms up or runs too cold.

Expect a reminder with each new reading

Temperature probe changed runs every time the reading changes, not only when it crosses your limit. While the probe stays out of range, every change sends another notification (up to once a minute while the TEMP-1B is awake, or once per wake-up while it sleeps) until the temperature is back inside your range. To pause the reminders while you deal with the freezer, switch the flow off in My Flows, and switch it back on afterwards.

docs.title: Test your flows
docs.text:
To check the alert without warming up your freezer, tap the play button next to a flow in My Flows. It runs its Then cards once, and a green check mark confirms it ran. Your phone gets the notification.

If a flow doesn't run when the freezer is out of range:

  • Check that Select probe is set to Temperature and that the Temperature Probe reading updates each time the TEMP-1B wakes.
  • Check that your limits are in °C.
  • Check that both flows are switched on in My Flows.

docs.title: Optional: sound the TEMP-1B's buzzer too
docs.text:
The TEMP-1B can also raise the alarm on its own. When you turn this on, the sensor checks every probe reading against a minimum and maximum you store on the device and sounds a short siren from its buzzer when the reading is outside them. It works alongside your flows, so anyone near the freezer hears it even if their phone is on silent. Like your flows, it only checks readings the TEMP-1B takes while it's awake.

  1. Open your TEMP-1B's Settings.
  2. Under Probes and offsets for TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B, set Minimum probe temperature and Maximum probe temperature in °C, for example -30 and -10.
  3. Under Temperature range and alarm settings for TEMP PRO-1, turn on Alarm when temperature outside configured range. The group is named for the TEMP PRO-1, but this setting also switches the TEMP-1B's alarm on and off.

The TEMP-1B now sounds the siren with each probe reading outside your range, until the reading is back inside it.

Use the probe settings, not the TEMP PRO-1 ones

Minimum temperature and Maximum temperature in the TEMP PRO-1 group belong to the TEMP PRO-1 and don't change anything on a TEMP-1B. Set the range with Minimum probe temperature and Maximum probe temperature instead.

Next step: know when dinner is ready

Your freezer is covered. The automation examples put the food probe to work: a flow that lights your TEMP-1B green and sends you one notification when your food reaches its target temperature.

Build the food probe flow

docs.title: Automation examples using a TEMP-1B
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 2

🌱 New here? Try these first:

TEMP-1B alert outside a temperature range Difficulty: Level 1

Your Apollo TEMP-1B sends every probe reading to Homey while it's awake, and each new reading can start a flow. This page has two flows to build in the Homey mobile app: a freezer alert, and a food probe flow that lights the TEMP-1B green and messages you when dinner is almost ready.

Before you start

  • Add your TEMP-1B to Homey with the Apollo Automation app. See Getting started.
  • Install the Homey mobile app on every phone that should get a notification.
  • For the freezer flow, plug in the temperature probe. For the food flow, plug in the food probe.

docs.title: How probe readings reach Homey
docs.text:
The Apollo Automation app gives each probe its own reading on the TEMP-1B and its own trigger card. Which one reports depends on the Select probe setting: open your TEMP-1B's Settings and find it under Probes and offsets for TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B.

Probe Reading in Homey Trigger card How often it reports while awake Set Select probe to Temperature probe Temperature Probe Temperature probe changed About once a minute Temperature Food probe Food Probe Food probe changed Every few seconds Food

Both cards hand the new reading to the flow as a Temperature token, always in °C. The probe that isn't selected sends no readings, so its card never runs.

The cards run each time the reading changes, not only when it crosses your limit. That's why each flow below checks the Temperature token in an And... condition, and why the food flow adds a second condition so it alerts you once instead of every few seconds.

docs.title: Readings and sleep
docs.text:
The TEMP-1B only sends readings while it's awake. With Prevent sleep on, it stays connected and reports as shown in the table. With Prevent sleep off, it reports once each time it wakes, every 12 hours unless you change Sleep duration (in hours). Both settings are under Battery settings (if battery is present) in your TEMP-1B's Settings, and Prevent sleep walks you through changing them.

Change settings while the TEMP-1B is awake

Homey can only change the TEMP-1B's settings, including Select probe and Prevent sleep, while it's awake. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up., wake the sensor and try again. See How to wake up your sensor.

docs.title: Freezer over its maximum temperature
docs.text:
This flow sends a push notification whenever the freezer probe reads warmer than your maximum. It is Flow 1 from TEMP-1B alert outside a temperature range, which walks through every tap and shows you how to pick a limit and a Sleep duration that suit your freezer.

Column Card Set it to When... Temperature probe changed, from Apollo Automation for your TEMP-1B Nothing to set And... Homey's built-in condition for comparing numbers Temperature token greater than -10 Then... Send Message to User, from Push Notifications A message such as Check the freezer! with the Temperature token, sent to Everyone

Once it's saved, any probe reading above -10 °C sends the alert, with a reminder each time the reading changes until the freezer cools down again.

docs.title: Food probe reaches a target temperature
docs.text:
Chicken is safe to eat at 74 °C (165 °F), and it keeps rising a few degrees while it rests. This flow fires at 71 °C (160 °F) so you can take it off the heat in time. When the food probe gets there, the TEMP-1B's light turns green and your phone gets one notification.

The light also stops the alert from repeating. The food probe reports every few seconds, so the flow only runs while the light is off; once the flow has turned it green, later readings leave it alone.

Keep the TEMP-1B away from the heat

Only the food probe and its cable can go on the grill or in the oven. Set the TEMP-1B itself somewhere cool and dry, such as a side shelf.

Before you build the flow, wake your TEMP-1B, turn on Prevent sleep so it reports for the whole cook, and set Select probe to Food. Check that the Food Probe reading on your TEMP-1B changes when you hold the probe tip in your hand.

  1. In the Homey mobile app, tap Flow in the bottom bar, then tap + at the top right (or Create a Flow if you have none yet).
  2. Under When..., tap Add Card. Open Apollo Automation under Apps, choose your TEMP-1B, and choose Food probe changed.
  3. Under And..., tap Add Card and add Homey's built-in condition for comparing numbers. Set it to check that the Temperature token is greater than 71.
  4. Under And..., tap Add Card again. Find your TEMP-1B under Zones & Devices and choose its condition for whether it is turned on. Turn on Invert, so the card checks that the TEMP-1B is turned off. On a TEMP-1B, turned on and off means its RGB light.
  5. Under Then..., tap Add Card. Find your TEMP-1B under Zones & Devices and choose Turn on.
  6. Under Then..., tap Add Card again. Choose Set a color for your TEMP-1B, pick green, and tap the check mark.
  7. Under Then..., add Send Message to User from Push Notifications. Type a message such as Check the food! The food probe reads, add the Temperature token after it, and pick a User.
  8. Tap Next. Name the flow, for example Food is ready, and tap Save Flow.

The flow now shows in My Flows. When the food probe passes 71 °C, your TEMP-1B glows green and your phone gets one notification.

docs.title: Reset it for the next cook
docs.text:
When the food is off the heat, open your TEMP-1B in the Homey app and turn it off, which turns its light off. With the light off, the flow is ready to alert you again. The TEMP-1B also turns its light off whenever it goes to sleep.

Then turn Prevent sleep off again if you want to save battery, and switch the flow off in My Flows until your next cook.

docs.title: Test your flows
docs.text:
To check the alert without cooking anything, wake your TEMP-1B and tap the play button next to the flow in My Flows. It runs its Then cards once, and a green check mark confirms it ran: the TEMP-1B lights green and the notification arrives. Turn the TEMP-1B's light off afterwards so the flow is ready for the real thing.

If a flow doesn't run:

  • Check that Select probe matches the probe the flow uses: Temperature for the freezer flow, Food for the food flow.
  • Check that the TEMP-1B is awake, or wait for its next wake-up.
  • Check that your limits are in °C.
  • For the food flow, check that the TEMP-1B's light is off before the food reaches its target.
  • Check that the flow is switched on in My Flows.

docs.title: Take it further
docs.text:
• More probes: with the Multi-Probe Splitter, the extra probes each get their own trigger card: Temperature probe 2 changed, Temperature probe 3 changed, and Temperature probe 4 changed. Build the freezer flow once per probe to watch a fridge and a freezer from one TEMP-1B.
  • Other targets: change the number in the food flow's condition for other dishes, and give each one its own message.

docs.title: Coming from the Home Assistant cook chicken example
docs.text:
The Home Assistant version of the cook chicken example, shared by Discord user RalphP, does a few things the Homey flow above handles differently or leaves out:

  • A dashboard button to start and stop monitoring. In Homey, switch the flow on in My Flows when you start cooking and off when you're done.
  • A blinking light when the food is ready. The TEMP-1B has pulse effects for its light, but the Apollo Automation app has no card for them, so in Homey the light stays solid green.
  • A spoken announcement on smart speakers. The Home Assistant version uses text-to-speech. This guide doesn't cover speakers.

docs.title: Use cases for the TEMP-1B
docs.text:
1. Monitoring fridge / freezer: There are settings to set the maximum temperature the sensor should reach. It can alert through the onboard buzzer if it rises above that temperature. The cable on the probe is flat to not interfere with fridge seals.

2. Monitoring fish tank, hot tub ( if covered ), pool ( if covered or in sealed box ) with the waterproof probe.

3. Monitoring grilling, baking, or other food activities with the food safe probe

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This will walk you through the process of connecting your new Apollo Automation sensor to Homey. If at any point you get stuck, join our Discord for some help.

docs.title: Connecting through hotspot:
docs.text:
To get your new Apollo sensor connected to your Wi-Fi, follow the steps below!

1. Plug the sensor into a quality power brick. They require 5v and under an amp so most phone chargers will be fine. ESP devices are sensitive to power fluctuations and users have had some issues with really cheap power bricks. If your device is restarting or unavailable please try a different power brick.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to "Apollo MSR2 Hotspot", it might take a minute for the Wi-Fi network to show up.

3. Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your sensor.

If this does not automatically open the dashboard, please open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

4. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your sensor to connect to or scroll to the bottom and type in your Wi-Fi network then click "Save".

Tip for Mesh Wi-Fi systems or multiple Access Points

If you have multiple access points or a mesh system please manually type in your Wi-Fi network so it will join with the strongest signal!

5. Once connected, the sensor's dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your sensor to your Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Adding Apollo Automation app in Homey:
docs.text:
You'll install the Apollo Automation app on your Homey from a desktop PC or a browser.

1. Navigate to this website and click "Install App". For now this needs to be done from a desktop PC or a browser.

2. Select the Homey device you want to install it on and then click "Install App" again!

3. Your device will install the Apollo Automation Homey App then move to the next section.

docs.title: Connecting to Homey:
docs.text:
Next, you'll add your Apollo sensor to Homey from the Homey app on your phone.

1. Open the Homey App on your phone and navigate to the Devices tab at the bottom then select the (+) icon in the top right and choose "New Device". Choose "Allow" if it pops up asking to find Bluetooth devices, or you can change this later in settings.

2. Select Apollo Automation under Brands in the bottom left then choose "Every Apollo Sensor". When prompted, click "Connect".

3. Your Apollo devices will automatically show up and if not, please first connect it to your Wi-Fi following the steps outlined here.

4. Select the device you want to add, in this case an Apollo MTR-1 and click Continue at the bottom.

5. Click Continue Setup and choose a Zone to place your device in. If you are new to Homey you can choose Home and move it to another Zone later after you create more zones!

6. Change any other default settings like the Name, icon, etc or click Finish in the bottom right.

7. You are done! Your sensor is now ready to create flows and add as a favorite to your dashboard!

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: How to insert the battery
docs.text:
16340 AKA RC-CR123A and charger required!

The TEMP-1B is a very neat sensor but it does NOT include a battery nor a charging circuit. You will have to buy your own rechargeable RC-CR123A aka 16340 battery and also a separate 16340 charger such as a Nitecore 2 or 4bay model.

Follow these steps to open the case, insert the battery, and close it again.

1. Gently pry open the case lid as shown in the image below.

2. Once the lid is removed either lift the PCB out or gently dump the pcb out by turning it upside down.

3. Align the battery as shown in the image below.

4. Insert the battery with the positive terminal facing the + sign.

5. Begin reassembly by placing the battery side down with the RGB led in the top right corner.

6. You will use the "ledge" of the case to set the PCB down and then it will lay down and rest on the ledge of the other side as well.

7. Align the RGB led in the top right with the small hole in the lid.

8. Gently press down until the lid seats.

9 You have now installed or reinstalled the battery!

docs.title: Prevent sleep
docs.text:
Your Apollo TEMP-1B can sleep between readings: it wakes up, reports to Homey, and goes back to sleep until the next report. Sleeping is what makes the battery last. It also keeps the board from warming itself up, so the temperature readings need less offset.

The TEMP-1B ships with Prevent sleep turned on, so it stays awake and reports all the time. That's handy while you set it up, but it drains the battery far faster. Once the sensor is in place, turn Prevent sleep off and let it sleep.

Before you start

  • Add your TEMP-1B to Homey. See Getting started.
  • Homey can only change these settings while the sensor is awake and connected. If it's asleep, Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. In that case, keep it awake first.

docs.title: The sleep settings in Homey
docs.text:
Both settings sit in your TEMP-1B's Settings in the Homey app, under Battery settings (if battery is present). They're device settings only, so there's no flow card that turns sleep on or off.

Setting What it does Prevent sleep Checked, the sensor stays awake. Unchecked, it sleeps between reports. A new TEMP-1B has it checked. Sleep duration How many hours the sensor sleeps between reports, from 0 to 800, with up to two decimals: 0.5 is 30 minutes. The default is 12.

docs.title: Let your TEMP-1B sleep
docs.text:
Set how long the sensor sleeps first, then let it go to sleep. Make the two changes one at a time: the sensor falls asleep the moment Prevent sleep turns off, so a change sent along with it may never arrive.

Read this before you uncheck Prevent sleep

The TEMP-1B goes to sleep as soon as Prevent sleep is off, and Homey can't reach it again until it wakes up. Put the sensor where you want it and finish any other settings first.

  1. In the Homey app, open your TEMP-1B's Settings.
  2. Under Battery settings (if battery is present), set Sleep duration to the hours you want between reports, and save the change. Leave it at 12 unless you need fresher readings.
  3. Uncheck Prevent sleep and save.

Your TEMP-1B is now asleep. It wakes up after each Sleep duration, connects to Homey, sends fresh readings, and goes back to sleep about 20 seconds after it connects.

Device disconnected is normal between reports

While the TEMP-1B sleeps, Homey shows it as Device disconnected. That's expected: Homey reconnects on its own each time the sensor wakes up.

docs.title: Keep your TEMP-1B awake again
docs.text: To change a setting, update the firmware, or troubleshoot, the sensor has to stay awake. Turn Prevent sleep back on from the sensor itself or from the Homey app.

docs.title: With the buttons on the sensor
docs.text:
The buttons work even when Homey can't reach the sensor, which makes this the most reliable way. The sensor connection check has photos of the reset and boot buttons.

Watch how long you hold the boot button

Hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds, no longer. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets the TEMP-1B to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi, and you'd have to connect it to Wi-Fi again. A short press of under 3 seconds runs the connection check instead.

  1. Press and release the reset button to wake the sensor. You can also take the battery out and put it back in.
  2. Wait a few seconds, then press and hold the boot button for 4 to 5 seconds and let go.

The sensor turns Prevent sleep on and stays awake. In Homey, Prevent sleep shows as checked again once the sensor is connected. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, the sensor was already on its way back to sleep. It still remembers Prevent sleep, so press the reset button once more and it stays awake this time.

docs.title: From the Homey app
docs.text:
The sensor stays awake for only about 20 seconds after Homey connects, so have the Homey app open and ready before you start.

  1. Wake the sensor with the reset button, or take the battery out and put it back in.
  2. In the Homey app, open your TEMP-1B and wait until it no longer shows Device disconnected.
  3. Right away, open its Settings, check Prevent sleep under Battery settings (if battery is present), and save.
  4. If Homey loses the connection again a few seconds later, press the reset button once more.

Your TEMP-1B now stays awake until you uncheck Prevent sleep again. If the sensor was already on its way back to sleep at step 3, it still keeps the change and starts up with Prevent sleep on after the reset in step 4. If Homey shows The device is asleep. Settings can be changed when it next wakes up. instead, the change didn't reach the sensor: start again from step 1, or use the buttons.

Keep your TEMP-1B dry

Don't leave the TEMP-1B outside for long periods or let it get wet. If it will sit in damp air or could see rain, put it inside another, protective case.

Next step: check your sensor's connection

Not sure whether your TEMP-1B woke up and reached Homey? The light on the sensor tells you in a few seconds.

Run the sensor connection check

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your TEMP-1B. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The Default Update column is how often each entity refreshes while the TEMP-1B is awake. The TEMP-1B runs on a battery, and by default Prevent Sleep is on, so it stays awake and reports continuously at these intervals (which drains the battery). Turn Prevent Sleep off to let it deep-sleep between readings and conserve the battery: it wakes, reports, then sleeps for the Sleep Duration before waking again.

To update firmware on a sleeping device, click Update on the Firmware Update entity and it installs the next time the device wakes (the firmware keeps itself awake until the update finishes, so you don't need to do anything else). The optional OTA helper is a separate toggle that overrides Prevent Sleep to keep a device awake on demand.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light One RGB Neopixel LED. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Alarm Outside Temp Range Sounds the onboard buzzer when the selected probe's temperature crosses the Min Probe Temp or Max Probe Temp thresholds. Defaults to off. Select Probe Chooses which probe the TEMP-1B reads: Temperature (the Dallas DS18B20 probe, available in long or short versions) or Food (the stainless steel, food-safe probe for grilling and cooking). Sensor Default Update Details Temperature Probe 60s Reading from the Dallas DS18B20 probe. Active when Select Probe is set to Temperature. Good for fridge/freezer, aquariums, hot tubs, and covered pools. Adjusted by the Temp Probe Offset. Food Probe 3s Reading from the stainless steel food-safe NTC probe for grilling, baking, and other cooking. Active when Select Probe is set to Food. Adjusted by the Food Probe Offset. Board Temperature 60s Onboard temperature from the AHT20 sensor. Adjusted by the Board Temperature Offset. Board Humidity 60s Onboard relative humidity from the AHT20 sensor. Adjusted by the Board Humidity Offset. Battery level 60s Remaining battery charge from the MAX17048, reported 0-100%. Battery voltage 60s Current battery voltage from the MAX17048 for real-time monitoring. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. Board Temperature Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset applied to the Board Temperature reading. Board Humidity Offset 0 % Calibration offset applied to the Board Humidity reading. Temp Probe Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset for the Temperature Probe reading. Disabled by default. Food Probe Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset for the Food Probe reading. Disabled by default. Max Probe Temp 125.0 °C Upper temperature threshold used by the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Min Probe Temp -55.0 °C Lower temperature threshold used by the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Probe Temp Difference Threshold 0.0 °C How much the probe temperature must change to trigger the Notify Only Outside Temp Difference wake. Disabled by default. Notify Only Outside Temp Difference Off When on, the device only wakes and reports when the probe temperature changes by more than the Probe Temp Difference Threshold. Disabled by default. Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it reports continuously. Required for OTA updates and live readings; turn it off to save power on battery. While sleeping the TEMP-1B will not respond to Home Assistant until it wakes again. Sleep Duration 12 h How many hours the device stays in deep sleep between wake cycles (only used when Prevent Sleep is off). Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode
Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the TEMP-1B into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
Use this method to put your device into boot mode by pressing the boot button through the opening in the side of the case.

1. Position the TEMP-1B so that the USB-C port is facing you. On the right side of the device, locate a small opening where you can use a paperclip to press the boot button.

If you prefer, please remove the lid by gently prying up on the small slit by the top of the case.

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your TEMP-1B then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
Use this method to put your device into boot mode with the case removed, by holding the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and remove the case as shown in the images above

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your TEMP-1B in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (labeled BOOT, shown above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (labeled RST, at the opposite end of the board from boot).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the TEMP-1B. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash TEMP-1B
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the below guide.

This needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

If your device has already been added to Homey, please remove it from Homey before continuing.

1. Put your device in boot mode by holding down the boot button and then plugging in the USB cable.

2. Navigate to the Apollo TEMP-1 installer. The TEMP-1B uses the same page as the TEMP-1.

Remove the battery!

This will not work properly if the battery is still supplying power to the TEMP-1B. Please remove the battery if you are having issues!

3. Choose Battery Power since you are using a TEMP-1B, then click Connect & Install.

Use R2 version unless instructed to use R1 by support!

The Apollo installer installs the Revision 2 (R2) firmware. R2 is what all of our devices use except a very small batch of TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B boards. If support tells you your board needs Revision 1 (R1), click Connect under Battery Firmware Revision 1 on the classic TEMP-1 installer instead. In the next steps, the firmware option is named Install ApolloAutomation.TEMP-1B.

4. Select the open com port then click Connect.

5. Click Install Apollo.TEMP-1B_R2.

6. Click "INSTALL".

7. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

8. Please proceed to the getting started guide and set up your sensor as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your TEMP-1B
Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your TEMP-1B
docs.text:
Follow these steps to clear your device's saved Wi-Fi credentials so it broadcasts its hotspot again and you can enter new Wi-Fi details.

1. Plug the device into power.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo TEMP1B Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: ESPHome Starter Kit FAQ
docs.text:
1. What is the ESPHome Starter Kit?

  • The ESPHome Starter Kit is the first official kit for learning to build your own smart home devices using ESPHome. Designed and engineered by Apollo Automation in partnership with the Open Home Foundation, it pairs the modern ESP32-C6 chip with snap-together modules that connect with a single ribbon cable. No soldering, breadboards, parts sourcing, or code required.

2. Do I need to know how to code?

  • No. The kit is configured through ESPHome Desktop, a free download for Mac, Windows, and Linux that handles every step through a simple visual interface. Users who want to learn YAML directly can do so at any time.

3. Do I need to solder anything?

  • No. Every connection in the kit is made with a single FPC ribbon cable. No breadboards, no jumper wires, no solder joints.

4. Which way does the ribbon cable go in?

  • Insert the ribbon cable with the blue side facing upwards (blue side to the sky), so the exposed metal contacts face the pins inside the FPC connector. Flip up the latch, slide the cable in straight until it seats, then press the latch back down to lock it. The latches are small and the cable is fragile, so lift the latch with a fingernail and never pull on the cable itself.

5. Does it require Home Assistant?

  • No. The ESPHome Desktop app runs as a standalone download on Mac, Windows, and Linux, so you can build with the kit without installing Home Assistant or running a server first. The devices then work as standalone ESPHome devices over Wi-Fi, reachable at their .local hostname, and integrate with Home Assistant whenever you want to add it. Home Assistant finds them automatically over mDNS. See Connect to Home Assistant when you are ready.

6. Can the kit run on battery power?

  • Yes. The ESP32-C6 supports a rechargeable 3.7V LiPo battery that charges over the same USB-C cable, so the kit can be deployed cable-free around the home. See Adding the Battery for how to connect it.

7. What is the ESPHome Desktop app?

  • ESPHome Desktop is the free, open source desktop version of the ESPHome Device Builder. It runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux. For the first time, new users no longer need to install Home Assistant first, set up a Raspberry Pi, or run a server to use ESPHome. Download it, plug in the kit, and a guided setup walks you through the rest. Open esphome.io/install to download the latest release for your operating system, then follow First Steps to set up your first device. For a deeper look at how ESPHome and the app fit together, see Explaining ESPHome.

8. What can I build with it?

  • By the end of the included learning path, you will have built four working devices: a motion sensor, an environment monitor (temperature and humidity), a button trigger, and a notification light. Two modules can run on the ESP32-C6 at the same time, turning the kit into a multi-purpose sensor for any room. Beyond the lessons, every skill carries straight into the wider ESPHome ecosystem.

9. What happens when I am "done" learning?

  • Every module is built to last and designed to keep working long after the lessons end. Unlike most learning kits, where the hardware ends up in a drawer, the ESPHome Starter Kit's modules become real, useful smart home devices that earn a permanent place in the home.

10. Does the kit support Zigbee?

  • The kit officially supports Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE, and Thread. The ESP32-C6 chip inside also has Zigbee at the hardware level, so it is possible at the chip level for advanced users who want to experiment, though it is not part of the supported out-of-the-box experience.

11. Does it require a cloud service or account?

  • No. Everything runs 100% locally. No cloud, no account, no subscription, no telemetry. Your data stays in your home, and what leaves it is only what you choose to share.

12. How does this connect to the Open Home Foundation?

  • Apollo Automation is a commercial partner of the Open Home Foundation, the non-profit that owns and stewards ESPHome, Home Assistant, and over 250 other open source projects. The majority of profits from every ESPHome Starter Kit are contributed directly to the Open Home Foundation, funding the long-term development of the open source smart home and its founding principles of privacy, choice, and sustainability.

13. What is the difference between this and other ESP starter kits?

  • Other kits typically focus on broad electronics learning with breadboards and individual components. The ESPHome Starter Kit is purpose-built for smart home device construction, uses a solder-free ribbon-cable system, and is paired with the ESPHome Desktop app and a learning wiki that bridges into the wider ESPHome ecosystem. Most learning kits end with the lessons. The ESPHome Starter Kit's modules are designed to keep working as real smart home devices long after the kit is finished.

14. Why a ribbon cable instead of a breadboard?

  • Breadboards and jumper wires are the most common source of frustration for new builders: loose connections, wrong pins, wires that pop out. The ESPHome Starter Kit uses a single FPC (flexible printed circuit) ribbon cable that connects each module to the ESP32-C6 in seconds. Every connection is identical, foolproof, and reliable. Components snap together and stay together.

15. Why the ESP32-C6 chip?

  • The ESP32-C6 is a modern microcontroller from Espressif that brings Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE, and Thread support to a single chip. It is the same family of silicon used in commercially certified smart home products, and gives learners a future-ready platform that supports the same open standards used in production smart home devices.

16. Why won't my LEDs light up, my buzzer play, or my module respond?

  • Check the Accessory Power Rail first. The Onboard RGB LED and every module get their power from it, so if your project doesn't include it, or its Accessory Power switch is off, they don't get enough power to work. Projects created from the ESPHome Starter Kit board include the rail and turn it on at boot. If yours is missing it, see Accessory Power Rail to add it back.

docs.title: Welcome to the ESPHome Starter Kit!
docs.text:
Welcome to the start of your ESPHome journey with the all-new ESPHome Starter Kit!

Buy the ESPHome Starter Kit

By the end of this wiki you'll know how to:

  • Remove the modules off the panel safely
  • Identify each part of your kit

docs.title: What's in the kit
docs.text: Your kit arrives as a single snap-apart panel that includes the ESP32-C6 along with a selection of interchangeable modules. The kit also includes three ribbon cables for connecting modules to the ESP32-C6, one more than any project uses at once so you always have a spare, plus a stand for the LED & Buzzer module.

docs.title: Snapping the panel apart
docs.text:
Each module is connected to the panel by small breakaway tabs. Follow the steps below to separate them.

Take it slow

Bend the panel gradually, not all at once. The PCB is sturdy, but the components on the modules prefer a gentle snap.

  1. Hold the panel flat on a table with one hand on the module you want to remove.
  2. Gently flex the panel along the tab line until the tab snaps cleanly.

docs.title: Meet the modules
docs.text:
ESP32-C6

  • The brain of every project you'll build with the kit. It handles Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, runs your ESPHome config, and exposes the GPIO pins the modules plug into.

LED & Buzzer module

  • The starter kit's notification module, a strip of ten addressable RGB LEDs and a small piezo buzzer behind the ESPHome logo silkscreen. Use the included stand to show it off!

Motion module

  • Detects movement in a room and a great way to get started automating your home. It comes in two parts, and the PIR sensor plugs into the PIR module board.

Button module

  • Premium feel button perfect to trigger automations for lights and more.

Temperature and Humidity module

  • Extremely accurate temp and humidity sensor trustworthy enough to track a room comfort level with ease!

FPC cables

  • Each module connects to the ESP32-C6 through the FPC connector using one of the three provided cables. Tear the brown paper bag open from one of the ends. Please DO NOT use scissors as you could accidentally cut the cables!

docs.title: Next: bring it online
docs.text:
Once you've identified your modules and snapped them off the panel, the next step is to connect the ESP32-C6 to your computer and walk through your first ESPHome configuration.

Next - First Steps

docs.title: Build a button-controlled RGB light
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

This tutorial uses the Button module and the RGB & Buzzer module connected to the ESP32-C6, all sitting in the starter kit case.

Before you start

Work through these pages first. This tutorial assumes your device is flashed and both modules are connected:

  • First Steps to create your starter kit device in ESPHome Device Builder.
  • Adding the Button Module to wire up the input.
  • Adding the LED & Buzzer Module to wire up the RGB output.

docs.title: Build the automation
docs.text:
ESPHome Device Builder has a new GUI for building automations, so you can wire a trigger to an action without hand-writing YAML. The trigger is the when of the automation, the thing that makes it fire. The action is the then do, what happens when it fires. If you've built automations in Home Assistant, this is the same mental model.

  1. Open your starter kit device in ESPHome Device Builder and click Edit. If you need a refresher on the editor, see the Device Builder Tour.

  2. In the editor's left pane, expand the Automations dropdown and click Add Automation.

  3. Set up the trigger:

    • What should this automation react to? → A configured component
    • Which configured component? → Button Module (binary_sensor.gpio)
    • Which trigger? → Binary Sensor → On Click (1)
    1. The trigger dropdown also offers On Double Click, On Multi Click, On Press, On Release, On State, and On State Change for other button gestures. Swap any of these in once you're comfortable with the On Click flow.

  4. Click Continue. You land on the Binary Sensor → On Click editor with the Target already set to your Button module.

  5. Set up the action:

    • Under Actions, click + Add action.
    • In the Add action dialog, stay on the By target tab and scroll down towards the bottom, then choose Light → Toggle under the RGB LED group.
    • On the new action, click the ID dropdown and select RGB LEDs. (1)
    1. The ID dropdown only needs changing if your device also has an Onboard RGB LED component configured. If RGB LEDs is the only light, it's already selected.
What the GUI built in YAML

The form pane and the YAML editor on the right of the editor stay in sync, so the GUI you just used and the YAML pane are two views of the same config. Your button section now grows an on_click trigger with a light.toggle action:

binary_sensor:
  - platform: gpio
    name: Button Module
    pin:
      inverted: true
      mode:
        input: true
        pullup: true
      number: 6
    id: button_module
    on_click:
      then:
        - light.toggle: rgb_leds

See Device Builder Tour → YAML editor (right) for the full breakdown of the YAML pane.

docs.title: Install the software
docs.text:
Your automation is saved in Device Builder, but the device is still running its old software. Compile and install the new code to push the change.

  1. Click Save in the bottom right of the editor.

  2. Click Install, then pick On the Network to push the new software over Wi-Fi. (1)

    1. We say software because it's the friendlier word. The technically correct term is firmware: code that runs directly on the chip instead of on a computer. That's the word ESPHome's own docs use.

  3. Wait for the compile and flash to finish. The device reboots once the install is done.

docs.title: Test the automation
docs.text:
With the device back online, press the button on the Button module. You should hear a soft click, and the RGB LEDs turn on. Press it again and they turn off.

You've built your first GUI automation!

The same trigger-then-action pattern works for every automation you'll build in Device Builder. Swap the trigger (motion, temperature crossing a threshold, a schedule) or the action (turn on, dim, play a buzzer tone) and you have a new automation.

Next: Light Effects

docs.title: Turn on a light with motion
Turn on a light with motion
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

This tutorial uses the Motion module and the LED & Buzzer module connected to the ESP32-C6. When the PIR sensor detects movement, the RGB light turns on, and when the movement stops, the light turns back off. It's the same trigger-then-action pattern as the Button Controlled LEDs automation, swapping the button trigger for a motion trigger.

Before you start

Work through these pages first. This tutorial assumes your device is flashed and both modules are connected:

  • First Steps to create your starter kit device in ESPHome Device Builder.
  • Adding the Motion Module to wire up the PIR sensor.
  • Adding the LED & Buzzer Module to wire up the RGB light.

docs.title: Build the automation
docs.text: ESPHome Device Builder has a GUI for building automations, so you can wire a trigger to an action without hand-writing YAML. The trigger is the when, the thing that makes it fire. The action is the then do, what happens when it fires. You'll build two automations on the same Motion module: one that turns the lights on when motion is detected, and one that turns them off when motion stops.

docs.title: Turn the lights on
docs.text:
Start with the automation that turns the RGB light on when your Motion module detects movement.

  1. Open your starter kit device in ESPHome Device Builder and click Edit. If you need a refresher on the editor, see the Device Builder Tour.

  2. In the editor's left pane, expand the Automations dropdown and click Add Automation.

  3. Set up the trigger:

    • What should this automation react to? → A configured component
    • Which configured component? → Motion Module (binary_sensor.gpio)
    • Which trigger? → Binary Sensor → On Press (1)
    1. On Press fires the moment the sensor detects motion. The dropdown also offers On Release (the moment motion stops) and On State for other occupancy behaviors. You'll use On Release in the next section to turn the lights back off.

  4. Click Continue. You land on the Binary Sensor → On Press editor with the Target already set to your Motion module.

  5. Set up the action:

    • Under Actions, click + Add action.
    • In the Add action dialog, stay on the By target tab and scroll down towards the bottom, then choose Light → Turn On under the RGB LED group.
    • On the new action, click the ID dropdown and select RGB LEDs. (1)
    1. The ID dropdown only needs changing if your device also has an Onboard RGB LED component configured. If RGB LEDs is the only light, it's already selected.

What the GUI built in YAML

The form pane and the YAML editor on the right of the editor stay in sync. Your motion section now grows an on_press trigger with a light.turn_on action:

binary_sensor:
  - platform: gpio
    name: Motion Module
    pin: 3
    device_class: motion
    id: motion_module
    on_press: # (1)!
      then:
        - light.turn_on: rgb_leds
  1. on_press is the YAML name for the On Press trigger you picked in the GUI.

See Device Builder Tour → YAML editor (right) for the full breakdown of the YAML pane.

docs.title: Turn the lights off
docs.text:
Right now the lights turn on with motion but never turn off. Add a second trigger to the same Motion module so the lights switch off once motion clears.

  1. Add another automation, this time choosing Binary Sensor → On Release as the trigger for the Motion module. (1)

  2. Give it a Light → Turn Off action targeting RGB LEDs. (2)

  1. PIR sensors hold their "motion detected" state for a few seconds after movement stops, so On Release fires shortly after the room goes still, not the instant you stop moving.
  2. As before, the ID dropdown only needs changing if your device also has an Onboard RGB LED component configured. If RGB LEDs is the only light, it's already selected.
What the GUI built in YAML

Your motion section now has both triggers:

binary_sensor:
  - platform: gpio
    name: Motion Module
    pin: 3
    device_class: motion
    id: motion_module
    on_press: # (1)!
      then:
        - light.turn_on: rgb_leds
    on_release: # (2)!
      then:
        - light.turn_off: rgb_leds
  1. The On Press trigger from the first automation.
  2. on_release is the YAML name for the On Release trigger, firing when the sensor stops reporting motion.

docs.title: Install the software
docs.text:
Your automation is saved in Device Builder, but the device is still running its old software. Compile and install the new code to push the change.

  1. Click Save in the bottom right of the editor.

  2. Click Install, then pick On the Network to push the new software over Wi-Fi. (1)

    1. We say software because it's the friendlier word. The technically correct term is firmware: code that runs directly on the chip instead of on a computer. That's the word ESPHome's own docs use.

  3. Wait for the compile and flash to finish. The device reboots once the install is done.

docs.title: Test the automations
docs.text:
You've built a motion-activated light!

Same trigger-then-action pattern, new trigger. Swap the action (play a buzzer tune, dim the light, send a notification) or the trigger (a button, a temperature threshold, a schedule) and you have a new automation.

With the device back online, wave your hand in front of the PIR sensor. The RGB light turns on as soon as motion is detected, then turns off shortly after the sensor stops seeing movement. If the light triggers right after boot with nothing moving, give the sensor a moment. PIR sensors need a brief warm-up after powering on, usually 5 to 10 seconds, before their readings stabilize.

Next: Temp-Reactive LEDs

docs.title: Play a tune with the button
Play a tune with the button
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

This tutorial uses the Button module and the LED & Buzzer module connected to the ESP32-C6. When you click the button, the piezo buzzer plays a short tune. It's the same trigger-then-action pattern as the Button Controlled LEDs automation, swapping the light action for a buzzer action.

Before you start

Work through these pages first. This tutorial assumes your device is flashed and both modules are connected:

  • First Steps to create your starter kit device in ESPHome Device Builder.
  • Adding the Button Module to wire up the input.
  • Adding the LED & Buzzer Module to wire up the buzzer output.
  • Accessory Power Rail to confirm your project includes it. The LED & Buzzer module gets its power from the rail, and the buzzer doesn't get enough power to play without it.

docs.title: How the buzzer plays tunes
docs.text:
The buzzer plays songs written in RTTTL (Ring Tone Text Transfer Language), the same compact text format old phones used for ringtones. A tune is a single line that names the song, sets the tempo and default note length, then lists the notes:

scale_up:d=32,o=5,b=100:c,c#,d,d#,e,f,f#,g,g#,a,a#,b

When you added the LED & Buzzer module, Device Builder created an rtttl component with the id rtttl_player wired to the buzzer output. The automation below hands that component a tune string to play.

docs.title: Build the automation
docs.text:
ESPHome Device Builder has a GUI for building automations, so you can wire a trigger to an action without hand-writing YAML. The trigger is the when, the thing that makes it fire. The action is the then do, what happens when it fires.

  1. Open your starter kit device in ESPHome Device Builder and click Edit. If you need a refresher on the editor, see the Device Builder Tour.

  2. In the editor's left pane, expand the Automations dropdown and click Add Automation.

  3. Set up the trigger:

    • What should this automation react to? → A configured component
    • Which configured component? → Button Module (binary_sensor.gpio)
    • Which trigger? → Binary Sensor → On Click (1)
    1. The trigger dropdown also offers On Double Click, On Multi Click, On Press, On Release, On State, and On State Change for other button gestures. Swap any of these in once you're comfortable with the On Click flow.

  4. Click Continue. You land on the Binary Sensor → On Click editor with the Target already set to your Button module.

  5. Set up the action:

    • Under Actions, click + Add action.
    • In the Add action dialog, click By type then search Rtttl and choose Rtttl → Play.
    • In the Rtttl (tune) field, paste an RTTTL string. Copy the one below to get started, or use one of the examples below. (1)
    1. If your device has more than one rtttl component, set the ID to rtttl_player. With a single buzzer it's already selected.

    Copy this tune and paste it into the Rtttl field:

    The Simpsons:d=4,o=5,b=160:c.,e,f#,8a,g.,e,c,8a4,8f#4,8f#4,8f#4,2g4,8p,8p,8f#4,8f#4,8f#4,8g4,a4.,8c,16p,8c,16p,8c,2c

What the GUI built in YAML

The form pane and the YAML editor on the right of the editor stay in sync. Your button section now grows an on_click trigger with an rtttl.play action:

binary_sensor:
  - platform: gpio
    name: Button Module
    pin:
      inverted: true
      mode:
        input: true
        pullup: true
      number: 6
    id: button_module
    on_click:
      then:
        - rtttl.play: "The Simpsons:d=4,o=5,b=160:c.,e,f#,8a,g.,e,c,8a4,8f#4,8f#4,8f#4,2g4,8p,8p,8f#4,8f#4,8f#4,8g4,a4.,8c,16p,8c,16p,8c,2c"

See Device Builder Tour → YAML editor (right) for the full breakdown of the YAML pane.

docs.title: Install the software
docs.text:
Your automation is saved in Device Builder, but the device is still running its old software. Compile and install the new code to push the change.

  1. Click Save in the bottom right of the editor.

  2. Click Install, then pick On the Network to push the new software over Wi-Fi. (1)

    1. We say software because it's the friendlier word. The technically correct term is firmware: code that runs directly on the chip instead of on a computer. That's the word ESPHome's own docs use.

  3. Wait for the compile and flash to finish. The device reboots once the install is done.

docs.title: Test the automation
docs.text:
With the device back online, press the button on the Button module. You should hear the buzzer play your tune. Press it again to replay it.

No sound?

The buzzer is an output, not a switch, so it has no web server control of its own. The only way to hear it is to trigger it, like the button click above. If it stays silent:

  • Check that the Accessory Power switch is on in the web server and still in your project's Components section. The LED & Buzzer module gets its power from the Accessory Power Rail, and the buzzer doesn't get enough power to play without it.
  • Confirm the LED & Buzzer module is connected and that the install finished without errors.

docs.title: Find more tunes
docs.text:
Swap the tune string in your action for any valid RTTTL line. Here are a few to get started, copy the whole line into the Rtttl field:

Mario 
smb:d=4,o=5,b=100:16e6,16e6,32p,8e6,16c6,8e6,8g6,8p,8g,8p,8c6,16p,8g,16p,8e,16p,8a,8b,16a#,8a,16g.,16e6,16g6,8a6,16f6,8g6,8e6,16c6,16d6,8b,16p,8c6,16p,8g,16p,8e,16p,8a,8b,16a#,8a,16g.,16e6,16g6,8a6,16f6,8g6,8e6,16c6,16d6,8b,8p,16g6,16f#6,16f6,16d#6,16p,16e6,16p,16g#,16a,16c6,16p,16a,16c6,16d6,8p,16g6,16f#6,16f6,16d#6,16p,16e6,16p,16c7,16p,16c7,16c7,p,16g6,16f#6,16f6,16d#6,16p,16e6,16p,16g#,16a,16c6,16p,16a,16c6,16d6,8p,16d#6,8p,16d6,8p,16c6
Cantina 
Cantina:d=4,o=5,b=250:8a,8p,8d6,8p,8a,8p,8d6,8p,8a,8d6,8p,8a,8p,8g#,a,8a,8g#,8a,g,8f#,8g,8f#,f.,8d.,16p,p.,8a,8p,8d6,8p,8a,8p,8d6,8p,8a,8d6,8p,8a,8p,8g#,8a,8p,8g,8p,g.,8f#,8g,8p,8c6,a#,a,g
Star Wars Imperial Death March 
StarWars/Imp:d=4,o=5,b=112:8d.,16p,8d.,16p,8d.,16p,8a#4,16p,16f,8d.,16p,8a#4,16p,16f,d.,8p,8a.,16p,8a.,16p,8a.,16p,8a#,16p,16f,8c#.,16p,8a#4,16p,16f,d.,8p,8d.6,16p,8d,16p,16d,8d6,8p,8c#6,16p,16c6,16b,16a#,8b,8p,16d#,16p,8g#,8p,8g,16p,16f#,16f,16e,8f,8p,16a#4,16p,2c#

Want more? Browse a big list of RTTTL ringtones here, and preview any tune in your browser here before pasting it in. Paste the song into the Rtttl field of your action, then Save and Install again to hear the new tune.

You've built a button-triggered buzzer!

Same trigger-then-action pattern, new action. Swap the trigger (motion, a temperature threshold, a schedule) or the tune, and you have a new automation.

The trigger here is a button press on the device. To play tunes from a Home Assistant automation, script, or the Developer Tools page instead, see Play a Tune from Home Assistant.
