docs.title: Take control of your CAST-1
docs.text:
Taking control adopts your device into the ESPHome Device Builder so you can rename it or edit its YAML.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder.

2. Click Show next to Discovered at the top, then click Take Control next to your CAST-1. Change the Name and Friendly Name if you'd like, or leave them, then click Take Control again.

3. Click Install (the up arrow icon), then click On the network and watch it finish installing. (1)

  1. This takes 5 to 10 minutes depending on how fast your device is.

4. Once it completes, click Stop, then press the Reset button on your device. Your CAST-1 will reboot and it's now ready to test out!

You're all set!

Your CAST-1 is now adopted into the ESPHome Device Builder, where you can rename it or edit its YAML.

docs.title: Add the Ethernet module to CAST-1
Adding the Ethernet module
docs.text:
The Ethernet add-on gives your CAST-1 a wired network connection. It's a small header board that presses onto the top of the CAST-1, so there's no case to open and nothing to solder.

1. Unplug your CAST-1 from power.

2. Find the two rows of female header pins on the top of the case.

3. Line the module's pins up with those two rows, pin side down, and press it straight down until it sits flat. (1)

  1. Press evenly on both ends. If the module won't sit flat against the case, lift it off and line the pins up again rather than forcing it.

4. Plug an Ethernet cable into the module, then plug the CAST-1 back into power.

That's it. Your CAST-1 picks the wired connection up on its own. Check the Network Connection sensor on the device page to confirm it reads Ethernet. (1)

  1. It reads Ethernet + WiFi if your CAST-1 is on both at once, which is what you want. Home Assistant keeps talking to the device that way while you plug or unplug the cable.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Add an LED strip to CAST-1
Add an LED strip
docs.text:
Your CAST-1 has three exposed pins, 5V, GND and IO1, that can drive an addressable LED strip. Once it's wired up, the strip shows up in Home Assistant as a light with effects, and it can switch on by itself whenever music is playing.

Firmware 26.10.13.1 or newer

LED strip support arrived in firmware 26.10.13.1. If your CAST-1 is on an older version, update it from the Firmware Update entity on its device page. Until this release reaches the Stable channel, switch to the Beta channel first.

docs.title: What you'll need
docs.text:
• An addressable RGB strip that uses a single data wire. WS2812B is the most common. WS2812, SK6812 (RGB), WS2811, APA106 and SM16703 also work.
  • Three wires to connect the strip to the CAST-1.

Strips with separate data and clock wires (APA102, SK9822), RGBW strips, and plain 12V RGB strips with no data wire won't work.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Every LED draws current. A WS2812B LED pulls up to about 60 mA at full white, so a strip adds up fast: 30 LEDs can draw about 1.8 A, and a 5 m roll of 150 LEDs about 9 A.

  • Short strips can run from the CAST-1's 5V pin. Keep LED Strip Max Brightness at its default of 50% or lower.
  • Long strips need their own 5V power supply sized for the strip. Connect the supply to the strip's 5V and GND, connect the CAST-1's GND to the strip's GND as well, and run only the data wire from IO1. Don't connect the CAST-1's 5V pin to a strip that has its own supply.

Too much load reboots the CAST-1

If the CAST-1 restarts or the audio cuts out when the strip gets bright, the strip is drawing more than the 5V pin can supply. Lower LED Strip Max Brightness or give the strip its own power supply.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
You'll connect the strip's power, ground and data wires to the matching pins on your device.

1. Unplug your CAST-1 from power.

2. Find the input end of the strip. Its pads are labelled DIN or DI, and the arrows printed on the strip point away from it. (1)

  1. Data only travels one way along the strip. Wired to the DOUT end, the strip stays dark.

3. Connect the wires:

CAST-1 LED strip 5V 5V (or +5V) GND GND IO1 DIN

4. Plug your CAST-1 back into power.

docs.title: Turn on the LED strip controls
docs.text:
The LED strip controls are hidden until you turn them on, so CAST-1s without a strip don't show extra controls.

1. In Home Assistant, go to Settings > Devices & services > ESPHome and open your CAST-1.

2. Under Controls, Configuration and Diagnostic, select +N entities not shown and turn on each entity whose name starts with LED Strip. Home Assistant adds them after about 30 seconds.

3. Set LED Strip Count to the number of LEDs on your strip. (1)

  1. Multiply the strip's length by its LEDs per meter. A 5 m roll of a 30 LEDs/m strip has 150 LEDs. LEDs past the count stay off.

4. Press LED Strip Test. The strip shows red, green, blue and white, then a rainbow, and turns off.

If the colors come out in the wrong order (for example, green when the test shows red), change LED Strip Color Order until they match. GRB is right for most WS2812B strips.

docs.title: LED strip controls
docs.text:
Entity What it does LED Strip The strip itself. Turn it on and off, pick a color and brightness, or choose an effect: Rainbow, Color Wipe, Scan, Twinkle, Random Twinkle, Fireworks, Flicker, Pulse or Strobe. LED Strip Count How many LEDs to drive, up to 300. LED Strip Max Brightness Caps the brightness of every LED to keep the current draw down. Defaults to 50%. LED Strip Color Order The order your strip expects its colors in. LED Strip Chipset The type of LED on your strip. Leave it on WS2812 unless the strip flickers or shows random colors. LED Strip Music Mode Turns the strip on with the Music Effect whenever music is playing, and off about 3 seconds after it stops. LED Strip Music Effect The effect Music Mode uses. LED Strip Test Runs the color test from the steps above.

Music Mode follows playback, not the beat

Music Mode turns the strip on and off with playback. The effects run at their own pace and don't react to the music itself.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Nothing lights up

  • Check the data wire goes to the DIN end of the strip.
  • Make sure the strip's GND is connected to the CAST-1's GND, even when the strip has its own power supply.
  • Check the LED Strip light is turned on.

Random colors or flickering

  • Try a different LED Strip Chipset.
  • Keep the data wire short. The CAST-1 sends a 3.3V data signal, which most strips accept over a short wire.

Only part of the strip lights up

  • Set LED Strip Count to the number of LEDs on your strip.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: TTS and announcements
docs.text:
Your CAST-1 can speak. Send it a text-to-speech message and it plays over whatever is already going, ducking the music down and bringing it back when it's done. Nothing stops or resumes, the two run at once.

You'll need a text-to-speech engine set up in Home Assistant first. The examples below use Piper, which runs locally and sounds good, but any engine works since the CAST-1 plays what Home Assistant sends it.

docs.title: Which player to use
docs.text:
Your CAST-1 has two media players and either one handles announcements.

  • Apollo CAST-1 Player is the ESPHome media player with the announcement pipeline.
  • Apollo CAST-1 Sendspin Player is the Music Assistant streaming target. Announcements sent here get forwarded to the announcement pipeline, so your music still ducks.

docs.title: Send an announcement
docs.text:
You'll send a test announcement from Developer Tools and hear it play over your music.

1. Open Developer Tools in Home Assistant (Settings → Tools in Home Assistant 2026.8 and newer) and go to the Actions tab.

2. Switch to YAML mode and paste this: (1)

  1. The number in the entity ID comes from your CAST-1's MAC address, so yours won't be 722124. Copy the real one from your device page in Home Assistant.
action: tts.speak
target:
  entity_id: tts.piper
data:
  media_player_entity_id: media_player.apollo_cast_1_722124_player
  message: Testing announcements on the CAST dash one

3. Run it with music playing and you'll hear the music drop, the message play, then the music come back.

docs.title: What happens during an announcement
docs.text:
The CAST-1 ducks the music by 40 dB the instant an announcement starts, so speech stays clear without the music stopping. The onboard LEDs turn cyan while it's talking. When the message finishes, the music fades back over a second and the LEDs go out.

That LED change is a handy way to tell an announcement from a glitch when you're across the room.

docs.title: Announce a sound instead of speech
docs.text:
Anything you can play can be an announcement, not just speech. A doorbell chime works the same way, ducking the music and lighting the LEDs:

action: media_player.play_media
target:
  entity_id: media_player.apollo_cast_1_722124_player
data:
  media_content_id: media-source://media_source/local/doorbell.mp3
  media_content_type: music
  announce: true

The announce: true is what routes it to the announcement pipeline. Leave it out and the sound replaces your music instead of playing over it.

docs.title: Use it in an automation
docs.text:
Announce when the washing machine finishes 
alias: Announce laundry done
triggers:
  - trigger: state
    entity_id: sensor.washing_machine_status
    to: "off"
    for:
      minutes: 2
actions:
  - action: tts.speak
    target:
      entity_id: tts.piper
    data:
      media_player_entity_id: media_player.apollo_cast_1_722124_player
      message: The washing machine is finished
mode: single

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: WizMote control
docs.text:
A WizMote gives you physical control over playback on your CAST-1. The Apollo CAST-1 WizMote blueprint maps each of the nine buttons to a playback action, a light toggle, or any Home Assistant action you want, all set up without leaving Home Assistant.

Every button ships with a sensible default, so your WizMote works the moment you import the blueprint. Open any button's dropdown to change it, or set one to Send HA Event to run a custom action like playing a Music Assistant playlist.

Button Default action On Play Off Pause Night Toggle Light Brightness Up Volume Up Brightness Down Volume Down Button 1 Previous Track Button 2 Next Track Button 3 Send HA Event Button 4 Send HA Event

Each dropdown offers the same choices: Nothing, Play, Pause, Play / Pause, Next Track, Previous Track, Volume Up, Volume Down, Toggle Light, or Send HA Event.

docs.title: Pair your WizMote
docs.text:
Before the blueprint can control anything, pair your WizMote with the CAST-1.

1. Open the ESPHome integration, then click through to your Apollo CAST-1 to open its device page.

2. Turn on WizMote Auto-Discovery.

3. Press any button on your WizMote. The CAST-1 pairs with it and WizMote Status updates to show the paired remote. (1)

  1. Pairing a different WizMote later? Use Clear WizMote Pairing on the device to unpair, then turn WizMote Auto-Discovery back on and press a button on the new remote.

Pairing takes longer on a CAST-1 running Ethernet only

A CAST-1 that's on Ethernet and not joined to any Wi-Fi network has no channel to follow, so it hops through radio channels 1 through 13 hunting for the WizMote, moving on every couple of seconds until it hears one. Keep pressing a button and it should pair within a minute.

docs.title: Import the blueprint
docs.text:
You'll import the blueprint, pick your device, and choose what each WizMote button does.

1. Click the Import Blueprint button below then click Open link.

2. Click Preview then click Import Blueprint.

3. Click on Apollo CAST-1 WizMote, then click Select a device and choose your Apollo CAST-1 from the dropdown.

4. Every button already has a default, so your WizMote works right away. To change one, open its dropdown and pick a different action.

5. For any button set to Send HA Event (Buttons 3 and 4 by default), click Add Action below it and choose what it should do, like playing a Music Assistant playlist or toggling a light.

6. Name your automation something like Apollo CAST-1 WizMote and click Save. Your WizMote now controls your CAST-1!

docs.title: CAST-1 getting started
docs.text: This will guide you through connecting your CAST-1 to your speakers, adding it to your Wi-Fi and Home Assistant, and streaming to it with Music Assistant.

docs.title: Physical setup
docs.text:
Run a 3.5mm cable from the CAST-1 into the line-in on your powered speakers, receiver, or active soundbar, then plug the CAST-1 into power with USB-C. A 5V 1A power supply is plenty. (1)

  1. The CAST-1 has no amplifier of its own, so it needs powered speakers or an amp. If your speakers use RCA or 6.35mm inputs, use a 3.5mm-to-RCA or 3.5mm-to-6.35mm adapter cable.

docs.title: Connect to your network
docs.text:
There are three ways to get your CAST-1 online. Pick whichever is easier, you only need to do one.

  • Hotspot works on any phone or computer. The CAST-1 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi network, you join it, then enter your Wi-Fi details. No extra hardware needed.
  • Improv via BLE sets the CAST-1 up over Bluetooth straight from Home Assistant. It's quick, but it needs Bluetooth on your Home Assistant host or an ESP32 Bluetooth proxy.
  • Ethernet is for a CAST-1 with the Ethernet add-on module fitted. It connects over a network cable straight to your router or switch.
HotspotImprov via BLEEthernet

1. Plug the CAST-1 in via USB-C. A 5V 1A power supply will work fine.

If your CAST-1 is restarting or not broadcasting Wi-Fi try another USB-C cable and power supply!

The CAST-1 is sensitive to power fluctuations and needs constant 5V power. Most quality phone chargers will work fine.

Still no hotspot? Follow the Reset Wi-Fi Credentials guide to make it broadcast again.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to "Apollo CAST 1 Hotspot". Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your CAST-1. If it doesn't, open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

3. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your CAST-1 to connect to and type in your Wi-Fi password, then click "Save".

4. Once connected, the dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your CAST-1 to your Wi-Fi.

Pre-requirement: Bluetooth proxy or Bluetooth Home Assistant hardware required

Bluetooth built in such as a Raspberry Pi or at least one ESP32 BLE Proxy is required to use this to set up your Apollo device.

1. Open your integrations page in Home Assistant.

2. Click the Add button on your discovered CAST-1, type in your Wi-Fi SSID and password, then click Submit.

3. Click Submit again, give it an Area, then click Finish.

Improv adds your CAST-1 to Home Assistant as part of setup, so skip ahead to installing Music Assistant.

With the CAST-1 unplugged, line the Ethernet module up with the two rows of female header pins on top of the case, pin side down, and press it straight down until it sits flat.

1. Plug an Ethernet cable into the module, then plug the CAST-1 into power.

2. Your CAST-1 picks up an address from your router on its own, so there's nothing to enter. (1)

  1. Unplug the cable later and your CAST-1 falls back to Wi-Fi on its own. The FAQ covers how the two connections work together.

3. Home Assistant discovers your CAST-1 automatically. Add it below, then check the Network Connection sensor on the device page to confirm it reads Ethernet.

docs.title: Add to Home Assistant
docs.text: Open the ESPHome Integration, then click Add and Submit. Edit the name and choose an Area then click Finish.

docs.title: Music Assistant
docs.text:
The CAST-1 streams through Music Assistant. Once Music Assistant is running, your CAST-1 shows up as a player automatically, no extra configuration needed.

Use Music Assistant 2.10.7 or newer

Newer CAST-1 firmware needs Music Assistant 2.10.7 or newer to connect. If Music Assistant is already installed, update it from its app page first.

docs.title: Install Music Assistant
docs.text:
You'll install the Music Assistant app, then add its integration in Home Assistant.

1. Head to the App Store to install Music Assistant.

2. Click Install, then click Start once it finishes.

3. Home Assistant discovers the Music Assistant integration automatically. Open your integrations page, find Music Assistant, then click Add and Submit.

docs.title: Stream to your CAST-1
docs.text:
With Music Assistant running, you can start playing music through your speakers.

1. Open Music Assistant from the Home Assistant sidebar.

2. Your CAST-1 appears in the player list in Music Assistant. Select it as your player.

3. Pick any song, playlist, or radio station and it plays through the speakers connected to your CAST-1.

docs.title: Play in multiple rooms
docs.text:
Have more than one CAST-1? Group them to play the same music in sync across every room.

1. In Music Assistant, open the player you're listening on.

2. Click the group/sync button and select the other CAST-1 players you want to join.

3. All grouped CAST-1 players now play the same audio together. Adjust the volume for the whole group or per player.

Add a WizMote for physical playback control!

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your CAST-1. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does Apollo CAST-1 Player The main media player for Home Assistant. Use it to play media, text-to-speech, and announcements to the speakers connected to your CAST-1. Announcements duck the music down, then bring it back when they finish. See TTS and Announcements. Apollo CAST-1 Sendspin Player The Music Assistant streaming player. This is the player your CAST-1 exposes to Music Assistant, and it's the one you group with other CAST-1s for synchronized multi-room audio. Announcements sent to it forward to the ESPHome player and duck the music the same way. RGB Light The four onboard RGB LEDs. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color, pick a Slow Pulse or Fast Pulse effect, or use the toggle to turn it on or off. Sensor What it reports Track Title Title of the track currently playing through the CAST-1. Artist Artist of the current track. Album Album of the current track. Setting Default What it does Firmware Channel Stable Which firmware channel the CAST-1 updates from. Beta gets new features earlier but is less tested than Stable. See Switch to Beta Firmware. Firmware Update n/a Checks for and installs a firmware update from the selected channel, straight from Home Assistant. See Updating Firmware for the full walkthrough. Bluetooth Proxy Off Lets the CAST-1 act as a Bluetooth proxy for Home Assistant, extending Bluetooth range to nearby devices. WizMote Auto-Discovery Off Turn on to pair a WizMote. While it's on, the next WizMote button press links that remote to your CAST-1. Clear WizMote Pairing n/a Unpairs the current WizMote so you can pair a different one. WizMote MAC Address n/a MAC address of the paired WizMote. Set automatically during pairing, or type one in manually. WizMote On Play Action the WizMote On button runs. Choose from Nothing, Play, Pause, Play / Pause, Next Track, Previous Track, Volume Up, Volume Down, Toggle Light, or Send HA Event. WizMote Off Pause Action the WizMote Off button runs. WizMote Night Toggle Light Action the WizMote Night button runs. WizMote Brightness Up Volume Up Action the WizMote Brightness Up button runs. WizMote Brightness Down Volume Down Action the WizMote Brightness Down button runs. WizMote Button 1 Previous Track Action the WizMote 1 button runs. WizMote Button 2 Next Track Action the WizMote 2 button runs. WizMote Button 3 Send HA Event Action the WizMote 3 button runs. WizMote Button 4 Send HA Event Action the WizMote 4 button runs. ESP Reboot n/a Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Factory Reset ESP n/a Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity What it shows WizMote Status Whether a WizMote is paired. Shows "No WizMote paired", "Discovery mode active", or "Paired:" with the remote's MAC address. Apollo Firmware Version The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.7.12.1). ESPHome Version The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Network Connection Which connection the CAST-1 is using: Ethernet, WiFi, Ethernet + WiFi when it's on both at once, Hotspot while it's waiting for Wi-Fi details, or Connecting. Ethernet IP Address The device's IP address on the wired connection. Needs the Ethernet module fitted. WiFi IP Address The device's IP address on your Wi-Fi network. Online Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. ESP Temperature Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Disabled by default. Uptime How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the CAST-1 in boot mode
Putting the CAST-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the CAST-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware. Both methods do the same thing, so use whichever is easier for you.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
1. With the CAST-1 unplugged, hold down the boot button (on the left) while plugging a USB-C data cable into the CAST-1. Once connected, release the button.

2. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
This method puts your device into boot mode with the boot and reset buttons.

1. Plug a USB-C cable that supports power and data into your computer and connect the other end to your CAST-1.

2. Locate the boot and reset buttons on the CAST-1.

3. Put your CAST-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (on the left). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (on the right).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the CAST-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Reflashing the CAST-1
docs.text:
Use this to put your CAST-1 back on the latest factory firmware.

Reflash if your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods, or to get onto the latest firmware.

1. Plug a USB-C cable that supports power and data into your computer and connect the other end to your CAST-1.

2. Locate the boot and reset buttons on your CAST-1. (1)

  1. Prefer to boot with a single button? Follow Method 1 on the Boot Mode page instead.

3. Put your CAST-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (on the left). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (on the right).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the CAST-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Open the Apollo CAST-1 Installer.

5. Click Connect & Install. In the browser popup, select USB JTAG/serial debug unit and click Allow. When the installer opens, click Install to flash the firmware, then click Install again to confirm.

6. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled, meaning power removed, to make it boot in a normal mode!

Head to the Getting Started article to set up your CAST-1 as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your CAST-1
docs.text:
Resetting the Wi-Fi credentials makes your device broadcast its hotspot again so you can enter new Wi-Fi details.

Using the Ethernet module? Unplug the cable first.

Your CAST-1 doesn't broadcast its hotspot while an Ethernet cable is connected, so take the cable out before you start.

1. Plug the CAST-1 into power.

2. Long press the boot button (on the left) for 10 seconds.

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo CAST 1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

Still not broadcasting a hotspot?

If your CAST-1 won't broadcast its hotspot after resetting, reflash it to restore the factory firmware and settings.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Make Any Speakers Smart: Connect the CAST PRO-1 to your speakers, receiver or soundbar, add it to Home Assistant, and it shows up in Music Assistant as a player you can stream to. It needs Music Assistant 2.10.7 or newer.

Analog or Optical Output: Use the analog output for powered speakers, or the optical output for a receiver or soundbar. Pick which one plays with the Audio Output setting on the device page.

Audio In: Plug in a turntable, TV or other source and turn on Line In to play it through the speakers connected to your CAST PRO-1.

Built-In Ethernet: The CAST PRO-1 has an Ethernet port on board, so it can run on a wired connection with no add-on. Without a cable, it works over WiFi.

Multi-Room Audio: Group the CAST PRO-1 with other CAST players to play the same music in sync across every room. Streaming runs locally through Music Assistant and Sendspin, so there's no cloud account and no subscription.

LED Strip Terminals: Connect an addressable LED strip to the terminals, with no soldering, and control it from Home Assistant. See Add an LED Strip.

WizMote Control: Pair a WizMote for physical control over playback without opening an app. Each button is configurable in Home Assistant.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Add an LED strip to CAST PRO-1
Add an LED strip
docs.text:
Your CAST PRO-1 has LED strip terminals, 5V, GND and IO1, for an addressable LED strip. There's no soldering: the strip's wires go straight into the terminals. Once it's connected, the strip shows up in Home Assistant as a light with effects, and it can switch on by itself whenever music is playing.

Coming in a firmware update

LED strip support for the CAST PRO-1 is coming in a firmware update. Once it's available, update your CAST PRO-1 from the Firmware Update entity on its device page.

docs.title: What you'll need
docs.text:
• An addressable RGB strip that uses a single data wire. WS2812B is the most common. WS2812, SK6812 (RGB), WS2811, APA106 and SM16703 also work.
  • A strip with bare wire ends (or wires you can connect to its pads) for the terminals.

Strips with separate data and clock wires (APA102, SK9822), RGBW strips, and plain 12V RGB strips with no data wire won't work.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Every LED draws current. A WS2812B LED pulls up to about 60 mA at full white, so a strip adds up fast: 30 LEDs can draw about 1.8 A, and a 5 m roll of 150 LEDs about 9 A.

  • Short strips can run from the CAST PRO-1's 5V terminal. Keep LED Strip Max Brightness at its default of 50% or lower.
  • Long strips need their own 5V power supply sized for the strip. Connect the supply to the strip's 5V and GND, connect the CAST PRO-1's GND terminal to the strip's GND as well, and run only the data wire from IO1. Don't connect the CAST PRO-1's 5V terminal to a strip that has its own supply.

Too much load reboots the CAST PRO-1

If the CAST PRO-1 restarts or the audio cuts out when the strip gets bright, the strip is drawing more than the 5V terminal can supply. Lower LED Strip Max Brightness or give the strip its own power supply.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
You'll connect the strip's power, ground and data wires to the matching terminals on your device.

1. Unplug your CAST PRO-1 from power.

2. Find the input end of the strip. Its pads are labelled DIN or DI, and the arrows printed on the strip point away from it. (1)

  1. Data only travels one way along the strip. Wired to the DOUT end, the strip stays dark.

3. Connect the strip's wires to the terminals:

CAST PRO-1 terminal LED strip 5V 5V (or +5V) GND GND IO1 DIN

4. Plug your CAST PRO-1 back into power.

docs.title: Turn on the LED strip controls
docs.text:
The LED strip controls are hidden until you turn them on, so a CAST PRO-1 without a strip doesn't show extra controls.

1. In Home Assistant, go to Settings > Devices & services > ESPHome and open your CAST PRO-1.

2. Under Controls, Configuration and Diagnostic, select +N entities not shown and turn on each entity whose name starts with LED Strip. Home Assistant adds them after about 30 seconds.

3. Set LED Strip Count to the number of LEDs on your strip. (1)

  1. Multiply the strip's length by its LEDs per meter. A 5 m roll of a 30 LEDs/m strip has 150 LEDs. LEDs past the count stay off.

4. Press LED Strip Test. The strip shows red, green, blue and white, then a rainbow, and turns off.

If the colors come out in the wrong order (for example, green when the test shows red), change LED Strip Color Order until they match. GRB is right for most WS2812B strips.

docs.title: LED strip controls
docs.text:
Entity What it does LED Strip The strip itself. Turn it on and off, pick a color and brightness, or choose an effect: Rainbow, Color Wipe, Scan, Twinkle, Random Twinkle, Fireworks, Flicker, Pulse or Strobe. LED Strip Count How many LEDs to drive, up to 300. LED Strip Max Brightness Caps the brightness of every LED to keep the current draw down. Defaults to 50%. LED Strip Color Order The order your strip expects its colors in. LED Strip Chipset The type of LED on your strip. Leave it on WS2812 unless the strip flickers or shows random colors. LED Strip Music Mode Turns the strip on with the Music Effect whenever music is playing, and off about 3 seconds after it stops. LED Strip Music Effect The effect Music Mode uses. LED Strip Test Runs the color test from the steps above.

Music Mode follows playback, not the beat

Music Mode turns the strip on and off with playback. The effects run at their own pace and don't react to the music itself.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Nothing lights up

  • Check the data wire goes to the DIN end of the strip.
  • Make sure the strip's GND is connected to the CAST PRO-1's GND, even when the strip has its own power supply.
  • Check the LED Strip light is turned on.

Random colors or flickering

  • Try a different LED Strip Chipset.
  • Keep the data wire short. The CAST PRO-1 sends a 3.3V data signal, which most strips accept over a short wire.

Only part of the strip lights up

  • Set LED Strip Count to the number of LEDs on your strip.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Apollo DEV-1 introduction
docs.text: The Apollo DEV-1 is a very small dev board that we use to prototype before creating other new products. It's a great starter device for tinkerers. You can buy it on its own, or with a breadboard and dupont wires (jumper wires) if you need those too.

docs.title: Pinout and power
docs.text:
• Built-in RGB light: on GPIO3.
  • 3.3V pin: supplies up to 600mA, but the microcontroller itself uses 100-200mA of that.

Use one power source at a time

You can power the DEV-1 through the USB-C port or back-feed power through the 5V and G (ground) pins, but not both at the same time.

docs.title: GPIO pins
docs.text:
These are the DEV-1's I2C, UART, ADC, and onboard RGB LED pins, written as ESPHome YAML:

#These are the i2c pins
i2c:
  sda: GPIO1
  scl: GPIO0

#These are the UART pins
uart:
  tx_pin: GPIO21
  rx_pin: GPIO20
  baud_rate: 115200 #match the device you connect

#ADC pins: GPIO0, GPIO1, GPIO2, GPIO4

#Onboard RGB LED: GPIO3

docs.title: Flash your DEV-1
docs.text: The DEV-1 doesn't come pre-flashed with ESPHome or WLED, so you flash it yourself. This getting started video we made walks you through it:

docs.title: Example ESPHome YAML
docs.text:
Use the example configuration below as a starting point for your DEV-1. Before you use it, give it your own API encryption key:

1. Open the ESPHome API documentation and copy the randomly generated API key from the code block, as shown in the red box below.

2. In the YAML below, find the key: line under api: and replace use-a-randomly-generated-key-here with the key you copied.

Your configuration now uses its own encryption key. Here's the full example for the DEV-1:

#Define Project
substitutions:
  name: apollo-dev-1
  version:  "1"
  device_description: ${name} made by Apollo Automation - version ${version}.

esphome:
  name: "${name}"
  friendly_name: Apollo DEV-1
  comment: Apollo DEV-1

  project:
    name: "ApolloAutomation.DEV-1"
    version: "${version}"

# Define Board
esp32:
  variant: esp32c3
  framework:
    type: esp-idf

# Enable logging
logger:

# Enable Home Assistant API
api:
  encryption:
    key: "use-a-randomly-generated-key-here"

ota:
  - platform: esphome
    password: !secret ota_password

wifi:
  ssid: !secret wifi_ssid
  password: !secret wifi_password

  # Enable fallback hotspot (captive portal) in case wifi connection fails
  ap:
    ssid: "Apollo-Dev-1 Fallback Hotspot"
    password: !secret wifi_password

captive_portal:

web_server:
  port: 80
  version: 3

#onboard LED using pin GPIO3 as shown below
light:
  - platform: esp32_rmt_led_strip
    id: rgb_onboard_light
    name: "RGB Onboard Light"
    pin: GPIO3
    default_transition_length: 0s
    chipset: WS2812
    num_leds: 1
    channel_colors: GRB
    effects:
      - pulse:
          name: "Slow Pulse"
          transition_length: 1000ms
          update_interval: 1000ms
          min_brightness: 50%
          max_brightness: 100%
      - pulse:
          name: "Fast Pulse"
          transition_length: 100ms
          update_interval: 100ms
          min_brightness: 50%
          max_brightness: 100%

button:
  - platform: restart
    icon: mdi:power-cycle
    name: "ESP Reboot"

sensor:
  - platform: internal_temperature
    name: "ESP Temperature"
    id: sys_esp_temperature

  - platform: uptime
    name: Uptime
    id: sys_uptime
    update_interval: 60s

  - platform: wifi_signal
    name: RSSI
    id: wifi_signal_db
    update_interval: 60s
    entity_category: "diagnostic"

text_sensor:
  - platform: wifi_info
    ip_address:
      name: "${name} IP"
      icon: "mdi:ip-outline"

docs.title: Choosing an mmWave sensor
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave sensors detect the moving and still energy of people and animals, which makes them excellent for presence detection in a room. They are not meant to detect vehicles, so for a car an ultrasonic sensor is a better fit. This guide compares our three current mmWave sensors so you can pick the right one for your space.

  • MSR-2

    Best still detection, for one person.

    MSR-2 overview

  • MTR-1

    Tracks multiple people across zones.

    MTR-1 overview

  • R PRO-1

    Best of both worlds, plus PoE.

    R PRO-1 overview

docs.title: Compare
docs.text: MSR-2 MTR-1 R PRO-1 Targets tracked 1 Up to 3 Up to 3 Multi-zone tracking  3 zones  3 zones Still detection  Excellent  Limited  With LD2412 add-on PoE / Ethernet Horizontal FoV 120° 120° 120°150° with LD2412 Vertical FoV 70° 70° 70° Power USB-C USB-C PoE (802.3af) or USB-C mmWave module LD2410B LD2450 LD2450, optional LD2412

docs.title: Field of view
docs.text:
Each sensor watches a cone that fans out in front of it, like the beam of a flashlight. The cone is wider side to side than it is top to bottom.

120° sensor Horizontal FoV: 120° side to side (up to 150° on the R PRO-1 with the LD2412) 70° sensor Vertical FoV: 70° top to bottom

docs.title: Zone tracking (MTR-1 and R PRO-1)
docs.text:
The LD2450 module tracks up to three moving targets and reports each one's X and Y position. You draw rectangular zones in those coordinates to decide where presence counts.

Setting LD2450 zone coordinates

  • X1 must always be less than X2, and Y1 must always be less than Y2.
  • The X axis is where you can get tripped up, especially when both values are negative: -3456 is less than -2345.
  • The Y axis is easier since it is never negative.
  • The Plotly chart still draws the rectangles even if the X1/X2 or Y1/Y2 values are reversed, so double-check the order.
  • Zones cannot overlap.

To set up zones, follow the guide for your device: MTR-1 zones or R PRO-1 (LD2450) zones.

Draw zones on a live map

Instead of typing coordinates, you can draw zones over the radar's live targets and get an occupancy sensor for each one. In Home Assistant, the Apollo mmWave dashboard has a zone map for every MTR-1 and R PRO-1, where you draw rectangles, ellipses, or polygons.

docs.title: Still detection (MSR-2 and R PRO-1 with the LD2412)
docs.text: The MSR-2, and the R PRO-1 once you add the optional LD2412, detect a single target using gates: fixed distance bands rather than X and Y coordinates. This is what makes them so good at catching someone who is barely moving, like sleeping or sitting still. To add the second module to an R PRO-1, follow Add the LD2412 to your R PRO-1.

docs.title: Reducing false triggers
docs.text:
mmWave detects motion, so things that move or reflect the radar signal can trigger a sensor even when no one is there. Common culprits include:

  • Mirrors and other reflective surfaces
  • Fans and spinning blades
  • Moving air from HVAC vents and registers
  • Curtains, blinds, or plants swaying in a draft

The MSR-2 (LD2410) and the R PRO-1 with the LD2412 let you tune the sensitivity of each gate, so you can dial down the distance bands where a fan or vent sits and tune these false positives out. With the LD2450 (MTR-1 and R PRO-1) you can instead draw your zones to exclude the problem area.

See the Radar Tuning guide to adjust sensitivity.

docs.title: 1. How much power do your sensors use?
docs.text: • All Apollo sensors use 1amp or less, some of them 350-500mA.

docs.title: 2. What all can the MSR-2 LD2410B mmWave sensor go through?
docs.text: • It can reliably go through drywall and some other materials such as thin wood and some couches.

docs.title: 3. My MSR-2 is triggering and no one is there.
docs.text: • We have seen this happen before. Please first try to restart your radar, then factory reset your radar, then try a factory firmware flash. We also see success with users re-seating their LD2410B mmWave sensor.

docs.title: 3. How do I reset my Wi-Fi?
docs.text: • Plug in your device then hold down the boot button for 10 seconds. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

docs.title: 4. My lux sensor doesn't seem to be working how do I fix it?
docs.text: • The default update_interval is 60 seconds which isn't great for automations revolving around measuring lux values. Please follow this short guide to edit the lux update_interval down to a more responsive 3-5 seconds.

docs.title: 5. Do I need to push the "Clean" button for my AIR-1 or set up an automation for it?
docs.text: • No, your AIR-1 will self-clean once a week per this recommended documentation from the manufacturer.

docs.title: 6. Can your sensors be used with OpenHAB?
docs.text: • Yes, please install this binding and then restart OpenHAB and our devices will show up to configure!

docs.title: 7. I am getting the error "Failed to import device" in ESPHome Dashboard when trying to adopt my Apollo device.
docs.text:
• Make sure you have enough free space in Home Assistant. Protip: check for old backups you can delete!
  • If your space is not an issue then please reboot or even try reinstalling the ESPHome Device Builder app and see if that helps!

docs.title: 8. My CO2 values are way off from my other Apollo devices.
Answer 8:
docs.text: • If your sensor is exposed to high levels of vibrations or too much airflow, the SCD40 CO2 sensor will have issues working properly. https://sensirion.com/products/catalog/SCD40

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Apollo Automation is a small startup based in Lexington, Kentucky, dedicated to creating innovative, high-quality, and affordable smart home automation hardware. Founded in 2023 by a group of friends, the company was born out of frustration with existing solutions that lacked transparency and customization options. Named after Trevor’s dog, Apollo, the team set out to build products that offer complete local control without reliance on cloud services or subscriptions!

Apollo Automation focuses on designing and manufacturing open-source hardware and software that puts control in the hands of its users. The company engages closely with the Home Assistant community, providing fully customizable devices that integrate with the platform. Their mission is to empower customers to build and control their own smart homes with ease, reliability, and privacy. Through monthly livestreams and an active Discord community, Apollo Automation remains accessible, transparent, and driven by user feedback, ensuring that their products meet the evolving needs of their customers.

docs.title: Temp and humidity calibration and offset examples
Simple and advanced temperature and humidity offsets
docs.text: Your Apollo device's temperature and humidity readings can differ from the true value. This page explains why, then shows how to correct them: simple offsets you set from the device page, or advanced template sensors that estimate the true values from all of your readings.

docs.title: Why readings can be off
docs.text:
The BME280 and SCD40 sensors are known for measuring temperature and humidity precisely. Like any sensor, though, they can sometimes give inaccurate readings. One significant cause is heat from the ESP chip, which warms the air inside the enclosure and skews the readings.

Temperature and humidity are also linked. When the air temperature rises, the air can hold more moisture, which can lower the relative humidity. When the temperature falls, the air can hold less moisture, so the humidity rises. This relationship plays a big part in how the sensors detect and interpret readings, which makes accurate readings even more important.

docs.title: Add simple offsets
docs.text:
Add two offset boxes to your device so you can correct its SCD40 temperature and humidity readings from Home Assistant.

1. In ESPHome Device Builder, open your device's YAML and paste the following at the bottom:

sensor:
  - id: !extend scd40
    humidity:
      name: "Humidity"
      id: "humidity"
      filters:
        - lambda: return x - id(scd40_humidity_offset).state;
    temperature:
      name: "Temperature"
      id: "temperature"
      filters:
        - lambda: return x - id(scd40_temperature_offset).state;
number:
  - platform: template
    name: SCD40 Humidity Offset
    id: scd40_humidity_offset
    restore_value: true
    initial_value: -18.86
    min_value: -70.0
    max_value: 70.0
    entity_category: "CONFIG"
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    optimistic: true
    update_interval: never
    step: 0.1
    mode: box
  - platform: template
    name: SCD40 Temperature Offset
    id: scd40_temperature_offset
    restore_value: true
    initial_value: 14.54
    min_value: -70.0
    max_value: 70.0
    entity_category: "CONFIG"
    unit_of_measurement: "°C"
    optimistic: true
    update_interval: never
    step: 0.1
    mode: box

2. Click Save, then Install.

3. In Home Assistant, open your device's page in the ESPHome integration. Fill in your offsets in the two new boxes, SCD40 Humidity Offset and SCD40 Temperature Offset.

Give the new offsets up to 1 minute to take effect. The next section explains how to choose the right values.

docs.title: How the offsets work
docs.text:
You can adjust the BME280 and SCD40 Temperature Offset entities by hand to match the conditions in your home. The firmware subtracts each offset from the raw temperature or humidity reading, and the result is what the sensor's entity shows in Home Assistant. For example, the scd40_temperature entity equals the raw SCD40 temperature reading minus scd40_offset.

The default offsets come from our NIST-certified thermometer and are calibrated for our environment, so they might not be accurate in your home. To fine-tune them, compare your sensor with a reference thermometer and adjust the offsets by the difference between the two readings.

You may also notice the bme280_humidity_calibrated, scd40_humidity_calibrated, bme280_temperature_calibrated, and scd40_temperature_calibrated entities. These use the linear filter in the ESPHome firmware to adjust the readings based on data we collected. Because every home is different, they might not always be precise either.

docs.title: Advanced: model the relationship between sensors
docs.text:
Another way to get accurate readings is to model how the ESP chip temperature and the other sensors relate to a reference temperature. A template sensor in Home Assistant does this for you: it combines your sensor's live readings into an estimated true temperature and humidity, using either a decision tree or our regression coefficients (the multipliers in the example below).

Add the example below to your Home Assistant configuration YAML. Its entity IDs belong to one Apollo MSR-1 (apollo_msr_1_a79e24), so replace them with your own device's entity IDs.

sensor:
  - platform: template
    sensors:
      estimated_reference_temperature:
        friendly_name: "Estimated Temperature"
        unit_of_measurement: '°C'
        value_template: >
          {{
            0.3228 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_esp_temperature') | float +
            0.8702 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature') | float +
            -0.1285 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature') | float +
            -0.0491 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity') | float +
            0.0851 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity') | float +
            -17.4840
          }}


      estimated_reference_humidity:
        friendly_name: "Estimated Humidity"
        unit_of_measurement: '%'
        value_template: >
          {{
            -1.2468 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_esp_temperature') | float +
            -2.1959 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature') | float +
            2.9604 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature') | float +
            0.2380 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity') | float +
            1.8283 * states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity') | float +
            40.1686
          }}

docs.title: Collect your own data
docs.text:
To gather your own data with a reference sensor and an MSR-1 in your home, we recommend logging the readings to a CSV file. The YAML below logs once a minute to match the reference sensor. As its comments show, the notify entry goes in configuration.yaml and the automation goes in automations.yaml.

#Configuration.yaml
notify:
  - platform: file
    name: sensor_csv_log
    filename: /config/sensor_log.csv
    timestamp: False

#Automations.yaml
  - id: log_sensor_data_to_csv
    alias: "Log Sensor Data to CSV"
    trigger:
      platform: time_pattern
      minutes: "/1"  # Log data every minute to match reference sensor
    action:
      - service: notify.sensor_csv_log
        data_template:
          message: >
            {{ now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_esp_temperature') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_temperature_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_humidity_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_bme280_humidity_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('number.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_scd40_temperature_offset') | default('NA') }},
            {{ states('sensor.apollo_msr_1_a79e24_uptime') | default('NA') }}

docs.title: Advanced accuracy with GPIO
docs.text: For the highest accuracy, connect a temperature and humidity sensor to the exposed mezzanine connector on the back of your Apollo board. This modification can dramatically improve both temperature and humidity readings, giving you data that's as accurate as possible.

docs.title: Apollo battery devices - Awake HA helper
Keep your sensor awake with a Home Assistant helper
docs.text:
When an apollo_ota_mode toggle in Home Assistant is on, your Apollo battery devices stay awake so you can update them. In this guide you create that toggle, then add an automation that turns it off again after one hour.

This keeps every Apollo device awake

While apollo_ota_mode is on, none of your Apollo devices go back to sleep. Finish the second part of this guide to create an automation that turns the helper off after it has been on for one hour.

docs.title: Create the OTA mode toggle
docs.text:
Start by creating the toggle helper and switching it on.

1. Go to Settings → Devices & services and select the Helpers tab at the top. Or use the button below to go straight there.

2. Select Create helper in the bottom right.

3. Scroll to the bottom of the list and select Toggle.

4. Name the toggle apollo_ota_mode, choose an icon such as mdi:sleep-off, and click Create.

5. Search the helpers list for apollo_ota_mode and click the helper that appears.

6. Switch the toggle on.

OTA mode is now on. The next time your Apollo device reboots or wakes up on its wake timer, it stays awake instead of going back to sleep.

docs.title: Turn OTA mode off after one hour
docs.text:
Next, create an automation that switches apollo_ota_mode off once it has been on for one hour, so you never leave your devices awake by accident.

1. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes and click Create automation.

2. Click Add trigger, then select Entity.

3. Select State.

4. In the Entity box, enter apollo_ota_mode. Set To to On, and enter 1 in the hours box under For. This trigger fires once apollo_ota_mode has been on for one hour.

5. Scroll down to Then do, click Add action, search for input boolean, and choose Input boolean: Turn off.

6. Click Choose entity and select apollo_ota_mode.

You're done. Turn apollo_ota_mode on whenever you want to update your devices, and the automation turns it off for you after one hour.

docs.title: Prevent Sleep
docs.text:
Put your sensors to sleep!

All of our battery powered devices are able to go to sleep to save battery life. Our non-battery sensor devices like the AIR-1 and PLT-1 can also sleep to get better temperature and humidity measurements.

The temperature offsets needed will be much lower for your sensors as the microcontroller will not put off as much heat when it is sleeping and then waking for short periods to report the sensor values.

You'll set how long your sensor sleeps, then turn off Prevent Sleep so it can start sleeping.

1. Head to the ESPHome Integrations page and click on the name of your Apollo device.

2. Scroll down until you see Prevent Sleep and Sleep Duration.

3. Type in how long you want your sensor to sleep in the Sleep Duration box. Check the unit next to the box: it is minutes on the AIR-1 (default 5), PLT-1 (default 5), and TEMP-1 (default 8), and hours on the BTN-1 (default 24), PLT-1B (default 12), and TEMP-1B (default 12). We recommend leaving the default values.

Read this before turning off Prevent Sleep!

When "Prevent Sleep" is toggled off, your sensor will immediately begin sleeping. Please make sure you are ready to make this sensor sleep before toggling off prevent sleep.

4. When you are ready, toggle off Prevent Sleep and your sensor will go to sleep. It will wake up on the Sleep Duration interval from step 3. If you need to keep your sensor awake, head to our OTA Awake helper tutorial!

5. You can wake your sensor by following this guide or you can power cycle your device. If there is a battery in it, the battery will need to be removed or the reset button pressed.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The AIR-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your AIR-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.
