docs.title: How to add temp and humidity from SCD40
How to add temp and humidity from SCD40
docs.text:
You add YAML in ESPHome Builder to get SCD40 temperature and humidity entities, with offsets you can adjust in Home Assistant.

1. Select the ESPHome Builder in the sidebar then click "EDIT" on the device you want to change. If it isn't in your sidebar, the button below opens the app.

2. Copy the YAML below and put it at the bottom on a new line with no spaces before it.

This example is for the AIR-1

It also works on the MSR-2 once the CO2 addon is installed. The MTR-1 firmware already includes SCD40 Temperature and SCD40 Humidity entities with their offsets (disabled by default), so on an MTR-1 with the CO2 addon, enable those entities on the device page instead of adding this YAML.

sensor:
  - id: !extend scd40
    temperature:
      name: "SCD40 Temperature"
      id: "temperature"
      filters:
        - lambda: return x - id(scd40_temperature_offset).state;
    humidity:
      name: "SCD40 Humidity"
      id: "humidity"
      filters:
        - lambda: return x - id(scd40_humidity_offset).state;

number:
  - platform: template
    name: SCD40 Temperature Offset
    id: scd40_temperature_offset
    restore_value: true
    initial_value: 14.54
    min_value: -70.0
    max_value: 70.0
    entity_category: "CONFIG"
    unit_of_measurement: "°C"
    optimistic: true
    update_interval: never
    step: 0.1
    mode: box
  - platform: template
    name: SCD40 Humidity Offset
    id: scd40_humidity_offset
    restore_value: true
    initial_value: -18.86
    min_value: -70.0
    max_value: 70.0
    entity_category: "CONFIG"
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    optimistic: true
    update_interval: never
    step: 0.1
    mode: box

3. In the top right of the same screen click "SAVE" and then "INSTALL".

4. Once you see "INFO OTA successful" you are done. Click "STOP" to exit.

5. Once you are finished, you will have two new boxes inside the Home Assistant ESPHome integration device page for your device where you can fill in an offset. Give them up to 1 minute to take effect!

docs.title: ESPHome integration - part 1
docs.text:
You rename the device in the ESPHome integration, then update its entity IDs to match.

1. Click the button below to open the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome).

2. On the device you want to rename, click the pencil icon and enter a new name. Click Update, then select the name you just created.

3. Click the 3 dots in the top right and select Recreate Entity IDs then select Update.

It's okay if there are some entities that cannot be regenerated!

You will likely run into a popup showing that 2 entity IDs cannot be regenerated because they are not available. This is fine, we can manually fix these later or ignore them as they are disabled entities and not expected to be used.

4. Scroll down to the Diagnostic section and click on +2 disabled entities. Select each entity and replace the old name with the new name. Make sure to replace spaces with underscores as shown in the gif below!

docs.title: ESPHome integration - part 2
docs.text:
This section only changes the device name shown in the ESPHome integration page. It is safe to skip, but we recommend doing it to keep naming consistent.

1. Click the button below to open the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome).

2. On the device you would like to rename, click the 3 dots icon and select Rename and type in your new name then click OK.

The next section is not necessary unless you use ESPHome Device Builder!

The next section is for ESPHome device builder which is for tinkerers and advanced users to take control of their device and edit the yaml. Please skip the next section if you do not use ESPHome Device Builder!

docs.title: ESPHome Device Builder
docs.text:
You change the device's hostname and friendly name in ESPHome Device Builder, then re-add it to Home Assistant under the new name.

1. Make sure you are already using the ESPHome Device Builder app as gone over in the getting started wiki articles.

2. Click the 3 dots next to your new Apollo device and select Rename hostname then enter in the new name of your sensor and click Rename. This cannot have any spaces or underscores only hyphens, numbers, and lowercase letters such as "smart-keys". Once it finishes it will say OTA successful and you can click close to get back to the main dashboard.

We are now ready to rename the friendly_name to a new name such as Smart Keys

This can have spaces and capital letters and will be the same name Home Assistant will give the device and all entity names!

3. Click Edit then replace the text after friendly_name with your new name such as Smart Keys. Click Save and Install in the top right once you are done with the rename and it will save and install. Once it finishes it will say OTA successful and you can click close to get back to the main dashboard.

4. Finally we should delete the device from the ESPHome Integration in Home Assistant and then add it back! Head to the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome). Next to the device you would like to remove, click the three dots and then Delete.

5. Scroll up and add the new auto-discovered device. The name should be the same Friendly name you put in the ESPHome Device builder and all of your entities should be the correct name to begin with!

docs.title: Switch to beta firmware
docs.text: Beta firmware gets new features and fixes before they reach Stable. It's a great way to help us test, and you can switch back at any time.

docs.title: With the Firmware Channel setting
docs.text:
This is the simpler way. Use it if your device has a Firmware Channel setting on its device page, like the CAST-1.

1. Open your device in Home Assistant: go to Settings > Devices & services > ESPHome and select it.

2. Under Configuration, set Firmware Channel to Beta.

3. Select Press next to Firmware Update.

4. Wait about a minute while it installs and restarts. It's done when Firmware Update shows Up-to-date.

Switching back to Stable

Set Firmware Channel to Stable and select Press next to Firmware Update again. Your device installs the current stable release, even if it's older than the beta.

No Press button?

Some devices only have the Firmware Update entity. Select it and choose Install once the beta version shows up.

docs.title: With ESPHome Device Builder
docs.text:
Use this if your device doesn't have a Firmware Channel setting, or if you build its firmware yourself.

1. In Home Assistant open the ESPHome Device Builder app.

Make sure you are running the latest version of ESPHome

You should be fully up to date with the ESPHome Device Builder before updating our sensors for ideal performance and ease of troubleshooting!

2. Find the sensor you want to edit and click the "EDIT".

This is code and requires you to follow the directions carefully.

Editing the YAML here means even a space matters. Follow the guide exactly as shown and ask questions if you need help!

3. Look for the line that starts with packages and the line below it and put a # in front of each line as shown in the second image below.

4. Select your product below, copy the code, and paste it below the two lines you just commented out.

    refresh: 1min

Do not change the name or friendly_name!

Changing the name can cause the install to fail due to mDNS issues. If you want to rename your device, follow this guide instead.

5. Click save then install in the top right and click Wirelessly when prompted.

6. Once you see "INFO OTA successful" you are done. Click "STOP" in the bottom right to exit.

docs.title: Connection issues
docs.text:
If your Apollo device keeps dropping offline or won't stay connected to your Wi-Fi, work through these checks in order.

1. Try a few different combinations of power cord and power brick. Power quality matters a lot more than you'd think.

2. On your phone or PC, open your Wi-Fi settings and look for the sensor's hotspot. If the hotspot shows up, the sensor isn't connected to a network. Connect it to your Wi-Fi through the hotspot again.

3. Check your router's list of connected devices. Your device shows up with the Apollo name and a 6-digit hex value taken from the end of its MAC address.

4. Turn off power save mode in ESPHome. The steps are in the next section.

docs.title: Turn off Wi-Fi power save mode
docs.text:
The Wi-Fi interface of every ESP chip offers three power save modes that cut the power spent on Wi-Fi. Some of them can lower the ESP's power use, but they generally make the Wi-Fi connection less reliable. The highest power saving mode causes frequent disconnections from the router.

  • NONE (least power saving, default for ESP8266)
  • LIGHT (default for ESP32)
  • HIGH (most power saving)

For the most reliable connection, set the mode to none. In your device's YAML file, the setting sits inside the wifi: section, where # ... stands for the lines already in that section:

wifi:
  # ...
  power_save_mode: none

Your sensor runs warmer

Turning off power save mode makes the sensor's internal temperature increase.

Follow these steps to turn power save mode off from the ESPHome app in Home Assistant.

1. Open the ESPHome app from your Home Assistant sidebar and click Edit under the device you want to change. If the app isn't in your sidebar, the button below opens it.

2. Add power_save_mode: none under the wifi: section of your device's YAML file, indented to line up with the other lines in that section. If your file doesn't have a wifi: line, add one. Then click Save and Install.

wifi:
  power_save_mode: none

Your device should now have a stronger connection to your Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Firmware updates not appearing
docs.text:
Apollo devices check for new firmware by downloading a small manifest file from apolloautomation.github.io over HTTPS. If the Firmware Update entity in Home Assistant always shows up to date even though a newer release exists, work through the list below.

1. Make sure the device can reach the internet.

  • The device needs outbound HTTPS (port 443) to apolloautomation.github.io. If your sensors live on an isolated IoT VLAN that blocks traffic leaving the network, the update check fails silently and the entity shows up to date forever.
  • To confirm, watch the device logs (ESPHome Device Builder → Logs, or the device's web page). A blocked check logs Failed to fetch manifest with ESP_ERR_HTTP_CONNECT.
  • Allow the device to reach apolloautomation.github.io on port 443 in your firewall rules, then reboot the device.

2. Give it a moment after a reboot, or update your firmware.

  • On older firmware the very first update check after a boot can be skipped if Wi-Fi isn't connected yet, and the next check only happens about 6 hours later. Newer firmware checks as soon as the network connects.
  • If the entity looks stale right after a reboot, either wait, reboot once more while the network is up, or update to the latest firmware release.

3. Devices adopted in the ESPHome Device Builder update differently.

  • If you have taken control of the device's configuration in the ESPHome Device Builder, Home Assistant manages updates through the Device Builder instead of the manufacturer Firmware Update entity. That is expected. Build and install updates from the Device Builder in that case.

Battery devices

Battery powered sensors only check for updates while they are awake and connected. If the update never appears, keep the device awake (see Prevent Sleep) and reboot it once.

docs.title: OPNsense mDNS auto discover issue
docs.text:
If mDNS is unchecked then Home Assistant and ESPHome will not auto discover new devices

If you have different networks that Home Assistant and ESPHome devices are on, then you will need mDNS working across both networks and firewall rules allowing access between them. Below is a guide for installing the mDNS Repeater plugin on OPNsense to fix this issue.

Install the mDNS Repeater

1. Click System -> Click Firmware -> Click Plugins -> Search for "mdns" -> Click the “+” symbol to install os-mdns-repeater.

2. Confirm that the installation was successful.

3. Refresh the page and then go to Services -> mDNS Repeater (if it isn't there after refreshing your screen, verify the plugin install was successful.)-> Check off "enable" -> select your networks containing Home Assistant / ESPHome IoT devices -> click save.

Now the Home Assistant/ESPHome auto-discover issue should be fixed!

docs.text:

Skip this step unless you took control of your device with the ESPHome Device Builder app!

This step is only necessary for advanced users who added the device to the ESPHome device builder to edit the yaml and customize the device. Please skip to the next step if you are only using the ESPHome or Apollo Automation integration!

2. On the device you would like to remove, click the three dots and select "Delete" then click Delete to confirm.

docs.title: Ubiquiti UniFi mDNS auto discover issue
Ubiquiti UniFi mDNS auto discover issue
docs.text:
If mDNS is unchecked then Home Assistant and ESPHome will not auto discover new devices

If your Home Assistant (or Homey) hub and your ESPHome devices are on different networks, you need mDNS working across both networks and firewall rules that allow traffic between them. Below are guides for fixing this from your PC or the UniFi mobile app.

docs.title: Method 1: Browser
docs.text:
You can turn on Multicast DNS for your Default Network from a browser on your PC.

1. Log into your UniFi network through your default IP address which is usually http://192.168.1.1

2. Select Network.

3. Select Settings.

4. Select Networks.

5. Select the Default Network

6. Check Multicast DNS

7. Now the Home Assistant/ESPHome auto-discover issue should be fixed!

docs.title: Method 2: UniFi mobile app
docs.text:
You can also turn on Multicast DNS for your Default Network from the UniFi mobile app.

1. Open the UniFi app.

2. Tap Settings/Gear Icon

3. Tap Networks

4. Tap Default Network

5. Tap the Multicast DNS slider

6. Now the Home Assistant/ESPHome auto-discover issue should be fixed!

docs.title: How to edit your sensor's CO2 update interval
How to edit your sensor's CO2 update interval
docs.text:
This guide will show you how to edit the CO2 updates down to 5 seconds, which is the fastest the SCD40 sensor supports. This is useful for use-cases that benefit from smoother graphs or quicker reaction to CO2 changes, such as grow rooms, offices, or sleep spaces.

Your sensor is defaulting to 60 seconds for updates to the state of the CO2 sensor.

This is the default for all ESPHome devices using the SCD40 because it uses less Wi-Fi airtime fairness and writes less to your Home Assistant Database. 5 seconds is the minimum. The SCD40 hardware cannot produce a new reading faster than that.

Sensor response time

Even at a 5 second update interval, the SCD40 itself takes roughly 90 seconds to fully reflect a real change in CO2 levels in the air. The number on your dashboard will refresh every 5 seconds, but a true spike (for example, someone walking into the room) will ramp in over a couple of minutes. That is normal sensor behavior, not a configuration issue. See the Sensirion SCD4x datasheet for full specs.

1. Select the ESPHome Builder in the sidebar then click "EDIT" on the device you want to change.

2. Copy this code and enter it exactly as shown in the next step. Make sure there are no extra spaces or any other characters. It needs to look exactly like the example in the next step.

#CO2 sensor update interval
sensor:
  - platform: scd4x
    id: !extend scd40
    update_interval: 5s

3. Paste the code you copied in step 2 below your sensor's existing yaml.

4. In the top right of the same screen click "SAVE" and then "INSTALL".

5. Once you see "INFO OTA successful" you are done. Click "STOP" to exit.

6. Once that is finished your sensor should now be reporting CO2 at your new update_interval such as 5 seconds!

docs.title: How to edit your sensor's lux update interval
How to edit your sensor's lux update interval
docs.text:
This guide will show you how to edit the lux updates down to 5 seconds.

Your sensor is defaulting to 60 seconds for updates to the state of the lux sensor.

This is the default for all ESPHome devices using lux because it uses less Wi-Fi airtime fairness and writes less to your Home Assistant Database. Suggested not to go below 5 seconds.

1. Select the ESPHome Builder in the sidebar then click "EDIT" on the device you want to change.

2. Copy this code and enter it exactly as shown in the next step. Make sure there are no extra spaces or any other characters. It needs to look exactly like the example in the next step.

#LUX sensor update interval
sensor:
  - platform: ltr390
    id: !extend ltr_390
    update_interval: 5s

3. Paste the code you copied in step 2 below your sensor's existing yaml as shown below.

4. In the top right of the same screen click "SAVE" and then "INSTALL".

5. Once you see "INFO OTA successful" you are done. Click "STOP" to exit.

6. Once that is finished your sensor should now be reporting at your new update_interval such as 5 seconds!

docs.title: Control an LED strip with the GPIO Header
Control an LED strip with the GPIO header
docs.text:
The GPIO Header addon brings the MSR-2's spare pins out to a row of headers, so you can hang your own hardware off the sensor. This guide wires a WS2812B strip to one of those pins and gets it into Home Assistant as its own light entity, color picker and effects included.

The same steps work on any Apollo device with a mezzanine port, including the MTR-1 and AIR-1. Click any photo to see it full size.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• An Apollo MSR-2, or any Apollo device with a mezzanine port.
  • The Apollo GPIO Header addon.
  • A WS2812B (neopixel) RGB strip. SK6812 RGBW strips work too.
  • Three male-to-male DuPont wires. A set comes with the header.
  • A USB-C cable and power brick.

Watch the current draw

The 5V pin supplies up to 350mA. A meter of 60 LEDs at full white draws far more than that, so anything longer than a short strip needs its own 5V supply. You can power the MSR-2 itself from the 5V and GND pins instead of the USB-C port, but use one or the other, never both.

docs.title: Choosing a data pin
docs.text: IO2, IO4, IO6, and IO7 are free for LED data, and you can drive more than one strip by giving each its own pin. IO18 and IO19 are unavailable, and IO0 and IO1 are reserved for I2C sensors. This guide uses IO7, plus the 5V and GND pins at the top of the header for power.

docs.title: Attaching the GPIO header
docs.text:
You'll seat the GPIO Header on your sensor's mezzanine connector, then fit the blue back plate that came with the addon.

  1. Unplug the MSR-2 from power and pull the back plate off.

  2. Line up the X marked on the MSR-2 PCB with the X on the GPIO Header. Both face the same way.

  3. Press the header down onto the small black mezzanine connector, then check it sits flat with no gap along either edge.

  4. Slide the blue GPIO back plate that came with the addon over the sensor and press until it clicks. If it needs more than light pressure, stop and check the orientation rather than forcing it.

docs.title: Wiring the strip
docs.text:
You'll run three wires from the header to your strip, then check which way the data flows.

  1. Run three wires from the header to the strip: 5V, GND, and data. Matching the colors to the strip's own wiring saves a lot of squinting later, so use red for 5V, white for GND, and green for data on IO7.

  2. Plug the other end into the strip. Most strips come with a JST-SM pigtail carrying the same three colors, so the wires match up directly. The connector is rated to 3A.

  3. Check the direction before you power anything on. Arrows printed along the strip show which way data flows, and they need to point away from the MSR-2.

A dab of hot glue across the outer shells of the three DuPont connectors stiffens them into a single plug. (1)

  1. Keep glue out of the header's female pins. It will ruin the addon.

docs.title: Adding the strip to your YAML
docs.text:
The MSR-2 knows nothing about the strip until you tell it how many LEDs there are and which pin they sit on.

  1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app, find your MSR-2, and click Edit.

  2. Add the block below at the bottom of the file, flush with the left margin so light: lines up with packages: and wifi:. Set num_leds to the number of LEDs on your strip, and change pin if you wired to a different port.

    light:
  - platform: esp32_rmt_led_strip
    id: bed_led
    name: "Bed LED"
    pin: GPIO7
    chipset: WS2812
    channel_colors: GRB
    num_leds: 60
    default_transition_length: 0s
    effects:
      - pulse:
          name: "Slow Pulse"
          transition_length: 1000ms
          update_interval: 1000ms
          min_brightness: 50%
          max_brightness: 100%
      - pulse:
          name: "Fast Pulse"
          transition_length: 100ms
          update_interval: 100ms
          min_brightness: 50%
          max_brightness: 100%
      - addressable_rainbow:

  3. Check that the editor shows no red error markers.

  4. Click Save, then Install, and pick Wirelessly. ESPHome compiles the firmware and sends it to the MSR-2. The first build takes a few minutes.

Older versions of this guide set rmt_channel: 1 on the light. ESPHome dropped that option, and leaving it in now fails validation, so the block above does not use it.

The ESPHome light effects reference covers everything else you can add under effects:, including addressable_scan.

docs.title: Controlling it from Home Assistant
docs.text:
Once the install finishes, the MSR-2 exposes a new light entity called Bed LED.

Click the entity name to open the light card. The color wheel covers the full range, and the effects list holds the two pulses and the rainbow from the YAML above.

That's all folks! Thanks to Smart Home Sellout for putting this tutorial together.

docs.title: Minimize activity spam
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave sensors report frequently by design, which can cause internal radar entities like target direction, target count, and zone occupancy to flood your Home Assistant Activity log. Adding a logbook.exclude block to your configuration.yaml tells Home Assistant to stop recording those entities.

Home Assistant Activity Documentation

For more details on activity filtering, see the Home Assistant Logbook integration docs.

1. Open your Home Assistant configuration.yaml file.

2. Select your sensor below and copy the snippet, then paste it into configuration.yaml.

MSR-1 / MSR-2MTR-1R PRO-1 
logbook:
  exclude:
    entity_globs:
      # LD2410
      - binary_sensor.*radar_moving_target
      - binary_sensor.*radar_still_target
      - binary_sensor.*radar_zone*occupancy

logbook:
  exclude:
    entity_globs:
      # LD2450
      - binary_sensor.*ld2450_*
      - sensor.*target_*_direction*
      - sensor.*target_count*

logbook:
  exclude:
    entity_globs:
      # LD2450
      - binary_sensor.*ld2450_*
      - sensor.*target_*_direction*
      - sensor.*target_count*
      # LD2412
      - binary_sensor.*ld2412_*

If you already have a logbook: section

Do not add a second logbook: key. Merge the exclude.entity_globs list into your existing section.

3. Save configuration.yaml and restart Home Assistant (Settings → System → Restart).

4. Open Activity in Home Assistant to confirm the noisy entities no longer appear.

docs.title: Apollo sensors + SmartThings direct control
docs.text:
Compatible Devices

This works with any Apollo ESPHome device running ESPHome: MTR-1, MSR-2, AIR-1, and others. The OAuth2 token block is fully device-agnostic: swap the packages: line for your device.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Since early 2025, Samsung SmartThings no longer supports permanent Personal Access Tokens (PAT). All API access now requires OAuth2 tokens that expire every 24 hours. This makes direct ESP32 integrations tricky, but not impossible.

This tutorial shows how to make your Apollo MTR-1 control SmartThings lights directly, with zero external servers, no Home Assistant, and no intermediate hub. The ESP32 handles the full OAuth2 token lifecycle autonomously, including persisting the refresh token across reboots using NVS flash storage. Once set up, it runs forever without any manual intervention.

What you will achieve:

  • Zone-based presence detection on the MTR-1 that triggers SmartThings lights on/off instantly
  • Fully autonomous OAuth2 token renewal every 20 hours
  • Token persistence across power cuts and reboots via NVS flash

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Apollo MTR-1 (the same pattern works for MSR-2, AIR-1, and other Apollo ESPHome devices)
  • A Samsung SmartThings account
  • ESPHome installed on your PC (pip install esphome)
  • One or more SmartThings-connected lights or switches
  • About 30 minutes for the initial setup

docs.title: Part 1: Create a SmartThings OAuth2 app
docs.text:
This is a one-time setup. You need to register an OAuth2 client in the SmartThings Developer Workspace to get your client_id and client_secret.

Step 1. Create a project:

  1. Go to https://developer.smartthings.com and sign in with your Samsung account
  2. Click "Create Project" → select "Automation for SmartThings"
  3. Give it any name, e.g. "Apollo MTR-1"

Step 2. Add an OAuth2 Client:

  1. Inside your project, go to Automation → OAuth2
  2. Set the Redirect URI to: https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback
  3. Set scopes: r:devices:* w:devices:* x:devices:*
  4. Save. You will receive a Client ID and a Client Secret. Note both down.

docs.title: Part 2: Get your first token pair (one-time via browser)
docs.text:
SmartThings requires a one-time browser-based authorization. After this, the ESP32 renews everything automatically.

Step 1. Open this URL in your browser (replace YOUR_CLIENT_ID):

https://api.smartthings.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&scope=x:devices:*+w:devices:*+r:devices:*&response_type=code&redirect_uri=https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback

Log in with your Samsung account and authorize the app. You will be redirected to a URL like:

https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback?code=XXXXXX

Copy the code value. It expires in about 60 seconds. Act fast.

Step 2. Exchange the code for tokens (PowerShell on Windows):

$b64 = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes("YOUR_CLIENT_ID:YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"))
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri "https://api.smartthings.com/oauth/token" `
  -Headers @{Authorization="Basic $b64"} `
  -ContentType "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" `
  -Body "grant_type=authorization_code&code=YOUR_CODE&redirect_uri=https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback"

You will receive a response like:

access_token  : xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
refresh_token : yyyyyyyy-yyyy-yyyy-yyyy-yyyyyyyyyyyy
expires_in    : 86399

Save both tokens. You will enter them into the ESPHome config exactly once.

How to generate the Base64 credential string you will need later:

[Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes("YOUR_CLIENT_ID:YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"))

Save this Base64 string too.

docs.title: Part 3: Create virtual switches and find device IDs
docs.text:
To map your physical MTR-1 zones to SmartThings routines without a hub, we need Virtual Switches. The MTR-1 will send ON/OFF commands to these virtual switches, which you can then use in SmartThings to trigger your actual lights.

Step 1. Create Virtual Switches

Log into your account @ my.smartthings.com > advanced > add device > cloud > switch

Step 2. Find Your SmartThings Device IDs

In the my.smartthings webapp you can copy your new virtual device IDs.

For each light or switch you want to control, you need its Device ID (format: xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx).

docs.title: Part 4: The ESPHome configuration
docs.text:
Below is the complete, production-tested YAML. Replace all YOUR_* placeholders with your actual values.

Key Design Decisions

  1. wifi: on_connect instead of on_boot: the ESP-IDF HTTP stack is not ready at boot time. Using on_connect with a 15-second delay guarantees the network is fully available before the first token refresh fires.
  2. script: mode: single: prevents a second token refresh from being triggered while the first one is still running. This is critical during router reboots or mesh Wi-Fi reconnects where wifi: on_connect can fire multiple times in rapid succession.
  3. restore_value: yes on st_refresh_token: saves the latest refresh token to NVS flash after every successful renewal. It survives reboots and power cuts. The initial_value in the YAML is only ever used on the very first flash.
  4. body: !lambda |-: plain string bodies are silently ignored by the ESP-IDF HTTP client. The lambda syntax is required for the POST body to actually be sent.
substitutions:
  name: "apollo-mtr1"
  friendly_name: "Apollo MTR-1"

esphome:
  name: ${name}
packages:
  - github://ApolloAutomation/MTR-1/Integrations/ESPHome/MTR-1_Factory.yaml

http_request:
  id: http_request_id
  verify_ssl: false
  timeout: 10s
  buffer_size_rx: 1024
  buffer_size_tx: 512

globals:
  - id: st_access_token
    type: std::string
    restore_value: no
    initial_value: '"Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN"'
  - id: st_refresh_token
    type: std::string
    restore_value: yes        # saved to NVS flash, survives reboots
    initial_value: '"YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN"'

script:
  - id: refresh_oauth_token
    mode: single              # ignore duplicate calls while refresh is in progress
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> Refresh START");
      - http_request.send:
          method: POST
          url: "https://api.smartthings.com/oauth/token"
          capture_response: true
          max_response_buffer_size: 1024
          request_headers:
            Authorization: "Basic YOUR_BASE64_CLIENT_ID_SECRET"
            Content-Type: "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
          body: !lambda |-
            return std::string("grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=") + id(st_refresh_token);
          on_response:
            then:
              - lambda: |-
                  ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> HTTP Status: %d", response->status_code);
                  if (response->status_code == 200) {
                    json::parse_json(body, [](JsonObject root) -> bool {
                      std::string new_access = root["access_token"] | "";
                      std::string new_refresh = root["refresh_token"] | "";
                      if (!new_access.empty()) {
                        id(st_access_token) = "Bearer " + new_access;
                        ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> Access token updated");
                      }
                      if (!new_refresh.empty()) {
                        id(st_refresh_token) = new_refresh;
                        ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> Refresh token updated and saved to NVS");
                      }
                      return true;
                    });
                  } else {
                    ESP_LOGW("oauth", ">>> Refresh FAILED: %s", body.c_str());
                  }

wifi:
  on_connect:
    - delay: 15s
    - lambda: |-
        ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> WiFi ready, firing token refresh");
    - script.execute: refresh_oauth_token

interval:
  - interval: 20h             # tokens expire after 24h, refresh safely at 20h
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> 20h interval token refresh");
      - script.execute: refresh_oauth_token

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# PRESENCE ZONES
# The MTR-1 uses the LD2450 radar which provides X/Y coordinates
# in mm for up to 3 simultaneous targets. Define rectangular zones
# based on your room layout. Use the ESPHome web UI live view to
# find the right coordinates by walking through your space.
# X = left/right from sensor center, Y = distance forward
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

sensor:
  - platform: ld2450
    target_1:
      x: { name: "My T1 X", id: my_t1_x, internal: true }
      y: { name: "My T1 Y", id: my_t1_y, internal: true }
    target_2:
      x: { name: "My T2 X", id: my_t2_x, internal: true }
      y: { name: "My T2 Y", id: my_t2_y, internal: true }
    target_3:
      x: { name: "My T3 X", id: my_t3_x, internal: true }
      y: { name: "My T3 Y", id: my_t3_y, internal: true }

binary_sensor:
  # Zone 1 — replace coordinates and device ID with your own
  - platform: template
    name: "SmartThings Zone Kitchen Counter"
    lambda: |-
      return (
        (id(my_t1_x).state >= -1400 && id(my_t1_x).state <= 950 && id(my_t1_y).state >= 700 && id(my_t1_y).state <= 2700) ||
        (id(my_t2_x).state >= -1400 && id(my_t2_x).state <= 950 && id(my_t2_y).state >= 700 && id(my_t2_y).state <= 2700) ||
        (id(my_t3_x).state >= -1400 && id(my_t3_x).state <= 950 && id(my_t3_y).state >= 700 && id(my_t3_y).state <= 2700)
      );
    on_press:
      - http_request.send:
          url: "https://api.smartthings.com/v1/devices/YOUR_DEVICE_ID_1/commands"
          method: POST
          request_headers:
            Authorization: !lambda return id(st_access_token).c_str();
            Content-Type: "application/json"
          body: '{"commands": [{"component": "main", "capability": "switch", "command": "on"}]}'
    on_release:
      - http_request.send:
          url: "https://api.smartthings.com/v1/devices/YOUR_DEVICE_ID_1/commands"
          method: POST
          request_headers:
            Authorization: !lambda return id(st_access_token).c_str();
            Content-Type: "application/json"
          body: '{"commands": [{"component": "main", "capability": "switch", "command": "off"}]}'

  # Zone 2 — add as many zones as you need, one per light/switch
  - platform: template
    name: "SmartThings Zone Dining Table"
    lambda: |-
      return (
        (id(my_t1_x).state >= 1000 && id(my_t1_x).state <= 2600 && id(my_t1_y).state >= 1000 && id(my_t1_y).state <= 2000) ||
        (id(my_t2_x).state >= 1000 && id(my_t2_x).state <= 2600 && id(my_t2_y).state >= 1000 && id(my_t2_y).state <= 2000) ||
        (id(my_t3_x).state >= 1000 && id(my_t3_x).state <= 2600 && id(my_t3_y).state >= 1000 && id(my_t3_y).state <= 2000)
      );
    on_press:
      - http_request.send:
          url: "https://api.smartthings.com/v1/devices/YOUR_DEVICE_ID_2/commands"
          method: POST
          request_headers:
            Authorization: !lambda return id(st_access_token).c_str();
            Content-Type: "application/json"
          body: '{"commands": [{"component": "main", "capability": "switch", "command": "on"}]}'
    on_release:
      - http_request.send:
          url: "https://api.smartthings.com/v1/devices/YOUR_DEVICE_ID_2/commands"
          method: POST
          request_headers:
            Authorization: !lambda return id(st_access_token).c_str();
            Content-Type: "application/json"
          body: '{"commands": [{"component": "main", "capability": "switch", "command": "off"}]}'

verify_ssl: false turns off certificate checking

This setting tells the device to skip certificate checks on every SmartThings API call it makes, including the token refresh. The example does this because the certificate bundle the ESP32 would need to check those certificates is too large to fit comfortably on the device. Anyone who can intercept your network traffic could read your SmartThings token, so keep the device on a trusted network.

docs.title: Part 5: Flash and verify
docs.text:
esphome run your_config.yaml --device 192.168.x.x

Within 15 seconds of connecting to Wi-Fi, you should see in the logs:

[oauth] >>> WiFi ready, firing token refresh
[oauth] >>> Refresh START
[oauth] >>> HTTP Status: 200
[oauth] >>> Access token updated
[oauth] >>> Refresh token updated and saved to NVS

Then walk into one of your defined zones. The SmartThings API response will show content-type: application/json (not text/html) and your light turns on.

If you see HTTP Request failed; Code: 401, the access token has expired. A simple reboot fixes it: the wifi: on_connect handler will fetch a fresh token automatically.

docs.title: How the token lifecycle works
docs.text:
First flash:   initial_value token → refresh → new access + refresh → saved to NVS
Every 20h:     NVS refresh token   → refresh → new access + refresh → saved to NVS
After reboot:  NVS token loaded    → refresh → new access + refresh → saved to NVS

After the first flash, the initial_value in the YAML is never used again. The NVS token takes over and the chain is fully self-sustaining.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
401 on SmartThings API calls

The access token has expired. Reboot the device. The wifi: on_connect handler will fetch a fresh pair automatically.

400 invalid_grant on token refresh

The refresh token was invalidated. This can happen if the device was offline for more than 30 days, or if a previous refresh failed mid-way. Re-run the browser OAuth flow from Part 2, update both initial_value fields in your YAML, flash once, and the self-sustaining chain resumes from there.

400 invalid_grant after router reboot or power outage

This is the trickiest failure mode. It happens when the device reconnects to Wi-Fi multiple times in quick succession (e.g. during a router restart), causing two parallel token refresh calls. Both use the same refresh token: one succeeds, one invalidates it. The broken token then gets saved to NVS flash and survives every reboot.

mode: single on the script prevents this going forward, but if you already have a broken NVS token, here is the recovery procedure (no USB required):

Step 1. Get a fresh refresh token via PowerShell:

$b64 = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes("YOUR_CLIENT_ID:YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"))
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri "https://api.smartthings.com/oauth/token" `
  -Headers @{Authorization="Basic $b64"} `
  -ContentType "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" `
  -Body "grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=LAST_KNOWN_GOOD_REFRESH_TOKEN"

If that returns 400 too, use the browser OAuth flow from Part 2 to get a completely fresh pair.

Step 2. Flash 1: add an on_boot override (priority 600 runs after NVS load but before Wi-Fi):

esphome:
  name: ${name}
  on_boot:
    priority: 600.0
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          id(st_refresh_token) = "YOUR_FRESH_REFRESH_TOKEN";
          ESP_LOGI("oauth", ">>> Boot: token override active");

Flash OTA and wait for HTTP Status: 200 and Refresh token updated and saved to NVS in the logs.

Step 3. Flash 2: remove the override immediately (while device is still running): Remove the entire on_boot block, keep restore_value: yes, and flash OTA again. You do not need to change initial_value, because the device has already saved the new refresh token to NVS.

The NVS now holds the correct token and the self-sustaining chain resumes.

Token refresh fires but on_response never runs

You are likely triggering the refresh from on_boot. The ESP-IDF HTTP stack is not ready at that point. Move to wifi: on_connect with a 15-second delay as shown above.

POST body is not being sent

Make sure you use body: !lambda |- return std::string("...");. Plain YAML string values for body: are silently dropped by the ESP-IDF HTTP client.

docs.title: Adapting for other Apollo devices
docs.text:
The OAuth2 token block (globals, script, wifi on_connect, interval) is completely device-agnostic. Swap the packages: line for your device and add your own triggers:

  • AIR-1: trigger a SmartThings ventilation fan when the CO₂ sensor exceeds 1200 ppm
  • MSR-2: simple presence-based lighting in smaller rooms

Tested continuously for 10+ days including multiple reboot cycles. The token chain has not required any manual intervention since initial setup.

Thanks to Matteo for putting this tutorial together!

docs.title: Putting the H-1 in boot mode
docs.text: This will cover how to put the H-1 into boot mode. Sometimes, this is needed to upload new firmware if the device is struggling.

docs.title: Boot button only
docs.text:
You can enter boot mode using only the boot button.

1. Make sure the device is not powered and see the photo above to help find the boot button

2. Press and hold the boot button, while holding the boot button plug the H-1 back into your computer/power and then release the boot button

3. Continue with uploading the firmware

docs.title: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You can also enter boot mode with the boot and reset buttons while the device is plugged in.

1. Plug in the device

2. Put your H-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (circled in the photo above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (also circled in the photo above).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the H-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware

docs.title: H-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What songs are pre-loaded on the Apollo H-1?

  • The H-1 comes with three classic holiday songs: Sleigh Bells, Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, and Let it Snow. You can play these songs by pressing the gold button on the back of the ornament: one press for Sleigh Bells, two for Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, and a long press for Let it Snow. Each song is paired with a unique LED effect for added festive flair.

2. Can I customize the songs and LED effects?

  • Yes! While the H-1 ships pre-loaded with three songs and light effects, you can integrate it with Home Assistant to further customize songs, LED patterns, and more. This makes the H-1 a versatile addition to your smart home holiday setup.

3. Is the Apollo H-1 “smart” right out of the box?

  • The H-1 is pre-flashed with a simple firmware that operates independently, allowing you to play songs with the gold button without needing any additional setup. For a full “smart” experience, you can connect the H-1 to Home Assistant, where you can program custom automations, change songs, and adjust LED effects.

4. How do I activate the pre-loaded songs?

  • To play the songs, press the gold button on the back of the ornament:
  • 1 press for Sleigh Bells
  • 2 presses for Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer
  • Long press for Let it Snow

5. What does purchasing the Apollo H-1 support?

  • All proceeds from the H-1 go to a local charity in Lexington, KY. This initiative allows us to give back to our community as a thank you for the support we receive from our customers, friends, and family.

6. Can the Apollo H-1 be used as a standard holiday ornament?

  • Absolutely! The H-1 is designed to look festive on any holiday setup, whether you choose to use the pre-loaded music and lights or integrate it as part of a smart home. It’s a fun and functional ornament that brings joy in multiple ways.

7. How do I set up the Apollo H-1 with Home Assistant?

  • To integrate the H-1 with Home Assistant, follow the getting started guide or reach out to our support team for assistance. Once connected, you can unlock additional functionality and customization.

8. Does the ornament require any additional power source?

  • The Apollo H-1 can operate on battery power, so you can hang and place it wherever you'd like in your holiday decorations. It uses a (rechargeable) RC-CR123A aka 16340 battery (ideally 850mAh). It can also be powered by the USB-C port. The H-1 USB-C port will NOT charge the battery, you need an external charger.

9. Can I gift the Apollo H-1 to friends or family?

  • Yes, the H-1 makes a wonderful gift! It’s unique, festive, and supports a good cause, making it a great option for holiday gifting.

10. My H-1 is draining battery too fast. How do I fix this?

  • Please make sure if you are on the smart firmware to disable the "prevent sleep" option on the Home Assistant device page!

11. Where can I find more information about the Apollo H-1 and similar products?

  • For more details, setups, guides, and other products please email us at support@apolloautomation.com

docs.title: Factory re-flash H-1
docs.text:
If your Apollo H-1 becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods, you can upload a fresh set of firmware to it by following this guide.

Before you start

  • Use Chrome or Edge. The install utility needs to run from one of them.
  • Already added this H-1 to Home Assistant? Remove it from Home Assistant first, then come back here.

Follow these steps to flash fresh firmware onto your H-1 and find it again in Home Assistant.

1. Hold the boot button, then plug your H-1 into your computer with a quality USB-C cable that supports data transfer. Let go of the boot button once the USB cable is plugged in.

2. Open the Apollo H-1 installer and click Connect & Install. The installer has one firmware for the H-1, the smart Wi-Fi firmware.

3. Select your Apollo device and click Connect. It shows with a name similar to the one below. If you aren't sure which device it is, unplug the H-1 and see which one disappears.

No device in the list?

Click Cancel, then install the recommended driver that shows on the popup. If you've installed the driver and tried different cables and it still won't work, put the H-1 in bootloader mode and then retry step 3.

4. Choose to install the new firmware.

Shown with the MSR-1 installer; the H-1 installer looks the same.

Seeing the error below?

If the installer shows this error, complete the H-1 boot mode guide and go back to step 3.

Shown with the MSR-1 installer; the H-1 shows the same error.

5. Wait for the installer to finish. If you see "ERROR Logger is not configured!", that's expected: the logger is disabled to make more room for other components on the microcontroller.

Shown with the MSR-1 installer; the H-1 installer looks the same.

6. Unplug your H-1 and plug it back in to leave boot mode. Don't skip this step. The H-1 stays in boot mode until you do.

7. Check for the Apollo hotspot and connect to it. The hotspot might not show if your H-1 was connected to your Wi-Fi before.

8. Log into Home Assistant, go to the ESPHome app, and check whether you can adopt the device.

Your H-1 is now running a fresh set of firmware.

docs.title: How To Wake Up Your Sensor
docs.text:
To wake a sleeping Apollo battery sensor, press the reset button. A BTN-1 also wakes when you press Button 1, 2, 3, or 4, and an H-1 or H-2 wakes when you press a gold song button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping device. Select your device below for the button locations.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1H-1H-2

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping TEMP-1B. Once the TEMP-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: TEMP-1B boot mode.

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping PLT-1B. Once the PLT-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: PLT-1B boot mode.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Buttons 1 to 4. Press and release Button 1, 2, 3, or 4. Home Assistant receives that press as a click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any automation you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping BTN-1. Once the BTN-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: BTN-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-1 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Method 2: Gold button. Press and release the gold button (SW1).

The boot button can't wake a sleeping H-1. Once the H-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

The unlabeled circled button at the lower left is the gold button (SW1), which plays the built-in songs.

Button locations: H-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-2 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Song buttons. Press and release any of the four gold song buttons on the back of the H-2. The H-2 wakes and plays that button's song.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping H-2. Once the H-2 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: H-2 boot mode.

Your device is now awake, but it will not stay awake on its own yet. Click the Prevent Sleep button on your device page in Home Assistant, or directly on the device web server such as plt-1.local or its IP address.

You can also turn on Prevent Sleep from the device itself. Once it's awake, press and hold the boot button for 4-5 seconds, then let go.

Watch how you use the boot button

Press the boot button only after the device has restarted. Holding it while you press reset puts the device in boot mode for flashing firmware instead. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets the device to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi.

Head to the awake helper wiki article

If you need to keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time we suggest using our OTA awake helper.

docs.title: H-2 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What songs are pre-loaded on the Apollo H-2?

  • The H-2 comes with four classic holiday songs: Jingle Bells, Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, Let it Snow, and Blue Christmas. You can play these songs by pressing the 4 different gold buttons on the back of the ornament. Each song is paired with a unique LED effect for added festive flair.

2. Can I customize the songs and LED effects?

  • Yes! While the H-2 ships pre-loaded with four songs and light effects, you can integrate it with Home Assistant and ESPHome to further customize songs, LED patterns, and more. This makes the H-2 a versatile addition to your smart home holiday setup. You can also use the buzzer to play any song in Home Assistant!

3. Is the Apollo H-2 “smart” right out of the box?

  • The H-2 is pre-flashed with a simple firmware that operates independently, allowing you to play songs with the gold button without needing any additional setup. For a full “smart” experience, you can reflash the H-2 to the smart firmware from the Apollo H-2 installer (choose Smart (Wi-Fi)), then join it to Home Assistant, where you can program custom automations, change songs, and adjust LED effects.

4. How do I activate the pre-loaded songs?

  • To play the songs, press the four different gold buttons on the back of the ornament.

5. What does purchasing the Apollo H-2 support?

  • All proceeds from the H-2 go to a local charity in Lexington, KY. This initiative allows us to give back to our community as a thank you for the support we receive from our customers, friends, and family. We also are donating to the Open Home Foundation!

6. Can the Apollo H-2 be used as a standard holiday ornament?

  • Absolutely! The H-2 is designed to look festive on any holiday setup, whether you choose to use the pre-loaded music and lights or integrate it as part of a smart home. It’s a fun and functional ornament that brings joy in multiple ways.

7. How do I set up the Apollo H-2 with Home Assistant?

  • To integrate the H-2 with Home Assistant, reflash it with the smart firmware: open the Apollo H-2 installer and choose Smart (Wi-Fi).

8. Does the ornament require any additional power source?

  • The Apollo H-2 can operate on battery power, so you can hang and place it wherever you'd like in your holiday decorations. It uses a 16340 rechargeable battery. It can also be powered by the USB-C port. The H-2 USB-C port will not charge the battery. You need a dedicated 16340 charger such as this nitecore model.

9. Can I gift the Apollo H-2 to friends or family?

  • Yes, the H-2 makes a wonderful gift! It’s unique, festive, and supports a good cause, making it a great option for holiday gifting.

10. My H-2 is draining battery too fast. How do I fix this?

  • Please make sure if you are on the smart firmware to disable the "prevent sleep" option on the Home Assistant device page!

11. Where can I find more information about the Apollo H-2 and similar products?

  • For more details, setups, guides, and other products please email us at support@apolloautomation.com

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

The Apollo H-2 is the second edition of our annual holiday ornament! It's our way of saying thank you for your support and giving back to our community.

The H-2 ships pre-flashed with a basic firmware featuring four classic holiday tunes. New for 2025: The H-2 features four dedicated song buttons (no more multi-click!), upgraded ESP32-C6 processor with 8MB flash, 58 RGB LEDs (up from 22), and a logo light for enhanced visual appeal.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Follow these steps to power up your ornament, play its pre-loaded songs, and optionally add it to Home Assistant.

1. Powering On the H-2

Insert a rechargeable RC-CR123A (16340) battery, preferably an 850 mAh model like the one available in our store. A normal CR123A will not work!

2. Turning On the Ornament

If the device is in sleep mode, press one of the gold buttons on the back to wake it.

3. Play Holiday Songs

After the ornament is awake, press one of the four gold buttons to play a pre-loaded song. The buttons are on the back of the H-2, one at the tip of each side arm.

Each button plays one of these songs:

  • Button 1: Jingle Bells
  • Button 2: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer
  • Button 3: Let It Snow
  • Button 4: Blue Christmas

4. Add to Home Assistant (Optional)

For additional customization, you will need to put the H-2 in boot mode then flash the smart firmware from the Apollo H-2 installer (choose Smart (Wi-Fi)) and finally connect to Home Assistant following the setup guide. With Home Assistant you can add new songs, change LED effects, and create custom automations.

5. Enjoy Your Ornament

Hang the H-2 on your tree, place it on a mantel, or incorporate it into any holiday setup for added joy. Your Apollo H-2 is now ready to spread holiday cheer! Enjoy the festive tunes and LED effects, and feel free to share your unique setup with us in the community!

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the H-2 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the H-2 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Boot button only
docs.text:
You can enter boot mode using only the boot button.

Make sure that the battery is removed prior to putting it in boot mode

Make sure that there is no battery in the device. The battery will prevent it from entering boot mode.

1. Disconnect your H-2 from power. With the device facing you, locate the boot button. It’s the small black button on the right.

2. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer.

3. Push and hold the boot button (the right button). While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your H-2 then let go of the button.

4. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You can also enter boot mode with the boot and reset buttons while the device is plugged in.

1. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer and connect the other end to your H-2. With the device facing you, locate the reset (left) and boot (right) buttons.

2. Put your H-2 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the H-2. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

3. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Reflashing the H-2
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the steps below.

This factory re-flash needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

1. Disconnect your H-2 from power. With the device facing you, locate the boot button. It’s the small black button on the right.

2. Plug in a USB cable that supports power and data into your computer.

3. Push and hold the boot button (the right button). While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your H-2 then let go of the button.

4. Open the Apollo H-2 installer with the button below, using a Chromium-based browser such as Chrome or Edge. Under Choose your firmware, click Smart (Wi-Fi) to join your Wi-Fi and Home Assistant, or Basic (No Wi-Fi) to go back to the firmware the ornament ships with. Then click Connect & Install, select the open com port, and click Connect.

Apollo H-2 installer

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.H-2 (Smart) or Install ApolloAutomation.H-2D (Basic), then click Install again.

6. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

Head to the Getting Started article to set up your H-2 as a new device!

docs.title: H-3 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What songs are pre-loaded on the Apollo H-3?

  • The H-3 comes with six holiday songs across the three buttons on the ornament. Press a button to play its first song, or hold it for about a second to play its second song. Button 1 plays Frosty the Snowman and Blue Christmas, button 2 plays Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer and Do You Want to Build a Snowman, and button 3 plays Jingle Bells and Barbie Girl. Each song is paired with its own LED effect.

2. Can I customize the songs and LED effects?

  • Yes! While the H-3 ships pre-loaded with six songs and light effects, you can integrate it with Home Assistant and ESPHome to further customize songs, LED patterns, and more. You can also use the buzzer to play any song in Home Assistant!

3. Is the Apollo H-3 "smart" right out of the box?

  • The H-3 is pre-flashed with a simple firmware that operates independently, so you can play songs with the buttons without any additional setup. For a full "smart" experience, reflash the H-3 to the smart firmware then join it to Home Assistant, where you can program custom automations, change songs, and adjust LED effects.

4. How do I activate the pre-loaded songs?

  • Press one of the three buttons on the ornament. If the ornament is asleep, the same press wakes it and plays the song.

5. What does purchasing the Apollo H-3 support?

  • 100% of the profits from the H-3 go to CASA of Lexington, who advocate for children in the family court system, and to the Open Home Foundation. This is our way of giving back as a thank you for the support we receive from our customers, friends, and family.

6. Can the Apollo H-3 be used as a standard holiday ornament?

  • Absolutely! The H-3 is designed to look festive on any holiday setup, whether you choose to use the pre-loaded music and lights or integrate it as part of a smart home.

7. How do I set up the Apollo H-3 with Home Assistant?

  • Put the ornament in boot mode, then reflash it with the smart firmware. It shows up in Home Assistant as an ESPHome device once it joins your Wi-Fi.

8. Does the ornament require any additional power source?

  • The H-3 runs on two AA batteries, so you can hang it wherever you like. We suggest non-rechargeable AAs. It can also be powered by the USB-C port.

9. Can I gift the Apollo H-3 to friends or family?

  • Yes, the H-3 makes a wonderful gift! It's unique, festive, and supports a good cause, making it a great option for holiday gifting.

10. My H-3 is draining battery too fast, how do I fix this?

  • On the smart firmware, make sure the "Prevent Sleep" switch is off on the device page in Home Assistant. With it on, the ornament stays awake instead of sleeping between button presses.

11. Where can I find more information about the Apollo H-3 and similar products?

  • For more details, setups, guides, and other products please email us at support@apolloautomation.com

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: H-3 introduction
docs.text:
Can be powered by USB-C or two AA batteries. We suggest non-rechargeable AAs.

The Apollo H-3 is the third edition of our annual holiday ornament! It's our way of saying thank you for your support and giving back to our community.

The H-3 ships pre-flashed with a basic firmware and six holiday tunes. Press one of the three buttons to play its first song, or hold a button for about a second to play its second song:

  • Button 1: Frosty the Snowman, hold for Blue Christmas
  • Button 2: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, hold for Do You Want to Build a Snowman
  • Button 3: Jingle Bells, hold for Barbie Girl

Each tune comes with its own LED effect.

You can also integrate it with Home Assistant to unlock more features, such as changing the songs and LED effects, Bluetooth proxy, and Bluetooth tracking. You will need to reflash it to the smart firmware first!

New for 2026: The H-3 has 37 RGB LEDs split into five zones you can control separately (body, hat, eyes, nose, and mouth), six songs across three buttons, and runs on two AA batteries.

docs.title: How to wake up your sensor
docs.text:
To wake a sleeping Apollo battery sensor, press the reset button. A BTN-1 also wakes when you press Button 1, 2, 3, or 4, and an H-1 or H-2 wakes when you press a gold song button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping device. Select your device below for the button locations.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1H-1H-2

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping TEMP-1B. Once the TEMP-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: TEMP-1B boot mode.

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping PLT-1B. Once the PLT-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: PLT-1B boot mode.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Buttons 1 to 4. Press and release Button 1, 2, 3, or 4. Home Assistant receives that press as a click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any automation you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping BTN-1. Once the BTN-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: BTN-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-1 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Method 2: Gold button. Press and release the gold button (SW1).

The boot button can't wake a sleeping H-1. Once the H-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

The unlabeled circled button at the lower left is the gold button (SW1), which plays the built-in songs.

Button locations: H-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-2 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Song buttons. Press and release any of the four gold song buttons on the back of the H-2. The H-2 wakes and plays that button's song.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping H-2. Once the H-2 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: H-2 boot mode.

Your device is now awake, but it will not stay awake on its own yet. Click the Prevent Sleep button on your device page in Home Assistant, or directly on the device web server such as plt-1.local or its IP address.

You can also turn on Prevent Sleep from the device itself. Once it's awake, press and hold the boot button for 4-5 seconds, then let go.

Watch how you use the boot button

Press the boot button only after the device has restarted. Holding it while you press reset puts the device in boot mode for flashing firmware instead. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets the device to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi.

Head to the awake helper wiki article

If you need to keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time we suggest using our OTA awake helper.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Follow these steps to power up your ornament, play its holiday songs, and optionally add it to Home Assistant.

1. Powering On the H-3

Insert two AA batteries. We suggest non-rechargeable AAs. You can also run the ornament from the USB-C port instead.

2. Turning On the Ornament

If the ornament is asleep, press one of the buttons to wake it.

3. Play Holiday Songs

Press a button to play its first song, or hold it for about a second to play its second song:

  • Button 1: Frosty the Snowman, hold for Blue Christmas
  • Button 2: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, hold for Do You Want to Build a Snowman
  • Button 3: Jingle Bells, hold for Barbie Girl

4. Add to Home Assistant (Optional)

For additional customization, put the H-3 in boot mode, then flash the smart H-3 firmware and connect it to Home Assistant following the setup guide. With Home Assistant you can add new songs, change LED effects, and create custom automations.

5. Enjoy Your Ornament

Hang the H-3 on your tree, place it on a mantel, or incorporate it into any holiday setup. Share your setup with us in the community!

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the H-3 in boot mode
docs.text:
Boot mode is what lets you reflash the firmware over USB. You need it to move between the basic firmware and the smart firmware, and to recover an ornament that has stopped responding.

1. Take the batteries out of the H-3. (1)

  1. With batteries in, the ornament stays powered, so plugging in USB never restarts it and it can't enter boot mode.

2. Locate the boot button on the back of the ornament.

3. Hold the boot button down, plug a USB-C cable that supports data into the ornament and your computer, then let go of the button.

4. You are now ready to reflash your device!

Click here to go to the reflashing guide!

docs.title: Reflashing the H-3
docs.text:
Reflash the H-3 if it stops responding, or to move between the basic and smart firmware.

Do this in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. The installer needs a browser that can talk to the USB serial port.

1. Put the ornament in boot mode and leave it plugged into your computer.

2. Open the Apollo installer and pick which firmware you want. Smart (Wi-Fi) joins your Wi-Fi and Home Assistant. Basic (No Wi-Fi) is the firmware the ornament ships with, where the buttons play the built-in tunes.

3. Click Connect & Install, then pick the serial port for your ornament. (1)

  1. If no port appears, the ornament is not in boot mode or the USB cable is charge-only. Try a different cable.

4. Follow the prompts to install. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

Head to the Getting Started article to set up your H-3 as a new device!

docs.title: LED-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What is the maximum power output of the LED-1?

  • The LED-1 is able to safely offer 10 amps of power using either 5 V, 12 V, or a 24 V when using an external power supply.
  • The device can also be powered via USB-C-PD (Power Delivery) with 5 V or 12 V at 3 amps.
  • The device can also be powered by USB-C with 5 V at 3 Amps.
  • The device has a built-in replaceable fuse that will trip if 10 Amps is exceeded. The output voltage is the same as the input voltage, so please make sure you buy the same 5 V, or 12 V, or 24 V power supply and LED strips.

2. How long of an LED strip can I use with the LED-1?

  • The length of LED strips depends more on other factors like voltage drop. Ultimately, we suggest going 3 meters with 5 V for each output, so 3 meters + 3 meters connected to separate outputs. You can go up to 5 meters at 24 V without seeing much voltage drop though!

3. Can I use a remote with the LED-1?

  • Although the device does not come with IR, it does support the WizMote over "ESP-NOW" and this works great inside of WLED!

4. How does the microphone work?

  • Audio-reactive WLED is built into the WLED firmware we ship with the LED-1. Make sure to enable it from the "info" pane and then try using an effect with the little Musical Note Image next to them!

5. My LEDs are the wrong color how do I fix it?

  • You might have SK6812 or some other leds other than the default WS2812B and WLED needs to be configured to know that you are using a different type of LEDs. Head to the LED Outputs section of wled docs to learn more.

6. Can I use the LED-1 without Home Assistant or even Wi-Fi? Even on my boat/RV?

  • Yes! You can directly connect to the access point of your WLED device without a network using a phone or laptop. Look for "WLED-AP" in your Wi-Fi client list and enter in the password "wled1234", head to http://4.3.2.1 or http://wled.me then control your device!

7. My LEDs are very dim how do I fix it?

  • Head to the settings of WLED and make sure the brightness limiter is off. You also might have a very long LED strip and you might need power injection to make it work properly.

8. How much power does it use?

  • The LED-1 uses under 1 Amp of power for itself but will use up to 10amps at 5-24 Volts based on the power supply used.

9. Can I reflash this with stock WLED firmware?

  • Yes! The LED-1 runs regular WLED. Flash it with the LED-1 reflash guide, then set the pins in WLED from the LED-1 pinout guide.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Apollo LED-1 is a compact, versatile LED Controller for Home Assistant. Fully open-source and expandable, the LED-1 integrates with Home Assistant using the WLED Integration, making it ideal for automating lighting. Access to support and customization resources is available via our Discord and GitHub.

Key Features:

  • Powered via either USB-C (5 V only), USB-C PD (5 V or 12 V) or external power supply (5 V, 12 V, or 24 V).
  • Two fused outputs able to handle 10 Amps total, either from one output or both but max of 10 Amps.
  • Built in MEMS digital microphone for WLED Audio Reactive functionality.
  • Built in relay to kill power to LEDs for less power usage (great for battery projects).

docs.title: Controlling Govee lights with the LED-1
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to use the Apollo LED-1 to control your Govee permanent outdoor lights fully locally, without a cloud-based app. So far, the steps cover preparing a project box, wiring power into the LED-1, and preparing the LED cable.

This guide is still being written

The steps below get the LED-1 connected. More steps are coming.

1. Gather the parts and tools for this project.

Parts

  • Apollo LED-1
  • Govee permanent lights
  • Project box
  • Barrel plug connector
  • White 3-wire LED connecting wire
  • Waterproof sealant

Tools

  • Screwdriver
  • Wire strippers
  • Hobby knife
  • Tweezers

2. Unscrew the 4 screws and remove the project box lid.

3. Remove two of the rubber grommets. Use the hobby knife to cut a small slit in each one for the power and data connections. For an outdoor setup, the two bottom grommets might be best, to help keep water from getting in.

4. Connect the barrel plug to the WAGO connector, the large white component at the bottom left of the board, below the USB-C port. Connect the RED (+) wire to the top terminal and the BLACK (-) wire to the bottom terminal. To insert each wire, use the tweezers to press down the top of the WAGO connector, insert the wire, and then release to lock it in place.

5. Use the hobby knife to remove the cable sheathing from the 3-pin LED connector. Cut carefully, because the cable can roll.

You've finished the steps written so far: the grommets are cut, the barrel plug is wired to the LED-1, and the 3-pin LED connector is stripped and ready.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Congrats on your new Apollo LED-1! This guide walks you through powering it, wiring up your LEDs, and connecting it to Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Choose how to power it
docs.text:
You can power the LED-1 in three ways:

  • USB Power: 5V, up to 3 amps
  • USB Power Delivery: 5V or 12V, up to 3 amps
  • External Power Supply: a dedicated power supply using either 5V, 12V, or 24V

Pick the tab that matches your setup.

USB PowerUSB Power DeliveryExternal Power Supply

1. Connect a USB-C cable to a 5V 3A or larger power supply, and plug the other end into your LED-1.

Use a cable rated for 3 amps

We suggest a quality USB-C cable that can handle 3 amps or more. If you're not sure whether yours supports 3 amps, buy a new cable from our store or a reputable seller such as Amazon or Monoprice.

1. Decide whether you're using 5V or 12V with USB-C PD. If you're using 12V, first flip the switch on the LED-1 board (the board render on the LED-1 introduction page shows where it is). If you're using 5V, skip to the next step.

2. Connect your USB-C PD wall charger to the USB-C cable, then plug the other end into the USB-C port of the LED-1.

Your LED-1 now outputs either 5V or 12V to the + and - terminals of Output 1 and Output 2.

An external power supply is the best way to get the longest distance and the most power out of your device. You can get up to 10 amps of power at 5V, 12V, or 24V.

1. Connect your power supply's output wires to the input terminals of your LED-1. Be very careful to connect the positive red wire to the + sign and the negative black wire to the - sign.

If you still need a power supply, check out our power supply suggestions.

Cut off the barrel connector

Most power supplies have a barrel connector that's only rated for 3 amps. We suggest cutting the barrel connector off and splitting out the red and black wires to put directly into the LED-1.

Unplug the power!

Before you move on to wiring up your LEDs, make sure to unplug your LED-1.

docs.title: Wire up LEDs
docs.text:
Use LEDs that match your power supply's voltage

The LED-1 outputs the same voltage that is input to the device. It protects itself, but not the LED strips connected to it. Connect 5V LED strips if you're using a 5V power supply, and do the same with 12V and 24V.

Next, connect your LED strip to the first output of the LED-1.

1. Grab a male JST-SM 3-pin connector, such as the extra one included with your LED strips. Carefully note which wire is which: red is positive, green is data, and white is ground.

2. Find the two WAGO connectors on the LED-1 labeled "Output 1" and "Output 2". Insert the wires into Output 1:

  • Red power wire: far left terminal of Output 1
  • Green data wire: middle terminal of Output 1
  • White ground wire: third terminal of Output 1

3. If you have a second LED strip, repeat step 2 for it using Output 2.

Your LEDs are wired up and ready for power.

docs.title: Connect to Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Your device is now ready to connect to your Wi-Fi. Once it's connected, you can control it from Home Assistant, the WLED app for iPhone and Android, or a web browser.

1. Plug in your power supply or USB-C power. The LED-1 boots within a couple of seconds.

2. On your phone, open the list of available Wi-Fi networks and select WLED-AP.

3. Wait for the "Welcome to WLED!" page to pop up. If it doesn't, open a web browser and go to http://4.3.2.1/. You should see the same page shown below.

When the "Welcome to WLED!" page opens, you're connected to your LED-1.

docs.title: Add the LED-1 to Home Assistant
docs.text: Home Assistant should discover your LED-1 automatically using the WLED integration.

docs.title: Power supplies
docs.text:
Meanwell power supplies are best but most power supplies off Amazon will be sufficient. As a rule of thumb, over 80% usage on a power supply is bad. So if you want to run with 3amps, buy a 4 or 5amp power supply so that the power supply is not running at its maximum potential amperage.

Most power supplies will have a barrel connector only rated for 3 amps on it, so we suggest that you cut the barrel connector off and split out the red and black wires to put directly into the LED-1.

The LED-1 will output the same voltage that is input and that could damage LEDs!

The LED-1 will protect itself, but not the led strips connected to it. So if you connect a 24 volt power supply to the device, it will send 24v out to the LED strips. Make sure to pair your LEDs and Power supplies with the same voltage!

docs.title: LED strips
docs.text:
• WS2812B which are 5V RGB LED strips.
  • SK6812 which are 5V RGBW LED strips.
  • WS2814 which are 24V RGBW-CCT FCOB LED strips.

Not all LEDs are the same!

We suggest buying only BTF Lighting off of amazon or directly from us (we source only BTF Lighting). They also have an Aliexpress store!

docs.title: LED connectors
docs.text:
JST-SM 3 pin connectors are helpful to connect multiple led strips or to solder them onto led strips to create multiple smaller sections. These have a maximum rating of 3 amps.

10mm Width Transparent Connector Kit You might want to use these 24v FCOB connectors for the WS2814 LEDs suggested above. Make sure to choose the same width of led strip + connector (10mm, 12mm, etc).

docs.title: Additional tools
docs.text:
Wago Connectors are a great option for connecting wires together without soldering.

Wire Strippers are very helpful especially if you need to cut the end off a barrel connector to expose the red and black wires for powering your device. Make sure they are able to strip 18/20/22 gauge wires.

Soldering Iron such as a TS80P. Here's a tutorial on how to use it.
