3. Replace the packages: line and the line directly below it with the code below.

packages:
  ApolloAutomation.MSR-2:
    url: https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/MSR-2
    ref: main
    files: [Integrations/ESPHome/MSR-2_BLE.yaml]
    refresh: 1min

4. Click Save then Install in the bottom right. Click On the network when prompted.

5. When you see the purple lines the device has booted successfully and the logs will show the Bluetooth Proxy section. Click Stop in the bottom right and you're finished!

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

The easiest way is to let ESPHome Device Builder add the component for you. You can also paste the single line by hand.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar and click Edit on your device. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Click Add Component in the editor toolbar, search for Bluetooth Proxy, and click Add.

Device Builder drops a single line into your config:

bluetooth_proxy:

That's all it needs. Active connections are on by default, and bluetooth_proxy automatically pulls in the ESP32 BLE Tracker it depends on, so there's nothing else to add. Prefer to type it? Paste that one line at the top level of your YAML instead of using Add Component.

3. Click Save, then Install, and choose On the Network to flash the new firmware over Wi-Fi.

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

docs.title: Adding 90 degree USB-C to MSR-2
docs.text:
You'll attach this addon to your sensor and plug it into a USB-C outlet.

1. Gather the MSR-2 and 90 degree addon.

2. Align the MSR-2 with the USB-C port facing you and align the 90 degree addon with the shorter end facing the MSR-2 USB-C port.

3. Gently push the short end of the 90 degree addon into the MSR-2 side USB-C port.

4. Gently push the longer end of the 90 degree addon into a USB-C outlet.

You're ready to begin using your device!

Make sure to head to our getting started guide to get your MSR-2 up and running!

docs.title: Add the articulating stand to your MSR-2
Adding articulating stand to MSR-2
docs.text:
You'll swap the back of your sensor for the articulating stand backplate, then seat the stand's ball in its mount.

1. Unplug your MSR-2 from power and remove the back.

2. Align the new backplate that came with the articulating stand addon and gently push down on two corners near the articulating ball mount then the other two corners until it seats flat.

3. Align the ball inside the articulating mount and then push down until it's fully seated.

docs.title: Add the SCD40 CO2 sensor to your MSR-2
Adding CO<sub>2</sub> to MSR-2
docs.text:
You'll slide your sensor out of its case, fit the SCD40 module onto its mezzanine connector, and put the case back together.

1. Unplug your MSR-2 from power and remove the back

2. Flip the MSR-2 upside down and gently tap the case on the table and your MSR-2 should slide out of the case.

3. With the case removed, identify the bottom right corner where the small black mezzanine connector lives. You will see an "X" indicating which corner needs to be lined up with the SCD40 CO2 sensor. There is an X on the SCD40 sensor's PCB as well, you can see it in the image below but it is slightly cut off on the PCB itself. There is also a "gold dot" in the top left of the SCD40 when oriented properly.

4. Gently push the SCD40 CO2 module onto the black mezzanine connector.

5. Slide the case back over the MSR-2, making sure that the case has the hole for the USB-C port facing the right direction.

6. Gently press the backplate of the MSR-2 case onto the MSR-2 until it lightly snaps into place. Please do not force it, if necessary please repeat steps above until it seats in the case without any force required.

7. Please refer to our CO2 calibration guide to calibrate the CO2 module after installation. This is required for all CO2 addons purchased from us separately from a product (such as buying it to add on to an existing Apollo device).

docs.title: Add the GPIO header to your MSR-2
Adding GPIO header to MSR-2
docs.text:
You'll seat the GPIO Header addon on the mezzanine connector on the back of your sensor, then fit the new back that came with it.

1. Unplug your MSR-2 from power and remove the back.

2. Identify the "X" on the PCB on the back of your MSR-2 and the "X" on the top left corner of the GPIO Header addon.

3. Keep the "X" aligned on both sides and gently push down until it securely seats in the small mezzanine connector.

4. Align the new back for your MSR-2 that came with the GPIO Header addon. Push down on the corners closest to the GPIO Header addon first, and then push the back on securely on the other two corners.

docs.title: GPIO header pinout
docs.text:
With the header installed, these are the pins you can wire to. IO18 and IO19 can't be used while you flash the MSR-2, and IO0 and IO1 carry the I2C bus (SDA and SCL).

Make sure to check out our MSR-2 GPIO Header LED Strip Tutorial!

Brandon AKA SmartHomeSellout made this neat tutorial for how to connect a short LED strip to your MSR-2

GPIO LED Strip Tutorial

docs.title: Add the rear female USB-C port to your MSR-2
Adding rear female USB-C to MSR-2
docs.text:
You'll seat the Female Rear USB-C addon on the mezzanine connector on the back of your sensor, then fit the new back that came with it.

1. Unplug your MSR-2 from power and remove the back

2. Identify the "X" on the PCB on the back of your MSR-2 and the "X" on the top left corner of the Female Rear USB-C addon.

3. Keep the "X" aligned on both sides and gently push down until it securely seats in the small mezzanine connector.

4. Align the new back for your MSR-2 that came with the Female USB-C addon. It's possible you might have a flat back version and you can print that yourself too!

5. Push down on the corners closest to the USB-C addon first, and then push the back on securely on the other two corners.

docs.title: MSR-2 outlet mount
docs.text:
You'll attach your sensor to a top facing USB-C plug with the Outlet Mount.

1. Gather a top facing USB-C plug, an MSR-2, and our MSR-2 Outlet Mount.

2. Align the MSR-2 with the USB-C port facing the left side and align the MSR-2 Outlet Mount as shown in the image below.

3. Push the MSR-2 Outlet Mount into the USB-C port until it's fully seated. Do not push hard, it will go in very smoothly.

4. Gently push the other USB-C port of the MSR-2 Outlet Mount into the top of the USB-C top facing plug.

You're ready to plug it in and begin using your device!

Make sure to head to our getting started guide to get your MSR-2 up and running!

docs.title: Control an LED strip with the GPIO header
Control an LED strip with the GPIO header
docs.text:
The GPIO Header addon brings the MSR-2's spare pins out to a row of headers, so you can hang your own hardware off the sensor. This guide wires a WS2812B strip to one of those pins and gets it into Home Assistant as its own light entity, color picker and effects included.

The same steps work on any Apollo device with a mezzanine port, including the MTR-1 and AIR-1. Click any photo to see it full size.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• An Apollo MSR-2, or any Apollo device with a mezzanine port.
  • The Apollo GPIO Header addon.
  • A WS2812B (neopixel) RGB strip. SK6812 RGBW strips work too.
  • Three male-to-male DuPont wires. A set comes with the header.
  • A USB-C cable and power brick.

Watch the current draw

The 5V pin supplies up to 350mA. A meter of 60 LEDs at full white draws far more than that, so anything longer than a short strip needs its own 5V supply. You can power the MSR-2 itself from the 5V and GND pins instead of the USB-C port, but use one or the other, never both.

docs.title: Choosing a data pin
docs.text: IO2, IO4, IO6, and IO7 are free for LED data, and you can drive more than one strip by giving each its own pin. IO18 and IO19 are unavailable, and IO0 and IO1 are reserved for I2C sensors. This guide uses IO7, plus the 5V and GND pins at the top of the header for power.

docs.title: Attaching the GPIO header
docs.text:
You'll seat the GPIO Header on your sensor's mezzanine connector, then fit the blue back plate that came with the addon.

  1. Unplug the MSR-2 from power and pull the back plate off.

  2. Line up the X marked on the MSR-2 PCB with the X on the GPIO Header. Both face the same way.

  3. Press the header down onto the small black mezzanine connector, then check it sits flat with no gap along either edge.

  4. Slide the blue GPIO back plate that came with the addon over the sensor and press until it clicks. If it needs more than light pressure, stop and check the orientation rather than forcing it.

docs.title: Wiring the strip
docs.text:
You'll run three wires from the header to your strip, then check which way the data flows.

  1. Run three wires from the header to the strip: 5V, GND, and data. Matching the colors to the strip's own wiring saves a lot of squinting later, so use red for 5V, white for GND, and green for data on IO7.

  2. Plug the other end into the strip. Most strips come with a JST-SM pigtail carrying the same three colors, so the wires match up directly. The connector is rated to 3A.

  3. Check the direction before you power anything on. Arrows printed along the strip show which way data flows, and they need to point away from the MSR-2.

A dab of hot glue across the outer shells of the three DuPont connectors stiffens them into a single plug. (1)

  1. Keep glue out of the header's female pins. It will ruin the addon.

docs.title: Adding the strip to your YAML
docs.text:
The MSR-2 knows nothing about the strip until you tell it how many LEDs there are and which pin they sit on.

  1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app, find your MSR-2, and click Edit.

  2. Add the block below at the bottom of the file, flush with the left margin so light: lines up with packages: and wifi:. Set num_leds to the number of LEDs on your strip, and change pin if you wired to a different port.

    light:
  - platform: esp32_rmt_led_strip
    id: bed_led
    name: "Bed LED"
    pin: GPIO7
    chipset: WS2812
    channel_colors: GRB
    num_leds: 60
    default_transition_length: 0s
    effects:
      - pulse:
          name: "Slow Pulse"
          transition_length: 1000ms
          update_interval: 1000ms
          min_brightness: 50%
          max_brightness: 100%
      - pulse:
          name: "Fast Pulse"
          transition_length: 100ms
          update_interval: 100ms
          min_brightness: 50%
          max_brightness: 100%
      - addressable_rainbow:

  3. Check that the editor shows no red error markers.

  4. Click Save, then Install, and pick Wirelessly. ESPHome compiles the firmware and sends it to the MSR-2. The first build takes a few minutes.

Older versions of this guide set rmt_channel: 1 on the light. ESPHome dropped that option, and leaving it in now fails validation, so the block above does not use it.

The ESPHome light effects reference covers everything else you can add under effects:, including addressable_scan.

docs.title: Controlling it from Home Assistant
docs.text:
Once the install finishes, the MSR-2 exposes a new light entity called Bed LED.

Click the entity name to open the light card. The color wheel covers the full range, and the effects list holds the two pulses and the rainbow from the YAML above.

That's all folks! Thanks to Smart Home Sellout for putting this tutorial together.

docs.title: How to use the MSR-2 with Alarmo
MSR-2 + Alarmo home security install
docs.text:
My grandmother wanted a security system that would alert her when there was movement in her home after she had gone to bed. So, I set up three of our Apollo Automation mmWave sensors. These devices, plus the Alarmo integration, quickly allowed me to install a fully local, private, cloud-free, and no monthly subscription security system. She can arm/disarm it with one button on her Home Assistant dashboard, and it makes her feel much safer. This guide assumes you already have a motion/presence sensor installed on HA.

1. Install HACS 2. Install Alarmo and the Alarmo Card (Pretty Arm and Disarm card for your HA dashboard)

The first button opens Alarmo in HACS and the second opens the Alarmo Card:

Restart Home Assistant once both are installed, then add the Alarmo integration under Settings → Devices & services → Add integration. Alarmo shows up in the sidebar after that.

3. Find Alarmo on the left, select the Sensors tab, and toggle on the sensor entities that you would like to use for your alarm system.

Shown with MSR-1 sensors; add your MSR-2 radar target entities the same way.

4. Now select the Actions tab and under Condition > Event > Select "Alarm is triggered". You can also select the device you would like to receive a notification on under Task > Target > Select Device (Phone, tablet, etc.)

5. You can change the Title, Message, and Name of the alarm notification.

6. After saving that action we can add another one that will turn on our sensor lights and/or make the onboard piezo buzzers play an alarm sound. Under Entity select your sensors RGB light.

Shown with AIR-1 and MSR-1 lights; pick your MSR-2 RGB light the same way.

7. Under Action select Turn On and now your sensors RGB lights will turn on when the alarm is triggered.

Shown with AIR-1 and MSR-1 lights; the MSR-2 steps are the same.

8. And that's it, seriously... Now you can enjoy a free and local security system.

We hope this was helpful and please let us know if there are any questions!

docs.title: Set up the Apollo mmWave dashboard for the MSR-2
Set up the Apollo mmWave dashboard for the MSR-2
docs.text:
A new Apollo radar sensor detects presence out of the box, but every room is different: a ceiling fan or a moving curtain can make it trigger with nobody there, and someone sitting still can be missed. The Apollo mmWave dashboard is where you fix that. On an Apollo MSR-1, MSR-2, or R PRO-1 with the LD2412 addon, one button, Calibrate with empty room, sets the radar's thresholds for your room in about a minute and a half. On an Apollo MTR-1 or R PRO-1, the same dashboard is where you draw zones over the radar's live targets.

The Apollo mmWave integration gives every Apollo radar sensor in your home its own workspace in Home Assistant. When you add it, it offers to add an Apollo mmWave dashboard to your sidebar with one tab per radar, built from the devices Home Assistant already knows about. Add a sensor later and its tab appears on its own; remove one and its tab goes away.

What each tab holds depends on the radar inside the sensor:

Sensor Radar chip What its tab shows Apollo MSR-1, Apollo MSR-2 LD2410 Radar tuning: setup checks, auto-calibration, distance and gate energy charts, thresholds, detection range, and occupancy Apollo R PRO-1 LD2450, plus the optional LD2412 addon The same radar tuning cards for the LD2412, plus a zone map for drawing occupancy zones over the LD2450's live targets, with the LD2450's setup check, live status, and controls beside it Apollo MTR-1 LD2450 A zone map, with the radar's setup check, live status, and controls beside it

Every tab starts with a Start here card that lists your sensor's first steps, and ends with a Device card that shows its firmware versions and restarts it. LD2410, LD2412, and LD2450 are the model numbers of the radar chips, and the card titles use them.

If you built the MSR-2 tuning dashboard by hand, this replaces it. The integration ships its own cards and updates them along with itself, so Streamline Card, Plotly Graph Card, and the YAML generator are no longer needed.

Before you start

  • You're running Home Assistant 2026.8.1 or newer. Settings → About shows your version.

  • HACS 2.0.5 or newer is installed and set up. HACS is a community store for Home Assistant that installs and updates custom integrations like this one. If you don't have it yet, follow the HACS download guide and then the initial configuration guide. Setup asks you to sign in with a free GitHub account. On Home Assistant OS, the button below opens the Get HACS app that the download guide uses.

  • Your Apollo sensor is already in Home Assistant through the ESPHome integration. If it isn't, work through getting started first.

docs.title: Install Apollo mmWave through HACS
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave installs from its GitHub repository, so you add that repository to HACS once as a custom repository. From then on HACS tracks updates for it like any other integration. The button under step 1 covers steps 1 to 5: it adds the repository, after HACS asks you to confirm, and opens Apollo mmWave so you can go on at step 6.

If you installed Apollo mmWave from the original repository, bharvey88/apollo-mmwave, which is no longer on GitHub, follow From the original Apollo mmWave repository instead. It switches HACS over without setting anything up again.

  1. Open HACS from your Home Assistant sidebar.

  2. Click the three-dot menu in the upper right corner and choose Custom repositories.

  3. Paste https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/apollo-mmwave-main into the Repository field.
  4. Set Type to Integration and click Add. The repository shows up in the list; close the dialog.
  5. Search HACS for Apollo mmWave and open it.
  6. Click Download, then confirm with Download in the dialog that opens.

  7. Restart Home Assistant: go to Settings → System, click the power icon in the upper right corner, choose Restart Home Assistant, then click Restart. Wait for it to come back.

Home Assistant only loads a new integration when it starts, so the restart is what makes Apollo mmWave available to add in the next step.

docs.title: Add the integration
docs.text:
This is the step that builds your dashboard. You add Apollo mmWave once and it covers every Apollo radar you own, so there's no need to repeat it per sensor. Adding it a second time stops with This entry is already configured.

  1. Go to Settings → Devices & services and click Add integration. Or use the button below, which opens the Apollo mmWave setup dialog directly, and skip to step 3.

  2. Search for Apollo mmWave and select it. If it isn't in the list, refresh the browser page (your browser may still hold the list from before the restart) and search again.

  3. The dialog notes that the integration serves its own cards and dashboard, with nothing else to download, and offers to add the dashboard for you. Leave both boxes ticked (they're on by default) to get the dashboard this guide describes:
    • Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard to the sidebar creates the dashboard once, when you click Submit. Untick it only if you'd rather place the cards on your own dashboards; you can still add the dashboard later from the integration options.
    • Only administrators can see it keeps the dashboard out of other users' sidebars. Untick it to show the dashboard to everyone in your home. You can change this later in the dashboard's settings under Settings → Dashboards.
  4. Click Submit, then Finish on the success message.

Apollo mmWave now appears under Settings → Devices & services. With the first box ticked, a new Apollo mmWave entry with a radar icon also sits in your sidebar, at the apollo-mmwave address. The integration registers its cards with Home Assistant itself, so they load in browser tabs that were already open without a refresh. If the dashboard couldn't be created, setup still finishes without it, and The Apollo mmWave dashboard isn't in the sidebar shows how to add it.

Created once, then it's yours

From Apollo mmWave 2.2.6, the dashboard is created once, when you click Submit. Apollo mmWave never recreates, rewrites, or deletes it on its own: not when Home Assistant restarts, and not when the integration reloads or updates. It's an ordinary dashboard, so you can rename it, change its icon, hide it, or delete it under Settings → Dashboards like any other. To add it again later, remove it, or add a second one, see Manage the dashboard.

docs.title: Open the dashboard
docs.text:
Click Apollo mmWave in the sidebar. With two or more radars you'll see one tab per radar along the top, each named after the device the way it appears in Home Assistant. With one radar, Home Assistant shows the dashboard title instead of a tab bar, and that radar's cards fill the page. The tabs keep themselves current: add a sensor and its tab appears, no page reload needed.

The cards on each tab are laid out in columns that stack into one on a phone. Here's what a working first load looks like for each sensor. A row only appears when its entity is enabled in Home Assistant, so some cards can be shorter than described.

docs.title: MSR-2 and MSR-1 tabs
docs.text:
Both sensors use the LD2410 radar chip, so their tabs look the same, and the tuning card titles start with LD2410.

  • Start here sits at the top. It names your sensor and lists five steps, from Fix anything the Radar setup card flags. to walking the room while you watch the Gate Energy chart. Its links open the tuning guide on this wiki and your sensor's own page in Home Assistant.

  • Under it, the Radar setup card checks the radar's settings and offers a fix when one is off. On a sensor that's ready to go it reads Radar settings look good.

  • Auto-calibrate comes next, with the Calibrate with empty room and Preview only buttons. If your sensor still has its factory thresholds and has never been calibrated, the card adds These look like factory thresholds. Calibrating sets them for your room.

  • The LD2410 Gate Energy chart is dimmed behind Turn on Radar Engineering Mode to see gate energy values, with a Turn on Radar Engineering Mode button below. That's expected: the radar only reports gate energy while Radar Engineering Mode, a diagnostic setting, is on. You don't need to press the button before calibrating; the calibration turns the mode on for its listen and puts it back the way it was afterward.

  • The other cards hold the radar's settings and live readings: controls, distances, detection range, occupancy, a threshold for each gate (from G0 (at the sensor) to G8, each named for how far out it reaches), and a day of occupancy history. The sliders on the range and threshold cards start locked, so a scroll can't move them: press Unlock above them to change one. The Device card at the bottom shows the firmware versions and restarts the sensor. The tour of the radar tab explains each one.

docs.title: R PRO-1 tabs
docs.text:
The R PRO-1 tab starts with the same tuning cards, titled LD2412 instead of LD2410, for the optional LD2412 radar addon, and adds a zone map for its LD2450 radar. Without the addon, the LD2412 cards still appear but have no radar behind them, so skip to the zone map, and Start here gives the zone map steps instead. The differences from an MSR-2 tab:

  • Start here says what each radar is for: the LD2412 senses people anywhere in range, even sitting still, and the LD2450 tracks where people are and drives the zone map.
  • LD2412 Controls adds Start Dynamic Background Correction and Background Correction Running. The Auto-calibrate card reminds you to run background correction first, with the room empty, and wait for its status to turn off before you calibrate.
  • LD2412 Detection Range holds Radar Timeout, Max Gate, and Min Gate, plus Distance Resolution if you've enabled that entity (it's hidden on a new sensor).
  • The thresholds cards and the Gate Energy chart cover 14 gates, G0 to G13.
  • There's no Zone Config card, and the LD2412 Distances chart shows the gates and your Max Gate and Min Gate limits without distance bars.
  • After the first column (Start here, the LD2412's Radar setup card, Auto-calibrate, LD2412 Controls, and LD2412 Target / Occupancy), a Zone Map heading introduces the LD2450's cards: its own Radar setup card, the zone map, Zone presence, LD2450 Live, and LD2450 Controls, described below. The rest of the LD2412 cards follow, so on a phone you reach the zone map before the 28 threshold rows.

docs.title: MTR-1 tabs
docs.text:
An MTR-1 tab is built around the zone map, with everything for its LD2450 radar beside it:

  • Start here lists three steps (fix anything the Radar setup card flags, set Cone rotation, then draw a zone and walk into it), says which presence sensor to use in automations, and links to your sensor's own page.
  • Radar setup checks Zone Type and Multi Target Tracking, the two radar settings that decide whether the map can show people, and fixes them when you press its button. Zone Type should be Disabled, because the zone map replaces the radar's own built-in zones.
  • The zone map, titled with your sensor's name, shows the radar's view, a cone 120 degrees wide and about 6 m (20 ft) out, with a dot for each target the LD2450 is tracking. It's in feet or meters to match Home Assistant, and the m / ft switch on the map changes it. A pencil button in the lower left opens the drawing tools, the lower right holds the unit switch and the undo and lock buttons, and a collapsed Configure section under the grid holds the cone rotation slider and the zone list.
  • Zone presence, LD2450 Live, and Occupancy History show each zone's presence sensor, what the radar reports right now, and the last 24 hours.
  • LD2450 Controls, the radar's built-in zones (only while Zone Type isn't Disabled), and the Device card end the tab.

The integration finds the sensor's target entities itself, so there's nothing to pick before you start drawing. The R PRO-1's zone map and the cards beside it work the same way.

docs.title: What to do first
docs.text:
Your dashboard is working. Follow the Start here card on each tab, from the top:

  1. Look at the Radar setup card near the top of the tab. If it flags a setting, follow what it says: most problems have a button that fixes them, and the card changes nothing until you press one. An R PRO-1 tab has a second one above the zone map, for the LD2450.

  2. On an MSR-1 or MSR-2 tab, or an R PRO-1 tab with the LD2412 addon, calibrate the radar. Skip this step on an R PRO-1 without the LD2412. On an R PRO-1, first clear the room, press Start Dynamic Background Correction on the LD2412 Controls card, and wait for Background Correction Running to turn off. Then press Calibrate with empty room on the Auto-calibrate card and leave the room for about a minute and a half. You don't need to turn on Radar Engineering Mode: the calibration does that for you. The tuning guide walks you through it.

  3. On an MTR-1 or R PRO-1 tab, draw your zones.

The rest of this page covers managing the dashboard, upgrading from an older setup, and troubleshooting, so come back to it when you need it.

docs.title: Manage the dashboard
docs.text:
After setup, Apollo mmWave changes its dashboard only when you ask it to, from the integration options: add the dashboard, remove it, or choose which sensors get a tab. Open Settings → Devices & services → Apollo mmWave → Configure to reach the Apollo mmWave options menu. It reads These actions change only the Apollo mmWave dashboard this integration created. Dashboards you made yourself are never changed. and lists the actions that fit:

  • Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard is listed while the integration has no dashboard of its own: you unticked the box during setup, setup couldn't create it, or you deleted it. It describes the dashboard it creates and asks Only administrators can see it again. Click Submit to create it, once, with the sensors you chose under Choose the dashboard's devices.
  • Remove the Apollo mmWave dashboard is listed while the integration has one. Click Submit to delete the Apollo mmWave dashboard at /apollo-mmwave that the integration created, along with any title, icon, or strategy options you changed on it. Your sensors, zones, and calibration values stay, and the cards still work on your own dashboards. You can add the dashboard again from the same menu.
  • Choose the dashboard's devices opens Dashboard devices, which is empty by default and shows every Apollo mmWave device Home Assistant knows about, online or not. Select one or more devices to show exactly those and hide the rest; a selected device keeps its tab even while it's offline. Clear the selection to go back to automatic detection. The picker only lists Apollo MSR-1, MSR-2, MTR-1, and R PRO-1 sensors added through ESPHome.

Each action takes effect as soon as you click Submit, with no restart, and an open dashboard picks up a new device selection without a reload. The device selection is written only into the dashboard the integration created. Without one, the selection is kept and used when you add the dashboard from the options.

You can also delete the dashboard under Settings → Dashboards, like any other. It stays deleted until you add it again from the options.

docs.title: Add another Apollo mmWave dashboard
docs.text:
Want a second dashboard, say one with only the bedroom sensors, or one at another address because something else already uses apollo-mmwave? Home Assistant's dashboard picker adds one that builds its tabs the same way as the integration's own:

  1. Go to Settings → Dashboards and click Add dashboard.

  2. Pick Apollo Radar Tuning under Community dashboards.

  3. Give it a title and a URL other than apollo-mmwave, then click Create.

A dashboard you add this way is yours from the start, and the integration options never change it. It shows every detected Apollo mmWave device; to limit it, set devices in its raw configuration, as the Apollo mmWave configuration guide shows. The URL matters: if you delete the integration's dashboard and add one of these at apollo-mmwave, Apollo mmWave can mistake it for the dashboard it created, and its options and removal would then act on yours.

docs.title: Use your own layout
docs.text:
Want to rearrange the cards? Click the pencil icon in the upper right corner of the dashboard and choose Take control in the dialog that opens. From then on the layout is yours: the integration stops offering to remove the dashboard, writes no device selection into it, and leaves it in place when you remove the integration. The dashboard also stops adding and removing tabs as sensors come and go. Changed your mind? Delete the dashboard under Settings → Dashboards, then choose Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard in the integration options to get a fresh one. If you add the Apollo tabs to a dashboard of your own, take control of that dashboard before you edit them; editing an auto-built tab directly discards its cards.

A dashboard you took control of keeps the cards it had, so it doesn't pick up new cards from later releases, such as the updated Start here steps, the Radar setup cards, the Device card, and the slider lock that came with 2.3.0. To get them, delete it and add a fresh one from the options as described above.

The cards also work on their own: in the card picker they're listed as Apollo Radar Auto-Calibrate, Apollo Radar Distance Chart, Apollo Radar Gate Energy Chart, Apollo Radar Setup, and Apollo Zone Map. The Apollo mmWave configuration guide has the YAML for placing them.

docs.title: Upgrade from an older setup
docs.text:
If this is your first Apollo dashboard, skip this section and calibrate your radar or draw your zones. Troubleshooting is at the end of this page if something didn't load.

Before any upgrade, make a full Home Assistant backup under Settings → System → Backups, so you can go back if something goes wrong. After you update Apollo mmWave in HACS, restart Home Assistant, then refresh the dashboard in your browser so it loads the new cards.

docs.title: Updating to Apollo mmWave 2.3.0
docs.text:
In most setups 2.3.0 needs nothing from you. After the restart and a refresh, each tab gets the new layout: Start here and Radar setup at the top, locked sliders, the zone map in your units with the LD2450's cards beside it, and the Device card at the bottom. Check these if they apply to you:

  • Zones drawn before 2.2.7 with Home Assistant in US customary units. Before 2.2.7, the zone map read the radar's positions in inches as if they were millimeters, so the dots sat at or near the sensor. A zone drawn around those dots may not cover where people show up now. Walk through the room, watch the dots, and redraw any zone that's off.
  • A dashboard you took control of keeps the cards it had. To get the new ones, see Use your own layout.
  • A zone map card you added from the card picker before 2.3.0 keeps the fixed grid saved in its YAML, with no distance labels or range caption. If you didn't choose that grid yourself (the card picker saved x_min: -6000, x_max: 6000, y_min: 0, y_max: 12000 with grid_units: mm), open the card's code editor, delete grid and grid_units, and set unit_display: true to get the map fitted to the radar's view, in your units. A grid you set on purpose can stay.
  • Dashboard resources managed in YAML. Replace both ?v= addresses with the ones the log warning lists (see An Apollo card shows an error after an update).

docs.title: From Apollo mmWave 2.2.5 or earlier
docs.text:
Up to 2.2.5, Apollo mmWave rebuilt its dashboard every time it loaded, and the Auto-create the Apollo mmWave dashboard option decided whether the dashboard existed. From 2.2.6 that option is gone: the dashboard is created once, and Apollo mmWave adds or removes it only when you ask in its options (see Manage the dashboard). The update needs nothing from you:

  • The dashboard you already have stays as it is, including who can see it. Dashboards made before 2.2.6 are visible to every user; to limit yours to administrators, turn on Admin-only in its settings under Settings → Dashboards.
  • If it still builds itself (you never took control of it), the integration records it as the dashboard it created. The options can then remove it or write a device selection into it, and deleting the integration deletes it too. A dashboard you took control of is yours, and the integration leaves it alone.
  • If you had turned the auto-create option off, the integration records no dashboard, and setup no longer deletes a dashboard you made yourself at apollo-mmwave. Add the integration's dashboard from the options whenever you want it.

Going back to 2.2.5 or earlier from HACS turns the old behavior back on, as if the auto-create option were on: the dashboard is recreated or rewritten at every start, even if you had turned the option off. To go back, restore the backup you made before updating.

docs.title: From the MSR-2 tuning dashboard
docs.text:
Your thresholds, detection range, and every other setting live on the sensor itself, and the new dashboard reads the same entities. There's nothing to migrate: once your MSR-2 tab works in the Apollo mmWave dashboard, you can delete the old view.

Back up before you edit raw YAML

The raw configuration editor holds your whole dashboard. Copy its contents somewhere safe before you delete anything, so you can paste it back if a cut goes wrong.

  1. Open the dashboard you pasted the old YAML into, click Edit dashboard, open the three-dot menu, and choose Raw configuration editor.

  2. Find the old view. It starts like this:

      - type: sections
    max_columns: 4
    title: MSR-2 Configuration
    path: msr-2-configuration

  3. Delete that view, from its - type: sections line down to the line before the next view (or before streamline_templates:). If you ran the generator for more than one MSR-2, repeat for each MSR-2 Configuration view.

  4. At the bottom, delete the ld2410_ templates under streamline_templates:. If nothing else on your dashboards uses Streamline Card, delete the whole streamline_templates: block.
  5. Click Save.

If no other cards use them, you can also remove Streamline Card and Plotly Graph Card from HACS. Apollo mmWave doesn't need either.

docs.title: From the original Apollo mmWave repository
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave used to install from the original repository, bharvey88/apollo-mmwave, which is no longer on GitHub. If HACS installed your copy from there, point HACS at the new repository, ApolloAutomation/apollo-mmwave-main, so you keep getting updates. It's the same integration in the same folder, so nothing needs to be set up again: what you already have carries over, such as your Apollo mmWave entry, its dashboard, your zones, the saved calibration values that Undo uses, and your entity IDs. The switch takes one Home Assistant restart.

If the old copy is version 1.x or 2.0, not everything carries over on its own. Read the upgrade notes in the changelog first. Some cards and automations need a change by hand, and From Apollo mmWave 1.x zone mapping below sums them up.

Keep your Apollo mmWave entry in Home Assistant

The switch happens in HACS only. If you choose Delete from the three-dot menu on the entry under Settings → Devices & services → Apollo mmWave, Home Assistant asks Delete Apollo mmWave? and warns that its devices and entities will be permanently deleted. Deleting it also deletes the Apollo mmWave dashboard it created, every zone, and the saved calibration values that Undo uses. Setting it up again starts from nothing.

Leave Remove and Redownload alone in HACS

Both Apollo mmWave entries in HACS use the same custom_components/apollo_mmwave folder. Remove, on either entry, first shows Integration is configured and tells you to delete the configuration. Don't: Navigate leads to the integrations page, where Delete wipes your zones. Ignore, or closing the box, opens a Remove box whose Remove button deletes the folder, new download included, so Apollo mmWave won't load after the next restart. Redownload on the old entry fails because its repository is gone, and the folder can end up missing. Step 3 takes the old entry off the list without touching any files.

  1. Check two versions first. Home Assistant needs to be 2026.8.1 or newer (Settings → About). In HACS, click the three-dot menu in the upper right corner, choose About HACS, and check that Integration version is 2.0.5 or newer. The new repository won't download on older versions. Then make a full Home Assistant backup under Settings → System → Backups (see Upgrade from an older setup).
  2. In HACS, click the three-dot menu in the upper right corner and choose Custom repositories.
  3. Find the row whose second line reads bharvey88/apollo-mmwave (integration) and click the trash can icon on that row. There's no confirmation, so read the second line before you click: removing the wrong row deletes no files, but you have to add that repository again. This only takes the old entry off the HACS list. The files in custom_components/apollo_mmwave stay where they are, and Apollo mmWave keeps running.
    • If you already added the new repository, there are two rows. Remove only the bharvey88/apollo-mmwave one.
    • If there's no bharvey88/apollo-mmwave row, there's nothing to remove. Go on to step 4.

  4. If the dialog closed after step 3, open Custom repositories again. Paste https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/apollo-mmwave-main into the Repository field, set Type to Integration, click Add, and close the dialog. Or use the button below instead: it shows an Add custom repository box, and clicking Add there opens the repository page in HACS for you.

  5. Search HACS for Apollo mmWave and open it. Only one entry is left, and if you used the button in step 4, it's already open. Click Download in the lower right corner, then click Download again in the dialog. The dialog says the files go to /config/custom_components/apollo_mmwave, the same folder as before. Wait for it to finish.

    • If it shows an error, don't restart. Fix the cause and click Download again until it finishes with no error. On a first download HACS saves no backup copy of the folder, so a download that stops partway can leave old and new files mixed together.
  6. Look at the HACS list. Apollo mmWave now shows Pending restart, and the old entry is gone.

  7. Restart Home Assistant: go to Settings → System, click the power icon in the upper right corner, choose Restart Home Assistant, then click Restart. The Restart required repair that HACS adds does the same when you click Submit.

After the restart, HACS shows one Apollo mmWave entry with the status Downloaded. Everything else is where you left it: your same entry under Settings → Devices & services → Apollo mmWave, the Apollo mmWave dashboard in the sidebar, your zones on the zone map, your previous calibration values behind Undo, and the same entity IDs. If a card looks old or doesn't load, do a hard refresh with Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac). From here on, HACS tracks updates from the new repository.

HACS may leave its own update entity for the old repository behind, showing as unavailable. It belongs to HACS, not Apollo mmWave, so deleting it is optional and doesn't touch your zones.

docs.title: From Apollo mmWave 1.x zone mapping
docs.text:
Most of the move to 2.x happens on its own the first time the integration starts. If you wrote cards or automations by hand, change these yourself:

  • Card name. A hand-written zone card set to custom:zone-mapper-card now shows as a missing card. Change it to custom:apollo-radar-zone-map-card and give it the radar's device_id (plus an optional title) in place of location.
  • The apollo_mmwave.update_zone action. Pass device_id. location still works as a deprecated alias, logs a warning once per restart, and will be removed in a later release.
  • Zone change triggers. The apollo_mmwave_zone_updated event now carries device_id where it used to carry location, so a trigger reading trigger.event.data.location stops matching.
  • Empty entities lists. In an update_zone call, an empty entities list now leaves the tracked targets alone instead of erasing them. To empty the list on purpose, pass clear_entities: true.
  • dark_mode. The zone map follows your Home Assistant theme now, and dark_mode in the card config is an override. Remove it if you want the card to track your theme.

And here's what changes without you doing anything:

  • Target sensors are found automatically. The old Device and Targets picker is gone; the integration locates each radar's LD2450 target sensors itself.
  • Zone entities move onto the radar's device page. Your entity IDs, custom names, and area assignments are kept, and you can rename the entities freely.
  • Renaming a radar no longer loses its zones, because zones are stored per device rather than per display name. If you renamed a radar before upgrading, its zones are kept but not shown: the card comes up empty and the zone entities read as unavailable. Rename the radar back to its old name and reload the integration to bring them back, or keep the new name and redraw the zones.
  • Zones from the standalone Zone Mapper integration are imported when Apollo mmWave has no zone data of its own yet: on a fresh install, or when upgrading from a version before 1.2.0. The import only reads; nothing belonging to Zone Mapper is renamed or removed. Upgrading from 1.2.0 or later, the import is skipped and your existing Apollo mmWave zones are kept. Redraw any Zone Mapper zones you want on the zone map, then remove the old integration once you're happy with them.

Keep Zone Mapper until your zones have moved over

Don't uninstall the standalone Zone Mapper integration until you've confirmed your zones moved over. Its restore data is the only copy, and it goes away with its entities.

If a zone you expected is missing, search your Home Assistant log for apollo_mmwave. When the same zone number exists both on a device and in leftover pre-2.0 data, the copy already on the device wins, and the dropped copy is written to the log.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If none of these match, send Apollo a support file with your question.

docs.title: The Apollo mmWave dashboard isn't in the sidebar
docs.text:
Work through these in order:

  • Sign in as an administrator. The dashboard is for administrators only unless you unticked Only administrators can see it. To show it to everyone, turn off Admin-only in its settings under Settings → Dashboards.

  • Look under Settings → Dashboards. Apollo mmWave is listed there even when it's hidden. If you find it, check that its Add to sidebar setting is on and that you haven't hidden it from your own sidebar in your profile.

  • If it isn't listed, the integration has no dashboard: you unticked Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard to the sidebar during setup, setup couldn't create it, or it was deleted. Apollo mmWave never recreates it on its own, so add it from the integration options with Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard (see Manage the dashboard).

  • If another dashboard already uses the apollo-mmwave address, such as one you made yourself, the integration leaves that one as it is and doesn't create its own. Adding it from the options then shows The dashboard could not be created. Another dashboard may already use /apollo-mmwave; the Home Assistant log says why. You can add one from Settings > Dashboards > Add dashboard > Apollo Radar Tuning instead.

  • Open Settings → System → Logs and look for a warning that starts with Apollo mmWave:. If setup or the options couldn't create the dashboard, the warning says why and points you to the dashboard picker: Add one from Settings > Dashboards > Add dashboard > Apollo Radar Tuning (strategy type 'custom:apollo-radar-tuning'). You'll also see a warning that apollo_mmwave is a custom integration Home Assistant hasn't tested. Every custom integration installed through HACS logs that one, so you can ignore it.

  • If the integration can't create the dashboard, add one yourself from the dashboard picker, as described in Add another Apollo mmWave dashboard.

docs.title: The integration options show an error
docs.text:
When an action in the integration options fails, it changes nothing, and its form stays open with the reason:

  • The dashboard could not be created. Another dashboard may already use /apollo-mmwave; the Home Assistant log says why. You can add one from Settings > Dashboards > Add dashboard > Apollo Radar Tuning instead. Check Settings → Dashboards for a dashboard at apollo-mmwave and the log for a warning that starts with Apollo mmWave:. Delete that other dashboard and try again, or add another Apollo mmWave dashboard at a different URL.
  • The dashboard could not be removed. The Home Assistant log says why. You can delete it in Settings > Dashboards. Delete it there instead. The next time you open the options, they offer to add it again.
  • The dashboard could not be updated. The Home Assistant log says why. The new device selection wasn't saved, and the dashboard keeps the one it had. Check the log for a warning that starts with Apollo mmWave:, then try again.

If the options open straight on Dashboard devices, with no menu, Apollo mmWave couldn't read Home Assistant's dashboards, so it offers only the device selection. A selection you save there is kept but not written into the dashboard. Check the log, then open the options again and save the selection once the menu is back.

docs.title: The dashboard shows no devices
docs.text: The dashboard starts with No Apollo mmWave devices found. It found no radar to build a tab for. Confirm your sensor shows up under Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome, and check that Dashboard devices, under Choose the dashboard's devices in the integration options, is empty or lists your current devices. On a dashboard you added from Community dashboards, check the devices list in its raw configuration instead.

docs.title: One sensor has no tab
docs.text:
Work through these in order:

  • If Dashboard devices has any devices selected, the dashboard shows only those. Add the missing sensor under Choose the dashboard's devices in the integration options, or clear the selection to go back to automatic detection.
  • A dashboard you took control of no longer adds tabs on its own. Add the sensor's cards yourself, or delete the dashboard and add a fresh one from the integration options.
  • The dashboard only picks up radars added through the ESPHome integration. A copy of the same sensor that another integration created (a network integration tracking it by its MAC address, for example) doesn't get a tab.
  • A sensor you added a moment ago gets its tab once Home Assistant has registered its entities. It appears on its own, without a page reload.
  • DIY builds that don't report an Apollo model only get a tab while one of their radar entities is live.

docs.title: A tab says the sensor is offline
docs.text: The Start here card adds Offline right now., and the Radar setup card reads Radar is offline. Its settings are checked once it reconnects. On an MSR-1, MSR-2, or R PRO-1 tab, the Auto-calibrate card reads Radar is offline. Calibration needs the radar online and its gate entities enabled. with its buttons disabled. On an MTR-1 or R PRO-1 tab, the zone map shows no targets until the sensor reconnects. The tab stays so the sensor isn't silently missing, and the cards fill in once it reconnects. Check its power and Wi-Fi, and that it shows as online on the ESPHome integration page. If you replaced or reflashed the sensor under a new name, the old device entry is what's showing as offline: delete the old device under Settings → Devices & services and its tab goes away.

docs.title: An Apollo card shows an error after an update
docs.text:
After you update Apollo mmWave through HACS and restart, a browser that still holds the previous version's files can show the Apollo cards as error boxes that read Custom element doesn't exist. Refresh the page. Each release loads its cards under a new versioned address, so a fresh page load picks up the current version. If the error is still there, do a hard refresh with Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac). If that doesn't clear it either, check Settings → System → Logs for a warning that starts with Apollo mmWave: about Lovelace resources. On a system that manages its dashboard resources in YAML, the warning lists the two resource addresses to add by hand.

If the element named in the error is zone-mapper-card, a refresh won't help: that's the old card name, so update the card as described in From Apollo mmWave 1.x zone mapping.

docs.title: The Auto-calibrate card is still loading
docs.text:
The card reads Apollo mmWave is still loading... right after a restart while the integration starts, and clears on its own. If it changes to Apollo mmWave is not loaded, so calibration is unavailable., check that Apollo mmWave is enabled under Settings → Devices & services, then click Retry on the card.

Next step: calibrate your radar or draw zones

Your dashboard is up and every sensor has its tab. Now put it to work: the usage guide walks you through calibrating with an empty room, reading the charts, adjusting thresholds by hand, and drawing zones on the zone map.

Use the Apollo mmWave dashboard

docs.title: Tune your MSR-2 radar with the Apollo mmWave dashboard
Tune your MSR-2 radar with the Apollo mmWave dashboard
docs.text:
The Apollo mmWave dashboard puts every setting your radar has on one screen, with live charts that show what the radar sees. On an Apollo MSR-1, Apollo MSR-2, or Apollo R PRO-1 with the optional LD2412 radar addon, it can teach the radar what your empty room looks like in about a minute and a half, so it stops reacting to the room itself and starts reacting to people. On an R PRO-1 or an Apollo MTR-1 it is also where you draw occupancy zones on a map of the room.

Every tab starts with a Start here card that lists your sensor's first steps in order, and this guide follows the same order: check the Radar setup card, calibrate, set how far the radar looks and how long presence stays on, then fine-tune by hand. If you only do one thing today, press Calibrate with empty room and leave the room: Calibrate with an empty room shows what to expect. On an MTR-1, or an R PRO-1 without the LD2412, go straight to drawing zones.

Here's the Start here card on an MSR-1. On an MTR-1, or an R PRO-1 without the LD2412, it lists three zone map steps instead, and on an R PRO-1 with the LD2412 it covers both radars.

Before you start

  • The Apollo mmWave integration is installed and its Apollo mmWave dashboard is in your Home Assistant sidebar. If it isn't, sign in as an administrator (from Apollo mmWave 2.2.6, the dashboard is for administrators only unless you unticked that box), or follow the Apollo mmWave dashboard setup guide to add it.
  • This guide shows Apollo mmWave 2.3.0. On an older version some cards look different, so update it first.
  • Your radar is online in Home Assistant through ESPHome.
  • Your sensor is mounted where it will stay. A calibration, and the zones you draw, describe the room from the sensor's position, so moving the sensor later means calibrating again or redrawing your zones.
  • A calibration needs the room empty for about a minute and a half: people and pets out, robot vacuum docked.

docs.title: How radar tuning works
docs.text:
The radar splits the space in front of it into distance bands called gates. G0 sits right at the sensor, G1 is the next band out, and so on to the far edge of its range. For every gate the radar measures two kinds of signal on a scale of 0 to 100: move energy, which rises when something moves at that distance (someone walking past), and still energy, which picks up the much smaller signal of someone who is there but not moving (sitting on the couch, breathing, typing).

Each gate has a move threshold and a still threshold. When a gate's energy rises above its threshold, that gate detects a target (the radar's word for a person, or anything else it picks up) and the radar reports presence. A lower threshold makes the gate more sensitive (and more likely to trigger on a fan or a curtain); a higher one makes it less sensitive. To see the live energy of every gate, the radar has to be in Radar Engineering Mode, a diagnostic setting that streams the per-gate readings to Home Assistant. With it off you still get presence, but the Gate Energy chart has nothing to show. It's safe to turn on and off whenever you like: it changes what the radar reports, not how it detects. The calibration turns it on for you while it listens. Left on, it saves every gate's energy to Home Assistant's database about once a second, so the Radar setup card reminds you to turn it off.

How far away is each gate?

Each gate is one step of the radar's gate size. Unless you changed it, that's 0.75 m (about 2.5 ft). You don't need to work the distances out: each row on the Move Thresholds and Still Thresholds cards is named for how far out its gate reaches, such as G4 (about 3 m), or G4 (about 10 ft) when Home Assistant uses US customary units. G4 covers 2.25 m to 3 m (about 7.4 ft to 9.8 ft) from the sensor. The gate size setting is Gate Size on an MSR-1 or MSR-2 and Distance Resolution on an R PRO-1, and it's hidden on a new sensor: it only shows on the Detection Range card after you enable its entity on the sensor's device page. The Gates row on the Distances chart draws each gate along the distance axis, so you can read it off the screen. It starts at G1, because G0 is the reading right at the sensor and has no width. On an R PRO-1, a smaller Distance Resolution (0.5 m) gives finer tuning over a shorter range, and a larger one (0.75 m) reaches farther.

docs.title: Start with the Radar setup card
docs.text:
The first step on Start here points at the Radar setup card right under it on an MSR-1, MSR-2, or R PRO-1 tab. It reads the radar's settings and flags anything that gets in the way of a good calibration. Its second line names the chip and the sensor, and when there's nothing to fix it reads Radar settings look good.

The card changes nothing on its own. When it flags something, it says what's wrong and, where it can, offers a button that names the one change it makes:

  • Radar Engineering Mode is on, so every gate's energy is saved to the database about once a second. Press Turn off Radar Engineering Mode once you're done watching the Gate Energy chart. While a calibration runs, the card says nothing about it, because the calibration needs the mode on.
  • The radar has not reported its gate thresholds yet, so those settings are blank. Press Read settings from the radar. It only asks the radar to send them; nothing on the radar changes.
  • A zone that can never turn on (MSR-1 and MSR-2), for example Zone 2 can never turn on. End Zone 2 (150 cm) must be larger than End Zone 1 (200 cm). The distances on the LD2410 Zone Config card are out of order, or a zone starts past how far the radar is set to look. Change the distances on the Zone Config card, or raise the max gates on the Detection Range card.
  • Min Gate at or above Max Gate (R PRO-1). The LD2412 only detects people from Min Gate out to Max Gate, so set Min Gate lower than Max Gate on the LD2412 Detection Range card.

The last two have no button: the card explains them and leaves the new values to you. On an MTR-1, the Radar setup card under Start here checks the LD2450 instead, and an R PRO-1 tab has a second Radar setup card above the zone map for its LD2450. Both are covered in Check the LD2450's Radar setup card.

docs.title: Calibrate with an empty room
docs.text:
Calibration is the fastest way to a well-tuned radar. Home Assistant listens to every gate while nobody is in the room, notes the highest energy each gate reaches from the room itself (fans, curtains, plants), and sets each threshold a little above that. Your current thresholds are saved first, so you can always put them back.

Run it when you first set up a radar, when it triggers with nobody there, and after you move the sensor or rearrange the room.

Before you press the button, the card's checklist asks for three things (an R PRO-1 adds a fourth, covered in R PRO-1 and its LD2412 radar):

  • Nobody in the radar's view: people, pets, and robot vacuums all count. Someone sitting still is the hardest case, because their still energy becomes the "background".
  • Leave fans, curtains, and plants that normally move as they usually are. They are part of the background you want the radar to ignore.
  • Radar Engineering Mode is handled for you. If it is off, Home Assistant turns it on for the listen and back off at the end. If it is already on, the card says Radar Engineering Mode is already on and will stay on.

On an MSR-1 or MSR-2 that has never been tuned, the card may also say These look like factory thresholds. Calibrating sets them for your room.

A threshold of 100 means that gate never triggers, so some people set a gate to 100 to turn it off. Calibration sets every gate the radar uses, including those, and the card warns you first, for example The G2 still threshold is off (set to 100). Calibrating will turn it back on. If you turned that gate off on purpose, calibrate anyway and set it back to 100 afterward on the Still Thresholds (or Move Thresholds) card.

docs.title: Run a calibration
docs.text:
You start the calibration from the card, then stay out of the room for about a minute and a half while it listens. On an R PRO-1, first clear the room, press Start Dynamic Background Correction on the LD2412 Controls card, and wait for Background Correction Running to turn off (see R PRO-1 and its LD2412 radar).

  1. Press Calibrate with empty room on the Auto-calibrate card. Take your phone with you if you'd like to watch the countdown and the listen from outside the room.
  2. Leave the room while the countdown runs and close the door behind you. Then move away from the door and the walls: the radar can see through drywall and thin doors, so waiting right outside can count as someone in the room. If the room has no door, go to another room, out of the sensor's view.
  3. Come back after about a minute and a half, once the card shows Thresholds updated, and read the result.

The job runs inside Home Assistant, so closing the browser or putting your phone away does not stop it. Open the dashboard again and the card picks up wherever the job is. Here is what the card shows along the way:

Stage What the card shows How long Starting (only if Radar Engineering Mode was off) Turning on Radar Engineering Mode... A moment Countdown Leave the room now. and Listening starts in 15 s., counting down 15 seconds Warm-up Waiting for gate energy from the radar..., only if the radar is slow to start sending energy A few seconds at most Listening Listening to the empty room... 60 s left, Keep the room empty. 12 samples so far., and two lines starting Highest so far, move: and Highest so far, still: with the peak of each gate so far 60 seconds Reading (R PRO-1 only) Reading the radar's current thresholds... A few seconds Writing Writing 16 thresholds to the radar... 7 of 16 and Values already written stay until you undo. The count is the number of thresholds that are changing. A few seconds Checking Checking that the radar accepted the new values... About 3 seconds Done Thresholds updated

Here is a whole run on an MSR-1, sped up: turning on Radar Engineering Mode, the countdown, the listen with the highest energy of each gate so far, the writing and checking stages, and the result.

From the countdown through the listen, the card also reminds you: Leave Radar Engineering Mode on until this finishes. Turning it off during the listen stops the calibration without changing anything.

A Stop button sits under the progress bar until the checking stage. Press it and it reads Stopping... for a moment. Stopped before the writing stage, the card says Stopped. Nothing was changed. Stopped partway through writing, it says how many values were written and that Undo restores the saved values.

Not ready to change anything yet? Preview only runs the same countdown and listen and shows you the thresholds it would set. The card explains: Computes new thresholds without changing any of them. Radar Engineering Mode is still turned on for the listen. The preview ends with Preview: no threshold was changed. and These are the thresholds calibration would set: above the result table, and two buttons: Calibrate and apply starts a full calibration (with a fresh countdown and listen), and Close returns the card to its start.

docs.title: Read the result
docs.text:
When the run finishes, the card shows Thresholds updated and a summary such as Calibrated at 02:32 PM from 60 samples. 16 of 18 thresholds changed. Times appear in your browser's format, so you might see 14:32 instead of 02:32 PM. An MSR-1 or MSR-2 has 18 thresholds (9 gates, move and still); an R PRO-1 has 28 (14 gates).

Below the summary is a table with one row per gate and the columns Gate, Move peak, Move threshold, Still peak, and Still threshold. The peak is the highest energy that gate reached while the room was empty. The new threshold is that peak plus some headroom, capped at 100. From Apollo mmWave 2.2.4, the headroom is 15 points or 35% of the peak, whichever is larger: a move peak of 14 becomes a threshold of 29, and a still peak of 60 becomes 81. Earlier versions used 10 points or a quarter of the peak, so calibrate again after updating to get the extra headroom.

What the threshold cells mean:

  • 50 → 24: the threshold changed from 50 to 24.
  • 24 (unchanged): the new value matched the old one, so nothing was written.
  • 100 → 15 (was off): that gate was turned off (set to 100) and calibration turned it back on. A line under the table says so and how to turn it off again.
  • 100 (off) or 40 → 100 (off): the background at that gate was so strong the threshold went to the top of the scale, so that gate can no longer trigger. On an MSR-1 or MSR-2, the G0 and G1 still thresholds often end up here, because those gates sit right at the sensor and their still energy idles near the top. That's normal and needs no action, so the card does not warn about them. For any other gate in use, including G0 and G1 move, the card warns you (see Warnings the card can show).
  • no data: the gate sent too few readings, so it was left as it was.
  • (spike seen) after a peak: one reading jumped well above the rest, as if something moved. The threshold still comes from that peak, so that gate ends up less sensitive. If nothing should have moved there, run the calibration again with the room empty.
  • not confirmed (radar offline) or (not confirmed): the radar did not report the new value back. See Thresholds did not change on the radar.

Gates outside the range the radar is set to use are dimmed, with a note under the table such as G7, G8: not used (beyond Max Move Gate 6). They are still calibrated, so they are ready if you extend the range later.

docs.title: Check the result or undo it
docs.text:
Under the table, the card suggests a walk test:

Now walk around, then sit still for a minute: the Radar Target row in Target / Occupancy should stay on the whole time you are in the room and turn off a few seconds after you leave (Radar Timeout).

  1. Press Turn on Radar Engineering Mode on the Gate Energy chart if you'd like to watch the gates as well.
  2. Walk through the room, then sit where you usually sit and stay still for a minute or two. Radar Target covers still presence as well as movement, so it should stay on the whole time. With Radar Engineering Mode on, the bars of the gates you're in should be outlined.
  3. Leave the room. Radar Target should turn off a few seconds later, once Radar Timeout runs out, and no gate inside the radar's range should stay outlined.
  4. If you turned on Radar Engineering Mode, press Turn off Radar Engineering Mode on the Radar setup card, or use the switch on the Controls card.

Below the walk-test line are three buttons: Undo (restore your previous values), Calibrate again (a fresh calibration with a new countdown and listen), and Close. If the radar now misses you, or behaves worse than before, press Undo (restore your previous values). The card shows Restoring saved thresholds... 3 of 16 and then Restored your previous values. Undo saves the values it replaces first, so the button then reads Redo (put the calibrated values back), and pressing it puts the calibrated values back. The saved copy survives a Home Assistant restart.

If someone walked in during the listen, press Stop: nothing is written before the writing stage. If you only notice afterward, press Undo, clear the room, and press Calibrate with empty room.

The next time you open the dashboard, the card starts on its checklist again with a line such as Last calibrated Oct 11, 02:32 PM, 16 of 18 thresholds changed. (in your browser's date and time format), the Undo (restore your previous values) button with the time those values were saved under it (Saved Oct 11, 02:31 PM.), and Show last result to open the last result table.

docs.title: Warnings the card can show
docs.text:
Warnings appear under the result table. Each one is a sign the result may not match your empty room:

  • The radar reported someone present for 40% of the listen. If someone was in the room, even sitting still, press Undo and run it again. The radar detected presence for more than a quarter of the listen. That is normal for a radar that was too sensitive (which is what you are fixing), but if a person or pet was in the room, the thresholds are too high. Press Undo, clear the room, and run it again. If you're sure the room was empty, keep the result and do the walk test in Check the result or undo it.
  • The G3 move threshold is now off (its background peaked at 92). If a fan or curtain moves there all day this is fine; if not, press Undo and run again with the room really empty. That gate can no longer detect anything. If something at that distance moves all day, that is the expected result. If not, something moved there during the listen: press Undo and run it again with the room empty.
  • The radar was unavailable for part of the listen; gates with too few readings were left as they were. The radar dropped off the network for a moment. Gates marked no data kept their old thresholds. Check the radar's connection and run it again.
  • The G2 still threshold was off (set to 100) and calibration turned it back on (now 15). If you turned it off on purpose, set it back to 100 on the Still Thresholds card, or press Undo to put back all your previous values. You had that gate turned off, and calibration set it like every other gate. If you want it off, set it back to 100 on the card the line names. A preview words it as what calibration would do.
  • 2 values could not be confirmed: G3 move threshold reads back 35 (asked for 27), G5 still threshold could not be read (radar offline). Check the Move / Still Thresholds cards. The radar did not report some of the new values back. The heading reads Thresholds updated, 2 could not be confirmed. Check those gates on the threshold cards, and press Undo or run it again once the radar is stable.

docs.title: A tour of the radar tab
docs.text: Open Apollo mmWave from your sidebar and, if you have more than one radar, pick your radar's tab. On a wide screen the cards sit in columns; on a phone they stack in the order below. Card titles start with the name of the radar chip: LD2410 on an MSR-1 or MSR-2, LD2412 on an R PRO-1. A card only shows rows for entities Home Assistant has, so a setting the firmware hides has no row.

docs.title: First column
docs.text:
• Start here: your sensor's name and its first steps, pictured at the top of this guide. It ends with two links. Full tuning guide → opens this guide on the wiki: on an MSR-1 or MSR-2 the general version, the one that covers every Apollo radar, and on an R PRO-1 the R PRO-1 version at its LD2412 section. All settings for this device → opens the sensor's own page in Home Assistant, where every setting the dashboard leaves out lives. On an R PRO-1, the card also says what each radar is for and which presence sensor to use in automations.
  • Radar setup: checks the radar's settings and offers a fix (see Start with the Radar setup card).
  • Auto-calibrate: the calibration card. It shows the chip and the device name under its title, a short checklist, and the Calibrate with empty room button. Everything about it is in Calibrate with an empty room above.

  • LD2410 Controls: the Radar Engineering Mode switch, plus Radar Bluetooth (HLK app), Restart Radar, and Factory Reset Radar. On an R PRO-1 the card also has Start Dynamic Background Correction and Background Correction Running (see R PRO-1 and its LD2412 radar). Radar Bluetooth (HLK app) is the radar chip's own Bluetooth for the HLK phone app, not your sensor's Bluetooth proxy. Restart Radar restarts the radar chip without changing any settings. Leave Factory Reset Radar alone unless Apollo support asks you to press it: it puts the radar chip's settings, every threshold included, back to factory values, so run Calibrate with empty room again if it happens. Both ask before they act. The restart for the whole sensor is on the Device card at the bottom of the tab.

  • LD2410 Zone Config (MSR-1 and MSR-2): Start Zone 1, End Zone 1, End Zone 2, and End Zone 3 split the radar's range into three distance bands, each with its own occupancy sensor (Radar Zone 1 Occupancy to Radar Zone 3 Occupancy). These are distances from the sensor, not areas you draw like on the R PRO-1 and MTR-1 zone map. The boxes are in cm, even when Home Assistant uses feet, and the zones sit back to back: Zone 1 runs from Start Zone 1 to End Zone 1, Zone 2 from there to End Zone 2, and Zone 3 from there to End Zone 3. They're optional: leave them as they are unless you want separate sensors for, say, the couch and the far end of the room.

docs.title: Second column
docs.text:
• LD2410 Distances: a chart laid out along the radar's range. From top to bottom it can show a Zones row with your three distance bands (Z1 to Z3, with a filled circle when someone is in that band), bars for the current Detection, Moving, and Still distance, the Gates row, and bars that mark how far the radar is set to look (Max Move and Max Still, or Max Gate and Min Gate on an R PRO-1). On a computer, hover over a row for a short explanation. Distances show in meters, or in inches if Home Assistant uses US units.

  • LD2410 Detection Range: Radar Timeout (how long presence stays on after the last detection), the gate size (hidden until you enable its entity), and the sliders that set how far the radar looks: Max Move Gate and Max Still Gate on an MSR-1 or MSR-2, Max Gate and Min Gate on an R PRO-1. The sliders start locked under a Sliders locked row (see Set the range and timeout). A note under the card explains each one and gives each gate's depth in your units.

  • LD2410 Target / Occupancy: Radar Target (anyone detected), Radar Moving Target, Radar Still Target, and on an MSR-1 or MSR-2 Radar Zone 1 Occupancy to Radar Zone 3 Occupancy and Any zone, which is on while someone is in any of the three zones. A row lights up while it's on. On an R PRO-1 this card sits in the first column instead.

docs.title: Third column
docs.text:
• LD2410 Gate Energy: the chart you tune with. Each gate has two bars, a purple one for move energy and a green one for still energy, on a 0 to 100 scale. While Radar Engineering Mode is on, a right-pointing triangle marks each gate's move threshold and a left-pointing triangle its still threshold, and a bar that rises above its threshold gets an outline in the threshold's color: outlined bar = above threshold (detecting). While Radar Engineering Mode is off, the chart is dimmed with Turn on Radar Engineering Mode to see gate energy values and a Turn on Radar Engineering Mode button you can press right there.
  • LD2410 Move Thresholds: one slider per gate (G0 to G8 on an MSR-1 or MSR-2, G0 to G13 on an R PRO-1) to set each gate's move threshold. Each row is named for how far out its gate reaches, from G0 (at the sensor) to G8 (about 6 m), in feet when Home Assistant uses US customary units. The sliders start locked, like the Detection Range ones. A note underneath recaps how thresholds work.

docs.title: Fourth column
docs.text:
• LD2410 Occupancy History: the last 24 hours of Detected, Moving, and Still (and, on an MSR-1 or MSR-2, Any zone and Zone 1 to Zone 3), so a false trigger overnight is still there in the morning. On an R PRO-1 it's titled Occupancy History, its lines read LD2412 Presence, LD2412 Moving, and LD2412 Still, and it also shows LD2450 Presence and each zone you drew.
  • LD2410 Still Thresholds: one slider per gate for the still thresholds, named and locked the same way.
  • Device: at the bottom of every tab. It shows Apollo firmware, the radar chip's firmware (LD2410 firmware on an MSR-1 or MSR-2, LD2450 firmware on an MTR-1; on an R PRO-1, both chips' versions are hidden until you enable them on the device page), and Firmware update, which opens Home Assistant's own update window when you tap it. An MTR-1 has no Firmware update row. Restart device restarts the whole sensor after you confirm. On an R PRO-1 with the LD2412 it reads Restart device (both radars), and on an MTR-1 or an R PRO-1 without the LD2412 it reads Restart device (also restarts the radar). Under the rows are the All settings for this device → link and how to download a support file. While the Wi-Fi signal is below -75 dBm, a Weak Wi-Fi note appears too.

On an R PRO-1, the Zone Map heading comes right after the first column, with the LD2450's own Radar setup card, the zone map, Zone presence, LD2450 Live, and LD2450 Controls, so on a phone you reach them before the LD2412's threshold cards (see Draw zones on the R PRO-1 and MTR-1). An MTR-1 tab has those cards, its own Start here, and the Device card, without the tuning cards.

docs.title: R PRO-1 and its LD2412 radar
docs.text:
Every R PRO-1 has an LD2450 radar, and the optional LD2412 addon adds a second one. The LD2412 handles presence and gets the tuning cards and the calibration, and the LD2450 tracks positions for the zone map. An R PRO-1 without the LD2412 still shows the LD2412 cards on its tab, but there's no radar behind them, so the calibration and this section don't apply to it; its Start here card gives the zone map steps instead, and its zone map works the same. With the LD2412, a few things differ from an MSR-1 or MSR-2:

  • The tab has two Radar setup cards. The one under Start here checks the LD2412, and its second line starts with LD2412. The one above the zone map checks the LD2450.
  • The LD2412 has 14 gates, G0 to G13, so a calibration sets 28 thresholds.
  • LD2412 Detection Range has Distance Resolution instead of Gate Size, and Max Gate and Min Gate instead of Max Move Gate and Max Still Gate. Gates below Min Gate or beyond Max Gate are dimmed in the result table, for example G0: not used (below Min Gate 1).
  • There is no Zone Config card, and the Distances chart shows the gates and the Max Gate and Min Gate bars without live distance bars.
  • Before it writes, the calibration asks the radar for its current thresholds (Reading the radar's current thresholds...), so what it saves for Undo matches the radar.

The LD2412 also has its own background learning, Start Dynamic Background Correction on the LD2412 Controls card. It runs on the radar chip and stores its result inside the radar. Background Correction Running shows whether it is still working. Use both, in this order:

  1. Clear the room and press Start Dynamic Background Correction.
  2. Wait for Background Correction Running to turn off. Until it does, the Auto-calibrate card says Background correction is running on the LD2412. Wait for its status to turn off. and its button stays disabled.
  3. Press Calibrate with empty room with the room still empty.

Run the calibration again after any later background correction. During a calibration on an R PRO-1, the card's reminder reads Leave Radar Engineering Mode on and do not press Start Dynamic Background Correction until this finishes. Pressing it during the listen stops the calibration without changing anything.

Undo cannot reverse a background correction

The Auto-calibrate card's Undo restores the thresholds Home Assistant saved. Dynamic Background Correction changes the radar itself, outside those thresholds, so Undo cannot reverse it.

docs.title: Set the range and timeout
docs.text:
Steps 3 and 4 on Start here point at the Detection Range card: how far the radar looks, and how long presence stays on after you stop moving. Its sliders, and the ones on the two threshold cards, start locked, so a finger that lands on one while you scroll a phone can't change a setting.

  1. Press Unlock on the Sliders locked row. That unlocks this sensor's sliders on all three cards, and the row reads Sliders unlocked.

  2. Lower Max Move Gate and Max Still Gate (Max Gate on an R PRO-1) to stop the radar looking past a certain distance, such as a hallway beyond the doorway. The note under the card gives each gate's depth. On an R PRO-1, raise Min Gate to ignore anything right next to the sensor.
