  3. Raise Radar Timeout if lights turn off while you sit still. It's how long Radar Target (LD2412 Presence on an R PRO-1) stays on after the radar last detects someone. It's a number box, so it's never locked.

The sliders lock again on their own after 5 minutes without a change, when you leave the tab, and each time the page loads, but never while you're dragging one. Lock on the same row locks them right away.

Touched a locked slider?

A locked slider is gray and still shows its value, and a scroll that starts on it scrolls the page. Touch one and it turns orange for a moment while Unlock flashes. Try again within 10 seconds and Home Assistant shows These sliders are locked. Press Unlock above them to change one. with an Unlock button. The lock lives in the browser page, so another phone or browser tab has its own, and Calibrate with empty room works whether the sliders are locked or not.

docs.title: Fine-tune gates by hand
docs.text:
Calibration gets most rooms right. If one spot still misbehaves, the Gate Energy chart shows you which gate to change. The outline is the signal to read: an outlined bar is a gate whose energy is above its threshold right now. Inside the range the radar uses, that means the gate is detecting a target.

  1. Press Turn on Radar Engineering Mode on the Gate Energy chart. The bars and threshold triangles appear.

  2. Leave the room and watch the chart from your phone, somewhere out of the radar's view (it can see through drywall, so step away from the wall too). A bar that is outlined while nobody is there is a gate causing false triggers. Gates outside the range the radar uses can be outlined too, but the radar ignores them: that range runs up to Max Move Gate for move bars and Max Still Gate for still bars, or from Min Gate to Max Gate on an R PRO-1.

  3. Press Unlock above the sliders, then raise the threshold of each gate causing false triggers on Move Thresholds (purple bar) or Still Thresholds (green bar) until its triangle sits a few points above the highest point the bar reaches.
  4. Sit or stand where the radar misses you. Your gate is the one whose bars rise when you shift in place; each threshold row names how far out its gate reaches, and the Gates row on the Distances chart shows it too. Lower that gate's threshold a few points at a time until its bar is outlined while you are there, but not after you leave.
  5. Turn off Radar Engineering Mode when you are done: press Turn off Radar Engineering Mode on the Radar setup card, or use the switch on the Controls card. The chart has no off button.

The Detection Range card helps too: Set the range and timeout covers it.

Calibrate first, then fine-tune

A new calibration sets every threshold again, including ones you changed by hand. If you calibrate after fine-tuning and prefer your own values, Undo brings them back.

docs.title: Draw zones on the R PRO-1 and MTR-1
docs.text:
The LD2450 radar in the R PRO-1 and MTR-1 tracks where up to three people are in the room. The zone map lets you draw areas on that map, such as the couch or the desk, and gives each area its own occupancy sensor. On an MTR-1 the tab is built around the zone map: Start here, the Radar setup card, and the map come first, with the radar's live status and controls beside them. On an R PRO-1, the LD2450's Radar setup card, the map, and the radar's live status and controls sit under the Zone Map heading, right after the first column of LD2412 cards, and its Start here card stays at the top of the tab.

The MTR-1's Start here card has three steps, and this section follows them: fix anything the Radar setup card flags, set Cone rotation to match how the sensor is mounted, then draw a zone and walk into it. An R PRO-1 without the optional LD2412 gets the same steps.

The zone map card shows your radar's name and the area the radar can see: a view cone 120 degrees wide and about 6 m (20 ft) out, with a caption at its edge such as Radar range 6 m (20 ft), 120°, and a dot for each person it tracks. The map fits that area, turned the way you set Cone rotation, plus any zone you drew outside it. Buttons sit in the bottom corners of the grid, with a row of zone buttons and a Configure section underneath.

The map is in feet when Home Assistant uses US customary units (Settings → System → General), and in meters otherwise. The m / ft switch in the bottom-right corner of the map changes it. When an administrator presses it, the choice is saved for that radar, so everyone who opens its map sees that unit. Anyone else changes only their own view, until they reload the page. Zones are stored in millimeters either way, so switching units never moves a zone.

docs.title: Check the LD2450's Radar setup card
docs.text:
The Radar setup card right above the map checks the two LD2450 settings that decide whether the map can show people. The radar chip keeps these itself, and Apollo firmware never sets them:

  • Zone Type should be Disabled, because the zone map replaces the radar's own built-in zones. On Detection, the radar reports only people inside those built-in zones, and with none set it reports nobody, so the map stays empty. On Filter, it hides people inside them.
  • Multi Target Tracking should be on. Off, the radar tracks only one person.

Press the button the card shows: Set Zone Type to Disabled, Turn on Multi Target Tracking, or Use recommended settings when both need fixing. The card changes nothing until you press one, and reads Radar settings look good. once both are right. On an R PRO-1, Home Assistant hides Multi Target Tracking by default, so the card checks only Zone Type until you enable that setting (see The zone map shows nobody, or only one person).

docs.title: Match the map to how the sensor is mounted
docs.text:
Turn the map so its view cone points the way your sensor faces. The tracked dots turn with it.

  1. Open Configure under the grid.
  2. If the Cone rotation: slider is gray, the map is locked: press Locked on the map first (see Lock and unlock).
  3. Drag Cone rotation: (from -180° to 180°) until the view cone points the way your sensor faces. When you let go, the angle is saved for the radar and the map fits the turned cone. Double-click the slider to reset it.

docs.title: Lock and unlock
docs.text:
The bottom-right corner has a lock toggle that reads Unlocked (🔓) or Locked (🔒). The map starts locked once the radar has zones, and your browser remembers your choice for each radar. A radar with no zones yet starts unlocked, so you can set Cone rotation and draw right away. While the map is locked:

  • Drawing on it shows Unlock the grid before drawing.
  • The Cone rotation slider is gray, and a scroll that starts on it scrolls the page. A tap or drag on it outlines Locked and shows Cone rotation is locked. Press Locked on the map to change it.
  • Clear All Zones, double-clicking a zone's button, ↶ (Undo last zone change), and Configure → Zones still change your zones.

On a phone or tablet, the grid takes every touch, so a swipe on it doesn't scroll the page, even while the map is locked. Scroll with your finger outside the grid, for example on the radar's name above it. Stay off the zone buttons while you scroll: a stray tap on Clear All Zones clears every zone's shape. Keep the map on Locked when you're not drawing: on an unlocked map, a swipe across the grid can draw a new shape for the selected zone and replace its old one.

From Apollo mmWave 2.2.6, only administrators can save zone changes. Other users still see the zones and their presence sensors, and a change they try to make shows a Could not save message.

docs.title: Add a zone
docs.text: Open Configure → Zones and press Add Zone. The new zone is named Zone 1 (then Zone 2, and so on), gets its own button under the grid, and is selected and ready to draw.

docs.title: Draw a zone
docs.text:
You draw each zone on the grid as a rectangle, ellipse, or polygon.

  1. Unlock the map and press the zone's button to select it.
  2. Press ✎ (Drawing modes) in the bottom-left corner and pick a shape: ▭ (Rectangle), ◯ (Ellipse), or ⬠ (Polygon).
  3. For a rectangle or ellipse, drag across the grid and let go to save.
  4. For a polygon, click each corner, then double-click or press ✓ (Finish polygon) to save. A polygon can have up to 32 points. ↺ (Undo last point) or Backspace removes the last point, and Esc cancels the shape.

Drawing a new shape for a zone replaces its old one. Made a mistake? ↶ (Undo last zone change) in the bottom-right corner puts the last change back. Drawing works with touch too, so you can draw zones from a phone or tablet.

docs.title: Rename a zone
docs.text: In Configure → Zones, type a new name next to the zone and press Save. The name appears on the zone's button.

docs.title: Clear or delete a zone
docs.text: Double-click a zone's button to clear its shape, or press Clear All Zones to clear every shape while keeping the zones. To remove a zone completely, along with its sensors, press Delete next to it in Configure → Zones.

docs.title: Use the zone sensors
docs.text:
Each zone gets an occupancy sensor named Zone 1 presence (and so on) on the radar's device page in Home Assistant. It turns on when a tracked person is inside the zone, ready to use in your automations. When you rename a zone on the card, its sensors follow, so a zone named Couch gets Zone 1 presence - Couch. A name you gave the sensor yourself in Home Assistant is kept.

To try a zone, reload the page after you draw it, then walk into it. The Zone presence card next to the map lists each zone's sensor and colors it while someone is in the zone, and Occupancy History adds a line for the zone, covering the last 24 hours.

Under it, LD2450 Live shows what the radar reports right now. If the map shows no dot with you in the room, look here first: Presence off means the radar itself reports nobody.

LD2450 Controls holds Zone Type, Multi Target Tracking, Radar Timeout, Radar Bluetooth (HLK app), Restart Radar, and Factory Reset Radar, whichever your sensor has (the MTR-1 has no Restart Radar). The restart and the reset ask before they act. Radar Timeout is how long LD2450 Presence stays on after the radar last sees someone. It doesn't hold the zones you draw: a zone turns off as soon as nobody is in it. While Zone Type isn't Disabled, a Radar's built-in zones card shows the radar chip's own zones, which are not the zones on the map.

While the radar is offline, or still reconnecting after a restart, zone presence reads off, not unavailable. An automation that waits for a zone to be clear for some minutes can't tell that apart from an empty zone, so have it also check that the radar itself is online.

docs.title: Calibrate from an automation
docs.text:
The Calibrate with empty room button runs the apollo_mmwave.calibrate_gates action, and your automations can run it too. When an automation already knows the room is empty, set settle_s: 0 to skip the countdown, and wait: true to get the result back when the run ends. This example recalibrates an office radar at 3:00 AM if nobody has been detected for 30 minutes, and sends a notification when the outcome is anything other than applied:

alias: Recalibrate the office radar overnight
triggers:
  - trigger: time
    at: "03:00:00"
conditions:
  - condition: state
    entity_id: binary_sensor.apollo_msr_2_abc123_radar_target
    state: "off"
    for: "00:30:00"
actions:
  - action: apollo_mmwave.calibrate_gates
    data:
      device_id: your_device_id
      settle_s: 0
      wait: true
    response_variable: calibration
  - if:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ calibration.outcome != 'applied' }}"
    then:
      - action: persistent_notification.create
        data:
          title: Radar calibration
          message: >
            Outcome {{ calibration.outcome }}
            {% if calibration.error %}({{ calibration.error.message }}){% endif %},
            {{ calibration.changed }} thresholds changed.

To use it, create a new automation under Settings → Automations & scenes, open the three-dot menu, choose Edit in YAML, and paste it in. Then replace binary_sensor.apollo_msr_2_abc123_radar_target with your radar's Radar Target sensor, and your_device_id with your radar. To fill in the device without looking up its ID, switch the action to the visual editor and pick your radar under Radar Device. If the action is refused before it starts (the radar is offline, for example), the automation stops with an error at that step instead of sending the notification.

Each call calibrates one radar. Two related actions round it out: apollo_mmwave.cancel_calibration stops a running job, and apollo_mmwave.restore_gate_thresholds does what Undo does. The card offers only the newest saved thresholds, while the action can restore an older set with its snapshot_id field. Settings → Tools → Actions lists every field, and the button below opens it with apollo_mmwave.calibrate_gates selected.

Only automate it for a room you know is empty

A person sleeping or a pet napping can look like an empty room to an automation. Pick a time and a room where nobody is, and remember each run replaces any thresholds you set by hand.

docs.title: The radar still triggers with nobody there
docs.text:
A calibration sets each threshold a margin above the highest energy it heard during a one-minute listen. Something that moves now and then, like a fan that cycles or the heating coming on, may not have moved during that minute.

  1. Update Apollo mmWave to 2.2.4 or newer and press Calibrate with empty room again. 2.2.4 leaves more headroom above the room's noise (15 points instead of 10).
  2. Calibrate while whatever usually runs in the room is running: the fan on, the heating or air conditioning cycling. If it only comes on now and then, listen for longer so a cycle falls inside the listen, for example 5 minutes (duration_s: 300, set the same way as margin in step 3).

  3. Still too sensitive? Raise margin, the points added above each gate's peak, for example to 20 or 25, and calibrate again. It sets the headroom on most gates. The percentage (margin_pct) only takes over on gates whose peak is 43 or more at the defaults, such as gates right at the sensor, so raising it changes little in most rooms. There are two places to set it:

    • For one run, on any dashboard: open Settings → Tools → Actions, pick Calibrate gate thresholds (empty room), choose your radar under Radar Device, tick Headroom (points) and set it to 20 (and Listen for (seconds) for a longer listen), then press Perform action and leave the room. The Auto-calibrate card shows the run as it goes.

    • For every run, on your own dashboard: add a calibration block to the Auto-calibrate card's YAML. Calibrate with empty room then uses it each time:

      type: custom:apollo-radar-calibrate-card
device_id: your_device_id
calibration:
  margin: 20
  duration_s: 300

      The keys go under calibration:. Typed at the card's top level, they are ignored. On the Apollo mmWave dashboard, the same block can go under strategy: in its raw configuration; the Apollo mmWave configuration guide has the details.

  4. If only one spot misbehaves, raise only that gate's threshold, as described in Fine-tune gates by hand.

If the radar now misses you instead, press Undo (restore your previous values), or calibrate again with a smaller margin.

docs.title: Calibration will not start
docs.text:
The Calibrate with empty room button is disabled when the card cannot run a calibration. The card says why:

  • Radar is offline. Calibration needs the radar online and its gate entities enabled. Check that the radar is powered and shows as online under Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome. If it is online, open your sensor's device page from that list and check that the Radar Engineering Mode switch and the gate threshold and gate energy entities are enabled. A disabled entity is listed under + N entities not shown: select it, open its settings (the cog), turn on Enabled, and click Update.

  • Background correction is running on the LD2412. Wait for its status to turn off. (R PRO-1) Wait for Background Correction Running to turn off.

  • Apollo mmWave is still loading... The integration is starting or reloading, and the card keeps trying on its own. If it changes to Apollo mmWave is not loaded, so calibration is unavailable., press Retry. If that keeps happening, check Settings → Devices & services for an error on the Apollo mmWave integration.

If the button works but the card answers with a line starting Calibration failed:, the rest of the line says what went wrong, and Try again runs it again once you have fixed it. The common ones:

  • The radar is unavailable right now. Check that it is online, then try again. The radar dropped off the network.
  • Home Assistant could not turn Radar Engineering Mode on within 10 s. Is the radar online? The radar did not respond to the switch.
  • No gate energy readings arrived within 20 s of turning Radar Engineering Mode on. Check that the radar is online and that Radar Engineering Mode on the Controls card brings the Gate Energy chart to life.
  • Radar Engineering Mode turned off during the listen. Nothing was changed. Someone, or an automation, turned it off during the listen. Leave it on and try again.
  • The radar has not reported 18 of its threshold values yet. The number is how many are missing: up to 18 on an MSR-1 or MSR-2, and up to 28 on an R PRO-1. The radar has not sent its thresholds to Home Assistant since it started, which can happen after it has been running for a long time. Press Read settings from the radar (the Radar setup card at the top of the tab offers it too): the card asks the radar for its settings, shows Reading settings from the radar..., and tries again a few seconds later. If the card can't find the radar's query params button, it says Open the radar's device page, press its Query Params button in the Diagnostic section, wait a few seconds, then try again.
  • Your Home Assistant user is not allowed to control this radar's entities. Run the calibration from a Home Assistant user that can control the radar.

On an R PRO-1 without the LD2412 addon, there's no radar behind the LD2412 cards, so the Auto-calibrate card can't calibrate. Depending on what the sensor reports, the card either reads Radar is offline. Calibration needs the radar online and its gate entities enabled. with its buttons disabled, or answers Calibrate with empty room with The radar has not reported 28 of its threshold values yet. Reading the settings from the radar can't fix either one. Skip the calibration: the zone map is what that sensor uses.

docs.title: Radar Engineering Mode was left on
docs.text:
The calibration only turns Radar Engineering Mode off if it was the one that turned it on. If you turned it on yourself, or with the button on the Gate Energy chart, it stays on until you turn it off. The Radar setup card at the top of the tab says so while it's on: press its Turn off Radar Engineering Mode button, or use the Radar Engineering Mode switch on the Controls card.

If Home Assistant restarted during the countdown or the listen, nothing was written: the calibration turns Radar Engineering Mode back off when Home Assistant starts again, and the card says, for example, Last calibration Oct 12, 12:37 AM was stopped by a Home Assistant restart. Nothing was changed. Press Calibrate with empty room to run it again.

If Home Assistant restarted while thresholds were being written, or the radar went offline before the calibration could turn the mode off, the Auto-calibrate card shows a banner the next time you open it. It starts with A calibration was interrupted by a restart. or The last calibration could not turn Radar Engineering Mode back off (the radar was offline). Press Turn it off next to Radar Engineering Mode may still be on. If the banner also says Some thresholds may have been written., press its Undo to put the saved thresholds back, then run the calibration again.

Keep Radar Engineering Mode out of your history

While Radar Engineering Mode is on, the radar updates its 18 (MSR-1 and MSR-2) or 28 (R PRO-1) gate energy sensors about once a second, and Home Assistant's recorder, the part that saves history, stores every update. Turning the mode off when you're done avoids this. If you like to leave it on to watch the chart, add the block below to your configuration.yaml (the File editor app is one way to open it), then restart Home Assistant. If the file already has a recorder: section, add the exclude: lines to it instead of adding a second recorder: key.

configuration.yaml
recorder:
  exclude:
    entity_globs:
      - sensor.*_g?_move_energy     # LD2410: g0 to g8
      - sensor.*_g?_still_energy
      - sensor.*_g??_move_energy    # LD2412: g00 to g13
      - sensor.*_g??_still_energy

docs.title: Thresholds did not change on the radar
docs.text:
• You ran a preview. Preview only never writes anything. Press Calibrate and apply, or Calibrate with empty room.
  • The new value matched the old one. Cells that read (unchanged) were already right, so nothing was written.
  • The gate had no data. Gates marked no data keep their old thresholds. Check the radar's connection and run the calibration again.
  • The radar did not confirm the value. Cells marked (not confirmed) and the warning that values could not be confirmed mean the radar did not report the new value back. Check the gates on the Move Thresholds and Still Thresholds cards, then run it again once the radar is stable, or set those gates by hand.
  • The run was stopped. Stopped. Nothing was changed. means nothing was written.

docs.title: The chart says to turn on Radar Engineering Mode
docs.text:
If the chart instead reads Radar unavailable and Waiting for the device to reconnect, the radar is offline and the button is hidden until it comes back: check its power and Wi-Fi. Otherwise, the Gate Energy chart only shows bars while Radar Engineering Mode is on. Press Turn on Radar Engineering Mode on the chart itself, or turn on Radar Engineering Mode on the Controls card. The bars appear within a few seconds, once the radar starts sending energy. If the calibration turned the mode on, it turns it back off when it finishes, so the overlay returning after a calibration is expected.

Prefer the radar maker's app?

The HLKRadarTool app connects over the radar's Bluetooth (the Radar Bluetooth (HLK app) row on the Controls card, or on LD2450 Controls for the LD2450) and has its own auto-calibration. Each sensor has its own guide: MSR-1, MSR-2, R PRO-1, and MTR-1.

docs.title: The zone map shows nobody, or only one person
docs.text:
Start with the LD2450's Radar setup card, right above the map.

No dot at all. The usual cause is Zone Type set to Detection: the radar then reports only people inside its own built-in zones, and with none set it reports nobody. Press Set Zone Type to Disabled, or Use recommended settings if the card shows that instead. If Zone Type is already Disabled and Presence on the LD2450 Live card stays off with you in front of the sensor, the radar itself sees nobody: check that it's online and facing the room.

One dot with several people in the room. Usually Multi Target Tracking is off. Press Turn on Multi Target Tracking (or Use recommended settings if the card shows that instead) on the Radar setup card. On an R PRO-1, Home Assistant hides that setting by default, so the card can't check it and shows no button. Enable it once:

  1. Open the sensor's device page with All settings for this device → on the Start here card.
  2. Under Configuration, open the entities that aren't shown and select LD2450 Multi Target Tracking.
  3. Open its settings (⚙), turn on Enabled, and select Update.
  4. Reload the dashboard after a minute. The Radar setup card then checks the setting and offers its button when it's off.

docs.title: The dots sit at the sensor, or a zone misses you
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave 2.2.7 fixed this. Before it, when Home Assistant used US customary units (or you changed a Target X or Target Y sensor's unit), the zone map read the radar's positions in inches as if they were millimeters. The dots sat at or right around the sensor, and zone presence didn't turn on. Update Apollo mmWave (see Upgrade from an older setup) and the dots land where people are.

A zone you drew while the dots were in the wrong place may not cover where people show up now. Walk through the room, watch the dots, and redraw any zone that's off.

docs.title: A slider won't move
docs.text: The sliders on Detection Range, Move Thresholds, and Still Thresholds start locked. Press Unlock on the Sliders locked row above them (see Set the range and timeout). The Cone rotation slider on the zone map locks with the map: press Locked on the map first.

docs.title: Send Apollo a support file
docs.text:
Still stuck? Send Apollo a support file with your question. It holds the Apollo mmWave and Home Assistant versions, the dashboard's state, and each radar's model, firmware, settings, zones, and last calibration. It leaves out MAC and IP addresses, Wi-Fi network names, and tokens, and downloading it changes nothing. Only administrators can download it.

  1. Go to Settings → Devices & services and open Apollo mmWave. The Device card at the bottom of each tab links there too.

  2. Open the three-dot menu and choose Download diagnostics.

  3. Attach the file to your message to Apollo support, or to your issue on GitHub.

Check the file before you post it publicly

The file includes your zones and their names, which can show the layout of your home. Send it to Apollo support, or look through it before you attach it to a public GitHub issue.

docs.title: mmWave Tuning Videos
docs.text:
Radar Engineering Mode (REM)

If you're experiencing false triggers, we recommend using Radar Engineering Mode (REM) to monitor the gate energy and adjust the gate threshold to eliminate them.

Quick introduction video of the LD2410B gates and zones.

How to tune the mmWave sensor using radar engineering mode.

To tune your sensor, you'll turn on Radar Engineering Mode and adjust the gate thresholds.

1. Go to Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome and click the name of your device.

2. Scroll down to the Configuration section.

3. Turn on Radar Engineering Mode (REM).

4. Scroll down to the Diagnostic section and you will see that REM shows the move and still energy for gates 0-8.

5. The gates are different distances from the sensor.

6. Moving the gate still and move threshold slider to the right increases the amount of energy needed to trigger the sensor. Do this if you want the gate to be less sensitive.

7. Moving the gate still and move threshold slider to the left decreases the amount of energy needed to trigger the sensor. Do this if you want the gate to be more sensitive.

Quote from popular YouTuber Make It Work Tech

I ended up maxing out the sliders on all gates and then bringing them down just enough to pick up human presence. Definitely easier than using the LD2410B app. - MakeItWorkTech

Open-Concept kitchen and living room with MSR-2 to activate the under-cabinet lights only when person in the kitchen

Here's how you tune the gates so the kitchen lights only come on when you're in the kitchen.

  1. Stand in the desired trigger locations.
  2. Observe the gate energy.
  3. Adjust the gate threshold slider to the right, increasing the energy required to trigger the mmWave sensor. This ensures that your kitchen lights only come on when you're actually in the kitchen, not just walking by in the living room. Also, you can lower the gate threshold in the kitchen by moving the slider to the left. This makes the mmWave sensor more sensitive, even when standing still. This way, you avoid having the lights go off while reading a recipe or doing the dishes.

References

  • https://youtu.be/dAzHXpP3FcI?t=431
  • https://community.home-assistant.io/t/ld2410-esphome-tips/477058/316
  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l212Lvo1R6s

docs.title: Light sensor (LTR-390UV)
docs.text:
When mounting the MSR-2, position it so the center vent slots (outlined in red above) are not covered. This lets more light reach the sensor and keeps the readings accurate.

The RGB LED will trigger the Light sensor!

Make sure that your automations do not interfere with each other. This includes being aware that your onboard LED can trigger the lux reading but not the uv reading of the LTR390 in your device.

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
The MSR-2 should be mounted 1.5-2 meters off the ground which will then provide a nice even 120-degree FOV of the mmWave radar.

The MSR-2 can also be mounted on the ceiling if you can provide power and mount our articulating stand on the ceiling.

These are some useful hints!

  • The FOV angle is -60 to 60 degrees (120 degrees total).
  • Gates are pre-defined by the radar module and are in 0.75 meter increments.
  • Zones are user-configurable and are in cm.

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your MSR-2. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The Default Update column is how often each entity refreshes. Radar entities update in real time as targets move. The LTR390 Light and LTR390 UV Index sensors use the interval set by the LTR390 Update Interval number (60s by default).

Ensure that the LD2410 firmware version is V2.04.23022511 or later for proper integration functionality.

The newer version of the firmware includes an "auto calibrate" function, so you might want to test it out.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light Three RGB Neopixel LEDs. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn them on or off. Calibrate SCD40 To 420ppm Forces a fresh-air calibration of the SCD40 CO₂ sensor to the outdoor baseline (about 420 ppm). Run it outdoors or next to an open window. Only needed when CO2 Auto Calibration is off. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Factory Reset Radar — Resets the LD2410 radar to its factory move and still thresholds. Restart Radar — Restarts the LD2410 radar module. Radar Timeout — How long presence stays detected, in seconds, after the target is lost. Radar Max Move Distance — Maximum distance gate for movement detection (gate 2 to 8). Use it to ignore movement past a chosen distance. Radar Max Still Distance — Maximum distance gate for still detection (gate 2 to 8). Use it to ignore still targets past a chosen distance. Radar Zone 1 Start 0 cm Start distance of Zone 1 from the sensor, in cm (0 to 800). Radar End Zone 1 50 cm End distance of Zone 1 from the sensor, in cm. From Radar Zone 1 Start to this value is Zone 1. Radar End Zone 2 150 cm End distance of Zone 2, in cm. From the end of Zone 1 to this value is Zone 2. Radar End Zone 3 250 cm End distance of Zone 3, in cm. From the end of Zone 2 to this value is Zone 3. Radar Engineering Mode — Enables the g0-g8 threshold sliders for mmWave tuning. g0-g8 move threshold — Movement sensitivity threshold for each gate (g0 through g8). See the radar tuning guide. g0-g8 still threshold — Stillness sensitivity threshold for each gate (g0 through g8). See the radar tuning guide. ld2410 Gate Size — Distance resolution per gate on the LD2410. Disabled by default. ld2410 Bluetooth Off Turns on the LD2410's Bluetooth so you can connect with the HLK Radartool phone app for tuning. Turned off at boot. LTR390 Update Interval 60 s How often the LTR390 light and UV sensors poll (1 to 300 seconds). Disabled by default. DPS310 Pressure Offset 0.0 hPa Calibration offset for the DPS310 pressure reading (-100 to +100 hPa in 0.1 hPa steps). Disabled by default. A small subset of devices do not include a DPS310 sensor; if this reads Unknown, your device may be one of these units. DPS Temperature Offset 14.54 °C Offsets heat from the ESP chip for a more accurate DPS310 temperature reading. A small subset of devices do not include a DPS310 sensor. CO2 Auto Calibration On Keeps the SCD40 CO₂ sensor calibrated automatically. The sensor assumes it sees fresh air (about 420 ppm) at least once a week and corrects its baseline to match. Turn it off if the device sits in a space that rarely gets fresh air, then calibrate manually with Calibrate SCD40 To 420ppm every 1 to 2 years. Reduce DB Reporting Off Applies filters so many entities only report when they cross a threshold, using less Wi-Fi airtime and less Home Assistant database space. Startup Light Blink On Blinks the RGB LED during the MSR-2's initial boot. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. Separate from the Apollo Firmware Version and ESPHome Version sensors above. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot. Radar Firmware Version on boot Firmware version installed on the LD2410 radar module. query params — Queries the LD2410's current parameters for debugging and advanced tuning. g0 move energy to g8 move energy real-time Live move-energy level for each gate (g0 through g8). g0 still energy to g8 still energy real-time Live still-energy level for each gate (g0 through g8).

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Air quality & light
docs.text: Sensor Default Update Details CO2 60s True NDIR reading from the SCD40. Shows Unknown if you do not have the CO₂ module. You can re-calibrate it to the outdoor baseline. DPS310 Pressure 30s Barometric air pressure. A small subset of devices do not include a DPS310 sensor. If this reads Unknown, your device may be one of these units. DPS310 Temperature 30s Ambient air temperature from the DPS310. Adjusted by the DPS Temperature Offset. A small subset of devices do not include a DPS310 sensor. LTR390 Light 60s* Ambient light level in lux. *Polls at the LTR390 Update Interval (60s by default). LTR390 UV Index 60s* UV index measured by the LTR390. *Polls at the LTR390 Update Interval.

docs.title: Radar (LD2410)
docs.text: Sensor Default Update Details Radar Target real-time Whether the radar detects a still or moving target. Good for triggering occupancy automations. Radar Moving Target real-time Whether a moving target is currently detected. Radar Still Target real-time Whether a stationary target is currently detected. Radar Moving Distance real-time Distance to a moving target in cm. Reports Unknown when no moving target is present. Radar Still Distance real-time Distance to a still target in cm. Reports Unknown when no still target is present. Radar Detection Distance real-time Last detected distance from the radar in cm. Holds the last value, so it can be misleading when nothing is present. Radar Move Energy real-time Amount of movement measured by the LD2410. Faster movement reads as a higher percentage. Radar Still Energy real-time Energy of the current still target. Radar Zone 1 Occupancy real-time Whether someone is in Zone 1. Zones are distance bands from the sensor, set with Radar Zone 1 Start and Radar End Zone 1. Radar Zone 2 Occupancy real-time Whether someone is in Zone 2, from the end of Zone 1 to Radar End Zone 2. Radar Zone 3 Occupancy real-time Whether someone is in Zone 3, from the end of Zone 2 to Radar End Zone 3. Radar Zone Occupancy real-time Whether any of Zone 1, 2, or 3 is occupied.

docs.title: MSR-2 tuning dashboard
docs.text:
There is a newer way to do this

The Apollo mmWave integration now builds this dashboard for you automatically, with nothing to paste. It also adds auto-calibration, which sets your gate thresholds from a one-minute listen to the empty room and saves your previous values so you can undo it. Follow the Apollo mmWave dashboard setup guide to get started. The steps below still work if you'd rather keep the YAML version.

Huge shoutout to Discord user MirkoP for creating this!

We all owe a huge thanks to MirkoP from Discord/GitHub for creating and sharing this with everyone! Source here.

This guide will create a beautiful and helpful dashboard to simplify configuration of your MSR-2 sensor. You can view the current gate and zone thresholds which will help tune your sensor for your environment!

1. First make sure you have HACS installed. If not, download it here and install it.

2. Install the Streamline Card in HACS here which is required for the steps below.

3. Install the Plotly Graph Card in HACS here which is also required for the steps below.

4. Open your Home Assistant dashboard and Take control of your dashboard by clicking Edit Dashboard in the top right then the 3 dots from the Edit Dashboard menu and click Take control. (this step is only necessary for new Home Assistant users).

5. Use the YAML generator below and enter in your device name such as apollo_msr_2_m4c4dd and then click Generate YAML. It will copy the YAML for you to use in the next step!

Create backups to restore to before moving forward!

Back up your Home Assistant instance and back up a copy of the Raw configuration editor mentioned below before you make any changes, to be safe!

6. Click Edit dashboard in the top right then click the 3 dots from the Edit Dashboard menu and click Raw configuration editor. Navigate to the end of the document and paste the code from the YAML generator at the very bottom of the Raw configuration editor. Click Save in the top right.

This file is used by Home Assistant and must be carefully edited.

Home Assistant depends on this file to function correctly. It is what displays your dashboard "views". Only make the changes exactly as outlined below. Do not add extra spaces or modify anything beyond what is specified in the instructions.

7. You should now have a new dashboard view called MSR-2 Configuration and you should be ready to configure your sensor!

docs.title: How to tune the MSR-2 using Home Assistant
docs.text:
Prefer a guided dashboard?

The Apollo mmWave integration gives your Apollo MSR-2 a tuning dashboard with a Gate Energy chart and a Calibrate with empty room button that sets the gate thresholds for you. The Apollo mmWave dashboard guide walks you through it as a guided alternative to the manual steps below.

If you're experiencing false triggers, Radar Engineering Mode (REM) lets you monitor the gate energy and adjust the gate thresholds to eliminate them.

Quick introduction video of the LD2410B gates and zones.

How to tune the mmWave sensor using radar engineering mode.

You'll turn on Radar Engineering Mode to see the move and still energy for each gate.

1. Head to the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome) and select your MSR-2.

2. Scroll down to the Configuration section and turn on "Radar Engineering Mode".

3. Scroll down to the Diagnostic section and you will see that when REM is enabled, the move and still energy for gates 0-8 are shown.

The gates are 0.75 meter increments from the sensor, allowing you to "tune" each 0.75 meter section until your sensor works as intended!

Gate Distance (m / ft) Default move threshold Default still threshold 0 0 m / 0' 50 0 1 0 - 0.75 m / 0' - 2.46' 50 0 2 0.75 - 1.5 m / 2.46' - 4.92' 40 40 3 1.5 - 2.25 m / 4.92' - 7.38' 40 40 4 2.25 - 3 m / 7.38' - 9.84' 40 40 5 3 - 3.75 m / 9.84' - 12.30' 40 40 6 3.75 - 4.5 m / 12.30' - 14.76' 30 15 7 4.5 - 5.25 m / 14.76' - 17.22' 30 15 8 5.25 - 6 m / 17.22' - 19.69' 30 15

Moving the gate still and move threshold slider to the right increases the amount of energy needed to trigger the sensor. Do this if you want the gate to be less sensitive.

Moving the gate still and move threshold slider to the left decreases the amount of energy needed to trigger the sensor. Do this if you want the gate to be more sensitive.

docs.title: How to tune MSR-2 using HLKRadarTool
Auto-calibration
docs.text:
You'll connect the HLKRadarTool app to your sensor, measure your room's background noise, and pick one of the auto-calibration settings.

1. Download the HLKRadarTool app.

iPhoneAndroid

Click Here to download

Click here to download

The default password to connect to the HLKRadarTool is "HiLink".

2. Head to the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome) then select your MSR-2 and scroll down until you see LD2410 Bluetooth.

3. Open the app and select your device

4. Turn on Engineering Mode

5. Select More and then select Parameter settings

6. Select Detect background noise

7. Insert Delay detection and Detection time values. (For iPhone users Delay detection cannot be 0). Then select Start. This will give us our reference values so we can auto-calibrate the mmWave sensor.

8. Select Back to navigate to the Parameter settings. Then select one of the auto-calibration buttons.

Average: Sets the gate sensitivity to the average move and still energy

Maximum: Sets the gate sensitivity to the maximum move and still energy

Intelligent: Sets the gate sensitivity equal to or just above the maximum move and still energy.

docs.title: Manual calibration
docs.text:
You'll set the motion and static sensitivity values yourself in the app.

1. Repeat steps 1-5 above.

2. Select Motion or Static sensitivity, change it to your desired value, and select Set.

3. Now your MSR-2 should be tuned to your environment!

docs.title: Putting the MSR-2 in boot mode
Putting the MSR-2 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the MSR-2 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You'll hold the boot button while you plug in the USB-C cable.

1. Position the MSR-2 as shown in the image below and locate the small opening to press the boot button (the right button).

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your MSR-2 then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You'll plug the device into your computer, then hold the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and locate the boot button (the right opening, shown in the image above) and the reset button (the left opening, shown in the image below).

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your MSR-2 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the MSR-2. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash MSR-2
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the steps below.

This factory re-flash needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

If your device has already been connected to Home Assistant please remove it from the ESPHome integration and the ESPHome Device Builder before continuing.

1. Position the MSR-2 as shown in the image below and locate the small opening to press the boot button (the right button).

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your MSR-2 then let go of the button.

3. Open the Apollo MSR-2 installer.

4. Click Connect & Install.

5. Select the open com port then click Connect.

6. Click Install ApolloAutomation.MSR-2_Factory.

7. Click "INSTALL".

8. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

9. Please proceed to the getting started guide and set up your sensor as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your MSR-2
docs.text:
You'll reset the device's Wi-Fi credentials, then connect it to your new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button (the button on the right) for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo MSR2 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: MTR-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. What sensors are included in the MTR-1?

  • The MTR-1 includes a multi-target mmWave radar sensor for detecting motion and positioning, as well as LUX, UV, temperature, and pressure sensors. There’s also an optional CO2 sensor available.

2. How does the mmWave radar sensor work?

  • The MTR-1’s mmWave radar sensor tracks movement by emitting radar waves and detecting changes in reflected signals. This sensor can detect multiple targets and their locations within a room, offering more precise tracking than traditional motion sensors. It can even detect through light walls.

3. How many targets can the MTR-1 track?

  • The MTR-1 can track up to three targets simultaneously, allowing it to monitor multiple people in a room and provide their positions within defined zones.

4. What is the maximum detection range of the mmWave radar?

  • The mmWave radar sensor in the MTR-1 has a maximum detection range of 6 meters (about 19.7 feet), making it ideal for monitoring large rooms or spaces.

5. Can the MTR-1 be used to track the exact location of people in a room?

  • Yes, the MTR-1 can detect people’s positions within zones, such as distinguishing if someone is near a door, on the couch, or standing by the kitchen counter. This enables precise automation based on a person’s location within the room.

6. What is the benefit of the LUX and UV sensor?

  • The LUX sensor measures the ambient light in the room, while the UV sensor tracks ultraviolet light exposure. This data can be used for automations like adjusting lighting levels, or providing alerts when sunlight is strong.

7. How does the optional CO2 sensor work?

  • The optional CO2 sensor measures the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air, which is important for monitoring air quality in enclosed spaces. High CO2 levels can lead to poor sleep, drowsiness, and other health issues, and the sensor can trigger automations to turn on fans or open windows.

8. What are some common use cases for the MTR-1?

  • The MTR-1 can be used to automate lights based on people’s presence in a room, trigger alarms or notifications when someone enters a space, and adjust HVAC settings based on CO2 levels. Its precise tracking capabilities also make it great for monitoring multiple zones within a room, such as distinguishing when someone is at the stove versus the sink.

9. How do I connect the MTR-1 to Home Assistant?

  • The MTR-1 connects to Home Assistant through ESPHome using Wi-Fi. Once connected, you can access data from all the sensors and create automations based on the sensor readings.

10. What kind of automations can I set up with the MTR-1?

  • You can create automations for turning lights on/off based on motion, adjusting air filtration when CO2 levels rise, and sending notifications when specific zones (like doorways) detect movement. The multi-target tracking allows for even more advanced automations, such as adjusting lights depending on where people are in the room.

11. How do I adjust the sensitivity of the motion detection?

  • Sensitivity can NOT be adjusted via the ESPHome configuration. The MTR-1 LD2450 mmWave sensor cannot be tuned like the MSR-2 can. The MTR-1 can set zones and track multiple users instead.

12. Can the MTR-1 detect motion through walls?

  • Yes, the mmWave radar in the MTR-1 can detect movement through certain materials, such as light walls or thin furniture, though you may need to adjust the zones to prevent false positives from nearby rooms. Please visit the tuning articles for more info!

13. Can the MTR-1 be used outdoors?

  • While the MTR-1 is primarily designed for indoor use, with proper weatherproofing and environmental protection, it could be used in sheltered outdoor environments. Be cautious of exposure to moisture or extreme weather.

14. Does the MTR-1 work with other smart home platforms?

  • The MTR-1 is designed to work with Home Assistant via ESPHome. While it could potentially be integrated into other smart home platforms through custom configurations, its primary use case is for Home Assistant.

15. How does the temperature and pressure sensor work?

  • The temperature and pressure sensor provides accurate measurements for air temperature and barometric pressure. This data can be used in automations, such as controlling heating/cooling systems or monitoring environmental conditions.

16. My DPS310 Pressure or DPS310 Temperature shows as "unknown" in Home Assistant. Is something wrong?

  • No, your device is fine. A small subset of units shipped without the DPS310 sensor because the part was discontinued by the manufacturer. If you see those entities reporting "unknown," your unit is one of these. Every other sensor on the device works normally.

17. How is the MTR-1 powered?

  • The MTR-1 is powered through a USB-C connection and can be plugged into a standard wall outlet using a 5V adapter.

18. What is the purpose of the RGB LED and piezo buzzer?

  • The RGB LED can display different colors for various events or alerts, such as turning red when air quality is poor or green for general notifications. The piezo buzzer can be used for sound alerts, such as a beep when motion is detected or a CO2 level warning.

19. Can I customize the MTR-1’s features?

  • Yes, the MTR-1 is fully customizable through ESPHome. You can modify sensor settings, change reporting intervals, and create custom automations based on the sensor readings.

20. What is the reporting frequency of the MTR-1’s sensors?

  • The reporting frequency for each sensor can be adjusted through the ESPHome YAML configuration. You can choose to report data as frequently as every second or extend the intervals to reduce power consumption.

21. Can I use multiple MTR-1 sensors in my smart home setup?

  • Yes, you can integrate multiple MTR-1 sensors into your Home Assistant system. Each one shows up as its own device with its own set of entities, so you can monitor multiple rooms or areas in your home at the same time.

22. What’s the difference between the MTR-1 and MSR-2?

  • The MTR-1 features multi-target radar tracking, allowing it to detect multiple people in a room and track their positions. The MSR-2, on the other hand, is designed more for single-target detection and has a slightly different sensor set, though both sensors offer robust environmental monitoring capabilities.

23. What accessories are available for the MTR-1?

  • Accessories for the MTR-1 include mounting brackets, stands, and a variety of expansion options, like additional sensor modules. These allow for greater flexibility in where and how you use the sensor.

24. What are the primary advantages of the MTR-1 over other motion sensors?

  • The MTR-1’s mmWave radar is significantly more advanced than traditional PIR (Passive Infrared) motion sensors. It can detect subtle movements, track multiple targets, and monitor precise locations within a room, making it ideal for sophisticated home automations. Its additional sensors (LUX, UV, temperature, pressure, optional CO2) also provide greater environmental awareness.

25. How do I install the MTR-1?

  • Installation is simple. The MTR-1 is powered via USB-C and connects to your Wi-Fi. From there, you configure it through ESPHome and integrate it into your Home Assistant setup. Detailed instructions are available on our documentation wiki, and we offer support via our Discord community.

26. How secure is the MTR-1?

  • The MTR-1 operates entirely on your local network, using ESPHome, which means no data is sent to external servers. This ensures that your home automation data remains private and secure.

27. Does the MTR-1 require cloud connectivity?

  • No, the MTR-1 works entirely within your local network through Home Assistant and ESPHome. You don’t need cloud access or a subscription to use the sensor.

28. How do I update the firmware on the MTR-1?

  • Firmware updates for the MTR-1 can be done directly through ESPHome. When updates are available, you can install them wirelessly over-the-air (OTA), making it simple to keep the sensor up to date.

29. What is the warranty on the MTR-1?

  • The MTR-1 comes with a one-year warranty. If you encounter any issues, we provide comprehensive support via email, Discord, or our website to ensure you’re fully satisfied with the product.

30. How long does it take to set up the MTR-1?

  • Setup is quick. Most users report being able to configure and integrate the MTR-1 into their Home Assistant setup within 10-15 minutes.

31. What’s in the box?

  • Each MTR-1 package includes the assembled board, case, support stand, and a link to documentation, open-source code, and CAD models. Additionally, you’ll receive an Apollo Automation sticker.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The Apollo MTR-1 is a compact, affordable multi-target radar multisensor designed for Home Assistant via ESPHome. It features a range of sensors, including mmWave radar, LUX/UV, and an optional CO2 sensor, all in a 49mm x 32mm design. With multi-target and multi-zone tracking, the MTR-1 can detect not only when someone enters a room but also where they are. It integrates with Home Assistant using Wi-Fi and offers features like RGB notifications, a piezo buzzer for alerts, and Bluetooth tracking. Open-source software and CAD files are available for customization, and the Apollo team provides full support through Discord and GitHub.

docs.title: Simon Says Home Assistant MTR-1 review
MTR-1 Bluetooth proxy
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to make your Apollo device act as a "BLE Proxy" which lets Bluetooth devices talk back to Home Assistant using Apollo devices as the "next hop"!

Select a method below. Method 1 switches your MTR-1 to the prebuilt MTR-1_BLE.yaml firmware. Method 2 adds the BLE proxy yaml to your existing config by hand.

Method 1: MTR-1_BLE.yaml firmwareMethod 2: Manually enter the BLE proxy yaml

You'll swap your device's firmware package for its prebuilt Bluetooth proxy version in ESPHome Device Builder, then install it over the network.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Find your device and click Edit.

3. Replace the packages: line and the line directly below it with the code below.

packages:
  ApolloAutomation.MTR-1:
    url: https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/MTR-1
    ref: main
    files: [Integrations/ESPHome/MTR-1_BLE.yaml]
    refresh: 1min

4. Click Save then Install in the bottom right. Click On the network when prompted.

5. When you see the purple lines the device has booted successfully and the logs will show the Bluetooth Proxy section. Click Stop in the bottom right and you're finished!

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

The easiest way is to let ESPHome Device Builder add the component for you. You can also paste the single line by hand.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar and click Edit on your device. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Click Add Component in the editor toolbar, search for Bluetooth Proxy, and click Add.

Device Builder drops a single line into your config:

bluetooth_proxy:

That's all it needs. Active connections are on by default, and bluetooth_proxy automatically pulls in the ESP32 BLE Tracker it depends on, so there's nothing else to add. Prefer to type it? Paste that one line at the top level of your YAML instead of using Add Component.

3. Click Save, then Install, and choose On the Network to flash the new firmware over Wi-Fi.

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

docs.title: Adding 90 degree USB-C to MTR-1
docs.text:
You'll attach this addon to your sensor and plug it into an outlet.

1. Gather the MTR-1, 90 degree addon, and optional top facing USB-C Plug.

2. Insert the shorter end of the 90 degree addon into the MTR-1.

3. Align the other end of the 90 degree addon to the optional top facing USB-C Plug.

4. Gently push the connector into one of the top USB-C ports.

5. Plug into an outlet and enjoy your sensor!

You're ready to begin using your device!

Make sure to head to our getting started guide to get your MTR-1 up and running!

docs.title: Adding articulating stand to MTR-1
docs.text:
You'll swap the back of your sensor for the articulating stand backplate, then seat the stand's ball in its mount.

1. Unplug your MTR-1 from power and remove the stand if attached.

2. Remove the backplate of the MTR-1.

3. Align the new backplate that came with the articulating stand addon and gently push down on two corners near the articulating ball mount then the other two corners until it seats flat.

4. Align the ball inside the articulating mount and then push down until it's fully seated.

docs.title: Adding CO<sub>2</sub> to MTR-1
docs.text:
You'll slide your sensor out of its case, fit the SCD40 module onto its mezzanine connector, and put the case back together.

1. Unplug your MTR-1 from power and remove the stand if attached.

2. Flip the MTR-1 upside down and gently tap the case on the table and your MTR-1 should slide out of the case.

3. With the case removed, identify the bottom right corner of where the small black mezzanine connector lives. You will see an "X" indicating which corner needs to be lined up with the SCD40 CO2 sensor. There is an X on the SCD40 sensor's PCB as well, you can see it in the image below. There is also a "gold dot" in the top left of the SCD40 when oriented properly.

4. Gently push the SCD40 CO2 module onto the black mezzanine connector.

5. Slide the case back over the MTR-1, making sure that the case has the hole for the LUX Sensor facing the right direction (to the right).

6. Flip the MTR-1 back over to prepare to put the back case on.

7. Gently press the backplate of the MTR-1 case onto the MTR-1 until it lightly snaps into place. Please do not force it, if necessary please repeat steps above until it seats in the case without any force required.

8. Put the stand back on if applicable.

9. Please refer to our CO2 calibration guide to calibrate the CO2 module after installation. This is required for all CO2 addons purchased from us separately from a product (such as buying it to add on to an existing Apollo device).

docs.title: Adding GPIO header addon to MTR-1
Adding GPIO header to MTR-1
docs.text:
You'll seat the GPIO Header addon on the mezzanine connector on the back of your sensor, then fit the new back that came with it.

1. Unplug your MTR-1 from power and remove the stand if attached.

2. Remove the backplate of the MTR-1.

3. Identify the "X" on the PCB on the back of your MTR-1 and the "X" on the top left corner of the GPIO Header addon.

4. Keep the "X" aligned on both sides and gently push down until it securely seats in the small mezzanine connector.

5. Align the new back for your MTR-1 that came with the GPIO Header addon. Push down on the corners closest to the GPIO Header addon first, and then push the back on securely on the other two corners.

6. The case should sit flush and you're now ready to add functionality to your device!

Click here to head to the GPIO Header LED Strip Tutorial!

docs.title: Adding rear male USB to MTR-1
Adding rear male USB-C to MTR-1
docs.text:
You'll seat the Rear Male USB-C addon on the mezzanine connector on the back of your sensor, then fit the new back that came with it.

1. Unplug your MTR-1 from power and remove the stand if attached.

2. Remove the backplate of the MTR-1.

3. Identify the "X" on the PCB on the back of your MTR-1 and the "X" on the top left corner of the male Rear USB-C addon.

4. Keep the "X" aligned on both sides and gently push down until it securely seats in the small mezzanine connector.

5. Align the new back for your MTR-1 that came with the Male USB-C addon. Push down on the corners closest to the USB-C addon first, and then push the back on securely on the other two corners.

6. The case should sit flush and you're now ready to plug into a USB-C Outlet!

docs.title: MTR-1 corner mount STL by user CrookedToe
MTR-1 + Alarmo home security install
docs.text:
My grandmother wanted a security system that would alert her when there was movement in her home after she had gone to bed. So, I set up three of our Apollo Automation mmWave sensors. These devices, plus the Alarmo integration, quickly allowed me to install a fully local, private, cloud-free, and no monthly subscription security system. She can arm/disarm it with one button on her Home Assistant dashboard, and it makes her feel much safer. This guide assumes you already have a motion/presence sensor installed on HA.

1. Install HACS 2. Install Alarmo and the Alarmo Card (Pretty Arm and Disarm card for your HA dashboard)

The first button opens Alarmo in HACS and the second opens the Alarmo Card:

Restart Home Assistant once both are installed, then add the Alarmo integration under Settings → Devices & services → Add integration. Alarmo shows up in the sidebar after that.

3. Find Alarmo on the left, select the Sensors tab, and toggle on the sensor entities that you would like to use for your alarm system.

Shown with MSR-1 sensors; add your MTR-1 target entities the same way.

4. Now select the Actions tab and under Condition > Event > Select "Alarm is triggered". You can also select the device you would like to receive a notification on under Task > Target > Select Device (Phone, tablet, etc.)

5. You can change the Title, Message, and Name of the alarm notification.

6. After saving that action we can add another one that will turn on our sensor lights and/or make the onboard piezo buzzers play an alarm sound. Under Entity select your sensors' RGB light.

Shown with AIR-1 and MSR-1 lights; pick your MTR-1 RGB light the same way.

7. Under Action select Turn On and now your sensors' RGB lights will turn on when the alarm is triggered.

Shown with AIR-1 and MSR-1 lights; the MTR-1 steps are the same.

8. And that's it, seriously... Now you can enjoy a free and local security system.

We hope this was helpful and please let us know if there are any questions!

docs.title: Set up the Apollo mmWave dashboard for the MTR-1
Set up the Apollo mmWave dashboard for the MTR-1
docs.text:
A new Apollo radar sensor detects presence out of the box, but every room is different: a ceiling fan or a moving curtain can make it trigger with nobody there, and someone sitting still can be missed. The Apollo mmWave dashboard is where you fix that. On an Apollo MSR-1, MSR-2, or R PRO-1 with the LD2412 addon, one button, Calibrate with empty room, sets the radar's thresholds for your room in about a minute and a half. On an Apollo MTR-1 or R PRO-1, the same dashboard is where you draw zones over the radar's live targets.

The Apollo mmWave integration gives every Apollo radar sensor in your home its own workspace in Home Assistant. When you add it, it offers to add an Apollo mmWave dashboard to your sidebar with one tab per radar, built from the devices Home Assistant already knows about. Add a sensor later and its tab appears on its own; remove one and its tab goes away.

What each tab holds depends on the radar inside the sensor:

Sensor Radar chip What its tab shows Apollo MSR-1, Apollo MSR-2 LD2410 Radar tuning: setup checks, auto-calibration, distance and gate energy charts, thresholds, detection range, and occupancy Apollo R PRO-1 LD2450, plus the optional LD2412 addon The same radar tuning cards for the LD2412, plus a zone map for drawing occupancy zones over the LD2450's live targets, with the LD2450's setup check, live status, and controls beside it Apollo MTR-1 LD2450 A zone map, with the radar's setup check, live status, and controls beside it

Every tab starts with a Start here card that lists your sensor's first steps, and ends with a Device card that shows its firmware versions and restarts it. LD2410, LD2412, and LD2450 are the model numbers of the radar chips, and the card titles use them.

If you built the MSR-2 tuning dashboard by hand, this replaces it. The integration ships its own cards and updates them along with itself, so Streamline Card, Plotly Graph Card, and the YAML generator are no longer needed.

Before you start

  • You're running Home Assistant 2026.8.1 or newer. Settings → About shows your version.

  • HACS 2.0.5 or newer is installed and set up. HACS is a community store for Home Assistant that installs and updates custom integrations like this one. If you don't have it yet, follow the HACS download guide and then the initial configuration guide. Setup asks you to sign in with a free GitHub account. On Home Assistant OS, the button below opens the Get HACS app that the download guide uses.

  • Your Apollo sensor is already in Home Assistant through the ESPHome integration. If it isn't, work through getting started first.

docs.title: Install Apollo mmWave through HACS
docs.text:
Apollo mmWave installs from its GitHub repository, so you add that repository to HACS once as a custom repository. From then on HACS tracks updates for it like any other integration. The button under step 1 covers steps 1 to 5: it adds the repository, after HACS asks you to confirm, and opens Apollo mmWave so you can go on at step 6.

If you installed Apollo mmWave from the original repository, bharvey88/apollo-mmwave, which is no longer on GitHub, follow From the original Apollo mmWave repository instead. It switches HACS over without setting anything up again.

  1. Open HACS from your Home Assistant sidebar.

  2. Click the three-dot menu in the upper right corner and choose Custom repositories.

  3. Paste https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/apollo-mmwave-main into the Repository field.
  4. Set Type to Integration and click Add. The repository shows up in the list; close the dialog.
  5. Search HACS for Apollo mmWave and open it.
  6. Click Download, then confirm with Download in the dialog that opens.

  7. Restart Home Assistant: go to Settings → System, click the power icon in the upper right corner, choose Restart Home Assistant, then click Restart. Wait for it to come back.

Home Assistant only loads a new integration when it starts, so the restart is what makes Apollo mmWave available to add in the next step.

docs.title: Add the integration
docs.text:
This is the step that builds your dashboard. You add Apollo mmWave once and it covers every Apollo radar you own, so there's no need to repeat it per sensor. Adding it a second time stops with This entry is already configured.

  1. Go to Settings → Devices & services and click Add integration. Or use the button below, which opens the Apollo mmWave setup dialog directly, and skip to step 3.

  2. Search for Apollo mmWave and select it. If it isn't in the list, refresh the browser page (your browser may still hold the list from before the restart) and search again.

  3. The dialog notes that the integration serves its own cards and dashboard, with nothing else to download, and offers to add the dashboard for you. Leave both boxes ticked (they're on by default) to get the dashboard this guide describes:
    • Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard to the sidebar creates the dashboard once, when you click Submit. Untick it only if you'd rather place the cards on your own dashboards; you can still add the dashboard later from the integration options.
    • Only administrators can see it keeps the dashboard out of other users' sidebars. Untick it to show the dashboard to everyone in your home. You can change this later in the dashboard's settings under Settings → Dashboards.
  4. Click Submit, then Finish on the success message.

Apollo mmWave now appears under Settings → Devices & services. With the first box ticked, a new Apollo mmWave entry with a radar icon also sits in your sidebar, at the apollo-mmwave address. The integration registers its cards with Home Assistant itself, so they load in browser tabs that were already open without a refresh. If the dashboard couldn't be created, setup still finishes without it, and The Apollo mmWave dashboard isn't in the sidebar shows how to add it.

Created once, then it's yours

From Apollo mmWave 2.2.6, the dashboard is created once, when you click Submit. Apollo mmWave never recreates, rewrites, or deletes it on its own: not when Home Assistant restarts, and not when the integration reloads or updates. It's an ordinary dashboard, so you can rename it, change its icon, hide it, or delete it under Settings → Dashboards like any other. To add it again later, remove it, or add a second one, see Manage the dashboard.

docs.title: Open the dashboard
docs.text:
Click Apollo mmWave in the sidebar. With two or more radars you'll see one tab per radar along the top, each named after the device the way it appears in Home Assistant. With one radar, Home Assistant shows the dashboard title instead of a tab bar, and that radar's cards fill the page. The tabs keep themselves current: add a sensor and its tab appears, no page reload needed.

The cards on each tab are laid out in columns that stack into one on a phone. Here's what a working first load looks like for each sensor. A row only appears when its entity is enabled in Home Assistant, so some cards can be shorter than described.

docs.title: MSR-2 and MSR-1 tabs
docs.text:
Both sensors use the LD2410 radar chip, so their tabs look the same, and the tuning card titles start with LD2410.

  • Start here sits at the top. It names your sensor and lists five steps, from Fix anything the Radar setup card flags. to walking the room while you watch the Gate Energy chart. Its links open the tuning guide on this wiki and your sensor's own page in Home Assistant.

  • Under it, the Radar setup card checks the radar's settings and offers a fix when one is off. On a sensor that's ready to go it reads Radar settings look good.

  • Auto-calibrate comes next, with the Calibrate with empty room and Preview only buttons. If your sensor still has its factory thresholds and has never been calibrated, the card adds These look like factory thresholds. Calibrating sets them for your room.

  • The LD2410 Gate Energy chart is dimmed behind Turn on Radar Engineering Mode to see gate energy values, with a Turn on Radar Engineering Mode button below. That's expected: the radar only reports gate energy while Radar Engineering Mode, a diagnostic setting, is on. You don't need to press the button before calibrating; the calibration turns the mode on for its listen and puts it back the way it was afterward.

  • The other cards hold the radar's settings and live readings: controls, distances, detection range, occupancy, a threshold for each gate (from G0 (at the sensor) to G8, each named for how far out it reaches), and a day of occupancy history. The sliders on the range and threshold cards start locked, so a scroll can't move them: press Unlock above them to change one. The Device card at the bottom shows the firmware versions and restarts the sensor. The tour of the radar tab explains each one.

docs.title: R PRO-1 tabs
docs.text:
The R PRO-1 tab starts with the same tuning cards, titled LD2412 instead of LD2410, for the optional LD2412 radar addon, and adds a zone map for its LD2450 radar. Without the addon, the LD2412 cards still appear but have no radar behind them, so skip to the zone map, and Start here gives the zone map steps instead. The differences from an MSR-2 tab:

  • Start here says what each radar is for: the LD2412 senses people anywhere in range, even sitting still, and the LD2450 tracks where people are and drives the zone map.
  • LD2412 Controls adds Start Dynamic Background Correction and Background Correction Running. The Auto-calibrate card reminds you to run background correction first, with the room empty, and wait for its status to turn off before you calibrate.
  • LD2412 Detection Range holds Radar Timeout, Max Gate, and Min Gate, plus Distance Resolution if you've enabled that entity (it's hidden on a new sensor).
  • The thresholds cards and the Gate Energy chart cover 14 gates, G0 to G13.
  • There's no Zone Config card, and the LD2412 Distances chart shows the gates and your Max Gate and Min Gate limits without distance bars.
  • After the first column (Start here, the LD2412's Radar setup card, Auto-calibrate, LD2412 Controls, and LD2412 Target / Occupancy), a Zone Map heading introduces the LD2450's cards: its own Radar setup card, the zone map, Zone presence, LD2450 Live, and LD2450 Controls, described below. The rest of the LD2412 cards follow, so on a phone you reach the zone map before the 28 threshold rows.

docs.title: MTR-1 tabs
docs.text:
An MTR-1 tab is built around the zone map, with everything for its LD2450 radar beside it:

  • Start here lists three steps (fix anything the Radar setup card flags, set Cone rotation, then draw a zone and walk into it), says which presence sensor to use in automations, and links to your sensor's own page.
  • Radar setup checks Zone Type and Multi Target Tracking, the two radar settings that decide whether the map can show people, and fixes them when you press its button. Zone Type should be Disabled, because the zone map replaces the radar's own built-in zones.
  • The zone map, titled with your sensor's name, shows the radar's view, a cone 120 degrees wide and about 6 m (20 ft) out, with a dot for each target the LD2450 is tracking. It's in feet or meters to match Home Assistant, and the m / ft switch on the map changes it. A pencil button in the lower left opens the drawing tools, the lower right holds the unit switch and the undo and lock buttons, and a collapsed Configure section under the grid holds the cone rotation slider and the zone list.
  • Zone presence, LD2450 Live, and Occupancy History show each zone's presence sensor, what the radar reports right now, and the last 24 hours.
  • LD2450 Controls, the radar's built-in zones (only while Zone Type isn't Disabled), and the Device card end the tab.

The integration finds the sensor's target entities itself, so there's nothing to pick before you start drawing. The R PRO-1's zone map and the cards beside it work the same way.

docs.title: What to do first
docs.text:
Your dashboard is working. Follow the Start here card on each tab, from the top:

  1. Look at the Radar setup card near the top of the tab. If it flags a setting, follow what it says: most problems have a button that fixes them, and the card changes nothing until you press one. An R PRO-1 tab has a second one above the zone map, for the LD2450.

  2. On an MSR-1 or MSR-2 tab, or an R PRO-1 tab with the LD2412 addon, calibrate the radar. Skip this step on an R PRO-1 without the LD2412. On an R PRO-1, first clear the room, press Start Dynamic Background Correction on the LD2412 Controls card, and wait for Background Correction Running to turn off. Then press Calibrate with empty room on the Auto-calibrate card and leave the room for about a minute and a half. You don't need to turn on Radar Engineering Mode: the calibration does that for you. The tuning guide walks you through it.

  3. On an MTR-1 or R PRO-1 tab, draw your zones.

The rest of this page covers managing the dashboard, upgrading from an older setup, and troubleshooting, so come back to it when you need it.

docs.title: Manage the dashboard
docs.text:
After setup, Apollo mmWave changes its dashboard only when you ask it to, from the integration options: add the dashboard, remove it, or choose which sensors get a tab. Open Settings → Devices & services → Apollo mmWave → Configure to reach the Apollo mmWave options menu. It reads These actions change only the Apollo mmWave dashboard this integration created. Dashboards you made yourself are never changed. and lists the actions that fit:

  • Add the Apollo mmWave dashboard is listed while the integration has no dashboard of its own: you unticked the box during setup, setup couldn't create it, or you deleted it. It describes the dashboard it creates and asks Only administrators can see it again. Click Submit to create it, once, with the sensors you chose under Choose the dashboard's devices.
  • Remove the Apollo mmWave dashboard is listed while the integration has one. Click Submit to delete the Apollo mmWave dashboard at /apollo-mmwave that the integration created, along with any title, icon, or strategy options you changed on it. Your sensors, zones, and calibration values stay, and the cards still work on your own dashboards. You can add the dashboard again from the same menu.
  • Choose the dashboard's devices opens Dashboard devices, which is empty by default and shows every Apollo mmWave device Home Assistant knows about, online or not. Select one or more devices to show exactly those and hide the rest; a selected device keeps its tab even while it's offline. Clear the selection to go back to automatic detection. The picker only lists Apollo MSR-1, MSR-2, MTR-1, and R PRO-1 sensors added through ESPHome.

Each action takes effect as soon as you click Submit, with no restart, and an open dashboard picks up a new device selection without a reload. The device selection is written only into the dashboard the integration created. Without one, the selection is kept and used when you add the dashboard from the options.

You can also delete the dashboard under Settings → Dashboards, like any other. It stays deleted until you add it again from the options.

docs.title: Add another Apollo mmWave dashboard
docs.text:
Want a second dashboard, say one with only the bedroom sensors, or one at another address because something else already uses apollo-mmwave? Home Assistant's dashboard picker adds one that builds its tabs the same way as the integration's own:
