docs.title: LD2412 configuration
docs.text:
The LD2412 works differently than the LD2450. Instead of drawing rectangular zones on a 2D map, you work with distance gates. Each gate covers 0.75m of radial distance from the sensor, so Gate 1 is 0-0.75m away, Gate 2 is 0.75-1.5m, and so on out to Gate 12 at 8.25-9m (see the gate table on the General Tips page). You define what the sensor reacts to by setting a sensitivity threshold at each gate distance.

The same HLKRadarTool app is used for both sensors.

iPhoneAndroid

Click here to download

Click here to download

1. Head to the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome) then select your R PRO-1 and scroll down until you see LD2412 Bluetooth. Toggle it on.

2. Open the HLKRadarTool app. Your R PRO-1 should appear in the device list. Tap it to connect.

You need to be close to your device!

The LD2412 connects over Bluetooth, which means you need to be within a few feet of the sensor for it to appear in the app. If it doesn't show up, move closer and pull down to refresh the list.

3. Once connected, enable Engineering Mode as shown above. This turns on the live energy graph, which shows you what the sensor is actually seeing at each distance gate in real time.

Reading the engineering mode graph

The horizontal axis represents distance gates (each gate = 0.75m from the sensor). Two sets of bars are shown: one for moving targets and one for still targets. The colored threshold line is the sensitivity setting you've configured for each gate. When the live energy bar at a gate exceeds that threshold, the sensor reports detection at that distance.

Think of it like a ruler pointing away from the sensor, where each column is one step further out (0.75m per step). The taller a bar rises, the stronger the signal at that distance. When a bar crosses the threshold line, the sensor reports detection there. Walk around in front of it to see your movement show up in real time.

4. Leave the room empty and make sure nothing is moving, then tap Auto in the app. The sensor scans the environment for about 10 seconds and automatically sets thresholds to filter out static interference from electronics, HVAC, and other background sources. When it's done you'll see Completed and the app will return to showing the detection distance. This gives you a clean baseline before any manual tuning.

5. Tap Settings in the top right and use the Detection Range slider to set which gates the sensor monitors. You can set both a start and end gate. For example, Gate 3 to Gate 6 means the sensor only looks between 1.5m and 4.5m from the device. Limiting the range prevents the sensor from picking up movement through walls or in adjacent rooms.

Gate to distance reference

Each gate covers 0.75m. Gate 1 = 0-0.75m, Gate 2 = 0.75-1.5m, Gate 3 = 1.5-2.25m, Gate 4 = 2.25-3m, Gate 5 = 3-3.75m, Gate 6 = 3.75-4.5m, Gate 7 = 4.5-5.25m, Gate 8 = 5.25-6m.

6. To fine-tune which distances trigger detection, head to the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome), select your R PRO-1, and use the gate threshold sliders on the device page.

  • Raise a gate's threshold to make it harder to trigger at that distance (useful for ignoring a fan, HVAC vent, or a window where cars pass).
  • Lower a gate's threshold to make it easier to trigger at that distance (useful for reliably detecting someone sitting still in a chair).

7. Tap Settings at the top of the app and set the Unmanned Duration. This controls how many seconds the sensor waits after it stops detecting before it reports "no one present." The default is 10 seconds. Increase it if you're getting false "nobody home" readings in your space. In Home Assistant, this same setting is called LD2412 Timeout.

8. Head back to the ESPHome integration page (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome), select your R PRO-1, and toggle LD2412 Bluetooth back off. Leaving Bluetooth on increases power consumption and can interfere with nearby Bluetooth devices.

docs.title: Putting the R PRO-1 in boot mode
Putting the R PRO-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the R PRO-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You'll open the case, then hold the boot button while you plug in the USB-C cable.

1. Unplug your R PRO-1 from power and remove the back.

2. Gently remove the PCB from the case and flip it over.

3. Locate the boot button on the bottom right side of the PCB.

4. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your R PRO-1 then let go of the button.

5. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You'll open the case, plug the board into your computer, then hold the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug your R PRO-1 from power and remove the back.

2. Gently remove the PCB from the case and flip it over.

3. Locate the boot button on the bottom right side of the PCB.

4. Locate the reset button on the bottom left side of the PCB.

5. Plug your R PRO-1 into your computer, then put it in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (the right button, shown in step 3). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (the left button, shown in step 4).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the R PRO-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

6. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash R PRO-1
docs.text:
If your Apollo R PRO-1 becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods, you can re-flash the factory firmware by following the steps below. You'll put the R PRO-1 in boot mode, flash it from the Apollo installer in your browser, and then set it up as a new device.

Before you start

  • Do this factory re-flash in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium-based browser.
  • If your device has already been connected to Home Assistant, remove it from the ESPHome integration and the ESPHome Device Builder before continuing.

1. Put your R PRO-1 in boot mode. The boot button is on the bottom right of the board, so first unplug the R PRO-1, remove the back, and take the board out of the case. The boot mode guide shows each part.

With the board out of the case:

  • Push and hold the boot button.
  • While still holding the button down, plug a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your R PRO-1.
  • Let go of the button.

2. Open the Apollo R PRO-1 installer.

3. Under Choose your firmware, pick WiFi if your R PRO-1 connects over Wi-Fi, or Ethernet if it connects over PoE or Ethernet. Then click Connect & Install.

4. In the browser pop-up, select the open COM port (the R PRO-1's serial port, shown as USB JTAG/serial debug unit in the example below), then click Connect.

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.R-PRO-1-W if you chose WiFi, or Install ApolloAutomation.R-PRO-1-ETH if you chose Ethernet.

6. Click INSTALL.

7. When you see Installation complete!, you're finished. Click Next, then close the browser window.

Your R PRO-1 now has the factory firmware again.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else

Your R PRO-1 is still in boot mode. Unplug it, then plug it back in so it starts in normal mode.

8. Follow the getting started guide to set up your R PRO-1 as a new device.

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your R PRO-1
docs.text:
You'll reset the device's Wi-Fi credentials, then connect it to your new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button (the button on the right) for 10 seconds.

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo R PRO 1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: Teardown and reassembly of R PRO-1
Disassembly:
docs.text:
You'll remove the back, take the PCB out of the case, and remove both mmWave sensors.

1. Unplug your R PRO-1 from power and remove the back.

2. Gently remove the PCB from the case and flip it over.

3. Gently remove the LD2412 as shown below.

4. Gently remove the LD2450 as shown below.

docs.title: Reassembly
docs.text:
To put everything back together, you'll reinstall both mmWave sensors, place the PCB back in the case, and snap the lid on.

1. Place the LD2450 on the 8 pin header.

2. Place the LD2412 on the 4 and 3 pin headers (only fits one way).

3. Place back into the case with the ethernet module facing up and the USB-C port facing you.

4. Snap the lid back into place!

docs.title: TEMP-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. How is the TEMP-1 powered?

  • The TEMP-1 operates with USB-C at 5 volts using less than 1 amp of power.

2. What are the Optional Probe Addons?

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.
  • 1m (~3ft) Stainless Steel Food-Safe Probe (NTC): Max 350°C (662°F). Perfect for grilling, baking, and food prep (not dishwasher safe).

3. Is the TEMP-1 weatherproof? Can I use it outdoors?

  • The TEMP-1 is primarily designed for indoor use, but components like the waterproof temperature probe are suited for harsh conditions. The main body is not rated for outdoor use without additional protection.

4. How does the TEMP-1 connect to Home Assistant?

  • The TEMP-1 connects via Wi-Fi to ESPHome on Home Assistant, enabling data monitoring, automations, and alerts directly within Home Assistant.

5. How often does the TEMP-1 send sensor data?

  • The TEMP-1’s reporting frequency is adjustable in ESPHome but most things default to 60 seconds. You can set it for more frequent updates or longer intervals.

6. Can I customize the TEMP-1 functionality?

  • Absolutely! With ESPHome, users can modify firmware, settings, and even print custom cases for the TEMP-1. Our YAML is on GitHub and our .STEP and .STL CAD files are available for community use.

7. What are the RGB LED and piezo buzzer used for?

  • The RGB LED provides visual alerts, while the piezo buzzer offers audio notifications for events like the probe temperature going outside the Min/Max Probe Temp range you set (with Alarm Outside Temp Range turned on).

8. Is the TEMP-1 compatible with other smart home platforms?

  • While designed for Home Assistant via ESPHome, it may be compatible with other platforms using the ESPHome API or MQTT.

9. Do I need coding knowledge to use the TEMP-1?

  • Basic knowledge of Home Assistant and ESPHome is helpful, but most users can utilize it out of the box. For advanced customization, YAML knowledge is recommended.

10. Can I access data from the TEMP-1 remotely?

  • Yes, you can access sensor data remotely via the Home Assistant dashboard if your setup is configured for remote access.

11. What’s the difference between the battery and non-battery versions?

  • The TEMP-1B is battery-operated and slightly larger, while the non-battery (NB) version is compact and connects directly to a USB-C power source.

12. Can I use multiple TEMP-1 sensors in one Home Assistant setup?

  • Yes, you can add multiple TEMP-1 sensors, each appearing as a separate device, for comprehensive monitoring across multiple fridges, freezers, or spaces.

13. Can I use an extender to make the TEMP-1 temp probe cable longer?

  • Yes, you can, however at some point you will begin getting "voltage drop" and likely run into issues with bad data from the probe. We suggest 1.5 meters or less!

14. Can I use the probe in a salt water tank?

  • Yes, however a very high concentration of salt will likely eventually lead to corrosion and should be checked from time to time. The stainless steel used is "SS304" grade.

15. What is the wiring for the 3.5mm temp probe?

  • Tip is 3.3V, ring is data, and sleeve is GND. See the temp probe pinout for a picture.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The TEMP-1 can be used with an optional temperature probe which comes in two lengths or a food safe grill probe. The TEMP-1 itself can be used with an optional magnetic mount to mount it to a fridge, grill, or other surface while taking measurements. It also features an AHT20-F air temperature and humidity sensor, which includes dust protection, an RGB LED, and a piezo buzzer.

Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.
  • 1m (~3ft) Stainless Steel Food-Safe Probe (NTC): Max 350°C (662°F). Perfect for grilling, baking, and food prep (not dishwasher safe).

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The TEMP-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your TEMP-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: TEMP-1 Bluetooth proxy
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to make your Apollo device act as a "BLE Proxy" which lets Bluetooth devices talk back to Home Assistant using Apollo devices as the "next hop"!

Select a method below. Method 1 switches your TEMP-1 to the prebuilt TEMP-1_BLE.yaml firmware. Method 2 adds the BLE proxy yaml to your existing config by hand.

Method 1: TEMP-1_BLE.yaml firmwareMethod 2: Manually enter the BLE proxy yaml

You'll swap your device's firmware package for its prebuilt Bluetooth proxy version in ESPHome Device Builder, then install it over the network.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Find your device and click Edit.

3. Replace the packages: line and the line directly below it with the code below.

packages:
  ApolloAutomation.TEMP-1:
    url: https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/TEMP-1
    ref: main
    files: [Integrations/ESPHome/TEMP-1_BLE_R2.yaml]
    refresh: 1min

4. Click Save then Install in the bottom right. Click On the network when prompted.

5. When you see the purple lines the device has booted successfully and the logs will show the Bluetooth Proxy section. Click Stop in the bottom right and you're finished!

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

The easiest way is to let ESPHome Device Builder add the component for you. You can also paste the single line by hand.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar and click Edit on your device. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Click Add Component in the editor toolbar, search for Bluetooth Proxy, and click Add.

Device Builder drops a single line into your config:

bluetooth_proxy:

That's all it needs. Active connections are on by default, and bluetooth_proxy automatically pulls in the ESP32 BLE Tracker it depends on, so there's nothing else to add. Prefer to type it? Paste that one line at the top level of your YAML instead of using Add Component.

3. Click Save, then Install, and choose On the Network to flash the new firmware over Wi-Fi.

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

docs.title: Prevent Sleep
docs.text:
Put your sensors to sleep!

All of our battery powered devices are able to go to sleep to save battery life. Our non-battery sensor devices like the AIR-1 and PLT-1 can also sleep to get better temperature and humidity measurements.

The temperature offsets needed will be much lower for your sensors as the microcontroller will not put off as much heat when it is sleeping and then waking for short periods to report the sensor values.

You'll set how long your sensor sleeps, then turn off Prevent Sleep so it can start sleeping.

1. Head to the ESPHome Integrations page and click on the name of your Apollo device.

2. Scroll down until you see Prevent Sleep and Sleep Duration.

3. Type in how long you want your sensor to sleep in the Sleep Duration box. Check the unit next to the box: it is minutes on the AIR-1 (default 5), PLT-1 (default 5), and TEMP-1 (default 8), and hours on the BTN-1 (default 24), PLT-1B (default 12), and TEMP-1B (default 12). We recommend leaving the default values.

Read this before turning off Prevent Sleep!

When "Prevent Sleep" is toggled off, your sensor will immediately begin sleeping. Please make sure you are ready to make this sensor sleep before toggling off prevent sleep.

4. When you are ready, toggle off Prevent Sleep and your sensor will go to sleep. It will wake up on the Sleep Duration interval from step 3. If you need to keep your sensor awake, head to our OTA Awake helper tutorial!

5. You can wake your sensor by following this guide or you can power cycle your device. If there is a battery in it, the battery will need to be removed or the reset button pressed.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The AIR-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your AIR-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: TEMP-1 food probe
docs.text:
The TEMP-1 comes with an optional food probe which can be used to monitor food temperatures when baking, grilling, etc. It includes a heat-resistant cable but the TEMP-1 itself needs to stay in a cool environment.

1. To use your food probe, take it out of the package and insert it into the 3.5mm port on your TEMP-1.

2. Once inserted, press the reset button or power cycle your TEMP-1 so it detects the probe (see the tip below), then continue to step 3.

If you have it plugged into power you need to push the reset button.

The TEMP-1 looks for the food probe when it boots and if it is not there then the sensor is marked as failed and will not work properly in Home Assistant. You need to click the reset button if you have it plugged in or power cycle your TEMP-1 to make it reliably use the new food temperature probe.

3. Go to the device page of your TEMP-1 in Home Assistant (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome) and choose probe "Food".

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The TEMP-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your TEMP-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

1. To use your magnetic mount place it with the magnet facing upwards as shown:

2. Align the lid with the hole in the top right and place your TEMP-1 inside the magnetic mount and gently press down.

docs.title: TEMP-1 multi-probe splitter guide
docs.text:
The TEMP-1 comes with an optional 3.5mm Multi-Probe Splitter which can be used to monitor a fridge, freezer, fish tank, pool, hot tub, etc with up to 4 probes.

Firmware version 25.11.20.1 or newer required for TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B

The multi probe support was added in November of 2025. If you are using an old TEMP-1 or TEMP-1B that hasn't been updated then please visit our reflashing guide for the TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B. Alternatively you can update your devices following this guide!

1. To use your TEMP-1 Multi-Probe Splitter gently plug it into the 3.5mm port on your device.

2. Plug in your long or short temp probes into the Multi-Probe Splitter.

Power on your TEMP-1 after plugging in all of your probes!

The TEMP-1 will look for the probes at boot and mark them failed if you power on and plug in the probes after. Power cycle your device and they should show up!

3. Go to the device page of your TEMP-1 in Home Assistant and confirm the Temperature Probe is selected from the dropdown.

4. Enable the disabled 3rd and 4th temp probe entities if you have more than 2 probes!

5. Once completed you will see all four probes updating the temperature!

6. To rename the probes you can edit each probe and choose a unique name such as "Fridge Probe" and "Freezer Probe" as shown below!

docs.title: Keep Your Sensor Awake With HA Helper
Keep your sensor awake with a Home Assistant helper
docs.text:
When an apollo_ota_mode toggle in Home Assistant is on, your Apollo battery devices stay awake so you can update them. In this guide you create that toggle, then add an automation that turns it off again after one hour.

This keeps every Apollo device awake

While apollo_ota_mode is on, none of your Apollo devices go back to sleep. Finish the second part of this guide to create an automation that turns the helper off after it has been on for one hour.

docs.title: Create the OTA mode toggle
docs.text:
Start by creating the toggle helper and switching it on.

1. Go to Settings → Devices & services and select the Helpers tab at the top. Or use the button below to go straight there.

2. Select Create helper in the bottom right.

3. Scroll to the bottom of the list and select Toggle.

4. Name the toggle apollo_ota_mode, choose an icon such as mdi:sleep-off, and click Create.

5. Search the helpers list for apollo_ota_mode and click the helper that appears.

6. Switch the toggle on.

OTA mode is now on. The next time your Apollo device reboots or wakes up on its wake timer, it stays awake instead of going back to sleep.

docs.title: Turn OTA mode off after one hour
docs.text:
Next, create an automation that switches apollo_ota_mode off once it has been on for one hour, so you never leave your devices awake by accident.

1. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes and click Create automation.

2. Click Add trigger, then select Entity.

3. Select State.

4. In the Entity box, enter apollo_ota_mode. Set To to On, and enter 1 in the hours box under For. This trigger fires once apollo_ota_mode has been on for one hour.

5. Scroll down to Then do, click Add action, search for input boolean, and choose Input boolean: Turn off.

6. Click Choose entity and select apollo_ota_mode.

You're done. Turn apollo_ota_mode on whenever you want to update your devices, and the automation turns it off for you after one hour.

docs.text:
1. Press the reset button and let go to restart the deviceTEMP-1B reset button

PLT-1B reset button

2. Press the boot button and let goTEMP-1B boot button

PLT-1B boot button

The RGB Light on your device should flash green if connected to Wi-Fi, blue if connected to Wi-Fi and Home Assistant, or yellow if no Wi-Fi or Home Assistant connection.

Head to the awake helper wiki article

docs.title: How To Wake Up Your Sensor
docs.text:
To wake a sleeping Apollo battery sensor, press the reset button. A BTN-1 also wakes when you press Button 1, 2, 3, or 4, and an H-1 or H-2 wakes when you press a gold song button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping device. Select your device below for the button locations.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1H-1H-2

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping TEMP-1B. Once the TEMP-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: TEMP-1B boot mode.

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping PLT-1B. Once the PLT-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: PLT-1B boot mode.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Buttons 1 to 4. Press and release Button 1, 2, 3, or 4. Home Assistant receives that press as a click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any automation you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping BTN-1. Once the BTN-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: BTN-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-1 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Method 2: Gold button. Press and release the gold button (SW1).

The boot button can't wake a sleeping H-1. Once the H-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

The unlabeled circled button at the lower left is the gold button (SW1), which plays the built-in songs.

Button locations: H-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-2 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Song buttons. Press and release any of the four gold song buttons on the back of the H-2. The H-2 wakes and plays that button's song.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping H-2. Once the H-2 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: H-2 boot mode.

Your device is now awake, but it will not stay awake on its own yet. Click the Prevent Sleep button on your device page in Home Assistant, or directly on the device web server such as plt-1.local or its IP address.

You can also turn on Prevent Sleep from the device itself. Once it's awake, press and hold the boot button for 4-5 seconds, then let go.

Watch how you use the boot button

Press the boot button only after the device has restarted. Holding it while you press reset puts the device in boot mode for flashing firmware instead. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets the device to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi.

Head to the awake helper wiki article

If you need to keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time we suggest using our OTA awake helper.

docs.title: Hot water recirculation with TEMP-1
docs.text:
Contributed by Donovan

Big thanks to Donovan for building this and sharing his whole setup, automations included, so we could package it up as the blueprint below.

There are two normal ways to get hot water at a sink, and each has a catch. A small under-sink tank gives you instant hot water with very little energy, but it runs out after a gallon or two. The main house water heater never runs out, but you either wait while cold water runs down the drain, or you get a cold-water sandwich when the tank water hands off to the line water.

Donovan's setup uses an Apollo TEMP-1 to get both. Small draws come from a 2.5 gallon Bosch mini tank. When he knows he needs more, a button starts a recirculation loop that pulls hot water up from the house heater without running the tap, and the TEMP-1 tells Home Assistant the moment that line is hot enough to switch over. No water goes down the drain, and there is no cold-water sandwich.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The TEMP-1 probe is zip-tied to the hot-water angle stop, so it reads the temperature of the hot line coming from the house heater. Everything else, the Bosch tank, the circulator pump, the motorized valve, and the TEMP-1 itself, plugs into a Kasa smart power strip that Home Assistant controls.

  1. Idle. The 3-way valve is unpowered, so the sinks are fed by the Bosch mini tank. Instant hot water, low energy.
  2. Request hot water. Donovan presses an Aqara Zigbee button when he knows he'll use more than a gallon or two.
  3. Recirculate. Home Assistant switches the circulator pump on. It pumps the cooled water from the hot line back into the cold line, pulling fresh hot water up from the house heater. Nothing runs down the drain.
  4. Watch the line. The TEMP-1 reports the angle-stop temperature every few seconds. The pump also has its own temperature sensor, and the smart strip watches its energy use, so the system knows when the pump finishes.
  5. Switch over. Once the line is hot, Home Assistant powers the valve so the sinks draw from the house heater, and shuts the pump outlet off so it won't run again when the water cools. Alexa announces "The hot water is ready."
  6. Revert. When the TEMP-1 sees the line drop below a set temperature, Home Assistant cuts power to the valve. A capacitor inside the valve stores just enough energy to rotate it back, so the sinks return to the Bosch tank.

docs.title: Physical layout
docs.text: Here's the real thing under Donovan's sink: the Bosch mini tank with the smart strip on top, the 3-way valve strapped to the wall behind it, and the circulator pump bolted to the floor on the right.

docs.title: Control logic
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IDLE["Idle:<br/>Bosch feeds the sinks<br/>(valve off)"]
    PUMP["Pump ON:<br/>recirculate the wall loop,<br/>no water wasted"]
    Q1{"Wall line<br/>up to temp?"}
    WALL["Valve powered:<br/>house heater feeds the sinks<br/>(Alexa: hot water ready)"]
    Q2{"Wall line<br/>cooled off?"}

    IDLE -->|press Aqara button| PUMP --> Q1
    Q1 -->|no| PUMP
    Q1 -->|yes| WALL --> Q2
    Q2 -->|no| WALL
    Q2 -->|"yes: valve off, back to Bosch"| IDLE

    classDef bosch fill:#4379AA,stroke:#2d5a8a,color:#fff;
    classDef wall fill:#d64545,stroke:#a83232,color:#fff;
    classDef temp fill:#2e7d46,stroke:#1f5630,color:#fff;
    class IDLE bosch;
    class WALL wall;
    class Q1,Q2 temp;

docs.title: Parts
docs.text: Part Role in the loop Apollo TEMP-1 + short temperature probe Reads the hot line at the angle stop and reports it to Home Assistant Bosch ES2.5 mini tank (2.5 gal, 120 V) Instant hot water for small draws AquaMotion AMH3K-7N circulator pump Recirculates the loop to pull hot water up from the house heater US Solid 1/2" 3-way L-type motorized ball valve Selects the hot source: unpowered feeds the Bosch, powered feeds the house heater Smart plugs with power monitoring (we suggest Zooz Z-Wave, like the ZEN04; Donovan used a TP-Link Kasa strip) Switch the pump and valve, and report the pump's power so Home Assistant knows when it finishes Aqara wireless mini switch (Zigbee) The "I want hot water" button Alexa speaker Announces when the line is ready

docs.title: TEMP-1 configuration
docs.text:
For this to react quickly, the probe needs to report faster than its 60 second default. Donovan reports it every 3 seconds and keeps a 60 second heartbeat, so Home Assistant reacts fast while you can still tell at a glance that the probe is alive. Two guards keep the data clean: the 85.0 reading a DS18B20 sends at power-on is dropped, and readings are ignored when the Select Probe option is set to Food.

The probe zip-ties straight onto the hot-water angle stop, so it reads the line coming from the house heater.

For the full walkthrough of overriding probe YAML in the ESPHome Builder, including the simpler delta-plus-heartbeat pattern, see How To Change The Temperature Probe Update Interval.

sensor:
  - platform: dallas_temp
    id: !extend temp_probe
    update_interval: 3s
    filters:
      - lambda: |-
          if (isnan(x)) {
            return NAN;
          }
          if (x == 85.0) {
              return NAN;
          }
          auto selected_probe = id(temp_probe_select).current_option();
          if (selected_probe == "Food") {
            return NAN;
          }
          return x - id(dallas_temperature_offset).state;
      - or:
          - delta: 1.1    # ~2°F; change to 2.0 for 2°C (~3.6°F) instead
          - heartbeat: 60s

docs.title: Set it up in Home Assistant
docs.text:
Donovan's whole system is one blueprint. Import it, pick your entities, set your temperatures, and save. There are no helpers to create and no automations to copy and rename.

Before you import

Two things need to be in place: your TEMP-1 probe should report quickly (see TEMP-1 configuration above), and your pump and valve should be on smart plugs Home Assistant can switch, with power monitoring on the pump.

docs.title: Import the blueprint
docs.text:
1. Click the button below, then click Open link.

2. Click Preview, then Import blueprint.

3. Click Apollo Automation Hot Water Recirculation (TEMP-1), create an automation from it, and fill in the inputs below.

docs.title: What you'll fill in
docs.text:
Input What to pick Start trigger The press that starts a cycle, like your Aqara button's single click. Pick it from the trigger editor like any automation. You can add more than one (see the tip below). Circulator pump plug The smart plug powering the pump. Circulator pump power That plug's power (W) sensor, how the system knows the pump has finished. 3-way valve plug The smart plug powering the valve. Hot line temperature (TEMP-1) Your TEMP-1 probe. Activate / Return temperature When to switch to the house heater, and when to revert. Both default to 90 °F. Pump finished below (W) The power level that means the pump's thermostat cut the motor. Default 20 W. Pump / Valve safety timeout Backstops that force the pump and valve off if a signal is missed. Default 5 and 60 minutes. Actions when the water is ready Optional. Runs the moment the valve opens: announce on a speaker, turn on the shower fan, flash a light.

Starting by button, voice, or dashboard

The blueprint runs a cycle whenever the Start trigger fires, so it works with whatever you give it. Add your button's single-press for the physical button. To also start from a dashboard tap or a voice assistant (Donovan uses a Nabu Casa voice command), add a second trigger: your pump plug turning on. Then tapping that plug on a card, or saying "turn on the circulator," kicks off the whole cycle.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Both temperatures default to 90 °F. The probe reads the outside of the angle stop through a zip-tie, so it lags the water by a few degrees. Nudge Activate up if the valve flips before the water is genuinely hot, or down if you're left waiting.

Pump finished below should sit under the pump's running draw but above its standby. 20 W suits the AquaMotion AMH3K; check yours on the plug's power sensor.

The two safety timeouts are backstops. If a signal is ever missed, the pump and valve still shut themselves off, so the 5 and 60 minute defaults are deliberately generous.

Donovan's extras

Donovan also flashes the shower lights as a silent "ready" cue, and ties his shower exhaust fan into a Moen Flo that switches it off once the shower's water stops. Both drop straight into the Actions when the water is ready slot, alongside (or instead of) the spoken announcement.

docs.title: TEMP-1 alert outside temp range example
TEMP-1 alert outside temp range example
docs.text:
This will guide you through how to set up the built in alarm using the temperature probe in your freezer!

1. Place the temperature probe into your freezer (not the entire TEMP-1, just the probe!) and then wait for it to normalize around 0 degrees F aka -18C.

2. Once normalized, look at the graph and determine a good value to set for both the maximum and minimum temperatures. My mini freezer seems to max out at 30F so I would want to go slightly above that range. However, in most freezers they should NOT reach above 0F so you will likely need to input a lower value than me. My minimums are around -20F.

3. We now need to convert F to C since the max and min temps are measured in Celsius. My new values I will input are max probe temp 2C and a min probe temp of -30C. Reminder, yours will likely be different values, especially your max probe temp.

4. Enable the "Alarm Outside Temp Range" toggle and now your TEMP-1 will play an audible alert with its buzzer when the temp thresholds are reached. If the temp goes under the min or over the max the alarm will go off

docs.title: Automation examples using a TEMP-1
docs.text: These three examples show you how to put your Apollo TEMP-1 to work in Home Assistant: get an alert when your freezer warms up, know when your food reaches temperature, and run a whole chicken-cooking routine from one dashboard button.

docs.title: Freezer temperature probe example
docs.text:
This example walks you through setting up an automation in Home Assistant with the temperature probe in your freezer. At the end, you'll have an automation that sends your phone a notification when the freezer goes above the temperature you set.

Only the probe goes in the freezer

Only the temperature probe and its wire can withstand the temperatures in a fridge, freezer, and similar places. Keep your TEMP-1 itself in a cool, dry place.

1. Place the temperature probe in your freezer and wait for it to settle around 0°F (-18°C).

2. Once it has settled, look at the probe's history graph in Home Assistant (shown below) and decide on good values for both the maximum and minimum temperatures. In this example, the mini freezer seems to max out at 30°F, so the maximum goes slightly above that range. However, most freezers should not reach above 0°F, so you'll likely need a lower value than this example. The minimums in this example are around -20°F.

3. Convert your values to Celsius, because Max Probe Temp and Min Probe Temp are set in Celsius, then enter them. This example uses a Max Probe Temp of 2°C and a Min Probe Temp of -30°C. Yours will likely be different, especially your Max Probe Temp. These settings control the TEMP-1's built-in buzzer alarm.

Next, create the automation that sends the notification to your phone.

4. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation.

5. Click Add trigger → Entity → Numeric state and search for your TEMP-1 temperature probe, such as "temp-1 temperature probe". In the box labeled Above, type the maximum temperature you decided on in step 2. Prefer YAML? Skip ahead to the freezer automation YAML.

6. Click Add action, type "iPhone", and select your phone. If you don't see your phone, or you have an Android phone, type "notify" instead and scroll down until you find your phone in the list.

Still don't see your phone?

You need the Home Assistant mobile app installed on your phone for this step to work. If you don't have it, try another notification instead of your phone, such as a TTS notification on your speakers. This could be a fun way to announce that dinner is ready!

7. Type your message. If you want a title too, check the box for the title and type it in. This example's message is "The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and your freezer might be having issues." and its title is "Check the freezer!".

8. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and, optionally, a description and a category.

You're done. Your phone now gets a notification whenever the freezer probe goes above your maximum temperature.

docs.title: Freezer automation YAML
docs.text:
If you'd rather work in YAML, here's the finished automation. Use your own entity ID and phone in place of the ones shown.

alias: Freezer Over Max Temp Automation
description: Warning for the freezer when it reaches the max temperature.
triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id:
      - sensor.apollo_temp_1_temperature_probe
    # in the unit Home Assistant shows for the probe (°F here); use your own entity ID
    above: 30
conditions: []
actions:
  - action: notify.mobile_app_brandons_iphone
    metadata: {}
    data:
      title: Check the freezer!
      message: >-
        The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and
        your freezer might be having issues.
mode: single

docs.title: Food probe example
docs.text:
This example walks you through setting up an automation in Home Assistant with the food probe while chicken (or anything else) cooks to 165°F (73.9°C). At the end, you'll have an automation that sends your phone a notification when your food reaches that temperature.

Only the probe goes on the grill

Only the food probe and the wire can withstand temperatures on a grill, in the oven, and similar places. Keep your TEMP-1 itself in a cool, dry place.

1. Set your Max Probe Temp to 73.9°C. Max Probe Temp is always set in Celsius, even if you use °F in the automation below.

2. Place the food probe inside your food once it's on the grill.

3. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation.

4. Click Add trigger → Entity → Numeric state and search for your TEMP-1 food probe, such as "temp-1 food probe". In the box labeled Above, type the temperature you want for your food. This example uses 165°F (73.9°C), the temperature it's safe to cook chicken to. Prefer YAML? Skip ahead to the food probe automation YAML.

5. Click Add action, type "iPhone", and select your phone. If you don't see your phone, or you have an Android phone, type "notify" instead and scroll down until you find your phone in the list.

Still don't see your phone?

You need the Home Assistant mobile app installed on your phone for this step to work. If you don't have it, try another notification instead of your phone, such as a TTS notification on your speakers. This could be a fun way to announce that dinner is ready!

6. Type your message. If you want a title too, check the box for the title and type it in. This example's message is "The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and your food is ready." and its title is "Check the food!".

7. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and, optionally, a description and a category.

You're done. Your phone now gets a notification when your food reaches the temperature you set.

docs.title: Food probe automation YAML
docs.text:
If you'd rather work in YAML, here's the finished automation. Use your own entity ID and phone in place of the ones shown.

alias: Food Over Max Temp Automation
description: Warning for the food when it reaches the max temperature.
triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id:
      - sensor.apollo_temp_1_food_probe
    # in the unit Home Assistant shows for the probe (°F here); use your own entity ID
    above: 165
conditions: []
actions:
  - action: notify.mobile_app_brandons_iphone
    metadata: {}
    data:
      title: Check the food!
      message: >-
        The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and your food is ready.
mode: single

docs.title: Cook chicken example
docs.text:
This example walks you through adding a "Chicken Monitor" button to your dashboard and an automation that runs when you press it. The automation:

  • Turns the RGB LED green while it's running.
  • Messages your phone when it starts, when the temperature is reached, and when it finishes.
  • Turns the RGB LED off at the end.

Thanks to Discord user RalphP for this!

The automation has three triggers, each with its own trigger ID, and one Choose action with an option for each trigger ID. You'll build it in that order.

docs.title: Create the button
docs.text:
1. Create a new toggle helper called "Chicken Monitor". For step-by-step directions on creating a toggle helper, see this guide.

2. Edit your dashboard, add a button card, select Chicken Monitor, and then save.

docs.title: Create the automation and its triggers
docs.text:
Next, you'll create the automation and add its three triggers, each with its own trigger ID.

3. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation.

4. Click Add trigger → Entity → State and search for "Chicken Monitor". In the box labeled To, select On.

5. Create a trigger ID for this trigger called "Chicken Monitor On".

6. Click Add trigger → Entity → State and search for "Chicken Monitor". In the box labeled To, select Off. Create a trigger ID for this trigger called "Chicken Monitor Off".

7. Click Add trigger → Entity → Numeric state and search for your TEMP-1 food probe entity, such as "temp-1 food probe". In the box labeled Above, type the temperature you want for your food. This example uses 160°F (71.1°C), because the chicken will rest and reach 165°F once it's removed from the oven or grill.

8. Create a trigger ID for this trigger called "Temp Reached".

docs.title: Option 1: Monitoring starts
docs.text:
Option 1 runs when you turn Chicken Monitor on. It turns the LED green and tells your phone that monitoring has started.

9. Click Add action, search "choose", and select it.

10. Under Option 1, select Add condition, search "trigger id", and select Triggered by.

11. Check State changed to on, the first trigger in the list. It's the trigger you gave the Chicken Monitor On ID in step 5.

12. Still under Option 1 in the Choose action, click Add action, search "light", and select Light: Turn on.

13. Click Choose entity and search for your device, such as "TEMP-1 RGB Light".

14. Click Advanced options, check the box for Color name, then select a color from the drop-down, such as Green.

15. Still under Option 1 in the Choose action, click Add action, search "mobile", and select your phone in the list.

16. Write a custom title and message. The message is required, but the title is not.

17. Check your work. When you're done with this part, Option 1 looks like this:

docs.title: Option 2: Temperature reached
docs.text:
Option 2 runs when the food probe reaches your temperature. It blinks the LED until you turn Chicken Monitor off, and messages your phone.

18. Click Add option at the bottom. Under Option 2, select Add condition, search "trigger id", and select Triggered by.

19. Check Temp Reached, the trigger ID you created in step 8.

20. Still under Option 2 in the Choose action, click Add action, search "repeat", and select Until in the drop-down.

21. Under Until conditions, select Add condition and search "state".

22. Type "Chicken Monitor" and select it, then select Off in the drop-down for the state of the sensor.

23. Click Add action under the Until condition you just created. Be very careful to select the correct Add action button, as shown below.

24. Search "light toggle" in the search bar, then select Choose entity and select the RGB LED for your device.

25. Go down to Add action under Option 2, search "mobile", and select your phone, as you did in step 15. Give it a message and a title, as shown below.

26. (Optional) Add another action here to speak out loud on your smart speakers, such as HomePods. Click Add action and search "TTS". This requires you to have Piper and a few other things already set up.

docs.title: Option 3: Monitoring stops
docs.text:
Option 3 runs when you turn Chicken Monitor off. It turns the LED off and tells your phone that monitoring has stopped.

27. Click Add option (this is now Option 3). Select Add condition, search "triggered by", and choose the "Chicken Monitor Off" trigger ID you created in step 6.

28. Still under Option 3 in the Choose action, click Add action, search "light", and select Light: Turn off.

29. Click Choose entity and search for your device, such as "TEMP-1 RGB Light".

30. Click Add action, search "mobile" as you did above, and select your phone. Give it an optional title and message, as shown below.

31. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and save it.

You now have one automation that ties together the button you created in the dashboard and alerts you when your chicken is almost done, with a phone notification, a blinking green LED, and an optional TTS notification on your smart speakers. Thanks again to Discord user RalphP for this example!

docs.title: Use cases for the TEMP-1
docs.text:
1. Monitoring fridge / freezer: There are settings to set the maximum temperature the sensor should reach. It can alert through the onboard buzzer if it rises above that temperature. The cable on the probe is flat to not interfere with fridge seals.

2. Monitoring fish tank, hot tub ( if covered ), pool ( if covered or in sealed box ) with the waterproof probe.

3. Monitoring grilling, baking, or other food activities with the food safe probe

docs.title: Prevent Sleep
docs.text:
Put your sensors to sleep!

All of our battery powered devices are able to go to sleep to save battery life. Our non-battery sensor devices like the AIR-1 and PLT-1 can also sleep to get better temperature and humidity measurements.

The temperature offsets needed will be much lower for your sensors as the microcontroller will not put off as much heat when it is sleeping and then waking for short periods to report the sensor values.

You'll set how long your sensor sleeps, then turn off Prevent Sleep so it can start sleeping.

1. Head to the ESPHome Integrations page.

2. Click on the name "1 device" below your Apollo device's name.

3. Scroll down until you see "Prevent Sleep" and "Sleep Duration".

4. Type in the amount of minutes you want your sensor to sleep in the "Sleep Duration" box. Defaults to 8 minutes.

Read this before turning off Prevent Sleep!

When "Prevent Sleep" is toggled off, your sensor will immediately begin sleeping. Please make sure you are ready to make this sensor sleep before toggling off prevent sleep.

5. When you are ready, toggle off "Prevent Sleep" and your sensor will go to sleep. It will wake up every 8 minutes, or on the interval you set in step 4. If you need to keep your sensor awake, head to our OTA Awake helper tutorial!

6. You can wake your sensor by following this guide or you can power cycle your device. If there is a battery in it, the battery will need to be removed or the reset button pressed.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The TEMP-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your TEMP-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: How to change the temperature probe update interval
How to change the temperature probe update interval
docs.text:
By default the TEMP-1 reports its Temperature Probe every 60 seconds. You can make it report faster, such as every 10 seconds, by overriding the sensor's YAML in the ESPHome Builder. This is useful for smoother graphs or quicker reactions when you are watching a fridge, freezer, fish tank, or hot tub.

This controls reporting while your TEMP-1 is awake

The update interval only changes how often the probe reports while the device is awake. If you turn Prevent Sleep off, the TEMP-1 deep-sleeps between wake cycles and reports when it wakes instead. See Sensor Definitions for how sleep and reporting work together. You can go as low as 1s, but every reading is written to Home Assistant, so a 1 second interval floods your database and grows it quickly.

1. Select the ESPHome Builder in the sidebar then click "EDIT" on your TEMP-1. If it isn't in your sidebar, the button below opens the app.

2. Paste this YAML below your device's existing config. The !extend keyword edits the probe that is already defined in the firmware, so you only need the lines you want to change.

Start on a fresh line with no spaces in front

The sensor: line has to start at the very beginning of a new line. If you press Enter from the end of the wifi_password line, the editor indents your cursor one space, which makes the YAML invalid. The fix is to press Enter twice, then Backspace once. That drops you to a fresh line with no leading space.

sensor:
  - platform: dallas_temp
    id: !extend temp_probe
    update_interval: 10s

3. In the top right click "SAVE" and then "INSTALL". When the install options appear, choose "On the network".

4. Once you see the logs showing the new update interval of 10 seconds the flash has succeeded and you can click "STOP" to exit.

Your Temperature Probe will now report at the new interval.

docs.title: Report only when the temperature changes
docs.text:
A fast interval reacts quickly, but it also writes every single reading to Home Assistant and grows your database fast. If you want a quick response without that flood, read the probe often and only report when the temperature actually moves. ESPHome's delta filter does this: it reads on your interval but only sends a value when it differs enough from the last one it reported.

The threshold is in the probe's native unit, Celsius. 0.5 means 0.5°C, which is roughly 0.9°F.

Intermediate: report on a threshold jumpAdvanced: threshold jump plus a heartbeat

This reads the probe every second but only reports when the reading moves at least 0.5°C from the last value it sent. Steady temperatures stay quiet, and a real change shows up within about a second.

sensor:
  - platform: dallas_temp
    id: !extend temp_probe
    update_interval: 1s
    filters:
      - delta: 0.5

To think in percentages instead, pass a string with a %. The probe then reports when the reading changes by that much from the last value.

    filters:
      - delta: 5%

The delta filter on its own can stay silent for a long time when the temperature is stable, which can look like the probe stopped working. Wrapping it in or with a heartbeat guarantees at least one reading on a slower schedule, on top of any threshold reports.

sensor:
  - platform: dallas_temp
    id: !extend temp_probe
    update_interval: 1s
    filters:
      - or:
          - delta: 0.5
          - heartbeat: 60s

This reports the moment the temperature moves 0.5°C, and otherwise sends a reading once a minute so you always know the probe is alive.

1 second is about as fast as the probe can go

The DS18B20 probe needs around 750 ms to take a full-resolution reading, so 1s is close to its limit. If you see missed or blank readings, raise the interval to 2s.

Make sure the right probe is selected

The Temperature Probe only reads when Select Probe is set to Temperature. If it is set to Food, the probe reports nothing regardless of the update interval.

docs.title: TEMP-1 general tips
docs.text: The TEMP-1 has an optional Dallas temperature probe (long or short variants) and an optional food-safe probe.

docs.title: Physical buffered temperature
docs.text: For accurate vaccine storage monitoring, the CDC recommends using buffered temperature probes, a principle the Dallas temperature probe can follow using a glycol or glass bead vial. Buffering mimics the thermal behavior of stored vaccines, filtering out brief air temp fluctuations (e.g., door openings) that don’t reflect true vaccine exposure. This results in more reliable, regulation-aligned readings when using Dallas sensors like the DS18B20 in a buffered medium. You can also achieve better results by placing the probe inside a bottle of water (for the fridge not freezer).

docs.title: Virtual temperature buffering
docs.text: Instead of placing your Dallas temperature probe (like a DS18B20) in a vial of glycol or glass beads to mimic how vaccines warm up or cool down, you can use a software method called Virtual Temperature Buffering. It filters out quick air temperature changes (like when you open the fridge door) and gives a more stable, realistic reading similar to a physical buffer. This means you get accurate, regulation-friendly temps without needing messy liquids or bulky containers.

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your TEMP-1. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The Default Update column is how often each sensor refreshes while the TEMP-1 is awake. By default Prevent Sleep is on, so the device stays awake and reports continuously at these intervals. Turn Prevent Sleep off to let the TEMP-1 deep-sleep between readings for more accurate onboard AHT20 temperature and humidity (the ESP chip's heat skews them while it is awake); it then wakes for about 90 seconds, reports, and sleeps for the Sleep Duration.

To update firmware on a sleeping device, click Update on the Firmware Update entity and it installs the next time the device wakes (the firmware keeps itself awake until the update finishes, so you don't need to do anything else). The optional OTA helper is a separate toggle that overrides Prevent Sleep to keep a device awake on demand.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light One RGB Neopixel LED. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Alarm Outside Temp Range Sounds the onboard buzzer when the selected probe reads outside the Min Probe Temp to Max Probe Temp range. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Defaults to off. Select Probe Chooses which probe the TEMP-1 reads: Temperature (the Dallas DS18B20 probe, available in long or short versions) or Food (the stainless steel, food-safe probe for grilling and cooking). Sensor Default Update Details Board Temperature 60s Onboard air temperature from the AHT20. Adjusted by the Board Temperature Offset. Board Humidity 60s Onboard relative humidity from the AHT20. Adjusted by the Board Humidity Offset. Temperature Probe 60s Reading from the Dallas DS18B20 probe. Active when Select Probe is set to Temperature. Adjusted by the Temp Probe Offset. Ideal for fridge/freezer and aquatic monitoring. Food Probe 3s Reading from the stainless steel, food-safe NTC probe. Active when Select Probe is set to Food. Adjusted by the Food Probe Offset. Designed for grilling, baking, and other cooking. Temperature Probe 2 60s Second Dallas DS18B20 probe on the one-wire bus. Disabled by default. Temperature Probe 3 60s Third Dallas DS18B20 probe on the one-wire bus. Disabled by default. Temperature Probe 4 60s Fourth Dallas DS18B20 probe on the one-wire bus. Disabled by default. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Board Temperature Offset 0.0 °C Calibrates the Board Temperature reading to a known value. Range is -70 to +70 °C. Board Humidity Offset 0 % Calibrates the Board Humidity reading to a known value. Range is -70 to +70 %. Temp Probe Offset 0.0 °C Calibrates the Temperature Probe reading to a known value. Range is -70 to +70 °C. Disabled by default. Food Probe Offset 0.0 °C Calibrates the Food Probe reading to a known value. Range is -70 to +70 °C. Disabled by default. Max Probe Temp 125.0 °C Upper threshold for the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Min Probe Temp -55.0 °C Lower threshold for the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Probe Temp Difference Threshold 0.0 °C Temperature change that triggers a report when Notify Only Outside Temp Difference is on. Disabled by default. Notify Only Outside Temp Difference Off Wakes the device to report only when the probe temperature changes by more than the Probe Temp Difference Threshold, instead of every wake cycle. Disabled by default. Sleep Duration 8 min How long the TEMP-1 stays in deep sleep between wake cycles (only used when Prevent Sleep is off). Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it reports continuously. Turn it off to let the TEMP-1 deep-sleep between readings for more accurate onboard AHT20 temperature and humidity. Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the TEMP-1 in boot mode
Putting the TEMP-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the TEMP-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You can put your device into boot mode with only the boot button and a paperclip.

1. Position the TEMP-1 so that the USB-C port is facing you. On the right side of the device, locate a small opening where you can use a paperclip to press the boot button.

If you prefer, please remove the lid by gently prying up on the small slit by the top of the case.

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your TEMP-1 then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You can also open the case and put your device into boot mode by holding the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and remove the case as shown in the images above

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your TEMP-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (labeled BOOT, shown above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (labeled RST, shown below).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the TEMP-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash TEMP-1
docs.text:
If your Apollo TEMP-1 becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods, you can reflash the factory firmware by following this guide.

Before you start

  • Use Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium-based browser. The installer needs one of them.
  • If your TEMP-1 has already been connected to Home Assistant, remove it from the ESPHome integration and the ESPHome Device Builder before continuing.

Follow these steps to put your TEMP-1 in boot mode, flash the factory firmware from the installer page, and set it up again.

1. Put your TEMP-1 in boot mode: hold down the boot button, then plug in the USB cable.

2. Open the Apollo TEMP-1 installer page.

3. Choose USB Power, then click Connect & Install. USB Power is the right choice because you're using a TEMP-1.

Use R2 unless support tells you to use R1

The Apollo installer installs the Revision 2 (R2) firmware. R2 is what all of our devices use, except a very small batch of TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B boards. Support will tell you if yours needs Revision 1 (R1). If it does, click Connect under Non Battery Firmware Revision 1 on the classic TEMP-1 installer instead. In the next steps, the firmware option is named Install ApolloAutomation.TEMP-1.

4. In the browser's serial port pop-up, select the open COM port (USB JTAG/serial debug unit in the screenshot below), then click Connect.

5. Click Install Apollo.TEMP-1_R2.

6. Click INSTALL.

7. When the installer shows Installation complete!, the flash is finished. Click Next, then close the browser window.

Power cycle your TEMP-1 before doing anything else

Your TEMP-1 is still in boot mode. Remove its power by unplugging the USB cable, then plug it back in so it starts in normal mode.

8. Go to the getting started guide and set up your TEMP-1 as a new device.

Once it's set up, your TEMP-1 is back on its factory firmware and ready to use.

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your TEMP-1
docs.text:
You can clear the Wi-Fi details saved on your device and connect it to a new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo TEMP1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: TEMP-1B FAQ
docs.text:
1.How is the TEMP-1B powered?

  • The TEMP-1B operates with a rechargeable 16340 Flat Top battery (not included), giving it portability for temp monitoring without being tied to an outlet.

2. How long does the battery last in the TEMP-1B?

  • Battery life depends on sleep/wake intervals. Waking every 12 hours provides around 6+ months of battery life.

3. Can you charge the battery by plugging in the device?

  • No, you cannot charge the battery through the USB port. You need a separate 16340 charger such as a nitecore 2 or 4 bay.

4. Can the TEMP-1B be powered by USB-C instead of battery?

  • Yes. The USB-C port can power the device directly (5V, 1A or less). When USB-C is connected, the 16340 battery acts as a backup and keeps the TEMP-1B running if power is lost.

5. What are the Optional Probe Addons?

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.
  • 1m (~3ft) Stainless Steel Food-Safe Probe (NTC): Max 350°C (662°F). Perfect for grilling, baking, and food prep (not dishwasher safe).

6. Is the TEMP-1B weatherproof? Can I use it outdoors?

  • The TEMP-1B is primarily designed for indoor use, but the waterproof DS18B20 temperature probes are suited for harsh conditions. The main body is not rated for outdoor use without additional protection.

7. How does the TEMP-1B connect to Home Assistant?

  • The TEMP-1B connects via Wi-Fi to ESPHome on Home Assistant, enabling data monitoring, automations, and alerts directly within Home Assistant.

8. How often does the TEMP-1B send sensor data?

  • The TEMP-1B’s reporting frequency is adjustable in ESPHome but most things default to 60 seconds. You can set it for frequent updates or extend intervals to conserve battery life.

9. Can I customize the TEMP-1B’s functionality?

  • Absolutely! With ESPHome, users can modify firmware, settings, and even print custom cases for the TEMP-1B. Our YAML is on GitHub and our .STEP and .STL CAD files are available for community use.

10. What are the RGB LED and piezo buzzer used for?

  • The RGB LED provides visual alerts, while the piezo buzzer offers audio notifications for events like a probe temperature going above or below the range you set.

11. Is the TEMP-1B compatible with other smart home platforms?

  • While designed for Home Assistant via ESPHome, it may be compatible with other platforms using the ESPHome API or MQTT.

12. Do I need coding knowledge to use the TEMP-1B?

  • Basic knowledge of Home Assistant and ESPHome is helpful, but most users can utilize it out of the box. For advanced customization, YAML knowledge is recommended.

13. Can I access data from the TEMP-1B remotely?

  • Yes, you can access sensor data remotely via the Home Assistant dashboard if your setup is configured for remote access.

14. What’s the difference between the battery and non-battery versions?

  • The TEMP-1B runs on a 16340 battery (or USB-C) and is slightly larger, while the non-battery TEMP-1 is compact and requires USB-C power at 5 volts using 1 amp or less (5W). They both have the same AHT20 air temperature/humidity sensor, RGB LED, piezo buzzer, and 3.5mm probe port.

15. Can I use multiple TEMP-1B sensors in one Home Assistant setup?

  • Yes, you can add multiple TEMP-1B sensors, each appearing as a separate device, for comprehensive monitoring across multiple fridges, freezers, rooms, or other spaces.

16. Can I use an extender to make the TEMP-1 temp probe cable longer?

  • Yes, you can, however at some point you will begin getting "voltage drop" and likely run into issues with bad data from the probe. We suggest 1.5 meters or less!

17. Can I use the probe in a salt water tank?

  • Yes, however a very high concentration of salt will likely eventually lead to corrosion and should be checked from time to time. The stainless steel used is "SS304" grade.

18. What is the wiring for the 3.5mm temp probe?

  • Tip is 3.3V, ring is data, and sleeve is GND. See the temp probe pinout for a picture.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The TEMP-1B (16340 battery) can be used with an optional temperature probe which comes in two lengths or a food safe grill probe. The TEMP-1B itself can be used with an optional magnetic mount to mount it to a fridge, grill, or other surface while taking measurements. It also features an AHT20-F air temperature and humidity sensor, which includes dust protection, an RGB LED, and a piezo buzzer.

Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20): -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.
  • 1m (~3ft) Stainless Steel Food-Safe Probe (NTC): Max 350°C (662°F). Perfect for grilling, baking, and food prep (not dishwasher safe).

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The TEMP-1B should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your TEMP-1B if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: TEMP-1B Bluetooth proxy
docs.text:
This guide shows you how to make your Apollo device act as a "BLE Proxy" which lets Bluetooth devices talk back to Home Assistant using Apollo devices as the "next hop"!

Select a method below. Method 1 switches your TEMP-1B to the prebuilt TEMP-1B_BLE.yaml firmware. Method 2 adds the BLE proxy yaml to your existing config by hand.

Method 1: TEMP-1B_BLE.yaml firmwareMethod 2: Manually enter the BLE proxy yaml

You'll swap your device's firmware package for its prebuilt Bluetooth proxy version in ESPHome Device Builder, then install it over the network.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Find your device and click Edit.

3. Replace the packages: line and the line directly below it with the code below.

packages:
  ApolloAutomation.TEMP-1:
    url: https://github.com/ApolloAutomation/TEMP-1
    ref: main
    files: [Integrations/ESPHome/TEMP-1B_BLE_R2.yaml]
    refresh: 1min

4. Click Save then Install in the bottom right. Click On the network when prompted.

5. When you see the purple lines the device has booted successfully and the logs will show the Bluetooth Proxy section. Click Stop in the bottom right and you're finished!

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

The easiest way is to let ESPHome Device Builder add the component for you. You can also paste the single line by hand.

1. Open the ESPHome Device Builder app from your Home Assistant sidebar and click Edit on your device. The button below opens the app's page, or offers to install it if you don't have it yet. Click Open Web UI there to reach your devices.

2. Click Add Component in the editor toolbar, search for Bluetooth Proxy, and click Add.

Device Builder drops a single line into your config:

bluetooth_proxy:

That's all it needs. Active connections are on by default, and bluetooth_proxy automatically pulls in the ESP32 BLE Tracker it depends on, so there's nothing else to add. Prefer to type it? Paste that one line at the top level of your YAML instead of using Add Component.

3. Click Save, then Install, and choose On the Network to flash the new firmware over Wi-Fi.

Verify it works

Once the device reboots, Home Assistant picks it up as a Bluetooth proxy automatically. Open the Bluetooth advertisement monitor with the button below to watch nearby BLE devices roll in through it. Anything that shows up is ready to add under Settings → Devices & Services → Bluetooth like any other device.

docs.title: Prevent Sleep
docs.text:
Put your sensors to sleep!

All of our battery powered devices are able to go to sleep to save battery life. Our non-battery sensor devices like the AIR-1 and PLT-1 can also sleep to get better temperature and humidity measurements.

The temperature offsets needed will be much lower for your sensors as the microcontroller will not put off as much heat when it is sleeping and then waking for short periods to report the sensor values.

You'll set how long your sensor sleeps, then turn off Prevent Sleep so it can start sleeping.

1. Head to the ESPHome Integrations page and click on the name of your Apollo device.

2. Scroll down until you see Prevent Sleep and Sleep Duration.

3. Type in how long you want your sensor to sleep in the Sleep Duration box. Check the unit next to the box: it is minutes on the AIR-1 (default 5), PLT-1 (default 5), and TEMP-1 (default 8), and hours on the BTN-1 (default 24), PLT-1B (default 12), and TEMP-1B (default 12). We recommend leaving the default values.

Read this before turning off Prevent Sleep!

When "Prevent Sleep" is toggled off, your sensor will immediately begin sleeping. Please make sure you are ready to make this sensor sleep before toggling off prevent sleep.

4. When you are ready, toggle off Prevent Sleep and your sensor will go to sleep. It will wake up on the Sleep Duration interval from step 3. If you need to keep your sensor awake, head to our OTA Awake helper tutorial!

5. You can wake your sensor by following this guide or you can power cycle your device. If there is a battery in it, the battery will need to be removed or the reset button pressed.

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The AIR-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your AIR-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.text:
The TEMP-1B comes with an optional food probe which can be used to monitor food temperatures when baking, grilling, etc. It includes a heat-resistant cable but the TEMP-1B itself needs to stay in a cool environment.

1. To use your food probe, take it out of the package and insert it into the 3.5mm port on your TEMP-1B.

2. Once inserted, proceed to step 3 unless you have a battery in it

If you are using it with a battery you need to push the reset button.

The TEMP-1B looks for the food probe when it boots and if it is not there then the sensor is marked as failed and will not work properly in Home Assistant. You need to click the reset button if you have a battery in it or power cycle your TEMP-1B to make it reliably use the new food temperature probe.

3. Go to the device page of your TEMP-1B in Home Assistant (Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome) and choose probe "Food".

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The TEMP-1B should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your TEMP-1B if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain.

docs.title: TEMP-1 multi-probe splitter guide

The TEMP-1 comes with an optional 3.5mm Multi-Probe Splitter which can be used to monitor a fridge, freezer, fish tank, pool, hot tub, etc with up to 4 probes.

Firmware version 25.11.20.1 or newer required for TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B

The multi probe support was added in November of 2025. If you are using an old TEMP-1 or TEMP-1B that hasn't been updated then please visit our reflashing guide for the TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B. Alternatively you can update your devices following this guide!

1. To use your TEMP-1 Multi-Probe Splitter gently plug it into the 3.5mm port on your device.

2. Plug in your long or short temp probes into the Multi-Probe Splitter.

Power on your TEMP-1 after plugging in all of your probes!

The TEMP-1 will look for the probes at boot and mark them failed if you power on and plug in the probes after. Power cycle your device and they should show up!

3. Go to the device page of your TEMP-1 in Home Assistant and confirm the Temperature Probe is selected from the dropdown.

4. Enable the disabled 3rd and 4th temp probe entities if you have more than 2 probes!

5. Once completed you will see all four probes updating the temperature!

6. To rename the probes you can edit each probe and choose a unique name such as "Fridge Probe" and "Freezer Probe" as shown below!

docs.title: Keep Your Sensor Awake With HA Helper
Keep your sensor awake with a Home Assistant helper
docs.text:
When an apollo_ota_mode toggle in Home Assistant is on, your Apollo battery devices stay awake so you can update them. In this guide you create that toggle, then add an automation that turns it off again after one hour.

This keeps every Apollo device awake

While apollo_ota_mode is on, none of your Apollo devices go back to sleep. Finish the second part of this guide to create an automation that turns the helper off after it has been on for one hour.

docs.title: Create the OTA mode toggle
docs.text:
Start by creating the toggle helper and switching it on.

1. Go to Settings → Devices & services and select the Helpers tab at the top. Or use the button below to go straight there.

2. Select Create helper in the bottom right.

3. Scroll to the bottom of the list and select Toggle.

4. Name the toggle apollo_ota_mode, choose an icon such as mdi:sleep-off, and click Create.

5. Search the helpers list for apollo_ota_mode and click the helper that appears.

6. Switch the toggle on.

OTA mode is now on. The next time your Apollo device reboots or wakes up on its wake timer, it stays awake instead of going back to sleep.

docs.title: Turn OTA mode off after one hour
docs.text:
Next, create an automation that switches apollo_ota_mode off once it has been on for one hour, so you never leave your devices awake by accident.

1. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes and click Create automation.

2. Click Add trigger, then select Entity.

3. Select State.

4. In the Entity box, enter apollo_ota_mode. Set To to On, and enter 1 in the hours box under For. This trigger fires once apollo_ota_mode has been on for one hour.

5. Scroll down to Then do, click Add action, search for input boolean, and choose Input boolean: Turn off.

6. Click Choose entity and select apollo_ota_mode.

You're done. Turn apollo_ota_mode on whenever you want to update your devices, and the automation turns it off for you after one hour.
