docs.title: How To Wake Up Your Sensor
docs.text:
To wake a sleeping Apollo battery sensor, press the reset button. A BTN-1 also wakes when you press Button 1, 2, 3, or 4, and an H-1 or H-2 wakes when you press a gold song button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping device. Select your device below for the button locations.

TEMP-1BPLT-1BBTN-1H-1H-2

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping TEMP-1B. Once the TEMP-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: TEMP-1B boot mode.

Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Boot button. The boot button can't wake a sleeping PLT-1B. Once the PLT-1B is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: PLT-1B boot mode.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Buttons 1 to 4. Press and release Button 1, 2, 3, or 4. Home Assistant receives that press as a click of that button once the BTN-1 reconnects, so any automation you've tied to a click of that button runs. Use the reset button when you only want to wake it.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping BTN-1. Once the BTN-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: BTN-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-1 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset button to restart the device.

Method 2: Gold button. Press and release the gold button (SW1).

The boot button can't wake a sleeping H-1. Once the H-1 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

The unlabeled circled button at the lower left is the gold button (SW1), which plays the built-in songs.

Button locations: H-1 boot mode.

Smart firmware only

The H-2 only sleeps when running the smart firmware. These steps apply when it is running that firmware.

Method 1: Reset button. Press and release the reset (left) button to restart the device.

Method 2: Song buttons. Press and release any of the four gold song buttons on the back of the H-2. The H-2 wakes and plays that button's song.

The boot (right) button can't wake a sleeping H-2. Once the H-2 is awake, you can use the boot button to keep it awake, as described below.

Button locations: H-2 boot mode.

Your device is now awake, but it will not stay awake on its own yet. Click the Prevent Sleep button on your device page in Home Assistant, or directly on the device web server such as plt-1.local or its IP address.

You can also turn on Prevent Sleep from the device itself. Once it's awake, press and hold the boot button for 4-5 seconds, then let go.

Watch how you use the boot button

Press the boot button only after the device has restarted. Holding it while you press reset puts the device in boot mode for flashing firmware instead. Holding it for 10 seconds or more resets the device to factory settings and erases its Wi-Fi.

Head to the awake helper wiki article

If you need to keep your sensor awake for extended periods of time we suggest using our OTA awake helper.

docs.title: Hot water recirculation with TEMP-1
docs.text:
Running this on a TEMP-1B

This loop needs the probe reporting every few seconds, so it has to stay powered. Run your TEMP-1B on USB power with Prevent Sleep turned on, or use a mains-powered TEMP-1. On battery with deep sleep, it can't react fast enough to switch the valve in time.

Contributed by Donovan

Big thanks to Donovan for building this and sharing his whole setup, automations included, so we could package it up as the blueprint below.

There are two normal ways to get hot water at a sink, and each has a catch. A small under-sink tank gives you instant hot water with very little energy, but it runs out after a gallon or two. The main house water heater never runs out, but you either wait while cold water runs down the drain, or you get a cold-water sandwich when the tank water hands off to the line water.

Donovan's setup uses an Apollo TEMP-1 to get both. Small draws come from a 2.5 gallon Bosch mini tank. When he knows he needs more, a button starts a recirculation loop that pulls hot water up from the house heater without running the tap, and the TEMP-1 tells Home Assistant the moment that line is hot enough to switch over. No water goes down the drain, and there is no cold-water sandwich.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The TEMP-1 probe is zip-tied to the hot-water angle stop, so it reads the temperature of the hot line coming from the house heater. Everything else, the Bosch tank, the circulator pump, the motorized valve, and the TEMP-1 itself, plugs into a Kasa smart power strip that Home Assistant controls.

  1. Idle. The 3-way valve is unpowered, so the sinks are fed by the Bosch mini tank. Instant hot water, low energy.
  2. Request hot water. Donovan presses an Aqara Zigbee button when he knows he'll use more than a gallon or two.
  3. Recirculate. Home Assistant switches the circulator pump on. It pumps the cooled water from the hot line back into the cold line, pulling fresh hot water up from the house heater. Nothing runs down the drain.
  4. Watch the line. The TEMP-1 reports the angle-stop temperature every few seconds. The pump also has its own temperature sensor, and the smart strip watches its energy use, so the system knows when the pump finishes.
  5. Switch over. Once the line is hot, Home Assistant powers the valve so the sinks draw from the house heater, and shuts the pump outlet off so it won't run again when the water cools. Alexa announces "The hot water is ready."
  6. Revert. When the TEMP-1 sees the line drop below a set temperature, Home Assistant cuts power to the valve. A capacitor inside the valve stores just enough energy to rotate it back, so the sinks return to the Bosch tank.

docs.title: Physical layout
docs.text: Here's the real thing under Donovan's sink: the Bosch mini tank with the smart strip on top, the 3-way valve strapped to the wall behind it, and the circulator pump bolted to the floor on the right.

docs.title: Control logic
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IDLE["Idle:<br/>Bosch feeds the sinks<br/>(valve off)"]
    PUMP["Pump ON:<br/>recirculate the wall loop,<br/>no water wasted"]
    Q1{"Wall line<br/>up to temp?"}
    WALL["Valve powered:<br/>house heater feeds the sinks<br/>(Alexa: hot water ready)"]
    Q2{"Wall line<br/>cooled off?"}

    IDLE -->|press Aqara button| PUMP --> Q1
    Q1 -->|no| PUMP
    Q1 -->|yes| WALL --> Q2
    Q2 -->|no| WALL
    Q2 -->|"yes: valve off, back to Bosch"| IDLE

    classDef bosch fill:#4379AA,stroke:#2d5a8a,color:#fff;
    classDef wall fill:#d64545,stroke:#a83232,color:#fff;
    classDef temp fill:#2e7d46,stroke:#1f5630,color:#fff;
    class IDLE bosch;
    class WALL wall;
    class Q1,Q2 temp;

docs.title: Parts
docs.text: Part Role in the loop Apollo TEMP-1 + short temperature probe Reads the hot line at the angle stop and reports it to Home Assistant Bosch ES2.5 mini tank (2.5 gal, 120 V) Instant hot water for small draws AquaMotion AMH3K-7N circulator pump Recirculates the loop to pull hot water up from the house heater US Solid 1/2" 3-way L-type motorized ball valve Selects the hot source: unpowered feeds the Bosch, powered feeds the house heater Smart plugs with power monitoring (we suggest Zooz Z-Wave, like the ZEN04; Donovan used a TP-Link Kasa strip) Switch the pump and valve, and report the pump's power so Home Assistant knows when it finishes Aqara wireless mini switch (Zigbee) The "I want hot water" button Alexa speaker Announces when the line is ready

docs.title: TEMP-1 configuration
docs.text:
For this to react quickly, the probe needs to report faster than its 60 second default. Donovan reports it every 3 seconds and keeps a 60 second heartbeat, so Home Assistant reacts fast while you can still tell at a glance that the probe is alive. Two guards keep the data clean: the 85.0 reading a DS18B20 sends at power-on is dropped, and readings are ignored when the Select Probe option is set to Food.

The probe zip-ties straight onto the hot-water angle stop, so it reads the line coming from the house heater.

For the full walkthrough of overriding probe YAML in the ESPHome Builder, including the simpler delta-plus-heartbeat pattern, see How To Change The Temperature Probe Update Interval.

sensor:
  - platform: dallas_temp
    id: !extend temp_probe
    update_interval: 3s
    filters:
      - lambda: |-
          if (isnan(x)) {
            return NAN;
          }
          if (x == 85.0) {
              return NAN;
          }
          auto selected_probe = id(temp_probe_select).current_option();
          if (selected_probe == "Food") {
            return NAN;
          }
          return x - id(dallas_temperature_offset).state;
      - or:
          - delta: 1.1    # ~2°F; change to 2.0 for 2°C (~3.6°F) instead
          - heartbeat: 60s

docs.title: Set it up in Home Assistant
docs.text:
Donovan's whole system is one blueprint. Import it, pick your entities, set your temperatures, and save. There are no helpers to create and no automations to copy and rename.

Before you import

Two things need to be in place: your TEMP-1 probe should report quickly (see TEMP-1 configuration above), and your pump and valve should be on smart plugs Home Assistant can switch, with power monitoring on the pump.

docs.title: Import the blueprint
docs.text:
1. Click the button below, then click Open link.

2. Click Preview, then Import blueprint.

3. Click Apollo Automation Hot Water Recirculation (TEMP-1), create an automation from it, and fill in the inputs below.

docs.title: What you'll fill in
docs.text:
Input What to pick Start trigger The press that starts a cycle, like your Aqara button's single click. Pick it from the trigger editor like any automation. You can add more than one (see the tip below). Circulator pump plug The smart plug powering the pump. Circulator pump power That plug's power (W) sensor, how the system knows the pump has finished. 3-way valve plug The smart plug powering the valve. Hot line temperature (TEMP-1) Your TEMP-1 probe. Activate / Return temperature When to switch to the house heater, and when to revert. Both default to 90 °F. Pump finished below (W) The power level that means the pump's thermostat cut the motor. Default 20 W. Pump / Valve safety timeout Backstops that force the pump and valve off if a signal is missed. Default 5 and 60 minutes. Actions when the water is ready Optional. Runs the moment the valve opens: announce on a speaker, turn on the shower fan, flash a light.

Starting by button, voice, or dashboard

The blueprint runs a cycle whenever the Start trigger fires, so it works with whatever you give it. Add your button's single-press for the physical button. To also start from a dashboard tap or a voice assistant (Donovan uses a Nabu Casa voice command), add a second trigger: your pump plug turning on. Then tapping that plug on a card, or saying "turn on the circulator," kicks off the whole cycle.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Both temperatures default to 90 °F. The probe reads the outside of the angle stop through a zip-tie, so it lags the water by a few degrees. Nudge Activate up if the valve flips before the water is genuinely hot, or down if you're left waiting.

Pump finished below should sit under the pump's running draw but above its standby. 20 W suits the AquaMotion AMH3K; check yours on the plug's power sensor.

The two safety timeouts are backstops. If a signal is ever missed, the pump and valve still shut themselves off, so the 5 and 60 minute defaults are deliberately generous.

Donovan's extras

Donovan also flashes the shower lights as a silent "ready" cue, and ties his shower exhaust fan into a Moen Flo that switches it off once the shower's water stops. Both drop straight into the Actions when the water is ready slot, alongside (or instead of) the spoken announcement.

docs.title: TEMP-1B alert outside temp range example
TEMP-1B alert outside temp range example
docs.text:
This will guide you through how to set up the built in alarm using the temperature probe in your freezer!

1. Place the temperature probe into your freezer (not the entire TEMP-1B, just the probe!) and then wait for it to normalize around 0 degrees F aka -18C.

2. Once normalized, look at the graph and determine a good value to set for both the maximum and minimum temperatures. My mini freezer seems to max out at 30F so I would want to go slightly above that range. However, in most freezers they should NOT reach above 0F so you will likely need to input a lower value than me. My minimums are around -20F.

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B graph looks the same.

3. We now need to convert F to C since the max and min temps are measured in Celsius. My new values I will input are max probe temp 2C and a min probe temp of -30C. Reminder, yours will likely be different values, especially your max probe temp.

4. Enable the "Alarm Outside Temp Range" toggle and now your TEMP-1B will play an audible alert with its buzzer when the temp thresholds are reached. If the temp goes under the min or over the max the alarm will go off

docs.title: Automation examples using a TEMP-1B
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 2

🌱 New here? Try these first:

TEMP-1B Alert Outside Temp Range Example Difficulty: Level 1

Your Apollo TEMP-1B's probes can drive Home Assistant automations. This page walks you through three of them: a freezer alert, a food probe alert, and a chicken monitor you start and stop from your dashboard.

docs.title: Freezer temperature probe example
docs.text:
Set up a Home Assistant automation that uses the temperature probe in your freezer. At the end, you'll have an automation that sends your phone a notification when the probe goes above your maximum temperature.

1. Place the temperature probe into your freezer, then wait for its reading to settle around 0°F (-18°C).

Only the probe goes in the freezer

Keep your TEMP-1B itself in a cool, dry place. Only the temp probe and its wire can withstand the temperatures in a fridge, freezer, and similar places.

2. Once the reading settles, look at the graph and pick a good value for both the maximum and the minimum temperature. In this example, the mini freezer seems to max out at 30°F, so the maximum goes slightly above that. However, most freezers should not reach above 0°F, so you'll likely need a lower maximum than this one. The minimums here are around -20°F.

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B graph looks the same.

3. Convert your maximum and minimum from °F to °C, then enter them in Max Probe Temp and Min Probe Temp. Both settings are measured in Celsius. This example uses a max probe temp of 2°C and a min probe temp of -30°C. Your values will likely be different, especially your max probe temp.

With your thresholds set, the automation is now ready to be created.

4. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation.

5. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then Numeric state, and search for your TEMP-1B temperature probe, such as "temp-1b temperature probe". In the box labeled Above, type the maximum temperature you picked in step 2. Enter the value in the unit your Home Assistant shows (°F in this example). Advanced users can skip to the YAML at the end of this section.

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP-1B entity instead.

6. Click Add Action, type "iPhone", and select your phone. If you don't see your phone, or you have an Android phone, type "notify" instead and scroll down until you find your phone in the list.

Still don't see your phone?

You need the Home Assistant mobile app installed on your phone for this step to work. If you don't have it, use another kind of notification instead, such as a TTS notification on your speakers. This could be a fun way to announce that dinner is ready!

7. Type in your message. If you want a title too, check the box for title and type it in. This example uses the message "The temperature probe on your TEMP-1B reached its max temperature and your freezer might be having issues." and the title "Check the freezer!".

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

8. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and, optionally, a description and a category.

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

You're done! Your phone now gets a notification whenever the freezer probe goes above your maximum.

YAML for advanced users

alias: Freezer Over Max Temp Automation
description: Warning for the freezer when it reaches the max temperature.
triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id:
      - sensor.apollo_temp_1b_temperature_probe
    above: 30
conditions: []
actions:
  - action: notify.mobile_app_brandons_iphone
    metadata: {}
    data:
      title: Check the freezer!
      message: >-
        The temperature probe on your TEMP-1B reached its max temperature and
        your freezer might be having issues.
mode: single

docs.title: Food probe example
docs.text:
Set up a Home Assistant automation that uses the food probe while you cook chicken (or anything else) to 165°F (73.9°C). At the end, you'll have an automation that sends your phone a notification when your food reaches that temperature.

1. Set your Max Probe Temp to 73.9°C. Max Probe Temp must be entered in Celsius, even if you use °F in the automation below.

2. Once your food is on the grill, place the food probe inside it.

Only the food probe goes on the grill

Keep your TEMP-1B itself in a cool, dry place. Only the food probe and its wire can withstand temperatures on a grill, in the oven, and similar places.

3. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation.

4. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then Numeric state, and search for your TEMP-1B device, such as "temp-1b food probe". In the box labeled Above, type the temperature you want for your food. This example uses 165°F (73.9°C), the temperature it's safe to cook chicken to. Enter the value in the unit your Home Assistant shows (°F in this example). Advanced users can skip to the YAML at the end of this section.

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP-1B entity instead.

5. Click Add Action, type "iPhone", and select your phone. If you don't see your phone, or you have an Android phone, type "notify" instead and scroll down until you find your phone in the list.

Still don't see your phone?

You need the Home Assistant mobile app installed on your phone for this step to work. If you don't have it, use another kind of notification instead, such as a TTS notification on your speakers. This could be a fun way to announce that dinner is ready!

6. Type in your message. If you want a title too, check the box for title and type it in. This example uses the message "The temperature probe on your TEMP-1B reached its max temperature and your food is ready." and the title "Check the food!".

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

7. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and, optionally, a description and a category.

You're done! Your phone now gets a notification when your food reaches its target temperature.

YAML for advanced users

alias: Food Over Max Temp Automation
description: Warning for the food when it reaches the max temperature.
triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id:
      - sensor.apollo_temp_1b_food_probe
    above: 165
conditions: []
actions:
  - action: notify.mobile_app_brandons_iphone
    metadata: {}
    data:
      title: Check the food!
      message: >-
        The temperature probe on your TEMP-1B reached its max temperature and your food is ready.
mode: single

docs.title: Cook chicken example
docs.text:
This example adds a button called "Chicken Monitor" to your dashboard, plus an automation that runs when you press it. While it runs, the RGB LED turns green. Your phone gets a message when monitoring starts, when the temperature is reached, and when monitoring finishes, and then the RGB LED turns off. Thanks to Discord user RalphP for this!

The automation has three triggers, each with its own trigger ID, and one Choose action with an option for each trigger ID:

  • Option 1 (Chicken Monitor On): turns the RGB LED green and messages your phone.
  • Option 2 (Temp Reached): toggles the RGB LED until Chicken Monitor is turned off, messages your phone, and optionally speaks on your smart speakers.
  • Option 3 (Chicken Monitor Off): turns the RGB LED off and messages your phone.

First, create the button.

1. Create a new toggle helper called "Chicken Monitor". For step-by-step directions, see creating a toggle helper.

2. Edit your dashboard, add a button card, select Chicken Monitor, and then save.

Next, create the automation and its three triggers.

3. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation.

4. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then State, and search for "Chicken Monitor". In the box labeled To, select On.

5. Create a Trigger ID for this trigger called "Chicken Monitor On".

6. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then State, and search for "Chicken Monitor". In the box labeled To, select Off. Create a Trigger ID for this trigger called "Chicken Monitor Off".

7. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then Numeric state, and search for your TEMP-1B food probe entity, such as "temp-1b food probe". In the box labeled Above, type the temperature you want for your food. This example uses 160°F (71.1°C), because the chicken will rest and reach 165°F once removed from the oven or grill.

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP-1B food probe instead.

8. Create a Trigger ID for this trigger called "Temp Reached".

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

Now add the Choose action. Option 1 runs when you turn Chicken Monitor on.

9. Click Add Action, search "choose", and select it.

10. Under Option 1, select Add Condition, search "trigger id", and select Triggered by.

11. Check State changed to on, the first trigger in the list. It's the trigger you gave the Chicken Monitor On ID in step 5.

12. While still under Option 1 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "light", and select Light: Turn on.

13. Click Choose entity and search for your device, such as "TEMP-1B RGB Light".

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP-1B RGB Light instead.

14. Click Advanced Options, check the box for Color name, and select a color from the dropdown, such as Green.

15. While still under Option 1 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "mobile", and select your phone in the list.

16. Write a custom title and message. The message is required, but the title is not.

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

17. Check your work. When you're done with this part, Option 1 looks like this:

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

Option 2 runs when the food probe reaches your target temperature.

18. Click Add Option at the bottom. Under Option 2, select Add Condition, search "trigger id", and select Triggered by.

19. Check Temp Reached, the trigger ID you created in step 8.

20. While still under Option 2 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "repeat", and select Until in the dropdown.

21. Under Until Conditions, select Add condition, then search "state".

22. Type in "Chicken Monitor" and select it, then select Off in the dropdown for the state of the sensor.

23. Click the Add Action button under the until condition you created. Be very careful to select the correct Add Action button, as shown below.

24. Search "light toggle" in the search bar, then select Choose entity and select the RGB LED for your device.

25. Go down to Add Action under Option 2, search "mobile", and select your phone as you did in step 15. Give it a message and a title, as shown below.

26. Optionally, add another action here that speaks out loud on your smart speakers, such as HomePods. Click Add Action, then search "TTS". This requires you to have Piper and a few other things already set up.

Option 3 runs when you turn Chicken Monitor off.

27. Click Add Option (this is now Option 3). Select Add Condition, search "triggered by", and then choose the "Chicken Monitor Off" trigger ID you created in step 6.

28. While still under Option 3 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "light", and select Light: Turn off.

29. Click Choose entity and search for your device, such as "TEMP-1B RGB Light".

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP-1B RGB Light instead.

30. Click Add Action, search "mobile" as you did above, and select your phone. Give it a message and, optionally, a title, as shown below.

31. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and save.

Shown on a TEMP-1; the TEMP-1B steps are the same.

You now have one automation that ties together the button you created on your dashboard and alerts you when your chicken is almost done, with a phone notification, a blinking green LED, and an optional TTS notification on your smart speakers. Thanks again to Discord user RalphP for this example!

docs.title: Use cases for the TEMP-1B
docs.text:
1. Monitoring fridge / freezer: There are settings to set the maximum temperature the sensor should reach. It can alert through the onboard buzzer if it rises above that temperature. The cable on the probe is flat to not interfere with fridge seals.

2. Monitoring fish tank, hot tub ( if covered ), pool ( if covered or in sealed box ) with the waterproof probe.

3. Monitoring grilling, baking, or other food activities with the food safe probe

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This will walk you through the process of connecting your new Apollo Automation sensor to Home Assistant through ESPHome. If at any point you get stuck, join our Discord for some help.

docs.title: Connecting through hotspot
docs.text:
To connect through the sensor's onboard hotspot follow the below:

1. Plug the sensor into a quality power brick. They require 5v and under an amp so most phone chargers will be fine. ESP devices are sensitive to power fluctuations and users have had some issues with really cheap power bricks. If your device is restarting or unavailable please try a different power brick.

2. On your phone or PC, open the Wi-Fi settings and connect to the sensor's hotspot, such as "Apollo MSR2 Hotspot". It might take a minute for the Wi-Fi network to show up.

3. Once connected it should automatically open a dashboard for your sensor

If this does not automatically open the dashboard, please open your web browser and go to http://192.168.4.1

4. Select the Wi-Fi network that you would like your sensor to connect to or scroll to the bottom and type in your Wi-Fi network then click "Save".

Tip for Mesh Wi-Fi systems or multiple Access Points

If you have multiple access points or a mesh system please manually type in your Wi-Fi network so it will join with the strongest signal!

5. Once connected, the sensor's dashboard will automatically close. You've successfully connected your sensor to your Wi-Fi.

Click here for next steps!

docs.title: Connecting with Improv via BLE
docs.text:
You connect your sensor to Wi-Fi from Home Assistant over Bluetooth, then finish adding it through ESPHome.

Pre-requirement:

Bluetooth built in such as a Raspberry Pi or at least one ESP32 BLE Proxy. If you have already followed the "Connecting through Hotspot" please skip this section.

1. Navigate to settings -> integrations then click the "ADD" button below your new Apollo device!

2. Click submit when it asks if you want to set up your new device and shows you the hostname of your device.

3. Type in your Wi-Fi name and password in the two fields.

4. Wait for it to finish, you will see the image below while it connects.

5. Click the link shown in the image below (do not click close). If the dialog is already gone, the button below opens the same ESPHome setup.

6. When successful, you will see this image appear!

docs.title: Connecting to ESPHome Device Builder
docs.text:
Skip the ESPHome Device Builder unless...

Feel free to skip to the next section by clicking here unless you need to rename your sensor or do manual edits to the yaml

You can add the ESPHome Device Builder app in Home Assistant to update your device or edit the yaml. If you don't have the ESPHome Device Builder app installed you can follow the steps here. The button below opens the app in your Home Assistant.

Make sure to fill out your Wi-Fi details in the SECRETS section by clicking on the SECRETS Image below.

# Your Wi-Fi SSID and password - keep the quotes and just replace the name and password between the quotes!
wifi_ssid: "your-wifi-ssid-here"
wifi_password: "your-wifi-pass-here"

1. Click "Show" in the top right to show your discovered devices!

2. Click the ESPHome Builder in your sidebar then click "TAKE CONTROL" for your new Apollo Device!

3. Rename your sensor here (this only renames the sensor in the ESPHome Device Compiler's Dashboard) or skip it and continue on by clicking "TAKE CONTROL" again as shown below.

4. Click "INSTALL" (DO NOT click skip!) and let your device get adopted into the ESPHome Device Builder. Please have patience as this takes a few minutes to compile and then install to your new Apollo device!

5. Once you see "INFO OTA successful" you are done. Click "STOP" to exit.

6. Your new device is now adopted into the ESPHome Device Builder and you can move on to Integrating with Home Assistant via the ESPHome Integration below!

docs.title: Connecting to Home Assistant via ESPHome integration:
docs.text:
Next, you add your new Apollo device to Home Assistant through the ESPHome integration.

1. Click the "Notifications" Icon in the bottom left.

2. Click "Check it out" to go to the integrations page and see the new device that was found.

3. Click "ADD" to begin adding the device to Home Assistant.

4. Click "SUBMIT" to confirm you want to add your new Apollo device to Home Assistant.

5. Give it an area and click "FINISH".

6. Your device is now added to Home Assistant via the ESPHome integration. To find it, go to Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome and click the name of your new device!

Click here to join our Discord for fast support!

docs.title: How to insert battery on TEMP-1B
How to insert the battery
docs.text:
16340 AKA RC-CR123A and charger required!

The TEMP-1B is a very neat sensor but it does NOT include a battery nor a charging circuit. You will have to buy your own rechargeable RC-CR123A aka 16340 battery and also a separate 16340 charger such as a Nitecore 2 or 4bay model.

You'll open the case, insert the battery with the positive terminal facing the + sign, and close the lid again.

1. Gently pry open the case lid as shown in the image below.

2. Once the lid is removed either lift the PCB out or gently dump the pcb out by turning it upside down.

3. Align the battery as shown in the image below.

4. Insert the battery with the positive terminal facing the + sign.

5. Begin reassembly by placing the battery side down with the RGB led in the top right corner.

6. You will use the "ledge" of the case to set the PCB down and then it will lay down and rest on the ledge of the other side as well.

7. Align the RGB led in the top right with the small hole in the lid.

8. Gently press down until the lid seats.

9 You have now installed or reinstalled the battery!

docs.title: TEMP-1 general tips
docs.text: The TEMP-1 has an optional Dallas temperature probe (long or short variants) and an optional food-safe probe.

docs.title: Physical buffered temperature
docs.text: For accurate vaccine storage monitoring, the CDC recommends using buffered temperature probes, a principle the Dallas temperature probe can follow using a glycol or glass bead vial. Buffering mimics the thermal behavior of stored vaccines, filtering out brief air temp fluctuations (e.g., door openings) that don’t reflect true vaccine exposure. This results in more reliable, regulation-aligned readings when using Dallas sensors like the DS18B20 in a buffered medium. You can also achieve better results by placing the probe inside a bottle of water (for the fridge not freezer).

docs.title: Virtual temperature buffering
docs.text: Instead of placing your Dallas temperature probe (like a DS18B20) in a vial of glycol or glass beads to mimic how vaccines warm up or cool down, you can use a software method called Virtual Temperature Buffering. It filters out quick air temperature changes (like when you open the fridge door) and gives a more stable, realistic reading similar to a physical buffer. This means you get accurate, regulation-friendly temps without needing messy liquids or bulky containers.

docs.title: Sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your TEMP-1B. Use the tabs below to see what each entity does, grouped the same way Home Assistant displays them.

How often readings update

The Default Update column is how often each entity refreshes while the TEMP-1B is awake. The TEMP-1B runs on a battery, and by default Prevent Sleep is on, so it stays awake and reports continuously at these intervals (which drains the battery). Turn Prevent Sleep off to let it deep-sleep between readings and conserve the battery: it wakes, reports, then sleeps for the Sleep Duration before waking again.

To update firmware on a sleeping device, click Update on the Firmware Update entity and it installs the next time the device wakes (the firmware keeps itself awake until the update finishes, so you don't need to do anything else). The optional OTA helper is a separate toggle that overrides Prevent Sleep to keep a device awake on demand.

ControlsSensorsConfigurationDiagnostic Control What it does RGB Light One RGB Neopixel LED. Click the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Use the toggle to turn it on or off. Alarm Outside Temp Range Sounds the onboard buzzer when the selected probe's temperature crosses the Min Probe Temp or Max Probe Temp thresholds. Defaults to off. Select Probe Chooses which probe the TEMP-1B reads: Temperature (the Dallas DS18B20 probe, available in long or short versions) or Food (the stainless steel, food-safe probe for grilling and cooking). Sensor Default Update Details Temperature Probe 60s Reading from the Dallas DS18B20 probe. Active when Select Probe is set to Temperature. Good for fridge/freezer, aquariums, hot tubs, and covered pools. Adjusted by the Temp Probe Offset. Food Probe 3s Reading from the stainless steel food-safe NTC probe for grilling, baking, and other cooking. Active when Select Probe is set to Food. Adjusted by the Food Probe Offset. Board Temperature 60s Onboard temperature from the AHT20 sensor. Adjusted by the Board Temperature Offset. Board Humidity 60s Onboard relative humidity from the AHT20 sensor. Adjusted by the Board Humidity Offset. Battery level 60s Remaining battery charge from the MAX17048, reported 0-100%. Battery voltage 60s Current battery voltage from the MAX17048 for real-time monitoring. Setting Default What it does ESP Reboot — Restarts the device. Helpful for troubleshooting or refreshing the connection. Firmware Update — Shows whether a firmware update is available and lets you update from inside Home Assistant. Board Temperature Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset applied to the Board Temperature reading. Board Humidity Offset 0 % Calibration offset applied to the Board Humidity reading. Temp Probe Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset for the Temperature Probe reading. Disabled by default. Food Probe Offset 0.0 °C Calibration offset for the Food Probe reading. Disabled by default. Max Probe Temp 125.0 °C Upper temperature threshold used by the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Min Probe Temp -55.0 °C Lower temperature threshold used by the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Probe Temp Difference Threshold 0.0 °C How much the probe temperature must change to trigger the Notify Only Outside Temp Difference wake. Disabled by default. Notify Only Outside Temp Difference Off When on, the device only wakes and reports when the probe temperature changes by more than the Probe Temp Difference Threshold. Disabled by default. Prevent Sleep On Keeps the device awake instead of deep-sleeping, so it reports continuously. Required for OTA updates and live readings; turn it off to save power on battery. While sleeping the TEMP-1B will not respond to Home Assistant until it wakes again. Sleep Duration 12 h How many hours the device stays in deep sleep between wake cycles (only used when Prevent Sleep is off). Factory Reset ESP — Erases settings and returns the device to factory firmware defaults. Disabled by default. Entity Default Update What it shows Apollo Firmware Version on boot The Apollo firmware build installed on the device (for example, 26.3.2.1). ESPHome Version on boot The ESPHome version the firmware was compiled with. IP Address on connect The device's IP address on your network. Online on change Connection status of the device to Home Assistant. RSSI 60s Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. Values closer to 0 are stronger; a weak signal can affect reliability. ESP Temperature 60s Internal temperature of the ESP32 chip. Runs warmer than the room because of the processor and Wi-Fi radio. Uptime 60s How long the device has been running since its last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode
Putting the TEMP-1B in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the TEMP-1B into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You'll hold the boot button while you plug in the USB-C cable.

1. Position the TEMP-1B so that the USB-C port is facing you. On the right side of the device, locate a small opening where you can use a paperclip to press the boot button.

If you prefer, please remove the lid by gently prying up on the small slit by the top of the case.

2. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your TEMP-1B then let go of the button.

3. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You'll open the case, plug the device into your computer, then hold the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and remove the case as shown in the images above

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your TEMP-1B in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (labeled BOOT, shown above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (labeled RST, shown below).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the TEMP-1B. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash TEMP-1B
docs.text:
If your device becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods you can reflash the factory firmware by following the below guide.

This needs to be done in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium based browser.

If your device has already been connected to Home Assistant please remove it from the ESPHome integration and the ESPHome Device Builder before continuing.

Follow these steps to put your device in boot mode and install the factory firmware.

1. Put your device in boot mode by holding down the boot button and then plugging in the USB cable.

2. Navigate to the Apollo TEMP-1 installer. The TEMP-1B uses the same page as the TEMP-1.

Remove the battery!

This will not work properly if the battery is still supplying power to the TEMP-1B. Please remove the battery if you are having issues!

3. Choose Battery Power since you are using a TEMP-1B, then click Connect & Install.

Use R2 version unless instructed to use R1 by support!

The Apollo installer installs the Revision 2 (R2) firmware. R2 is what all of our devices use except a very small batch of TEMP-1 and TEMP-1B boards. If support tells you your board needs Revision 1 (R1), click Connect under Battery Firmware Revision 1 on the classic TEMP-1 installer instead. In the next steps, the firmware option is named Install ApolloAutomation.TEMP-1B.

4. Select the open com port then click Connect.

5. Click Install Apollo.TEMP-1B_R2.

6. Click "INSTALL".

7. Once you see "Installation complete!" you are finished. Click Next then close out of the browser window.

Power cycle your device before doing anything else!

Your device is still in boot mode and needs to be power cycled aka power removed to make it boot in a normal mode!

8. Please proceed to the getting started guide and set up your sensor as a new device!

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your TEMP-1B
docs.text:
You'll reset the device's Wi-Fi credentials, then connect it to your new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo TEMP1B Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.text:
You'll pry open the case lid and take the board out, so you can replace parts, clean it, or swap cases.

1. Gently pry open the case lid as shown in the image below.

2. Once the lid is removed either lift the PCB out or gently dump the pcb out by turning it upside down.

3. The teardown is complete!

docs.title: TEMP Pro-1 FAQ
docs.text:
1. How is the TEMP Pro-1 powered?

  • PoE (802.3af compliant) powered or...
  • USB-C at 5 volts using less than 1 amp of power.

2. What are the Optional Probe Addons?

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.
  • 12.7cm (~5 in) dust-proof temperature & humidity sensor with waterproof probe (SHT20)

3. What other addons can I use with the TEMP Pro-1?

  • You can add the GPIO header and SCD40 CO2 sensor with the two mezzanine ports. It also includes a Sensirion port for a SEN55 and SEN6x, a QWIIC port and a DfRobot port.

4. Is the TEMP Pro-1 weatherproof? Can I use it outdoors?

  • The TEMP Pro-1 is primarily designed for indoor use, but components like the waterproof temp probe are suited for harsh conditions. The main body is not rated for outdoor use without additional protection.

5. How does the TEMP Pro-1 connect to Home Assistant?

  • The TEMP Pro-1 connects via Wi-Fi to ESPHome on Home Assistant, enabling data monitoring, automations, and alerts directly within Home Assistant.

6. How often does the TEMP Pro-1 send sensor data?

  • The TEMP Pro-1 reporting frequency is adjustable in ESPHome but most things default to 60 seconds.

7. Can I customize the TEMP Pro-1 functionality?

  • Absolutely! With ESPHome, users can modify firmware, settings, and even print custom cases for the TEMP Pro-1. Our YAML is on GitHub and our .STEP and .STL CAD files are available for community use.

8. What are the RGB LED and piezo buzzer used for?

  • The RGB LED provides visual alerts, while the piezo buzzer offers audio notifications for events like the temperature or humidity going outside the Min/Max range you set (turn on Alarm Outside Temp Range or Alarm Outside Humidity Range).

9. Is the TEMP Pro-1 compatible with other smart home platforms?

  • While designed for Home Assistant via ESPHome, it may be compatible with other platforms using the ESPHome API or MQTT.

10. Do I need coding knowledge to use the TEMP Pro-1?

  • Basic knowledge of Home Assistant and ESPHome is helpful, but most users can utilize it out of the box. For advanced customization, YAML knowledge is recommended.

11. Can I access data from the TEMP Pro-1 remotely?

  • Yes, you can access sensor data remotely via the Home Assistant dashboard if your setup is configured for remote access.

12. Can I use multiple TEMP Pro-1 sensors in one Home Assistant setup?

  • Yes, you can add multiple TEMP Pro-1 sensors, each appearing as a separate device, for comprehensive monitoring across multiple rooms, fridges, or spaces.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The TEMP Pro-1 can be used with an optional temperature probe which comes in two lengths and/or dust-proof temp and humidity probe (SHT20). It also features an AHT20-F air temperature and humidity sensor, 4x RGB LEDs, and a piezo buzzer.

It includes two mezzanine connectors for our GPIO Header addon, CO2 addon, and any future addons using that port. It also includes a Sen5x/Sen6x port which is used to connect the SEN55 on our AIR-1. It even includes a DFrobot port (MiCS port on AIR-1) and a QWIIC port!

Optional Probe Addons:

  • 1.5m (~5ft) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy. Ideal for fridges, freezers, fish tanks etc.
  • 20cm (~8in) Waterproof Flat Cable (DS18B20) -55°C to 85°C (-67°F to 185°F), ±0.5°C accuracy.
  • 12.7cm (~5 in) dust-proof temperature & humidity sensor with waterproof probe (SHT20)

Do not leave your sensor outside or let it get wet!

The TEMP Pro-1 should not be left outside for long periods of time or allowed to get wet. You will need to use another case around your TEMP Pro-1 if there will be high moisture content in the air or if it is expected to rain. This is also true of attics!

docs.title: TEMP-1 alert outside temp range example
TEMP-1 alert outside temp range example
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 1

Written for the TEMP-1

This example was written for the Apollo TEMP-1, and its steps and screenshots show a TEMP-1. The TEMP Pro-1 sensor definitions list the same Max Probe Temp, Min Probe Temp, and Alarm Outside Temp Range settings, so you can follow along with your TEMP Pro-1.

Set up the built-in alarm so your TEMP-1 sounds its buzzer when the temperature probe in your freezer reads outside the range you choose. You'll pick a range from the probe's readings, enter it on the device, and turn the alarm on.

1. Place the temperature probe into your freezer, then wait for its reading to settle around 0°F (-18°C). Only the probe goes in the freezer, not the entire TEMP-1.

2. Once the reading settles, look at the graph and pick a good value for both the maximum and the minimum temperature. In this example, the mini freezer seems to max out at 30°F, so the maximum goes slightly above that. However, most freezers should not reach above 0°F, so you'll likely need a lower maximum than this one. The minimums here are around -20°F.

3. Convert your maximum and minimum from °F to °C, then enter them in Max Probe Temp and Min Probe Temp. Both settings are measured in Celsius. This example uses a max probe temp of 2°C and a min probe temp of -30°C. Your values will likely be different, especially your max probe temp.

4. Turn on the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Your TEMP-1 now plays an audible alert with its buzzer when the temperature thresholds are reached: if the temperature goes under the min or over the max, the alarm goes off.

Your freezer alarm is set. The next time the probe reads outside your range, the TEMP-1 lets you know with its buzzer.

docs.title: Automation examples using a TEMP-1
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 2

🌱 New here? Try these first:

TEMP-1 alert outside temp range example Difficulty: Level 1

Written for the TEMP-1

This page was written for the Apollo TEMP-1. Every step, screenshot, and YAML example uses a TEMP-1 and its entity names. Before you follow along with a TEMP Pro-1, check the TEMP Pro-1 sensor definitions to see which of these sensors and settings your TEMP Pro-1 has.

Your TEMP-1's probes can drive Home Assistant automations. This page walks you through three of them: a freezer alert, a food probe alert, and a chicken monitor you start and stop from your dashboard.

docs.title: Freezer temperature probe example
docs.text:
Set up a Home Assistant automation that uses the temperature probe in your freezer. At the end, you'll have an automation that sends your phone a notification when the probe goes above your maximum temperature.

1. Place the temperature probe into your freezer, then wait for its reading to settle around 0°F (-18°C).

Only the probe goes in the freezer

Keep your TEMP-1 itself in a cool, dry place. Only the temp probe and its wire can withstand the temperatures in a fridge, freezer, and similar places.

2. Once the reading settles, look at the graph and pick a good value for both the maximum and the minimum temperature. In this example, the mini freezer seems to max out at 30°F, so the maximum goes slightly above that. However, most freezers should not reach above 0°F, so you'll likely need a lower maximum than this one. The minimums here are around -20°F.

3. Convert your maximum and minimum from °F to °C, then enter them in Max Probe Temp and Min Probe Temp. Both settings are measured in Celsius. This example uses a max probe temp of 2°C and a min probe temp of -30°C. Your values will likely be different, especially your max probe temp.

With your thresholds set, the automation is now ready to be created.

4. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation. Shortcut: go straight to a new automation (works if you reach Home Assistant at homeassistant.local).

5. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then Numeric state, and search for your TEMP-1 probe sensor, such as "temp-1 temperature probe". In the box labeled Above, type the maximum temperature you picked in step 2. Advanced users can skip to the YAML at the end of this section.

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP Pro-1 entity instead.

6. Click Add Action, type "iPhone", and select your phone. If you don't see your phone, or you have an Android phone, type "notify" instead and scroll down until you find your phone in the list.

Still don't see your phone?

You need the Home Assistant mobile app installed on your phone for this step to work. If you don't have it, use another kind of notification instead, such as a TTS notification on your speakers. This could be a fun way to announce that dinner is ready!

7. Type in your message. If you want a title too, check the box for title and type it in. This example uses the message "The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and your freezer might be having issues." and the title "Check the freezer!".

8. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and, optionally, a description and a category.

You're done! Your phone now gets a notification whenever the freezer probe goes above your maximum.

YAML for advanced users

alias: Freezer Over Max Temp Automation
description: Warning for the freezer when it reaches the max temperature.
triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id:
      - sensor.apollo_temp_1_temperature_probe
    # in the unit Home Assistant shows for the probe (°F here); use your own entity ID
    above: 30
conditions: []
actions:
  - action: notify.mobile_app_brandons_iphone
    metadata: {}
    data:
      title: Check the freezer!
      message: >-
        The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and
        your freezer might be having issues.
mode: single

docs.title: Food probe example
docs.text:
Set up a Home Assistant automation that uses the food probe while you cook chicken (or anything else) to 165°F (73.9°C). At the end, you'll have an automation that sends your phone a notification when your food reaches that temperature.

1. Set your Max Probe Temp to 73.9°C. Max Probe Temp is always set in Celsius, even if you use °F in the automation below.

2. Once your food is on the grill, place the food probe inside it.

Only the food probe goes on the grill

Keep your TEMP-1 itself in a cool, dry place. Only the food probe and its wire can withstand temperatures on a grill, in the oven, and similar places.

3. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation. Shortcut: go straight to a new automation (works if you reach Home Assistant at homeassistant.local).

4. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then Numeric state, and search for your TEMP-1 food probe sensor, such as "temp-1 food probe". In the box labeled Above, type the temperature you want for your food. This example uses 165°F (73.9°C), the temperature it's safe to cook chicken to. Advanced users can skip to the YAML at the end of this section.

Shown on a TEMP-1; pick your TEMP Pro-1 entity instead.

5. Click Add Action, type "iPhone", and select your phone. If you don't see your phone, or you have an Android phone, type "notify" instead and scroll down until you find your phone in the list.

Still don't see your phone?

You need the Home Assistant mobile app installed on your phone for this step to work. If you don't have it, use another kind of notification instead, such as a TTS notification on your speakers. This could be a fun way to announce that dinner is ready!

6. Type in your message. If you want a title too, check the box for title and type it in. This example uses the message "The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and your food is ready." and the title "Check the food!".

7. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and, optionally, a description and a category.

You're done! Your phone now gets a notification when your food reaches its target temperature.

YAML for advanced users

alias: Food Over Max Temp Automation
description: Warning for the food when it reaches the max temperature.
triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id:
      - sensor.apollo_temp_1_food_probe
    # in the unit Home Assistant shows for the probe (°F here); use your own entity ID
    above: 165
conditions: []
actions:
  - action: notify.mobile_app_brandons_iphone
    metadata: {}
    data:
      title: Check the food!
      message: >-
        The temperature probe on your TEMP-1 reached its max temperature and your food is ready.
mode: single

docs.title: Cook chicken example
docs.text:
This example adds a button called "Chicken Monitor" to your dashboard, plus an automation that runs when you press it. While it runs, the RGB LED turns green. Your phone gets a message when monitoring starts, when the temperature is reached, and when monitoring finishes, and then the RGB LED turns off. Thanks to Discord user RalphP for this!

The automation has three triggers, each with its own trigger ID, and one Choose action with an option for each trigger ID:

  • Option 1 (Chicken Monitor On): turns the RGB LED green and messages your phone.
  • Option 2 (Temp Reached): toggles the RGB LED until Chicken Monitor is turned off, messages your phone, and optionally speaks on your smart speakers.
  • Option 3 (Chicken Monitor Off): turns the RGB LED off and messages your phone.

First, create the button.

1. Create a new toggle helper called "Chicken Monitor". For step-by-step directions, see creating a toggle helper.

2. Edit your dashboard, add a button card, select Chicken Monitor, and then save.

Next, create the automation and its three triggers.

3. Go to Settings → Automations & scenes, click + Create automation in the bottom right, then Create new automation. Shortcut: go straight to a new automation (works if you reach Home Assistant at homeassistant.local).

4. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then State, and search for "Chicken Monitor". In the box labeled To, select On.

5. Create a Trigger ID for this trigger called "Chicken Monitor On".

6. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then State, and search for "Chicken Monitor". In the box labeled To, select Off. Create a Trigger ID for this trigger called "Chicken Monitor Off".

7. Click Add Trigger, then Entity, then Numeric state, and search for your TEMP-1 food probe entity, such as "temp-1 food probe". In the box labeled Above, type the temperature you want for your food. This example uses 160°F (71.1°C), because the chicken will rest and reach 165°F once removed from the oven or grill.

8. Create a Trigger ID for this trigger called "Temp Reached".

Now add the Choose action. Option 1 runs when you turn Chicken Monitor on.

9. Click Add Action, search "choose", and select it.

10. Under Option 1, select Add Condition, search "trigger id", and select Triggered by.

11. Check State changed to on, the first trigger in the list. It's the trigger you gave the Chicken Monitor On ID in step 5.

12. While still under Option 1 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "light", and select Light: Turn on.

13. Click Choose entity and search for your device, such as "TEMP-1 RGB Light".

14. Click Advanced Options, check the box for Color name, and select a color from the dropdown, such as Green.

15. While still under Option 1 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "mobile", and select your phone in the list.

16. Write a custom title and message. The message is required, but the title is not.

17. Check your work. When you're done with this part, Option 1 looks like this:

Option 2 runs when the food probe reaches your target temperature.

18. Click Add Option at the bottom. Under Option 2, select Add Condition, search "trigger id", and select Triggered by.

19. Check Temp Reached, the trigger ID you created in step 8.

20. While still under Option 2 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "repeat", and select Until in the dropdown.

21. Under Until Conditions, select Add condition, then search "state".

22. Type in "Chicken Monitor" and select it, then select Off in the dropdown for the state of the sensor.

23. Click the Add Action button under the until condition you created. Be very careful to select the correct Add Action button, as shown below.

24. Search "light toggle" in the search bar, then select Choose entity and select the RGB LED for your device.

25. Go down to Add Action under Option 2, search "mobile", and select your phone as you did in step 15. Give it a message and a title, as shown below.

26. Optionally, add another action here that speaks out loud on your smart speakers, such as HomePods. Click Add Action, then search "TTS". This requires you to have Piper and a few other things already set up.

Option 3 runs when you turn Chicken Monitor off.

27. Click Add Option (this is now Option 3). Select Add Condition, search "triggered by", and then choose the "Chicken Monitor Off" trigger ID you created in step 6.

28. While still under Option 3 in the Choose action, click Add Action, search "light", and select Light: Turn off.

29. Click Choose entity and search for your device, such as "TEMP-1 RGB Light".

30. Click Add Action, search "mobile" as you did above, and select your phone. Give it a message and, optionally, a title, as shown below.

31. Click Save in the bottom right, then give the automation a name and save.

You now have one automation that ties together the button you created on your dashboard and alerts you when your chicken is almost done, with a phone notification, a blinking green LED, and an optional TTS notification on your smart speakers. Thanks again to Discord user RalphP for this example!

docs.title: Use cases for the TEMP Pro-1
docs.text:
1. Monitoring fridge / freezer: There are settings to set the maximum temperature the sensor should reach. It can alert through the onboard buzzer if it rises above that temperature. The cable on the probe is flat which should not interfere with fridge seals.

2. Monitoring fish tank, hot tub ( if covered ), pool ( if covered or in sealed box ) with the waterproof probe.

3. Monitoring an attic by putting the TEMP Pro-1 in a waterproof enclosure or poking a hole to feed a temp probe into an attic or other environment not suitable for the TEMP Pro-1 PCB itself.

docs.title: TEMP Pro-1 sensor definitions
docs.text:
Once added to Home Assistant you can configure different settings for your sensor. Below is what each setting does.

Controls

Alarm Outside Humidity Range

  • Alarm that sounds when the thresholds are met for the sensor.
  • Click on the toggle to turn on or off. Defaults to OFF.

Alarm Outside Temp Range

  • Alarm that sounds when the thresholds are met for the sensor.
  • Click on the toggle to turn on or off. Defaults to OFF.

RGB Light

  • Four RGB LEDs. Click on the light bulb or color wheel to change the color. Click on the toggle to turn on or off.
Sensors

Board Humidity

  • Measures and reports the current humidity level on the board.

Board Temperature

  • Measures and reports the current temperature of the board.

Temperature Probe

  • The temperature sensor probe, offered in both long and short options, is ideal for monitoring fridge/freezer temperatures and aquatic environments like fish tanks, hot tubs, and covered pools. Its flat cable prevents interference with fridge seals, and it includes a customizable temperature threshold with an onboard buzzer to alert when the limit is exceeded.
Configuration

Board Humidity Offset

  • Offset for Board Humidity: values between 0-100%

Board Temperature Offset

  • Offset for Board Temperature: values in Celsius.

ESP Reboot

  • Button to press which reboots your TEMP Pro-1.

Firmware Update

  • Indicates whether an update is available or if you are Up-to-date.

Max Probe Temp

  • Max Temperature threshold used for the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle.

Min Probe Temp

  • Min Temperature threshold used for the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle.

Notify Only Outside Temp Difference

  • Notify on Outside temperature difference ONLY.
  • Click on the toggle to turn on or off. Defaults to OFF.

Prevent Sleep

  • Prevents the TEMP Pro-1 from going to sleep. When sleeping, your TEMP Pro-1 will NOT respond to Home Assistant it is effectively off until it wakes up again.
  • Click on the toggle to turn on or off. Defaults to ON.

Probe Temp Difference Threshold

  • Max temperature range threshold used for the Alarm Outside Temp Range toggle. Measured in Celsius.

Sleep Duration

  • The number of hours the device should remain in sleep mode before waking up. Defaults to 12 hours.
Diagnostic

ESP Temperature

  • Displays the current temperature of the ESP32 chip.

Online

  • Shows the connection status.

RSSI

  • Displays the Wi-Fi signal strength.

Uptime

  • Shows the time since last reboot.

Join our Discord if you need more help!

docs.title: Putting the TEMP Pro-1 in boot mode
Putting the TEMP Pro-1 in boot mode
docs.text:
This will cover how to put the TEMP Pro-1 into boot mode.

This is needed to force the device into boot mode to reflash the firmware.

docs.title: Method 1: Boot button only
docs.text:
You'll remove the lid, then hold the boot button while you plug in the USB-C cable.

1. Position the TEMP Pro-1 so that the USB-C port is facing you. Remove the lid by gently prying up on the small slit by the top of the case.

2. Locate the boot button as shown in the image below.

3. Push and hold the boot button. While still holding the button down, plug in a USB-C cable into the USB-C port of your TEMP Pro-1 then let go of the button.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Method 2: Boot and reset buttons
docs.text:
You'll open the case, plug the device into your computer, then hold the boot button down while you press and release the reset button.

1. Unplug the device and remove the case as shown in the images above

2. Plug it into your computer.

3. Put your TEMP Pro-1 in boot mode. Use both buttons, in this order:

  • Press and hold the boot button (labeled BOOT, shown above). Keep holding it.
  • While you're still holding boot, press and release the reset button (labeled RST, shown below).
  • Let go of boot.

Keep holding boot the whole time

Pressing reset by itself only restarts the TEMP Pro-1. It goes into boot mode only when boot is held down while you press and release reset.

4. Continue with uploading the firmware document.

docs.title: Factory re-flash TEMP Pro-1
docs.text:
If your Apollo TEMP Pro-1 becomes unresponsive and you've exhausted the other troubleshooting methods, you can reflash the factory firmware by following this guide.

Before you start

  • Use Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium-based browser. The installer needs one of them.
  • If your TEMP Pro-1 has already been connected to Home Assistant, remove it from the ESPHome integration and the ESPHome Device Builder before continuing.

Follow these steps to put your TEMP Pro-1 in boot mode, flash the factory firmware from the installer page, and set it up again.

1. Put your TEMP Pro-1 in boot mode: hold down the boot button, then plug in the USB cable.

2. Open the Apollo TEMP Pro-1 installer page.

3. Choose WiFi if your TEMP Pro-1 connects over Wi-Fi, or Ethernet if it connects over PoE or Ethernet. Then click Connect & Install.

4. In the browser's serial port pop-up, select the open COM port (USB JTAG/serial debug unit in the screenshot below), then click Connect.

5. Click Install ApolloAutomation.TEMP_PRO-1-W. If you chose Ethernet, click Install ApolloAutomation.TEMP_PRO-1-ETH instead.

6. Click INSTALL.

7. When the installer shows Installation complete!, the flash is finished. Click Next, then close the browser window.

Power cycle your TEMP Pro-1 before doing anything else

Your TEMP Pro-1 is still in boot mode. Remove all power from it, then reconnect the power so it starts in normal mode.

8. Go to the getting started guide and set up your TEMP Pro-1 as a new device.

Once it's set up, your TEMP Pro-1 is back on its factory firmware and ready to use.

docs.title: Reset Wi-Fi credentials on your TEMP Pro-1
docs.text:
You'll reset the device's Wi-Fi credentials, then connect it to your new Wi-Fi network through its hotspot.

1. Plug the device into power.

2. Long press the Boot button for 10 seconds

3. The Wi-Fi credentials should be reset and it will broadcast its hotspot again.

4. Connect to the hotspot titled "Apollo TEMP Pro-1 Hotspot" and enter your new Wi-Fi details!

docs.title: Teardown of TEMP Pro-1
docs.text:
Removing the case lid gives you access to the board inside your Apollo TEMP Pro-1, for example to replace parts, clean it, or swap cases.

1. Position the TEMP Pro-1 with the USB-C port facing you. Gently pry up the case lid at the small slit above the USB-C port, as shown in the image below.

With the lid off, the teardown is complete. Opening the case is also the first step of putting the TEMP Pro-1 in boot mode.
